individual_results.question: What types of works, undertakings, or businesses are considered 'federal work, undertaking or business' under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Federal Work, Undertakings, and Businesses: Definition

### Section 2: Interpretation - Definitions

Section 2 of the Canada Labour Code provides a comprehensive definition of "federal work, undertaking or business." It states:
"...federal work, undertaking or business means any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of Parliament, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, (a) a work, undertaking or business operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada, (b) a railway, canal, telegraph or other work or undertaking connecting any province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (c) a line of ships connecting a province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, (d) a ferry between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada, (e) aerodromes, aircraft or a line of air transportation, (f) a radio broadcasting station, (g) a bank or an authorized foreign bank within the meaning of section 2 of the Bank Act , (h) a work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces, (i) a work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislatures of the provinces, and (j) a work, undertaking or activity in respect of which federal laws within the meaning of section 2 of the Oceans Act apply pursuant to section 20 of that Act and any regulations made pursuant to paragraph 26(1)(k) of that Act..."

This definition is expansive, encompassing a wide array of activities. It explicitly lists sectors such as "navigation and shipping,"
"...other work or undertaking connecting any province with any other province..." "ferries," "aerodromes, aircraft, and a line of air transportation," "radio broadcasting stations," and "banks." Furthermore, it includes
"...a work or undertaking that, although wholly situated within a province, is before or after its execution declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces..." This highlights that federal work, undertaking, or business is not limited to those explicitly mentioned; it can also be those declared by Parliament to be for the national or interprovincial benefit. Finally, it covers activities
"...outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislatures of the provinces..." and those subject to federal laws within the Oceans Act.

### Section 5: Application - Canadian Carriers

Section 5 of the Canada Labour Code further clarifies the application of "federal work, undertaking or business" by specifically addressing "Canadian carriers." It states:
"This Part applies in respect of any Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and in respect of the employees of the carrier."

This indicates that Canadian carriers acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province are also considered federal work, undertaking, or business under this Part of the Code. The reference to "section 2 of the Telecommunications Act" provides a precise definition of what constitutes a Canadian carrier for the purposes of this section.

### Section 255: Combining Federal Works, Undertakings and Businesses

Section 255 deals with the possibility of two or more employers having common control or direction over associated or related federal works, undertakings, and businesses. It states:
"Where associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Minister may, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This section allows the Minister to consolidate multiple federal works, undertakings, and businesses under a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking, or business for the purposes of this Part of the Code, when they are operated by employers with common control or direction. This simplifies the application of the Part to such situations.

individual_results.question: Who does this part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) apply to?
individual_results.answer:
## Application of Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 4: General Application

Section 4 of Part I of the Canada Labour Code establishes the broad scope of its application. It states:
"This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."

This section clearly indicates that Part I applies to employees working on or in connection with federal work, undertakings, or businesses. It further extends its reach to the relationships between these employers and their employees, as well as to trade unions and employers' organizations that represent these employees or employers. This comprehensive application ensures that Part I governs a wide range of industrial relations activities within the federal government.

### Section 123: Application to Federal Public Administration and Crown Corporations

Section 123 provides more specific details on the application of Part I to certain entities within the federal government.

#### Application to Federal Public Administration
"Notwithstanding any other Act of Parliament or any regulations thereunder, this Part applies to and in respect of employment (a) on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut; (b) by a corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada; and (c) by a Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province."

This subsection reinforces the general application of Part I to federal work, undertakings, and businesses. It explicitly includes employment by corporations established to perform functions on behalf of the Government of Canada and Canadian carriers acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province.

#### Application to Provincial Crown Corporations
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

Section 121.1 grants the Governor in Council the authority to direct that Part I applies to employment within provincial Crown corporations whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This demonstrates the adaptability of Part I to the unique circumstances of provincial Crown corporations.

### Section 121.1: Exclusion from Application
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

While Section 121.1 grants the Governor in Council the power to *direct* the application of Part I to provincial Crown corporations, it also includes a marginal note: "Exclusion from application." This suggests that the Governor in Council could also direct the *exclusion* of Part I from the application to such corporations through regulation. This provision highlights the flexibility of Part I and its potential to be tailored to the specific needs of different entities within the federal government.

### Section 121.1: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations (Revisited)
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This repetition of Section 121.1 emphasizes the Governor in Council's power to determine whether Part I applies to provincial Crown corporations. The marginal note "Exclusion from application" further underscores this point, indicating that Part I could be excluded from the application to such corporations through regulation.

### Section 121.1: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations (Final)
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This final repetition of Section 121.1 reinforces the Governor in Council's authority to direct the application of Part I to provincial Crown corporations, including the potential for exclusion through regulation.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council exclude a corporation from the operation of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Exclusion of Corporations from Part I of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad authority of the Governor in Council to exclude corporations from the operation of Part I.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote establishes that the exclusion can be "in whole or in part" and applies to
"...any employment, or any class or classes of employment..." related to a work or undertaking whose activities are regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This indicates a specific category of corporations can be excluded, those involved in nuclear safety and control.

### Section 158 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 158 further elaborates on the exclusion power, linking it to federal Crown corporations acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province.
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This section clarifies that the exclusion can be applied to federal Crown corporations that are agents of a province and whose activities are also regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This creates a double layer of regulation and potential exclusion.

### Section 5 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 5 provides another avenue for exclusion, specifically for Canadian carriers acting as agents of Her Majesty in right of a province.
"Section 5 (1) This Part applies in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and in respect of the employees of any such corporation, except any such corporation, and the employees thereof, that the Governor in Council excludes from the operation of this Part."

This quote states that the Governor in Council can exclude corporations from the operation of Part I, but only those corporations that meet the criteria of being established to perform a function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and whose employees are also excluded. This suggests a more targeted exclusion based on the specific function of the corporation.

### Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 265 is very similar to Section 266, reiterating the Governor in Council's power to exclude corporations from Part I based on their activities being regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"Section 265 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote directly mirrors the language of Section 266, reinforcing the exclusion power in relation to nuclear safety and control activities.

### Section 121.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 121.1 also mirrors Section 266 and Section 265, confirming the Governor in Council's ability to exclude corporations from Part I based on their activities being regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"Section 121.1 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote further emphasizes the exclusion power in the context of nuclear safety and control regulated corporations.

In summary, the Governor in Council can exclude corporations from Part I of the Canada Labour Code under several circumstances, most notably when those corporations are involved in nuclear safety and control activities, as outlined in Sections 266, 265, and 121.1. Additionally, corporations that are federal Crown corporations acting as agents of a province and whose activities are also regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act can be excluded, as detailed in Sections 158 and 5. The exclusion can be "in whole or in part" and apply to any employment or class of employment related to a work or undertaking within the regulation.

individual_results.question: Who bears the burden of proof in determining whether a person is an employee of an employer in proceedings under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Burden of Proof in Canada Labour Code Proceedings

### Section 123.3 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 123.3 explicitly states:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This passage directly answers the question by identifying the party responsible for proving that a person is *not* an employee. It clarifies that when an employer raises this issue in a proceeding other than a criminal prosecution, they must present sufficient evidence to support their claim. This is a crucial aspect of the legal process, ensuring that the party making the assertion has the obligation to substantiate it.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 6.2 reinforces the burden of proof on the employer in situations where they contest the employee status of a person. It reads:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This section is virtually identical to Section 123.3, providing further confirmation of the employer's burden. The repetition of this statement underscores its importance in the context of Canada Labour Code proceedings. It leaves no room for ambiguity regarding who must prove the worker's status.

### Section 167.01(1) and (2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 167.01(1) establishes a presumption of employee status:
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

This presumption is a cornerstone of the Canada Labour Code. However, Section 167.01(2) provides a crucial caveat:
"The presumption does not apply for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part."

While the presumption exists for most proceedings, it is waived when the employer is pursuing criminal charges against the worker. In these cases, the burden of proof shifts back to the prosecution to demonstrate that the worker is *not* an employee. This demonstrates the dynamic nature of the burden of proof within the Code, adapting to the specific nature of the legal action being taken.

### IPG-069_12 and IPG-069_10

Interpretations and Policies and Guidelines (IPGs) further elaborate on the burden of proof. IPG-069_12 states:
"The employer can try to prove that the worker is not an employee, but they must provide strong enough evidence to support their claim."

This passage emphasizes that the presumption is not insurmountable. The employer has the opportunity to challenge the employee status, but they must do so with compelling evidence. IPG-069_10 also highlights this point, mentioning that the employer must "provide strong enough evidence to support their claim."

IPG-069_10 further explains the "total relationship" analysis, stating:
"It is the total relationship that is being examined." This means that the employer must present evidence across multiple factors to demonstrate that the worker is an independent contractor, not just one or two isolated aspects. The burden is not on the worker to prove they are an employee; it is on the employer to prove they are not.

### Section 167.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 167.1 prohibits an employer from treating an employee as if they were not their employee. While not directly addressing the burden of proof, it reinforces the legal framework that supports the presumption of employee status and the employer's obligation to overcome it.

individual_results.question: How can the Minister and the Board assist in collective bargaining for certain projects under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister and Board Assistance to Collective Bargaining for Major Projects

### Section 7: Major Projects

Section 7 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific ways the Minister and the Board can expedite collective bargaining for projects deemed "major projects."
"Nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to prevent the establishment of agreements on a project basis and where all the parties in a collective bargaining relationship identify themselves to the Minister as being engaged in a project that the Minister determines to be a major project, the Minister and the Board shall act as expeditiously as possible to facilitate the collective bargaining process involving those parties."

This passage directly addresses the question by stating that the Minister and the Board will "act as expeditiously as possible" to facilitate collective bargaining for projects identified as "major projects." This indicates a proactive role in streamlining the process, likely through dedicated resources, attention, and potentially intervention to overcome roadblocks. The provision also allows for the establishment of agreements on a project basis, which is a flexible approach to bargaining that can accommodate the unique needs of large undertakings.

### Section 80: Settlement of First Agreement

Section 80 details the Minister's authority to direct the Board to settle the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement.
"(1) Where an employer or a bargaining agent is required, by notice given under section 48, to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the first collective agreement between the parties with respect to the bargaining unit for which the bargaining agent has been certified and the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have otherwise been met, the Minister may, if the Minister considers it necessary or advisable, at any time thereafter direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and, if the Board considers it advisable, to settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties."

This section highlights the Minister's power to intervene in the initial stages of collective bargaining. The Minister can direct the Board to "inquire into the dispute" and ultimately
"...settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement..." This is a significant power, allowing the Minister to ensure a fair and reasonable outcome for the parties involved, especially when the bargaining process is stalled or unproductive. The Board's role is to consider the Minister's direction and, if deemed advisable, to proceed with the settlement.

### Section 80: Board's Settlement Process

Section 80 further elaborates on the Board's process when it settles the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement.
"(2) The Board shall proceed as directed by the Minister under subsection (1) and, if the Board settles the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement referred to in that subsection, those terms and conditions shall constitute the collective agreement between the parties and shall be binding on them and on the employees in the bargaining unit, except to the extent that such terms and conditions are subsequently amended by the parties by agreement in writing."

This passage clarifies the legal effect of the Board's settlement. The Board's settlement becomes the binding collective agreement for the bargaining unit, with the exception of any later amendments made in writing by the parties. The Board's settlement is not merely a recommendation; it is the agreement that governs the relationship between the employer and the employees.

### Section 80: Factors the Board May Consider

Section 80(3) lists the factors the Board may take into account when settling the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement.
"In settling the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement under this section, the Board shall give the parties an opportunity to present evidence and make representations and the Board may take into account (a) the extent to which the parties have, or have not, bargained in good faith in an attempt to enter into the first collective agreement between them; (b) the terms and conditions of employment, if any, negotiated through collective bargaining for employees performing the same or similar functions in the same or similar circumstances as the employees in the bargaining unit; and (c) such other matters as the Board considers will assist it in arriving at terms and conditions that are fair and reasonable in the circumstances."

This section emphasizes the Board's commitment to fairness and reasonableness in its settlement process. The Board will provide an opportunity for the parties to present their case and will consider a range of factors, including the good faith bargaining efforts of the parties, existing terms and conditions of employment for similar roles, and any other relevant information. This ensures that the settlement is not arbitrary but is based on a thorough understanding of the situation and the needs of both the employer and the employees.

individual_results.question: What freedoms do employees and employers have regarding joining and participating in trade unions and employers' organizations?
individual_results.answer:
## Employee and Employer Freedoms Regarding Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations

### Section 8: Employee and Employer Freedoms

#### Section 8(1): Employee Freedom to Join a Trade Union
"Every employee is free to join the trade union of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities."

This section of the Canada Labour Code explicitly guarantees employees the fundamental freedom to affiliate with a trade union of their choosing and to engage in its legitimate endeavors. The use of the word "lawful" is crucial, as it limits the scope of this freedom to activities that are not prohibited by the Code. This freedom is a cornerstone of collective bargaining and worker empowerment, allowing employees to collectively advocate for their interests.

#### Section 8(2): Employer Freedom to Join Employers' Organizations
"Every employer is free to join the employers’ organization of their choice and to participate in its lawful activities."

Correspondingly, employers also possess the freedom to join employers' organizations that align with their interests and to participate in their lawful activities. This allows employers to collectively address common concerns and advocate for their positions in the broader labour relations landscape. The inclusion of "lawful" again underscores the limitation to activities that are not contrary to the Code.

### Section 94: Employer Interference in Trade Unions

#### Section 94(1): Prohibition on Employer Interference
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..."

This section unequivocally prohibits employers from engaging in any form of interference with the formation or operation of a trade union or its ability to represent employees. This includes actions such as discouraging unionization, spreading misinformation about unions, or attempting to undermine union activities. The prohibition extends to both direct participation and indirect influence.

#### Section 94(3): Prohibition on Employer Actions Against Union Members
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) refuse to employ or to continue to employ or suspend, transfer, lay off or otherwise discriminate against any person with respect to employment, pay or any other term or condition of employment or intimidate, threaten or otherwise discipline any person, because the person (i) is or proposes to become, or seeks to induce any other person to become, a member, officer or representative of a trade union or participates in the promotion, formation or administration of a trade union..."

This subsection details a comprehensive list of prohibited employer actions against union members. It specifically forbids discrimination based on union membership or activity, as well as intimidation, threats, or other disciplinary measures. This aims to protect employees from retaliation for exercising their rights to unionize and participate in union activities.

#### Section 94(4): Prohibition on Employer Use of Replacement Workers During Strikes
"Subject to subsection (7), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall use the services of any of the following persons to perform all or part of the duties of an employee who is in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out..."

This section restricts employers from using replacement workers during a strike or lockout. This is intended to prevent employers from circumventing the collective bargaining process and forcing employees to accept terms and conditions of employment that they have rejected.

### Section 7: Concerted Activity Rights

#### Section 7(1): Right to Engage in Concerted Activity

individual_results.question: What is the structure and composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Structure and Composition of the Canada Industrial Relations Board

### Section 9: Establishment of Board

Section 9(1) of the Canada Labour Code formally establishes the Canada Industrial Relations Board, stating it
"...is established, to be known as the Canada Industrial Relations Board." This marks the foundational step in the Board's existence.

Section 9(2) then details the Board's composition, outlining a hierarchical structure. It includes:
"(a) a Chairperson, to hold office on a full-time basis..." This indicates a single, permanent leader at the helm of the Board.
"(b) two or more Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a full-time basis, and any other Vice-Chairpersons, to hold office on a part-time basis, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board..." This establishes a tiered leadership system with multiple Vice-Chairpersons to provide support and cover for the Chairperson.
"(c) not more than six other members, of which not more than three represent employees, and of which not more than three represent employers, to hold office on a full-time basis..." This defines the core membership of the Board, with a deliberate attempt at balance between employee and employer representation.
"(d) any other part-time members, representing, in equal numbers, employees and employers, that the Governor in Council considers necessary to discharge the responsibilities of the Board..." This allows for the appointment of additional part-time members to further refine the balance between employee and employer perspectives.
"(e) any other full-time or part-time members that the Governor in Council considers necessary to assist the Board in carrying out its functions under Parts II, III and IV." This provides flexibility for the Governor in Council to adjust the Board's size and composition based on evolving needs.

### Section 14: Panels

Section 14 further elaborates on the Board's operational structure by detailing the formation and powers of panels. It states,
"(1) Subject to subsections (3) and (3.1), a panel of not fewer than three members, at least one of whom is the Chairperson or a Vice-Chairperson, may determine any matter that comes before the Board under this Act." This establishes the panel as a key decision-making unit within the Board.

Section 14(2) emphasizes the importance of equal representation on panels, stating,
"Where a panel formed under subsection (1) is composed of one or more members representing employees, an equal number of members representing employers must also form part of the panel and vice versa." This ensures that panel decisions are informed by a diverse range of perspectives.

Section 14(5) clarifies the panel's authority, asserting,
"A panel has all the powers, duties and functions that are conferred on the Board by this Act with respect to any matter assigned to the panel." This underscores the panel's capacity to handle a wide range of cases.

### Section 15: Regulations

Section 15 grants the Board the power to make regulations of general application. This is a crucial mechanism for the Board to refine its procedures and adapt to changing circumstances. The regulations can cover a vast array of topics, including
"...the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings..." "the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining," and "the conduct of representation votes." This demonstrates the Board's ability to self-regulate and optimize its operations.

### Section 16: Powers of Board

Section 16 outlines the Board's extensive powers in relation to proceedings before it. These powers are broad and encompass a wide range of functions, from summoning witnesses and compelling evidence to entering on premises and issuing orders. For instance, it states,
"(a) to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce such documents and things as the Board deems requisite to the full investigation and consideration of any matter within its jurisdiction that is before the Board in the proceeding..." This highlights the Board's ability to gather information and ensure a thorough understanding of the issues at hand.

Furthermore, it mentions the Board's power to
"...determine any matter that comes before the Board under this Act." as reiterated in Section 14(1), and to
"...assist the Board in carrying out its functions under Parts II, III and IV." as stated in Section 15. These powers collectively paint a picture of a Board with significant authority to conduct fair and effective proceedings.

individual_results.question: Who appoints the members of the Board, and what are the general requirements for their appointment and terms?
individual_results.answer:
## Appointment of Board Members

### General Appointment Process

The members of the Board are appointed by the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister. This is a consistent method outlined in multiple sections of the Canada Labour Code.
"Subject to subsection (3), the members of the Board other than the Chairperson and the Vice-Chairpersons are to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation by the Minister with the organizations representative of employees or employers that the Minister considers appropriate, to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding three years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause." This passage from Section 10(2) details the appointment process for Board members who are not the Chairperson or Vice-Chairpersons. It specifies that the Minister will consult with organizations representing employees and employers before making the recommendation to the Governor in Council. These members hold office during "good behaviour" for terms not exceeding three years, with the Governor in Council having the power to remove them for cause.

Section 10(1) further clarifies the appointment of the Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons:
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons of the Board are to be appointed by the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister, to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding five years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause." This indicates that the Governor in Council makes the appointment based on the Minister's recommendation, with terms of office of up to five years.

### General Requirements for Appointment

The Canada Labour Code outlines several general requirements for Board members.
"The members of the Board must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act..." This requirement, found in Section 10(4), establishes the citizenship or permanent residency status of Board members.
"The Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons must have experience and expertise in industrial relations." This qualification, specified in Section 10(5), highlights the desired background for these leadership positions.

### Terms of Office

The terms of office for Board members vary depending on their position.
"...to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding five years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause." This states that the Chairperson and Vice-Chairpersons serve terms of up to five years, subject to removal for cause.
"...the members of the Board other than the Chairperson and the Vice-Chairpersons are to be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation by the Minister with the organizations representative of employees or employers that the Minister considers appropriate, to hold office during good behaviour for terms not exceeding three years each, subject to removal by the Governor in Council at any time for cause." This indicates that the other Board members serve terms of up to three years, also subject to removal for cause.

### Exception to Residence Requirement

Section 10.1(2) provides an exception to the general residence requirement for Board members.
"The Governor in Council may, by order, exempt a member from the requirement set out in subsection (1), subject to any conditions that the Governor in Council may prescribe." This allows the Governor in Council to waive the requirement for full-time Board members to reside in the National Capital Region, but this exemption can come with conditions.

individual_results.question: What are the restrictions on members of the Board in terms of holding other employment or office?
individual_results.answer:
## Restrictions on Board Members' Other Employment or Office

### Full-Time Members

Section 11(1) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states a restriction on full-time Board members:
"The full-time members of the Board must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration." This provision aims to ensure that full-time members are fully dedicated to their duties on the Board and are not divided by other financial obligations. The use of "must not" indicates a strict prohibition on such activities.

### Part-Time Members and Members Carrying Out Duties and Responsibilities Under Subsection 12(2)

Section 11(2) outlines a similar restriction for part-time Vice-Chairpersons and members appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e):
"A part-time Vice-Chairperson, or a member appointed pursuant to paragraph 9(2)(e), must not hold any other employment or office in respect of which they receive any remuneration and that is inconsistent with their duties under this Act." This addition introduces a nuance, allowing part-time members and those carrying out duties under subsection 12(2) to hold other employment or office *if* it is not inconsistent with their Board responsibilities. This acknowledges that individuals may have other commitments but ensures that these commitments do not interfere with their Board duties.

### Section 12.04 - Remuneration and Compensation

Section 12.04(1) further reinforces the restriction on full-time members' other employment by stating:
"The full-time members of the Board shall be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council." This indicates that full-time members are compensated for their work on the Board, making it incompatible with holding other remunerated employment. While part-time members and those carrying out duties under subsection 12(2) are also paid fees, the restriction on other remunerated employment remains, albeit with the caveat of not being inconsistent with their Board duties.

### Section 10.1 - Residence of Members

While not directly addressing restrictions on other employment, Section 10.1(1) does mention that full-time members must reside in the National Capital Region or within a distance determined by the Governor in Council. This suggests a requirement for full-time members to be geographically positioned to effectively carry out their Board duties, which could indirectly influence their ability to hold other employment in a different location.

individual_results.question: What happens to a member of the Board when their term of office expires or when they cease to be a member, and how does the Board ensure continuity in its operations?
individual_results.answer:
## Succession Rights and Obligations: Board to Determine Questions

### Reappointment

Section 12(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes that
"A member of the Board is eligible for reappointment on the expiration of any term of office in the same or another capacity." This indicates a mechanism for continuity, allowing experienced board members to return to their roles after their initial term ends. This is a direct response to the question about what happens to a member of the Board when their term expires.

### Completion of Duties

Section 12(2) further ensures continuity by outlining the Board's ability to allow departing members to complete outstanding duties. It states that
"Where a member of the Board ceases to be a member of the Board for any reason other than removal, the member may, despite anything in this Part, at the request of the Chairperson, carry out and complete any duties or responsibilities that the member would otherwise have had if the member had not ceased to be a member, in connection with any matter that came before the Board while the member was still a member of the Board and in respect of which there was any proceeding in which the member participated as a member." This provision prevents a sudden disruption to ongoing board work when a member leaves, ensuring that their unfinished tasks are addressed.

### Acting Chairperson

Section 12.03 addresses the continuity of leadership by detailing the process for an Acting Chairperson. It specifies that
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson." This ensures that the board can continue to function effectively even in the absence of the permanent Chairperson.

### Board's Role in Determining Questions

Section 46 of the Canada Labour Code highlights the Board's responsibility for ensuring continuity by determining any questions that arise under section 44. It states that
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business." This proactive approach allows the Board to address potential issues that could impact its operations or ongoing work, thereby maintaining its effectiveness.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of the Chairperson in terms of managing the work of the Board?
individual_results.answer:
## Responsibilities of the Chairperson in Managing the Work of the Board

### Section 12.01: Functions of Chairperson

Section 12.01 outlines the comprehensive supervisory and directional responsibilities of the Chairperson over the Board's work. It states that the Chairperson has
"...supervision over and direction of the work of the Board, including (a) the assignment and reassignment of matters that the Board is seized of to panels; (b) the composition of panels and the assignment of Vice-Chairpersons to preside over panels; (c) the determination of the date, time and place of hearings; (d) the conduct of the work of the Board; and (e) the management of the Board’s internal affairs."

This passage is crucial as it directly addresses the question. The Chairperson is not merely a presiding officer; they are actively involved in the operational aspects of the Board. This includes strategically distributing cases to different panels, ensuring panels are appropriately staffed with Vice-Chairpersons, setting the schedule for hearings, overseeing the overall process, and managing the Board's internal organization. The breadth of these responsibilities demonstrates the Chairperson's central role in ensuring the Board functions effectively.

### Section 12.02: Meetings | Acting Chairperson

Section 12.02 further elaborates on the Chairperson's role in managing Board meetings. It mentions that the Chairperson
"...convenes and presides over any meeting of the Board concerning the making of regulations under section 15." This highlights their responsibility for organizing and leading discussions and decisions related to the development of regulations.

Furthermore, Section 12.03 details the role of an Acting Chairperson when the Chairperson is absent or unable to perform their duties. It states,
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson." This ensures continuity in the Board's operations even in the absence of the primary Chairperson.

### Section 12.04: Remuneration | Compensation | Limitation of liability | Inquiries

Section 12.04 touches upon the Chairperson's financial aspects, stating that they are
"...be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council." While not directly managing the Board's work, this provision acknowledges the Chairperson's significant responsibilities and ensures they are appropriately compensated.

Section 12.06 mentions that the Chairperson
"...may request the Minister to decide whether any member of the Board should be subject to remedial or disciplinary measures for any reason set out in paragraphs 12.14(2)(a) to (d)." This indicates the Chairperson's involvement in addressing potential issues within the Board's membership, contributing to a productive and professional working environment.

In summary, the Chairperson's responsibilities in managing the Board's work are extensive and multifaceted. They are responsible for strategic case assignment, panel composition, hearing scheduling, overall conduct of Board business, and internal management. They also lead Board meetings, ensure continuity in leadership when necessary, and have a role in addressing potential issues within the Board's membership.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for a quorum at a meeting of the Board for making regulations, and how may the composition of the quorum vary?
individual_results.answer:
## Quorum Requirements for Board Meetings on Regulations

### General Quorum Composition

Section 12.02(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the general quorum for a meeting of the Board concerning the making of regulations under section 15. It states:
"For the purposes of subsection (1), the following persons constitute a quorum: (a) subject to paragraph (b), the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and two other members representing, respectively, employees and employers; or (b) at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members."

This indicates that the standard quorum consists of the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons, and two members each representing employees and employers. However, the composition of the quorum can vary depending on the subject matter of the meeting.

### Variation in Quorum Composition

Section 12.02(2)(b) details a variation in the quorum for meetings held for making regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I. It specifies:
"...at a meeting held for the making of regulations respecting matters that are not governed by Part I, the Chairperson, two Vice-Chairpersons and, if two or more full-time members have been appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e), two of those members."

This variation allows for the inclusion of up to two of the full-time members appointed under paragraph 9(2)(e) in the quorum, provided there are at least two such members appointed. This ensures that the Board has sufficient representation to make regulations on matters outside the scope of Part I.

### Section 85 on Sittings and Quorum

Section 85(1)(a) of the Canada Labour Code further clarifies the quorum for conciliation boards, which may be involved in the regulation-making process. It states:
"The chairperson of a conciliation board shall (a) after consultation with the other members of the board, fix the time and place of sittings of the conciliation board..."

While this section doesn't explicitly define the quorum for sittings, it implies that a quorum is necessary for the chairperson to fix the time and place of the sittings. Section 85(1)(2) then specifies:
"The chairperson and one other member of a conciliation board constitute a quorum but, in the absence of any member, the other members shall not proceed unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting."

This confirms that a quorum for sittings is at least the chairperson and one other member.

### Section 10 on Residence of Members

Section 10(1)(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines a requirement for full-time members of the Board:
"The full-time members of the Board must reside in the National Capital Region as described in the schedule to the National Capital Act or within the distance from the National Capital Region that is determined by the Governor in Council."

This residency requirement is a condition for appointment to a full-time position on the Board, but it does not directly impact the composition of the quorum.

### Section 12.03 on Acting Chairperson

Section 12.03 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the situation where the Chairperson is absent or unable to act. It states:
"If the Chairperson of the Board is absent or unable to act or the office of Chairperson is vacant, a Vice-Chairperson designated by the Minister acts as Chairperson for the time being, and a Vice-Chairperson so designated has and may exercise all the powers and perform all the duties and functions of the Chairperson."

This provision ensures that a quorum can still be maintained even if the Chairperson is unavailable, as a Vice-Chairperson can step in to lead the meeting.

individual_results.answer:
## Financial Provisions for Board Members

### Remuneration

Section 12.04(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the financial provisions for Board members. It states:
"The full-time members of the Board shall be paid any remuneration, and the part-time members of the Board and members of the Board carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2) shall be paid any fees, that may be fixed by the Governor in Council." This indicates that Board members, both full-time and part-time, are entitled to either remuneration or fees, the specific amounts of which are determined by the Governor in Council. This ensures that Board members are compensated for their time and effort.

### Travel and Living Expenses

Section 12.04(2) further details the financial support provided to Board members during their duties. It specifies:
"The members of the Board are entitled to be paid reasonable travel and living expenses incurred by them in the course of their duties under this Act while absent from, in the case of full-time members, their ordinary place of work and, in the case of part-time members and members carrying out duties and responsibilities under subsection 12(2), their ordinary place of residence." This provision covers reasonable expenses such as transportation and accommodation incurred while attending Board meetings or fulfilling their responsibilities outside their regular work location. This helps to alleviate the financial burden on Board members who may need to travel.

## Protection from Personal Liability

### Limitation of Liability

Section 12.051 of the Canada Labour Code provides significant protection from personal liability for Board members. It states:
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act." This means that Board members are shielded from being held personally responsible for any actions taken in good faith while performing their duties. This encourages Board members to act decisively and within their authority without fear of personal repercussions.

### Compensation

Section 12.05 also addresses Board members' entitlement to compensation. It declares:
"Each member of the Board is deemed to be an employee for the purposes of the Government Employees Compensation Act and to be employed in the federal public administration for the purposes of any regulations made under section 9 of the Aeronautics Act..." This deeming of Board members as employees under the Government Employees Compensation Act provides them with access to the same benefits and protections as other federal public administration employees, including compensation for work-related injuries or illnesses.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Minister take upon receiving a request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Actions Upon Receiving a Request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code

### Initial Actions and Information Gathering

Upon receiving a request under Section 12.07 of the Canada Labour Code, the Minister has several initial options.
"On receipt of the request, the Minister may take one or more of the following measures: (a) obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary..." This indicates that the Minister's first step is to gather information. The phrase "informal and expeditious manner" suggests a prompt and efficient approach to understanding the nature of the request. The Minister can request any information deemed relevant to the matter.

### Alternative Dispute Resolution

The Minister can also explore alternative methods of resolving the issue.
"(b) refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation..." This highlights the Minister's willingness to facilitate mediation between the parties involved. The Minister's satisfaction with the mediation potential is a key factor in this decision.

### Requesting an Inquiry

If the Minister believes the request warrants a more formal investigation, they can escalate the matter.
"(c) request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08..." This action involves formally requesting the Governor in Council to appoint an inquirer to conduct a thorough investigation into the request.

### Advising Against Further Measures

Finally, the Minister can determine that further action is not necessary.
"(d) advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section." This demonstrates the Minister's discretion to conclude that the request does not require further attention at that time. The Chairperson is formally informed of this decision.

### Appointment of Inquirer

Section 12.08 details the process of appointing an inquirer.
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry." This specifies that the Governor in Council makes the appointment based on the Minister of Justice's recommendation, and the appointed inquirer must be a judge of a superior court.

### Powers of the Inquirer

Section 12.09 outlines the extensive powers vested in the inquirer.
"The judge has all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court, including the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath." This demonstrates the inquirer's ability to compel testimony and evidence through summonses, oaths, and examinations.

### Staffing the Inquiry

Section 12.10 allows the inquirer to assemble a support team.
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses." This indicates that the inquirer can hire legal counsel and experts to aid in the investigation, with the Treasury Board's approval for compensation.

## General Principles Guiding Inquiries Under the Canada Labour Code

### Transparency

#### Public Conduct of Inquiries
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an inquiry must be conducted in public." This statement from Section 12.11(1) establishes a strong principle of transparency for inquiries conducted under the Canada Labour Code. It mandates that inquiries are, by default, open to the public. This allows for scrutiny of the evidence presented and the proceedings themselves, fostering accountability and public trust.

#### Rules of Evidence
"In conducting an inquiry, the judge is not bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence and may receive, and base a decision on, evidence presented in the proceedings that the judge considers credible or trustworthy in the circumstances of the case." This provision in Section 12.12(1) further supports transparency by granting the judge broad discretion in assessing the admissibility of evidence. The judge is not constrained by rigid legal rules, allowing for the consideration of information that may not meet traditional evidentiary standards but is deemed reliable in the context of the inquiry.

### Confidentiality

#### Application for Confidentiality
"The judge may, on application, take any appropriate measures and make any order that the judge considers necessary to ensure the confidentiality of the inquiry if, after having considered all available alternate measures, the judge is satisfied that (a) there is a real and substantial risk that matters involving public security will be disclosed; (b) there is a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the inquiry such that the need to prevent disclosure outweighs the societal interest that the inquiry be conducted in public; or (c) there is a serious possibility that the life, liberty or security of a person will be endangered." This section in Section 12.11(2) acknowledges the need for confidentiality in certain circumstances. It allows the judge to order confidentiality if there is a risk to public security, fairness of the inquiry, or the safety of individuals. This provision balances the public interest in transparency with the need to protect sensitive information.

#### Confidentiality of Hearing
"Where the judge considers it appropriate, the judge may take any measures and make any order that the judge considers necessary to ensure the confidentiality of a hearing held in respect of an application under subsection (2)." This subsection in Section 12.11(3) provides further flexibility for the judge to ensure confidentiality on a hearing-by-hearing basis. It allows for tailored measures to address specific confidentiality concerns that may arise during a particular hearing.

### Rights of Parties Involved

#### Right to be Heard
"The member who is the subject of the inquiry must be given reasonable notice of the subject-matter of the inquiry and of the time and place of any hearing and must be given an opportunity, in person or by counsel, to be heard at the hearing, to cross-examine witnesses and to present evidence." This section in Section 12.13(1) guarantees the subject of the inquiry the fundamental right to be heard. It mandates that the individual receives adequate notice of the inquiry's scope and hearing details, and is afforded the opportunity to present their case, cross-examine witnesses, and offer evidence.

#### Intervention in Inquiry
"An interested party may, with leave of the judge, intervene in an inquiry on the terms and conditions that the judge considers appropriate." This provision in Section 12.12(2) allows individuals or groups with a stake in the inquiry to participate. They can intervene with the judge's permission, subject to the judge's discretion regarding the terms and conditions of their involvement. This ensures that all relevant perspectives are considered during the inquiry.

#### Report to Minister
"The member who is the subject of the inquiry must be given reasonable notice of the subject-matter of the inquiry and of the time and place of any hearing and must be given an opportunity, in person or by counsel, to be heard at the hearing, to cross-examine witnesses and to present evidence." This section in Section 12.13(1) also specifies that the subject of the inquiry must receive a report of the inquiry's findings to the Minister. This ensures that the Minister is informed of the inquiry's outcome and can take appropriate action.

individual_results.question: What happens after an inquiry into a member's conduct is completed, and what actions can be taken as a result?
individual_results.answer:
## Post-Inquiry Actions and Outcomes

### Section 129: Internal Complaint Resolution Process: Head’s investigation

#### Head’s Decision and Notification
"The Head shall, on completion of an investigation made under subsection (1), make one of the decisions referred to in paragraphs 128(13)(a) to (c) and shall immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee." This passage outlines the immediate consequence of the Head's investigation. The Head must issue a decision based on the evidence gathered and communicate this decision in writing to both the employer and the employee involved in the inquiry.

#### Continuation of Work
"If the employee has exercised their right under subsection (1.3), the employer may, during the investigation and until the Head has issued a decision, require that the employee concerned remain at a safe location near the place in respect of which the investigation is being made or assign the employee reasonable alternative work, and shall not assign any other employee to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform the activity referred to in subsection (1) unless (a) the other employee is qualified for the work; (b) the other employee has been advised of the refusal of the employee concerned and of the reasons for the refusal; and (c) the employer is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the other employee will not be put in danger." This section details the employer's options regarding the employee's work status during the Head's investigation, particularly if the employee has exercised their right to refuse work. The employer can either require the employee to remain in a safe location or assign them alternative work, provided certain conditions are met.

#### Appeal Process
"If the Head makes a decision referred to in paragraph 128(13)(b) or (c), the employee is not entitled under section 128 or this section to continue to refuse to use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform that activity, but the employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, may appeal the decision, in writing, to the Board within 10 days after receiving notice of the decision." This passage specifies the appeal process available to the employee if the Head's decision falls under paragraphs 128(13)(b) or (c). The employee can appeal the decision to the Board within 10 days of receiving written notice.

### Section 30: Recourse After Investigator’s Report

#### Limited Appeal Process
"Under the Regulations, the resolution process is considered  complete once the employer implements the recommendations in the investigator’s  report. As such, there is no appeal process under the Code or Regulations if:  you are not satisfied with the conclusions or  recommendations in the investigator’s report, or  you believe the investigation was flawed   However, you should communicate these concerns to your  employer or designated recipient as soon as possible.  If your concerns are not resolved, you may be able to  request a judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court, within 30  days of receiving the investigator’s report. You should consult a lawyer  regarding this process, since it is not prescribed by the Regulations." This section clarifies that there is generally no formal appeal process within the Code or Regulations if the employee is dissatisfied with the investigator's report. However, the employee may be able to seek judicial review of the investigation by the Federal Court within 30 days of receiving the report, but this is not a prescribed process and legal counsel should be consulted.

#### Recommendations in the Investigator’s Report
"The investigator’s report should contain recommendations on  methods of eliminating or minimizing the risk of a similar occurrence in the  future. The recommendations should not reveal directly or indirectly the  identity of the persons involved in the occurrence or in the resolution process.  For example, the report could contain recommendations on methods to eliminate  systemic issues related to:   the organizational culture or structure, or  specific training that should be undertaken by  the parties involved..." This passage highlights the expected content of the investigator's report. It should include recommendations for preventing future incidents, while protecting the privacy of individuals involved. The recommendations should focus on systemic issues rather than individual blame.

### Section 12.07: Minister’s Powers

#### Minister’s Actions
"On receipt of the request, the Minister may take one or more of the following measures: (a) obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary; (b) refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation; (c) request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08; or (d) advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section." This section details the various actions the Minister can take upon receiving a request for an inquiry. These actions range from gathering information to referring the matter for mediation or requesting a formal inquiry from the Governor in Council. The Minister can also decline to take further action.

#### Appointment of Inquirer
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry." This passage specifies the process for appointing an inquirer when the Minister requests a formal inquiry. The Governor in Council makes the appointment on the Minister of Justice's recommendation, selecting a judge of a superior court.

#### Powers of the Inquirer
"The judge has all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court, including the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath." This section outlines the broad powers of the inquirer, which are equivalent to those of a superior court judge. These powers include issuing summonses, compelling testimony and document production, and administering oaths.

#### Staffing the Inquiry
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses." This passage explains that the inquirer can hire legal counsel and other experts to assist with the investigation. The inquirer can set the terms of their engagement and, with Treasury Board approval, determine their pay.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for determining a matter that comes before the Board, and who can determine such matters?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Determining a Matter Before the Board

### General Requirements for Board Determination

Section 16.1 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the Board's authority to make decisions without holding an oral hearing. This indicates a flexibility in the Board's approach to determining matters.
"The Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing."

### Determining the Wishes of the Majority of Employees

Section 17 specifically addresses the Board's role in determining the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit. It states:
"Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate."

This passage is crucial because it details the Board's obligation and the timeframe within which it must ascertain those wishes. The Board has discretion to set the date for this determination, but it must be either the date the application was filed or another date deemed suitable by the Board.

### Who Can Determine Matters Before the Board?

Several individuals and bodies have the authority to make decisions before the Board.

#### Panel Chairperson

Section 14.1 addresses the continuity of a panel's decision-making power in the event of a member's death or incapacity. It states:
"In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This means that if a panel member is unable to continue their duties, the chairperson has the power to make a decision on any outstanding matters, and that decision stands as the panel's decision.

#### Governor in Council

Section 12.08 outlines the Governor in Council's power to appoint an inquirer following a request. It specifies:
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry."

This indicates that the Governor in Council, acting on the Minister of Justice's advice, can appoint an inquirer to conduct a more in-depth investigation into a matter before the Board.

#### Chairperson

Section 14.2(1) states:
"A decision made by a majority of the members of a panel or, where there is no majority, by the chairperson of the panel is a decision of the Board."

This clarifies that even if a panel does not reach a majority decision, the chairperson's decision is considered the Board's decision.

#### Minister

Section 12.07 details the Minister's ability to take various measures upon receipt of a request, including referring the matter for mediation. It states:
"(b) refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation..."

This shows the Minister's role in attempting to resolve matters before they reach the Board through alternative dispute resolution methods.

#### Board

Section 46 explicitly states:
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This confirms that the Board has the ultimate authority to determine questions that fall within its purview, including those related to business sales and changes in activity.

## Section 15: General Power to Assist Parties

### Types of Matters the Board Can Make Regulations About

Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Board a broad power to make regulations of general application. This power encompasses a wide array of topics necessary for the Board to effectively carry out its duties.

### Establishing Rules of Procedure
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings..." This indicates that the Board can create detailed guidelines for how its proceedings will be conducted, from initial pre-hearing discussions to formal hearings. This ensures consistency and fairness in the Board's work.

### Telecommunication Use
"(a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings..." The Board can regulate the use of technology for communication during its proceedings. This can facilitate remote participation and streamline the process.

### Determining Units for Collective Bargaining
"(b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining..." This is a crucial function of the Board, and it can create regulations to guide its approach to defining bargaining units. This ensures that collective bargaining is conducted in a meaningful and representative manner.

### Certification of Trade Unions
"(c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units..." The Board can make regulations concerning the process by which trade unions are recognized as legitimate bargaining representatives for employees. This provides clarity and predictability for both unions and employers.

### Conduct of Representation Votes

"(d) the conduct of representation votes;" The Board can regulate how votes are conducted to determine whether employees want to be represented by a particular union. This ensures that the process is fair and transparent.

### Time Limits for Certification Applications
"(e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit..." The Board can set time limits for trade unions to re-apply for certification after a previous application was denied. This helps to avoid indefinite delays.

### Time Limits for Revocation Applications
"(f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit..." Similar to certification applications, the Board can set time limits for employees to seek the revocation of a union's certification.

### Hearing and Determination of Applications
"(g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board..." The Board can regulate how it handles various types of cases that are brought before it.

### Expedited Procedures
"(g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure..." The Board can create regulations for faster resolution of certain types of cases.

### Forms to be Used
"(h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board..." The Board can standardize the forms that are used for various types of filings and documents.

### Exercise of Powers Under Section 18
"(i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18..." Section 18 grants the Board broad powers to assist parties to reach agreements. The Board can regulate when and how it will exercise these powers.

### Inquiries
"(j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2)..." The Board can make regulations concerning any inquiries it may undertake.

### Evidence Presentation
"...the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part..." The Board can regulate how evidence related to union membership and employee preferences is submitted.

### Criteria for Union Membership
"(n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union..." The Board can make regulations to establish clear rules for determining who is considered a union member.

### Conditions for Valid Strike or Lockout Votes
"(o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes..." The Board can regulate the requirements for these types of votes to be legally valid.

### Authority of Board Representatives
"...the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions..." The Board can regulate the powers of its representatives.

### Other Incidental Matters
"(q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act." This provides a catch-all provision for any other regulations that the Board deems necessary to perform its functions.

In summary, Section 15 empowers the Board to make regulations on virtually every aspect of its work, from procedural rules to the determination of bargaining units and the conduct of certification votes. This broad power is essential for the Board to be an effective and efficient adjudicator of industrial relations disputes.
