## Assistance Provided by the Board and its Members

### General Power to Assist Parties

Section 15.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad authority of the Board, its members, external adjudicators, and authorized employees to assist parties in resolving disputes. It states:
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

This passage is crucial because it establishes a proactive role for the Board in facilitating resolution. The assistance is contingent upon the parties' agreement, ensuring that the Board's involvement is welcomed. Furthermore, the Board has discretion over the methods of assistance, allowing it to tailor its approach to the specific needs of the dispute. The phrase
"...without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled." is important as it clarifies that the Board's assistance is not intended to usurp its ultimate authority to make decisions on unresolved matters.

### Declaratory Opinions

Section 15.1(2) specifies another type of assistance the Board can provide: declaratory opinions. It states:
"The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."

This power allows the Board to provide formal interpretations of the Code or the application of its provisions to specific situations. This can be valuable for employers and unions seeking clarity on their rights and obligations. The Board's declaratory opinions are not binding on the parties in the same way as a decision on the merits of a dispute, but they can provide a useful framework for understanding the legal landscape.

individual_results.question: How does the Board determine the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit when an application is made under this Part?

## Section 17: Determination of the Wishes of the Majority of the Employees

### Timing of Determination

Section 17 outlines the Board's process for determining the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit when an application is made under this Part. It states:
"Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate."

This indicates that the Board has flexibility in choosing the date on which it will assess the majority view. The default is the date the application is formally submitted, but the Board can decide on a later date if it deems it necessary to gather more information or conduct further analysis. This adaptability allows the Board to respond effectively to different types of applications and situations.

### Section 31: Result of Representation Vote

Section 31 further elaborates on how the Board determines the wishes of the majority through a representation vote. It begins by stating:
"Subject to subsection (2), the Board shall determine the result of a representation vote on the basis of the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting."

This is the primary mechanism for the Board to ascertain the majority view. The Board will count the ballots cast and declare the union that receives the most votes as the bargaining agent, provided that at least thirty-five percent of the eligible employees have participated in the vote.

### Section 16.1: Board's Authority to Decide Without Oral Hearing

Section 16.1 grants the Board the authority to make decisions without holding an oral hearing. While not directly addressing the determination of the majority wish, it underscores the Board's capacity to act decisively when it has sufficient information. This power could be utilized in situations where the outcome of a representation vote is clear or where the Board has gathered sufficient data through other means.

### Section 30: Conduct of Representation Vote

Section 30 details the Board's responsibilities in conducting a representation vote. It specifies that the Board will:
"(a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

This highlights the Board's role in ensuring a fair and orderly voting process. By determining eligibility and making necessary arrangements, the Board lays the groundwork for a vote that accurately reflects the majority view of the employees.

### Section 18.1: Review of Bargaining Units

Section 18.1 discusses the Board's power to review the structure of bargaining units. While not a direct method for determining the majority wish, it can indirectly influence the outcome of a representation vote. If the bargaining units are determined to be inappropriate for collective bargaining, the Board may order a new vote with revised units, potentially leading to a different union being certified.

In summary, the Board primarily determines the wishes of the majority of employees in a unit through a representation vote, counting the ballots cast by those who voted. It also retains flexibility in choosing the date for its determination and can make decisions without an oral hearing when it has sufficient information. The Board's role in conducting fair votes and reviewing bargaining units further supports its ability to accurately reflect the majority view.

individual_results.question: What is the process for the Board to review the structure of bargaining units if it is deemed that they are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining, and what actions can the Board take if the parties do not reach an agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

### Section 18.1: Powers and Duties: Review of structure of bargaining units

Section 18.1(1) outlines the initial trigger for the Board to review bargaining unit structure:
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board's review is initiated either by a party seeking a change or by the Board itself upon its own assessment.

### Section 18.1(2): Actions the Board Can Take if Parties Do Not Reach an Agreement

Section 18.1(2) details the Board's course of action when the parties fail to reach an agreement within a reasonable timeframe. It states:
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This highlights the Board's obligation to facilitate an agreement and its authority to issue orders to put such an agreement into effect.

### Section 18.1(3): Board's Determination When Parties Fail to Agree

Section 18.1(3) addresses the scenario where the parties do not reach an agreement, and the Board must make a determination. It says:
"If the Board is of the opinion that the agreement reached by the parties would not lead to the creation of units appropriate for collective bargaining or if the parties do not agree on certain issues within the period that the Board considers reasonable, the Board determines any question that arises and makes any orders it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This emphasizes the Board's ultimate power to resolve outstanding issues and issue orders to establish appropriate bargaining units.

### Section 18.1(4): Content of Orders

Section 18.1(4) provides a comprehensive list of the types of orders the Board can issue when it makes a determination. These orders can cover a wide range of aspects, including:
"(a) determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each bargaining unit that results from the review; (b) amend any certification order or description of a bargaining unit contained in any collective agreement; (c) if more than one collective agreement applies to employees in a bargaining unit, decide which collective agreement is in force; (d) amend, to the extent that the Board considers necessary, the provisions of collective agreements respecting expiry dates or seniority rights, or amend other such provisions; (e) if the conditions of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met with respect to some of the employees in a bargaining unit, decide which terms and conditions of employment apply to those employees until the time that a collective agreement becomes applicable to the unit or the conditions of those paragraphs are met with respect to the unit; and (f) authorize a party to a collective agreement to give notice to bargain collectively." This demonstrates the Board's broad mandate to reshape bargaining units and their associated terms and conditions of employment.

In summary, the Board's review of bargaining unit structure is initiated by an application from a party or its own assessment. If the parties fail to reach an agreement, the Board is obligated to facilitate one and issue orders to implement it. When the parties do not agree, the Board makes a determination on any outstanding issues and issues orders to establish appropriate bargaining units, with the power to amend existing collective agreements and determine which collective agreement is in force.

individual_results.question: What flexibility does the Board have when making decisions or issuing orders under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Flexibility in Decision-Making and Orders under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 251.12: Broad Powers of the Board in Appeal Orders

Section 251.12 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the flexibility the Board possesses when making orders in an appeal. It states,
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal; (c) award costs in the proceedings; and (d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board."

This passage demonstrates the Board's wide latitude. It can
"...confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..." indicating it isn't bound by the original decision. Furthermore, it can issue orders related to payment, costs, and even penalties for delaying the appeal process. The phrase
"...any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision..." is key, highlighting that the Board's flexibility is driven by its need to implement its own findings.

### Section 243: Finality of Board Orders

Section 243(1) reinforces the Board's flexibility by declaring,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This provision is crucial because it means that once a Board order is issued, it is binding and cannot be challenged in the judicial system. This finality allows the Board to make decisions with a sense of authority and certainty, knowing that they will be enforced without further legal scrutiny. The lack of review in any court provides the Board with the freedom to make decisions without fear of them being overturned.

### Section 251.11: Scope of Appeal and Grounds

Section 251.11(2) further illustrates the Board's flexibility in the context of appeals. It specifies,
"Except in the case of a compliance order, the person may appeal the decision only on a question of law or jurisdiction."

This limitation on the grounds for appeal is a form of flexibility, as it allows the Board to focus on the legal aspects of its decision rather than getting bogged down in factual disputes. It also ensures that appeals are directed towards issues that the Board is equipped to handle.

### Section 244: Enforcement of Orders

Section 244(1) details the process for enforcing Board orders, which indirectly reflects the Board's flexibility in its decision-making. It states,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This provision provides a mechanism for the Board's orders to be given practical effect. The Federal Court can intervene to ensure compliance, demonstrating the Board's ability to make decisions that are ultimately enforceable. The flexibility lies in the fact that the Head can also initiate enforcement on behalf of someone affected by the order.

### Section 156: Decision Finality

Section 156(1) mirrors the finality established in Section 243, stating,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This reiteration of finality underscores the Board's power to make decisions that are not subject to judicial review. This allows the Board to act decisively and implement its findings without fear of them being overturned. The lack of review in any court provides the Board with the freedom to make decisions without fear of them being overturned.

In conclusion, the Board possesses considerable flexibility in its decision-making and issuance of orders under the Canada Labour Code. It can make orders that are "necessary to give effect to its decision," issue orders related to payment, costs, and penalties, and its orders are final and not subject to judicial review. This flexibility allows the Board to act decisively and implement its findings effectively.

Section 20(2) clarifies the legal status of such partial decisions:

## Conditions for Judicial Review or Questioning of Board Orders and Decisions

### Section 22: Review and Enforcement of Orders: Order and decision final

Section 22 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states the finality of Board orders and decisions, outlining the limited circumstances under which they can be challenged in a court.
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act."
This passage establishes a strong presumption against judicial review. It specifies that review is permissible *only* according to the Federal Courts Act and for reasons listed in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act. This indicates a narrow scope for judicial intervention.

### Section 243: Division XIV-Unjust Dismissal: Order final

Section 243 reinforces the finality of Board orders, specifically those made under Division XIV, which deals with unjust dismissal.
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This is a direct and unequivocal statement of finality, mirroring the language found in Section 22. It leaves no room for interpretation that judicial review is generally available for Board orders.

### Section 246.5: Decisions final

Section 246.5 further emphasizes the finality of Board decisions made under this Division.
"(1) Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This passage is a repetition of the finality principle established in Section 22 and Section 243, solidifying the point that Board decisions are not subject to standard judicial review.

### Section 251.12: Orders — Review and Appeal: Board decision

Section 251.12 discusses appeals from Board decisions, but it also maintains the finality of the Board's orders.
"(3) The order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This passage, like Sections 22, 243, and 246.5, reiterates the principle that Board orders are not generally reviewable in court. It only mentions the possibility of review according to the Federal Courts Act on specific grounds.

### Section 22 (2): No Proceedings in Any Court

Section 22(2) provides a comprehensive prohibition against initiating court proceedings to question, review, prohibit, or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Part.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Part."

This section explicitly states the primary purpose of filing a Board order or decision in the Federal Court: to make it enforceable. The filing is done
"...on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision..." This ensures that the filing is initiated by a party who has a direct interest in the order being legally binding. The exception to this rule is when the Board believes there is no risk of non-compliance or no practical benefit to filing.

### Section 246.6: Enforcement of Orders | Enforcement of orders
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

"...an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This means that the order can be enforced through all the same legal mechanisms available for judgments, such as execution, garnishment, and other court orders.

### Section 22: Review and Enforcement of Orders: Order and decision final

This means that once a Board order is registered in the Federal Court, it is legally binding and cannot be challenged in other courts on most grounds. The only exception is if the challenge is based on specific grounds outlined in the Federal Courts Act, such as jurisdiction or exceeding the Board's authority.

## Implications of Registration

individual_results.question: What are the rules and restrictions surrounding the timing of a trade union's application for certification as a bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Timing of Trade Union Certification Applications

### Section 24: General Application Timing

Section 24 outlines the various times a trade union can apply for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees. It states,
"Subject to subsection (3), an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made (a) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, at any time; (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time; (c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation; and (d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."

This section provides a comprehensive list of permissible application windows. The initial application can be made "at any time" if no collective agreement is in force and no union is certified. If a collective agreement exists, the application can be made after twelve months of certification or earlier with Board consent. For collective agreements lasting more than three years, the application is restricted to specific three-month periods before the end of each year of its operation and after the last three months of its operation.

### Section 33: Application Timing for Employers' Organizations

Section 33 addresses the application timing when a trade union seeks certification for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers' organization. It specifies,
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

This indicates that the application timing is similar to the general application timing, but with an additional consideration. The Board may designate the employers' organization as the employer if each employer within the organization has granted it the necessary authority. The application can be made "at any time" if no collective agreement is in force and no union is certified, or after twelve months of certification with Board consent if a collective agreement exists.

### Section 24(3): No Application During Strike or Lockout

Section 24(3) imposes a restriction on application timing during certain industrial actions. It states,
"An application for certification under subsection (2) in respect of a unit must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part and that involves employees in the unit."

This rule prohibits the filing of a certification application while a strike or lockout is in progress, unless the Board grants specific permission. This is likely intended to avoid undue disruption to ongoing collective bargaining efforts.

### Section 24(4): Terms or Conditions of Employment Not to Be Changed

Section 24(4) further restricts application timing by prohibiting employers from altering terms and conditions of employment after notification of an application. It says,
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board."

This provision aims to maintain stability in the workplace during the certification process. Employers are barred from making changes to employees' employment terms until the Board makes a decision or thirty days have passed after certification, unless such changes are part of an existing collective agreement or are approved by the Board.

### Section 24.1

Section 24.1 directly addresses the question, stating:
"A trade union that is not certified but has entered into a collective agreement the term of which has not expired may, despite paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d), make an application for certification at any time, in respect of the unit to which the collective agreement applies or substantially the same unit."

This passage explicitly confirms that a trade union that has already reached a collective agreement, even if it lacks official certification, has the right to apply for certification under specific conditions. The phrase "at any time" is particularly significant, indicating that the union is not bound by the usual time restrictions outlined in subsections (2)(c) and (d) of section 24. This exception provides flexibility for unions that have demonstrated their ability to bargain effectively through a tentative agreement. The union can pursue certification even before the agreement's expiration, or for a unit that is substantially similar to the one covered by the existing collective agreement.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions may the Board refuse to certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a unit of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Board Refusal of Certification

### Section 26: Prohibition on Certification for Multiple Units with the Same Employer
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This section explicitly outlines a condition under which the Board may refuse certification. It prohibits a single trade union from representing two separate bargaining units when those units are all employees of the same employer. This is a clear restriction designed to prevent a single union from wielding undue influence over multiple groups of workers within the same organization. The language is direct and unambiguous, stating that certification is barred in this scenario.

### Section 28: General Requirement for Certification
"The Board shall, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit if the Board (a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit; (b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining; and (c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent."

While Section 28 details the general requirements for certification, it does not list conditions under which the Board *may* refuse certification. It focuses on the affirmative steps the Board must take to grant certification. Therefore, this section does not directly answer the question about conditions for refusal.

### Section 29: Representation Vote Conditions
"Section 29 (1) The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

Section 29 discusses the Board's power to order a representation vote to determine employee preference. It does not specify conditions under which the Board would *refuse* certification, only when it would *order* a vote.

### Section 30: Conduct of Vote and Choice Provision
"(2) Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots."

Section 30 details the Board's responsibilities in conducting a representation vote. It mandates that a choice be included on the ballots for employees who do not wish to be represented by any of the unions listed. This does not outline conditions for refusal of certification, but rather the procedures followed when a vote is ordered.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification
"Section 36 (1) Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit; (b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees; (c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

Section 36 describes the consequences of certification, not the conditions for refusal. It details the exclusive bargaining authority granted to the certified union and the revocation of previous certifications.

### Section 24.1: Limitation on Mandatory Vote
"Subsection (2) does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under section 24.1."

This section provides a specific limitation on the Board's power to order a representation vote. It states that the mandatory vote provision in Section 29 does not apply to a trade union certified as a result of an application made under Section 24.1. This is a condition under which the Board would *not* order a vote, leading to certification.

Based on the analysis of the provided documents, the Board may refuse certification under the condition that a single trade union is seeking to represent two separate bargaining units that are all employees of the same employer, as explicitly stated in Section 26.

This passage is a clear and unambiguous prohibition. It explicitly forbids a single trade union from representing two separate bargaining units – one for private constables and another for other employees – when those employees are all employed by the same employer. The phrase
"...any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer." is crucial, as it establishes the condition under which the dual certification is prohibited. individual_results.question: What factors influence the Labour Board's decision when determining a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining?
individual_results.answer:
## Factors Influencing the Labour Board's Unit Determination

### Section 27: Determination of Appropriate Unit

Section 27 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the factors that guide the Labour Board's decision-making process when evaluating whether a unit proposed by a trade union is appropriate for collective bargaining.
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board shall determine the unit that, in the opinion of the Board, is appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage establishes the Board's ultimate authority in this matter. While the trade union may propose a unit, the Board's assessment is the final word.

### Section 27(2): Board's Flexibility in Unit Composition

The Board's determination is not a simple rubber stamp of the trade union's suggestion. It possesses considerable flexibility in adjusting the unit's composition.
"In determining whether a unit constitutes a unit that is appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board may include any employees in or exclude any employees from the unit proposed by the trade union." This indicates that the Board can broaden or narrow the unit based on its own considerations. It can add employees who it believes are essential to the bargaining process or remove employees who it deems less relevant.

### Section 27(3): Specific Considerations for Professional Employees

Section 27(3) highlights a specific set of factors that the Board considers when dealing with units comprised of or including professional employees.
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including professional employees, the Board, subject to subsections (2) and (4), shall determine that the unit appropriate for collective bargaining is a unit comprised of only professional employees, unless such a unit would not otherwise be appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage reveals that the Board generally aims for a unit consisting solely of professional employees. However, it acknowledges that this may not always be the optimal approach.

### Section 27(4): Board's Inclusion of Similar Occupations and Functions

Section 27(4) further elaborates on the Board's ability to include employees who may not strictly fit the definition of "professional employee" but perform similar functions.
"In determining that a unit is appropriate for collective bargaining under subsection (3), the Board may include in the unit (a) professional employees of more than one profession; and (b) employees performing the functions, but lacking the qualifications, of a professional employee." This demonstrates the Board's willingness to broaden the unit to include employees whose roles are closely related to those of professional employees.

### Section 27(5): Board's Consideration of Supervisory Employees

Section 27(5) addresses units comprised of employees whose duties include the supervision of other employees.
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of or including employees whose duties include the supervision of other employees, the Board may, subject to subsection (2), determine that the unit proposed in the application is appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage indicates that the Board generally accepts supervisory employee units, subject to its overall assessment of appropriateness.

### Section 27(6): Board's Exclusion of Private Constables

Section 27(6) provides a specific exclusion from the Board's unit determination.
"The Board shall not include a private constable in a unit with other employees." This is a clear directive against including private constables in bargaining units.

### Section 18.1: Board's Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

Section 18.1 outlines the Board's power to review the structure of bargaining units.
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage establishes that the Board can initiate a unit review process if it believes the existing units are no longer serving their intended purpose.

### Section 18.1(2): Board's Facilitation of Agreement

Section 18.1(2) details the Board's role in facilitating an agreement between the parties during a unit review.
"If the Board reviews, pursuant to subsection (1) or section 35 or 45, the structure of the bargaining units, the Board (a) must allow the parties to come to an agreement, within a period that the Board considers reasonable, with respect to the determination of bargaining units and any questions arising from the review; and (b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This passage highlights the Board's commitment to helping the parties reach a mutually acceptable unit structure.

### Section 18.1(3): Board's Independent Determination

Section 18.1(3) clarifies that if the parties cannot reach an agreement within the Board's timeframe, the Board will make an independent determination.
"If the Board is of the opinion that the agreement reached by the parties would not lead to the creation of units appropriate for collective bargaining or if the parties do not agree on certain issues within the period that the Board considers reasonable, the Board determines any question that arises and makes any orders it considers appropriate in the circumstances." This passage reinforces the Board's ultimate authority to resolve unit review issues when the parties are deadlocked.

### Section 45: Board's Determination in Successor Situations

Section 45 addresses the Board's role in determining appropriate bargaining units in the context of a sale or change of activity.
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This passage indicates that the Board can step in to determine units when a business undergoes a significant change.

## Requirements for Trade Union Certification

### Section 28: Duty to Certify Trade Union

#### Initial Steps by the Board
"The Board shall, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit if the Board (a) has received from the trade union an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit; (b) has determined the unit that constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining; and (c) is satisfied that, as of the date of the filing of the application or of any other date that the Board considers appropriate, a majority of the employees in the unit wish to have the trade union represent them as their bargaining agent."

This section outlines the initial obligations of the Board when a trade union submits a certification application. The Board must first receive the application, then determine the appropriate bargaining unit, and finally, be satisfied that a majority of the employees in that unit desire the union's representation. These three conditions must be met for the Board to proceed with the certification process.

### Section 29: Representation Vote

#### When a Vote is Ordered
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This section details the Board's power to order a representation vote. The Board can initiate a vote at any point during the certification process if it needs further assurance about the employees' preference for a specific union.

#### Mandatory Vote
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This subsection specifies a mandatory vote scenario. If a union applies for certification in a unit where no other union currently represents the employees, and the Board determines that between 35% and 50% of the unit members are union members, a vote *must* be conducted. This ensures that the employees have a direct say in their representation.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification

#### Exclusive Authority
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

This section highlights the significant consequence of certification: the union gains exclusive bargaining power. Once certified, the union is the *only* entity authorized to negotiate with the employer on behalf of the employees in the unit.

#### Revocation of Prior Certifications
"(b) the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees..."

This subsection clarifies that any prior certifications in the same unit are automatically cancelled to the extent they applied to the employees now seeking certification. This ensures a clear and single bargaining agent for the unit.

#### Substitution as Party to Collective Agreements
"(c) the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

This section details how the certified union becomes the official party to any existing or future collective agreements that cover the unit's employees. This provides legal recognition and enforceability to the union's bargaining outcomes.

#### Bargaining Agent for Purposes of Paragraph 50(b)
"(d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

This subsection provides a specific designation for the certified union, confirming its standing as the bargaining agent for a particular purpose outlined in the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 26: Certification Prohibited

#### Dual Bargaining Units
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This section establishes a prohibition against a single union representing two separate bargaining units that are part of the same employer. This is intended to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure clear representation for each distinct group of employees.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances may or must the Board order a representation vote among employees in a unit to determine their bargaining agent?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Orders Representation Votes

### Section 29: General Authority to Order a Representation Vote

Section 29(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the Board's broad power to order a representation vote. It states:
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."
This passage is fundamental to understanding when the Board *may* order a vote. The phrase "in any case" indicates that the Board has this discretion regardless of the specific circumstances surrounding a certification application. The purpose of the vote is
"...itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent..." This highlights the Board's need to gauge employee preference before making a certification decision.

### Section 29(2): Mandatory Vote Based on Union Membership

Section 29(2) outlines a specific circumstance *in which* the Board *must* order a representation vote. It specifies:
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."
This subsection establishes a threshold of union membership. If the Board determines that the union has between 35% and 50% of the employees in the unit as members, it is legally obligated to order a vote. This ensures that the Board has a mechanism to determine whether the union has sufficient support to be a legitimate bargaining agent.

### Section 29(3): Disregarding Charter Requirements

Section 29(3) provides a further exception to the 35%-50% rule. It states:
"Where the Board is satisfied that a trade union has an established practice of admitting persons to membership without regard to the eligibility requirements of its charter, constitution or by-laws, the Board may disregard those requirements in determining whether a person is a member of a trade union."
This passage clarifies that the Board can override a union's own membership rules when it finds that the union has a history of lax membership standards. This ensures that the vote accurately reflects the actual level of support for the union, even if the union's formal membership count is misleading.

### Section 30: Conduct of the Vote

Section 30 details the Board's responsibilities in conducting a representation vote. It states:
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."
This passage emphasizes the Board's role in ensuring a fair and orderly vote. It includes tasks such as identifying eligible voters, preparing ballots, establishing voting procedures, and securing the ballots. This comprehensive oversight is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the vote.

### Section 30(2): Choice on Ballots

Section 30(2) specifies that the ballots for a representation vote must include an option for employees to indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots. It states:
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots."
This passage highlights the Board's commitment to respecting individual employee preferences. The "choice" on the ballots allows employees to express their neutrality and not be forced into supporting a particular union.

### Section 30(3): No Choice for Second or Subsequent Votes

Section 30(3) provides an exception to the "choice" on the ballots for second or subsequent representation votes. It states:
"Notwithstanding subsection (2), where the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote."
This passage explains that if the first vote results in no single union receiving a majority, the Board is not required to include the "choice" option on the ballots for the next vote. This is because the first vote already established that no single union had overwhelming support.

## Section 30: Conduct of Vote - Responsibilities of the Board

### Determining Eligible Voters and Arrangements

Section 30(1)(a) outlines the Board's initial responsibility when ordering a representation vote: "determine the employees that are eligible to vote." This is a foundational step, ensuring that only those within the unit who meet the eligibility criteria can participate in the vote.

Section 30(1)(b) further details the Board's role in making necessary arrangements for the proper conduct of the vote. It states that the Board
"...make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes." This demonstrates the Board's comprehensive oversight, extending from the physical creation of the ballots to the secure handling of the votes cast.

### Choices to be Included on the Ballots

Section 30(2) specifies the choices that must be included on the ballots when the Board orders a representation vote on an application for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where no other trade union is currently the bargaining agent. It states:
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots." This "choice" is a crucial element, allowing employees to express their preference for not being represented by any of the unions listed.

Section 30(3) provides an exception to the inclusion of the "choice" on the ballots. It clarifies that if the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote, and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote. This exception acknowledges the possibility of a highly fragmented first vote and avoids unnecessary complexity in subsequent votes.

## Section 17: Determination of Wishes of the Majority of the Employees

Section 17 addresses the Board's responsibility when it is required to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit. It states:
"Where the Board is required, in connection with any application made under this Part, to determine the wishes of the majority of the employees in a unit, it shall determine those wishes as of the date of the filing of the application or as of such other date as the Board considers appropriate." This indicates that the Board's determination is made at a specific point in time, either the date the application is filed or another date deemed suitable by the Board. This ensures that the vote reflects the employees' preferences as they exist at that moment.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions does the Board consider a representation vote valid and how does it determine the outcome?
individual_results.answer:
## Validity of a Representation Vote

### Section 31: Determination of the Result of a Representation Vote
"Subject to subsection (2), the Board shall determine the result of a representation vote on the basis of the ballots cast by the majority of employees voting."

This section establishes the primary criterion for determining the result of a representation vote: the ballots cast by the majority of employees who participated. However, it immediately introduces an exception outlined in subsection (2).

### Section 31(2): Void Vote Due to Low Voter Turnout
"Where, on considering the result of a representation vote, the Board determines that less than thirty-five per cent of the employees who are eligible to vote have voted, the Board shall determine that the representation vote is void."

This subsection details the condition under which a representation vote is considered void. It specifies that the vote is void if the voter turnout is below 35% of the eligible employees. This threshold is crucial because it ensures that the outcome of the vote genuinely reflects the will of a significant portion of the workforce in the unit.

### Section 30: Conduct of Vote
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes."

This section outlines the Board's responsibilities in ensuring the proper conduct of a representation vote. It mandates the Board to first determine the employees who are eligible to vote. Furthermore, it requires the Board to make all necessary arrangements, including ballot preparation, casting and counting procedures, and ballot box security. These measures are essential for maintaining the integrity and fairness of the vote.

### Section 29: Mandatory Vote
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit."

This subsection specifies a mandatory vote scenario. If a trade union applies for certification and the Board determines that between 35% and 50% of the employees in the unit are members of that union, the Board *must* order a representation vote. This ensures that the employees have a direct say in whether they want that union to represent them.

### Section 30(2): Choice on Ballots
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken on an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, the Board shall include on the ballots a choice whereby an employee may indicate that they do not wish to be represented by any trade union named on the ballots."

This subsection clarifies the content of the ballots in a mandatory vote scenario. It mandates that the ballots include a "choice" option, allowing employees to explicitly state that they do not want to be represented by any of the unions listed. This ensures that employees have a full range of options and are not forced to vote for a union they do not support.

### Section 31(3): Majority Support vs. No Majority Support
"A vote by the majority of the employees voting in a representation vote is evidence that a majority of employees in the unit in respect of which the vote was ordered are of the opinion expressed in the vote of the majority of employees voting."

This passage reinforces the principle that the outcome of a representation vote is based on the majority of votes cast. It states that such a vote is "evidence" of the majority opinion within the unit. However, it also acknowledges that if no single union receives a majority of the votes, a second or subsequent vote may be required. This ensures that the outcome ultimately reflects the will of the majority.

individual_results.question: What are the implications for a council of trade unions and its member trade unions when the council is certified as the bargaining agent for a unit?
individual_results.answer:
## Implications of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions

### Section 32: Application and Certification of a Council of Trade Unions
"Where two or more trade unions have formed a council of trade unions, the council so formed may apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in the same manner as a trade union."

This section establishes the foundational principle for a council of trade unions seeking certification. It explicitly states that such a council has the same avenue for application to the Board as an individual trade union. This means the council doesn't need to navigate a separate or more complex process. It can follow the standard certification procedures outlined in the Canada Labour Code.
"The Board may certify a council of trade unions as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit where the Board is satisfied that the requirements for certification prescribed by or pursuant to this Part have been met."

This passage details the Board's discretion in certifying a council. It emphasizes that the certification hinges on the Board's satisfaction that all the necessary criteria for certification have been fulfilled. This suggests a thorough review process where the Board will assess the council's membership, its ability to represent the employees, and its adherence to the Code's requirements.

### Section 32: Binding Nature of Collective Agreements and Application of the Part
"Where a council of trade unions is certified by the Board as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."

This section outlines the crucial implications of certification for the council itself and its member trade unions.
"...the council of trade unions and each trade union forming the council of trade unions is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the council of trade unions and the employer concerned..."
This quote is central to understanding the council's legal standing. It declares that the council, along with each of its constituent trade unions, is legally obligated to abide by any collective agreement it has negotiated with the employer. This provides the council with the power to bargain and represent the employees effectively.
"...this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the council of trade unions were a trade union."
This passage further solidifies the council's status. It states that the entire Canada Labour Code applies to the council as if it were a single, unified trade union. This means the council inherits all the rights and responsibilities of a certified trade union, including the exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification - Notice to Bargain
"...is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section details the council's power to initiate collective bargaining. It states that upon certification, the council has the authority to demand that the employer begin negotiations for a new or revised agreement. This ensures that the council has the opportunity to address the employees' needs and concerns in a timely manner.

### Section 35: Board's Declaration of Single Employer
"Where, on application by an affected trade union or employer, associated or related federal works, undertakings or businesses are, in the opinion of the Board, operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Board may, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

While not directly about the certification of a council, this section is relevant because it can impact the certification process for a council. If the Board declares that multiple employers have common control or direction over associated federal works, undertakings, or businesses, it can treat them as a single employer for all purposes of the Code. This could streamline the certification process for a council representing employees across these entities.

individual_results.question: What happens when an employers' organization is designated as the employer for a unit of employees of two or more employers in the context of collective bargaining under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Designation of Employers’ Organization as Employer

### Section 33: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Designation of employers’ organization

Section 33 outlines the process by which an employers’ organization can be designated as the employer for a unit of employees of two or more employers. It states,
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

This indicates that the Board's decision to designate an employers’ organization as the employer hinges on the fact that each of the constituent employers has formally authorized the organization to act on their behalf in collective bargaining. This authorization is deemed "appropriate authority" and is crucial for the Board to proceed with the designation.

### Section 33: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Effect of Certification

Section 33 further elaborates on the consequences of such a designation. It specifies,
"Where the Board designates an employers’ organization as an employer pursuant to subsection (1), (a) the employers’ organization and each employer forming the employers’ organization is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the employers’ organization were an employer."

This is a significant point. When an employers’ organization is designated as the employer, it becomes bound by any collective agreement negotiated between itself and the trade union representing the employees. Furthermore, the entire Canada Labour Code applies to this unit as if the employers’ organization were a single, independent employer. This streamlines the collective bargaining process and provides a clear framework for the relationship between the employers’ organization and the union.

### Section 35: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Board may declare single employer

Section 35 provides a broader context for the designation of employers’ organizations. It states,
"Where, on application by an affected trade union or employer, associated or related federal works, undertakings or businesses are, in the opinion of the Board, operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Board may, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This section highlights that the Board can also declare a group of employers with common control or direction as a single employer, even if they have not formally established an employers’ organization. This declaration has the same effect as the designation outlined in Section 33, namely that the employers and their associated businesses are bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers’ organization and the trade union concerned, and the entire Canada Labour Code applies to this unit as if the employers’ organization were an employer.

individual_results.question: What is the process for determining a bargaining unit for employees in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries, and what is the role of the employer representative in collective bargaining?
individual_results.answer:
## Determining a Bargaining Unit for Employees in the Long-shoring Industry or Other Designated Industries

### Section 34: Certification in Long-shoring and Other Industries

Section 34 outlines the process for determining a bargaining unit for employees in the long-shoring industry or other designated industries. It states,
"Where employees are employed in (a) the long-shoring industry, or (b) such other industry in such geographic area as may be designated by regulation of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Board, the Board may determine that the employees of two or more employers actively engaged in the industry in the geographic area constitute a unit appropriate for collective bargaining and may, subject to this Part, certify a trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit."

This indicates that the Board has the authority to determine a bargaining unit for employees in these industries if they are actively engaged in the industry within a designated geographic area. The Board's determination is based on whether the employees constitute a unit appropriate for collective bargaining.

### Section 18.1: Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

Section 18.1 further elaborates on the Board's power to review bargaining unit structures. It mentions,
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining."

This power to review units is crucial for adapting units to changing industry dynamics. The Board can initiate a review based on an application from either party.

### Section 27: Determination of Appropriate Unit

Section 27 details the Board's process for determining an appropriate bargaining unit when a trade union applies for certification. It states,
"Where a trade union applies under section 24 for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers appropriate for collective bargaining, the Board shall determine the unit that, in the opinion of the Board, is appropriate for collective bargaining."

This highlights that the Board's determination is not solely based on the union's proposal but on its own assessment of what constitutes an appropriate unit for collective bargaining. The Board can modify the union's proposed unit by including or excluding employees.

### Section 33: Designation of Employers’ Organization

Section 33 addresses the situation where employees are employed by two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization. It states,
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

In such cases, the Board can designate the employers’ organization as the single employer for the bargaining unit, streamlining the collective bargaining process. This designation is contingent on the employers’ organization receiving proper authority from its members.

## The Role of the Employer Representative in Collective Bargaining

### Section 33: Employer Representative

Section 33 extensively details the role of the employer representative when an employers’ organization is designated as the employer. It states,
"An employer representative shall be deemed to be an employer for the purposes of this Part and, by virtue of having been appointed under this section, has the power to, and shall, discharge all the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part on behalf of all the employers of the employees in the bargaining unit, including the power to enter into a collective agreement on behalf of those employers."

This passage is fundamental to understanding the employer representative's power. It is legally considered an employer for all collective bargaining purposes, meaning it can negotiate and sign a collective agreement on behalf of all the employers within the bargaining unit.

### Section 33: Costs

Section 33 also covers the employer representative's financial responsibilities. It states,
"The employer representative may require each employer of employees in the bargaining unit to remit its share of the costs that the employer representative has incurred or estimates will be incurred in fulfilling its duties and responsibilities under this Part and under the terms of the collective agreement."

This allows the employer representative to recover the expenses associated with its role, including negotiation costs and administrative overhead.

### Section 33: Duty of Employer Representative

Section 33 further emphasizes the employer representative's obligation to act fairly and in good faith. It states,
"In the discharge of the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part, an employer representative, or a person acting for such a representative, shall not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith in the representation of any of the employers on whose behalf the representative acts."

This ensures that the employer representative represents all the employers within the bargaining unit equally and without bias.

### Section 34: Board to Determine Questions

Section 34 clarifies the Board's role in resolving any disputes that may arise under this section. It states,
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under this section, including any question relating to the choice or appointment of the employer representative."

This provides a mechanism for the Board to intervene and make decisions when the employers’ organization and its members cannot agree on an employer representative.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board declare multiple employers and their federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 35: Board May Declare Single Employer

### Circumstances for Declaration

Section 35(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific circumstances under which the Board can declare multiple employers and their associated federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes. It states:
"Where, on application by an affected trade union or employer, associated or related federal works, undertakings or businesses are, in the opinion of the Board, operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Board may, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This indicates that the Board's declaration is contingent upon two key factors: an application from either a trade union or an employer, and the Board's determination that the federal works, undertakings, or businesses are operated by two or more employers with "common control or direction." The Board is obligated to provide the affected employers and trade unions with an opportunity to make representations before making such a declaration.

### Effect of Declaration

Section 35(2) further clarifies the effect of the Board's declaration. It specifies:
"The Board may, in making a declaration under subsection (1), determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining."

This means that when the Board declares multiple employers and their federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity, it also has the authority to determine whether the employees within that single entity can be organized into one or more bargaining units. This is a crucial step in the certification process, as it establishes the scope of the collective bargaining agreement.

## Section 255: Minister's Order Combining Federal Works, Undertakings and Businesses

### Circumstances for Declaration

Section 255(1) of the Canada Labour Code details the circumstances under which the Minister can declare multiple federal works, undertakings, or businesses as a single entity for collective bargaining purposes. It states:
"Where associated or related federal works, undertakings and businesses are operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Minister may, after affording to the employers a reasonable opportunity to make representations, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

This mirrors the Board's power under Section 35(1), requiring the Minister to provide the employers with a reasonable opportunity to make representations before making the declaration. The declaration is based on the common control or direction of the federal works, undertakings, or businesses by two or more employers.

### Effect of Declaration

Section 255(2) outlines the legal consequences of the Minister's declaration. It states:
"Where an order is made under subsection (1), the employers to which it applies are jointly and severally liable to the employees employed in the federal works, undertakings and businesses to which the order applies for overtime pay, vacation pay, holiday pay and other wages or amounts to which the employees are entitled under this Part."

This means that the employers declared as a single entity are collectively responsible for providing all legally mandated wages and benefits to the employees working in the combined federal works, undertakings, and businesses. This simplifies the administration of these obligations and ensures that employees receive their full entitlements.

individual_results.question: What happens to the collective bargaining authority and existing collective agreements when a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 36: Effect of Certification

### Exclusive Authority to Bargain Collectively
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

Section 36(1)(a) directly addresses the outcome of a trade union's certification. It establishes that the certified union gains
"...exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..." This means that all future collective bargaining efforts must be conducted with this certified union. Any previous bargaining authority held by another union is immediately terminated.

### Revocation of Prior Certifications
"...the certification of any trade union that was previously certified as the bargaining agent for any employees in the bargaining unit is deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees..."

This passage from Section 36(1)(b) clarifies the impact on any existing certifications. It states that any prior certification is
"...deemed to be revoked to the extent that the certification relates to those employees..." This means that the previous union's certification is effectively cancelled for the employees covered by the new certification.

### Substitution in Existing Collective Agreements
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto..."

Section 36(1)(c) details the substitution of the certified union into any existing collective agreements. It specifies that the certified union becomes the new party to the agreement, replacing the previous bargaining agent. This ensures that the certified union has the full rights and responsibilities outlined in the agreement.

### Deemed Bargaining Agent for Other Purposes
"...the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)."

Finally, Section 36(1)(d) confirms the certified union's status as the bargaining agent for other relevant purposes, specifically "paragraph 50(b)." This provides a broader recognition of the certified union's authority beyond just the existing collective agreements.

In summary, when a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, it gains exclusive bargaining authority, all prior certifications are revoked for those employees, it is substituted into any existing collective agreements, and it is deemed the bargaining agent for other purposes. This certification process provides a clear and definitive transition of bargaining power to the newly certified union.
