individual_results.question: What are the protections in place for employees in an affected bargaining unit from the date of certification until a first collective agreement is entered into, specifically regarding dismissal or discipline?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Employees from Certification to First Collective Agreement

### Section 36.1: Just Cause Requirement During Certification Period

Section 36.1 of the Canada Labour Code establishes crucial protections for employees in an affected bargaining unit from the date of certification until a first collective agreement is reached. It states,
"During the period that begins on the date of certification and ends on the date on which a first collective agreement is entered into, the employer must not dismiss or discipline an employee in the affected bargaining unit without just cause." This provision is a cornerstone of employee security during the transition period.

The text elaborates on this by including a mechanism for arbitration in the event of a disagreement between the employer and the bargaining agent regarding dismissal or discipline. It specifies,
"Where a disagreement relating to the dismissal or discipline of an employee during the period referred to in subsection (1) arises between the employer and the bargaining agent, (a) the bargaining agent may submit the disagreement to an arbitrator for final settlement as if it were a difference; and (b) sections 57 to 66 apply, with the modifications that the circumstances require, to the disagreement." This ensures a fair and impartial process for resolving such disputes, preventing arbitrary actions by the employer.

### Section 36: Effect of Certification on Existing Agreements and Bargaining

Section 36 further reinforces these protections by detailing the impact of certification on existing collective agreements and future bargaining. It clarifies,
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..." This means that the previous bargaining agent loses its authority, and the certified union becomes the sole representative.

Furthermore, it addresses the employer's bargaining obligations during the certification period. It states,
"...the trade union so certified is substituted as a party to any collective agreement that affects any employees in the bargaining unit, to the extent that the collective agreement relates to those employees, in the place of the bargaining agent named in the collective agreement or any successor thereto; and (d) the trade union so certified is deemed to be the bargaining agent for the purposes of paragraph 50(b)." This ensures continuity in the bargaining process, with the certified union stepping into the shoes of the previous one.

### Section 24: Application for Certification and Employer Conduct

Section 24 outlines the process for a trade union to seek certification and places restrictions on employer conduct during this period. It specifies,
"...an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made (a) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, at any time; (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time; (c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation; and (d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation." This sets a timeline for certification applications.

Crucially, it includes a provision prohibiting employers from altering terms and conditions of employment after notification of a certification application. It states,
"Where an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit is made in accordance with this section, no employer of employees in the unit shall, after notification that the application has been made, alter the rates of pay, any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of such employees until (a) the application has been withdrawn by the trade union or dismissed by the Board, or (b) thirty days have elapsed after the day on which the Board certifies the trade union as the bargaining agent for the unit, except pursuant to a collective agreement or with the consent of the Board." This provides employees with a period of stability while the certification process is underway.

individual_results.question: What standard of behavior is expected of a trade union or its representative when representing employees in a bargaining unit with respect to their rights under the collective agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Standard of Behavior for Trade Unions Representing Employees

### Section 37: Duty of Fair Representation

Section 37 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the standard of behavior expected of a trade union or its representative when representing employees in a bargaining unit. It states:
"A trade union or representative of a trade union that is the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit shall not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith in the representation of any of the employees in the unit with respect to their rights under the collective agreement that is applicable to them."

This quotation is central to understanding the expected standard. It prohibits the union from acting "arbitrarily, discriminatorily or in bad faith." This means the union must treat all employees within the bargaining unit fairly and equitably, without bias or malicious intent. Their representation must be based on a reasonable and consistent application of the collective agreement. The standard extends to all aspects of representation, encompassing negotiations, grievance handling, and other activities related to the agreement.

### Section 94: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

While Section 94 primarily focuses on prohibitions against employers interfering with trade unions, it also indirectly supports the duty of fair representation. For instance, it prohibits employers from
"...participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..." This ensures that the union can operate freely and effectively in its role as bargaining agent, without undue pressure or manipulation from the employer.

Furthermore, Section 94(1)(b) prohibits employers from
"...contribute financial or other support to a trade union." This helps to maintain the union's independence and prevents the employer from unduly influencing its decisions.

### Section 95: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions (Further Detail)

Section 95 provides a more extensive list of prohibitions against trade unions, many of which are relevant to the duty of fair representation. For example, it prohibits unions from
"...attempt, at an employee’s place of employment during the working hours of the employee, to persuade the employee to become, to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union..." This protects employees from undue pressure from the union regarding their membership.

It also prohibits unions from
"...expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or deny membership in the trade union to an employee by applying to the employee in a discriminatory manner the membership rules of the trade union..." This ensures that the union's membership rules are applied fairly and consistently to all employees within the unit.

Finally, Section 95 prohibits unions from
"...take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by applying to that employee in a discriminatory manner the standards of discipline of the trade union..." This reinforces the need for fair and consistent application of the union's disciplinary procedures.

In summary, the standard of behavior expected of a trade union or its representative when representing employees in a bargaining unit with respect to their rights under the collective agreement is one of fairness, impartiality, and good faith. They must act without bias, consistently apply the terms of the collective agreement, and protect employees from undue pressure or discrimination. Section 37 provides the most direct articulation of this standard, while Sections 94 and 95 offer further context and prohibitions that support its implementation.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can an employee apply to revoke the certification of a trade union as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and are there any restrictions on when such an application can be made?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for an Employee to Apply for Revocation of Certification

### Section 38(1) - General Application for Revocation
"If a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order revoking the certification of that trade union."

This section establishes the primary condition for an employee to initiate a revocation process. An employee must demonstrate that they represent a majority of the employees within the bargaining unit. This claim is subject to a restriction outlined in subsection (5), which prohibits such an application during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part.

### Section 40 - Application Where Fraud
"Section 40 (1) Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This section provides an alternative condition for an employee to apply for revocation. If an employee alleges that the trade union's certification was obtained through fraud, they can apply to the Board at any time. This highlights that fraud is a specific ground for revocation, distinct from a simple claim of majority representation.

### Section 41 - Application for Revocation of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions
"Section 41 (1) Where a council of trade unions has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, in addition to any circumstances in which an application for revocation of the certification of the council of trade unions may be made pursuant to section 38 or subsection 40(1), any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This section specifically addresses the revocation of certification for a council of trade unions. It states that an employee, employer, or trade union member can apply for revocation on the ground that the council no longer meets the certification requirements. This expands the scope of who can apply for revocation beyond individual employees.

### Section 39(1) - Board's Determination
"Section 39 (1) If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This section details what happens after the Board receives an application for revocation. If the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees no longer want the union to represent them, it will issue an order either revoking the certification or declaring the union is no longer entitled to represent them, depending on the subsection under which the application was made.

## Restrictions on When Such an Application Can Be Made

### Section 38(5) - Prohibition During Strike or Lockout
"An application under subsection (1) or (3) must not, except with the consent of the Board, be made in respect of the bargaining agent for employees in a bargaining unit during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part."

This section imposes a restriction on when an employee can apply for revocation. Such an application cannot be made during a strike or lockout of those employees that is not prohibited by this Part, unless the Board grants consent. This is a measure to prevent disruption during labor disputes.

### Section 40(2) - One-Year Bargaining Period After Revocation
"...and (b) the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

This section outlines a restriction on collective bargaining for one year after the revocation of certification. The employer cannot bargain with the former union unless a new union is certified during that period. This provides a cooling-off period and prevents immediate resumption of negotiations with a non-certified union.

### Section 41(2) - Time for Application
"Where an application for revocation of certification is made under subsection (1), the Board may, by order, revoke the certification of the council of trade unions if, in the opinion of the Board, the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This section specifies the timeframe for an application for revocation of certification of a council of trade unions. The Board can issue an order revoking the certification if it determines that the council no longer meets the certification requirements.

### Section 39(2) - Limitation Without Collective Agreement
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This section places a limitation on the Board's ability to revoke certification of a union that has not yet entered into a collective agreement. The Board must be satisfied that the union has made a reasonable effort to negotiate a contract before it can issue a revocation order.

## Revocation of Certification and Related Matters: Conditions for Board Action

### Section 39: Order Revoking Certification or Declaring Bargaining Agent Not Entitled to Represent Bargaining Unit

Section 39 outlines the primary conditions under which the Board can revoke a trade union's certification or declare it not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit.
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This passage directly addresses the question by stating that the Board's action hinges on the Board's satisfaction that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit
"...no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them..." This determination is made
"...after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances..." This indicates a thorough process involving employee input and potentially further investigation by the Board. The Board has two options: revoke the certification entirely (for an application under subsection 38(1)) or declare the bargaining agent not entitled to represent the employees (for an application under subsection 38(3)).

### Section 40: Application Where Fraud

Section 40 details a specific condition for revocation: fraud in obtaining the certification.
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This section establishes that any party with evidence of fraud in the certification process can apply to the Board for revocation. The Board's response is automatic:
"On receipt of an application under subsection (1) in respect of a trade union certification as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the Board is satisfied that the evidence in support of the application (a) was not and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been presented to it in the certification proceeding; and (b) is such that the Board would have refused to certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the evidence had been presented to it in the certification proceeding." This highlights the Board's obligation to revoke the certification if the fraud is proven and the Board would have denied certification had the evidence been presented earlier.

### Section 42: Revocation of Certification and Related Matters: Effect of Revocation or Declaration

Section 42 further elaborates on the consequences of revocation or declaration.
"Where the Board makes an order under section 39, subsection 40(2) or section 41 revoking the certification of a trade union or council of trade unions, or declaring that a trade union is not entitled to represent the employees in a bargaining unit, (a) any collective agreement between the trade union or council of trade unions and the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit that applies to the bargaining unit ceases to have effect from the time the order is made or from such later time as the Board considers appropriate; and (b) the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

This section confirms that revocation or declaration of ineligibility has immediate legal ramifications. It states that any existing collective agreement between the union and the employer ceases to be in effect. Additionally, the employer is prohibited from bargaining with the union for a year unless the union is subsequently certified. This provides a period of stability and prevents immediate disruption to the bargaining process.

## Revocation of Certification: General Circumstances

### Section 39: Order Revoking Certification or Declaring Bargaining Agent Not Entitled to Represent Bargaining Unit

Section 39 outlines the circumstances under which the Board can issue an order revoking a trade union's certification or declaring that a bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit.
"If, on receipt of an application for an order made under subsection 38(1) or (3) in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, and after any inquiry by way of a representation vote or otherwise that the Board considers appropriate in the circumstances, the Board is satisfied that a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them, the Board shall, subject to subsection (2), by order, (a) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(1), revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit; or (b) in the case of an application made under subsection 38(3), declare that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This passage directly addresses the question by stating that the Board can revoke certification or declare a bargaining agent not entitled to represent the employees if it is satisfied that a majority of the employees no longer wish to have that bargaining agent represent them. This determination is made after an inquiry, which could involve a representation vote or other methods deemed appropriate by the Board.

### Section 40: Application Where Fraud

Section 40 details a specific circumstance where certification can be revoked: if it was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified.
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This section allows any party who alleges that the certification was obtained through fraud to apply to the Board for revocation.
"On receipt of an application under subsection (1) in respect of a trade union certification as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, the Board shall, by order, revoke the certification of the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the Board is satisfied that the evidence in support of the application (a) was not and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been presented to it in the certification proceeding; and (b) is such that the Board would have refused to certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit if the evidence had been presented to it in the certification proceeding."

The Board will only revoke certification upon satisfaction that the evidence supporting the fraud allegation was not reasonably presented during the certification proceeding and would have resulted in the Board refusing to certify the union.

### Section 42: Effect of Revocation or Declaration

Section 42 outlines the consequences of a certification revocation or declaration that a bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees.
"(a) any collective agreement between the trade union or council of trade unions and the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit that applies to the bargaining unit ceases to have effect from the time the order is made or from such later time as the Board considers appropriate; and (b) the employer shall not bargain collectively, or enter into a collective agreement with the trade union or council of trade unions, for a period of one year from the date of the order, unless the trade union or council of trade unions is certified by the Board under this Part during that period as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit comprised of employees of the employer."

This section clarifies that upon revocation, any existing collective agreement ceases to be in effect. Furthermore, the employer is prohibited from engaging in collective bargaining with the previously certified union for a period of one year, unless the union is subsequently re-certified.

### Section 38: Application for Revocation of Certification

Section 38 details the circumstances under which an employee can apply to the Board for a revocation of certification.
"(1) If a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order revoking the certification of that trade union."

This passage states that any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit can apply for revocation of certification.
"(2) An application for an order pursuant to subsection (1) may be made in respect of a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) where a collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made pursuant to section 24 unless the Board consents to the making of the application for the order at some other time; and (b) where no collective agreement applicable to the bargaining unit is in force, at any time after a period of one year from the date of certification of the trade union."

This subsection specifies the timeframes during which an employee can make such an application, depending on whether a collective agreement is in force.
"(3) If a collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force but the bargaining agent that is a party to the collective agreement has not been certified by the Board, any employee who claims to represent a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Board for an order declaring that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees in the bargaining unit."

This passage further clarifies that an employee can apply for a declaration that the bargaining agent is not entitled to represent the employees even if a collective agreement is in force but the union has not been officially certified.

## Revocation of Certification of a Council of Trade Unions: Circumstances for Application

### Section 41: General Grounds for Revocation

Section 41 outlines the primary circumstances under which an application can be made to revoke the certification of a council of trade unions as a bargaining agent. It states:
"Where a council of trade unions has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, in addition to any circumstances in which an application for revocation of the certification of the council of trade unions may be made pursuant to section 38 or subsection 40(1), any employee in the bargaining unit, the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit or a trade union that forms part of the council of trade unions may apply to the Board for revocation of the certification on the ground that the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This passage is crucial because it establishes that there are multiple avenues for revocation, including those detailed in sections 38 and 40(1), and a specific ground outlined in section 41. The new ground is that the council of trade unions
"...no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions." This broad criterion allows for applications based on a failure to maintain the necessary organizational structure, membership, or other qualifications stipulated in the Canada Labour Code for a council of trade unions to be recognized as a bargaining agent.

### Section 38: Application for Revocation Based on Failure to Make Reasonable Effort to Enter into a Collective Agreement

Section 38(2) specifies a time limitation for applications made under subsection (1), which is
"...only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made pursuant to section 24..." However, it also includes a condition:
"If no collective agreement applicable to a bargaining unit is in force, an order shall not be made under paragraph (1)(a) in relation to the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit unless the Board is satisfied that the bargaining agent has failed to make a reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement in relation to the bargaining unit."

This indicates that an application for revocation can be made if the council of trade unions has not made a "reasonable effort" to negotiate a collective agreement with the employer. The Board must be satisfied with this lack of effort before an order revoking the certification can be issued. This provision aims to hold councils of trade unions accountable for their bargaining obligations.

### Section 40: Application Where Fraud

Section 40(1) provides a specific ground for revocation:
"Where a trade union has been certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) any employee in the bargaining unit, (b) the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit, or (c) any trade union that appeared before the Board in the certification proceeding, that alleges that the certification was obtained by the fraud of the trade union so certified, may apply to the Board, at any time, for revocation of the certification."

This passage directly addresses revocation based on fraudulent activity during the certification process. It allows any party involved in the certification proceeding to apply for revocation if they have evidence that the certification was obtained through deceit. This provision is designed to safeguard the integrity of the certification process and prevent illegitimate bargaining agents from gaining control.

### Section 39: Application Based on Loss of Employee Support

Section 39(1) outlines a scenario where revocation can occur if a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit
"...no longer wish to have the bargaining agent represent them..." This is a direct measure of the council of trade unions' continued legitimacy. The Board will issue an order revoking the certification if it is satisfied with this loss of employee support.

### Section 41(2): Board's Discretion

Section 41(2) grants the Board discretion in revoking certification:
"Where an application for revocation of certification is made under subsection (1), the Board may, by order, revoke the certification of the council of trade unions if, in the opinion of the Board, the council of trade unions no longer meets the requirements for certification of a council of trade unions."

This passage highlights that the Board has the final say in whether or not to revoke the certification, even if other grounds for revocation have been presented. The Board's opinion is the determining factor.

individual_results.question: What happens to the rights, privileges, and duties of a trade union when it is succeeded by another trade union due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction?
individual_results.answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Mergers, etc., of Trade Unions (CLC-43)

### Acquisition of Rights, Privileges, and Duties

Section 43(1) of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the situation where a trade union succeeds another trade union due to a merger, amalgamation, or transfer of jurisdiction. It states:
"Where, by reason of a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, a trade union succeeds another trade union that, at the time of the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, is a bargaining agent, the successor shall be deemed to have acquired the rights, privileges and duties of its predecessor, whether under a collective agreement or otherwise."

This passage is fundamental to understanding successor rights. It establishes a presumption that the successor trade union automatically inherits all the legal standing and obligations of the predecessor union. This includes any existing collective agreements, arbitral awards, or other bargaining rights. The phrase "whether under a collective agreement or otherwise" is crucial, as it ensures that the successor union takes on all aspects of the predecessor's role, not just those explicitly mentioned in a written agreement.

### Board's Role in Determining Rights and Duties

Section 43(2) outlines the Board's role in clarifying any questions that may arise during such a change in union representation. It says:
"Where, on a merger or amalgamation of trade unions or a transfer of jurisdiction among trade unions, any question arises concerning the rights, privileges and duties of a trade union under this Part or under a collective agreement in respect of a bargaining unit or an employee therein, the Board, on application to it by a trade union affected by the merger, amalgamation or transfer of jurisdiction, shall determine what rights, privileges and duties have been acquired or are retained."

This indicates that the Board is available to intervene and make a determination if there is any ambiguity about which union holds which rights and responsibilities. The Board will consider the application from any union that feels its position has been affected by the change. This ensures a fair and impartial resolution to any disputes that may arise.

### Board's Inquiry and Representation Votes

Section 43(3) details the Board's methods for determining acquired rights and duties. It states:
"Before determining, pursuant to subsection (2), what rights, privileges and duties of a trade union have been acquired or are retained, the Board may make such inquiry or direct that such representation votes be taken as it considers necessary."

The Board has broad discretion in how it gathers information. It can conduct its own inquiries or order representation votes to gauge the preferences of the employees in the bargaining unit. This allows the Board to make a decision that is truly reflective of the employees' wishes and the interests of the successor union.

individual_results.question: What happens to the labour relations of employees when a business is sold, particularly in terms of their bargaining agent and collective agreements?
individual_results.answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Sale of Business

### Section 44(1) - Definition of Business and Sale

Section 44(1) defines "business" broadly, encompassing
"...any federal work, undertaking or business and any part thereof..." This broad definition is crucial for understanding the implications of a business sale. It establishes that the successor business is automatically subject to the Canada Labour Code.
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This passage directly addresses the question of bargaining agent and collective agreements. It states that the existing bargaining agent for the employees remains their bargaining agent even after the business is sold. Furthermore, a trade union that had previously applied for certification for those employees has the opportunity to be certified by the Board, subject to the provisions of this Part. Critically, the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that was in effect on the date of the sale. This ensures that the employees' existing terms and conditions of employment are preserved.

### Section 47(1)(a) - Continuation of Collective Agreements

Section 47(1)(a) further elaborates on the continuity of collective agreements following a business sale. It specifies that
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This means that the existing collective agreement or arbitral award remains in force until its scheduled expiration date. This provides stability for the employees and their bargaining agent during the transition period.

### Section 47.1 - Successor Rights and Obligations: Where Notice to Bargain Collectively Given Prior to Deletion

Section 47.1 provides additional context for successor rights and obligations, particularly when notice to bargain collectively has been given prior to the deletion or severance of a business portion. It states that
"(a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise; (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and..."

This section reinforces the continuity of collective agreements and arbitral awards, emphasizing that they remain in force until certain requirements are met or the employer and bargaining agent agree otherwise. It also clarifies that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of these agreements.

In summary, when a business is sold, the labour relations of the employees are largely preserved. Their bargaining agent remains the same, and any existing collective agreement or arbitral award continues in force until its expiration date. The successor business is bound by these agreements, ensuring that the employees' terms and conditions of employment are not immediately disrupted. The Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act continues to govern the interpretation and application of these agreements.

## The Board's Role in Sales or Changes of Activity Affecting Collective Bargaining Units

### Section 44: Definition of Business and Successor Rights

Section 44 of the Canada Labour Code establishes the definition of "business" for the purposes of successor rights and obligations. It clarifies that "business" encompasses
"...any federal work, undertaking or business and any part thereof..." This broad definition is crucial because it ensures that successor employers are bound by existing collective agreements and obligations of the predecessor employer.

Furthermore, Section 44 outlines the successor rights of trade unions. It states,
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent..." This passage is central to understanding the Board's role. The Board, through the definition of business, ensures that the existing bargaining relationship is preserved. The successor employer becomes bound by the existing collective agreement.

### Section 45: Board's Power to Determine Bargaining Units

Section 45 explicitly grants the Board the power to determine whether the employees affected by a sale or change of activity constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining. It states,
"In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board is actively involved in reviewing and potentially restructuring bargaining units following such events. The Board's determination is based on an application from either the employer or a trade union.

### Section 46: Board's Duty to Determine Questions Arising Under Section 44

Section 46 further elaborates on the Board's role by stating,
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business." This passage highlights the Board's comprehensive responsibility in resolving any ambiguities or disputes that may arise during a sale or change of activity. It acts as the ultimate arbiter on the factual matters related to the transaction.

### Section 47: Application of Successor Rights and Obligations

Section 47 details the application of successor rights and obligations. It addresses the continuation of collective agreements and arbitral awards. It states,
"(a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires; and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award." This passage underscores the Board's role in ensuring the continuity of existing agreements. The Board, through its orders, ensures that these agreements remain in force until their natural expiry date and that the relevant Act governs their interpretation and application.

### Section 18.1: Board's Review of Bargaining Unit Structure

Section 18.1 outlines the Board's power to review the structure of bargaining units. It states,
"On application by the employer or a bargaining agent, the Board may review the structure of the bargaining units if it is satisfied that the bargaining units are no longer appropriate for collective bargaining." This indicates that the Board proactively monitors bargaining unit structures and can initiate a review if it deems them inadequate.

Furthermore, Section 18.1 details the Board's authority to make orders to implement agreements reached by the parties during a review. It states,
"(b) may make any orders it considers appropriate to implement any agreement." This passage is crucial because it shows the Board's active role in facilitating and enforcing agreements that emerge from a bargaining unit review. It can make orders to amend certification orders, descriptions of bargaining units, or other relevant provisions of collective agreements.

### Section 49: Board's Role in Determining Bargaining Units

Section 49 specifies the Board's role in determining bargaining units when a sale or change of activity occurs. It states,
"Where no application for an order is made pursuant to subsection (3) within the period specified in that subsection, the corporation or business, as employer of the employees, or any bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by subsection (1), is continued in force, may, during the period commencing on the one hundred and fifty-first day and ending on the two hundred and tenth day after the date the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of the corporation or business, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively." This passage indicates that if the parties fail to agree on bargaining units within a specified timeframe, the Board will step in to make a determination. It can issue an order granting leave to serve a notice to bargain collectively.

In summary, the Board plays a multifaceted role in the event of a sale or change of activity affecting employees' collective bargaining units. It defines "business" to ensure successor employers are bound by existing agreements, it actively reviews bargaining unit structures, it determines whether employees constitute appropriate bargaining units, it ensures the continuity of existing collective agreements and arbitral awards, and it makes orders to implement agreements reached during a bargaining unit review. The Board acts as a central authority for resolving factual matters, facilitating agreements, and enforcing successor rights and obligations.

## The Board's Role in Business Sales and Changes in Business Activity

### Section 46: Board's Determination of Questions Arising Under Section 44

Section 46 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the Board's responsibility concerning questions related to business sales or changes in business activity.
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This passage is central to understanding the Board's role. It states unequivocally that the Board has the authority and obligation to make decisions on these specific issues. The Board doesn't merely provide guidance; it *shall* determine them. This includes not only the fact of a sale or change in activity but also the identity of the new owner. This power is crucial for ensuring the smooth transition of labour relations and collective agreements during such transactions, as detailed further in Section 44.

### Section 15: Board's Power to Make Regulations

Section 15 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Board broad regulatory powers.
"(g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part; (n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union; (o) the circumstances in which evidence referred to in paragraph (m) may be received by the Board as evidence that any employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, including the circumstances in which the evidence so received by the Board may not be made public by the Board; (o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes; (p) the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions; (p.1) the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators; and (q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act."

While Section 15 doesn't directly address business sales or changes in business activity, it establishes the Board's overarching power to make regulations "of general application" concerning its procedures and operations. This power could be used to create specific rules and processes for handling questions that arise during business transactions, such as timelines for notifying the Board or procedures for determining the identity of the purchaser.

### Section 248: Minister's Inquiry Powers

Section 248 grants the Minister the power to cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment.
"(a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."

While this section focuses on broader employment issues, it highlights the Minister's ability to initiate inquiries that could encompass business sales or changes in business activity if they raise significant labour relations concerns. The Minister could direct an inquiry to investigate the impact of a sale on existing collective agreements or employee benefits.

### Section 44: Successor Rights and Obligations - Board to Determine Questions

Section 44 further reinforces the Board's role in business sales and changes in business activity by stating that the Board
"...shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business." This is a direct repetition of the Board's power outlined in Section 46, emphasizing its central position in these types of transactions.

### Section 15.1: Board's Power to Assist Parties

Section 15.1 describes the Board's ability to assist parties in resolving issues in dispute.
"(1) The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

While Section 15.1 focuses on general dispute resolution, it indirectly supports the Board's role in business sales by facilitating communication and problem-solving between the outgoing and incoming employers and their respective bargaining agents. This assistance can be valuable in ensuring a smooth transition of labour relations.

individual_results.question: What happens to a collective agreement or arbitral award when a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 47: Successor Rights and Obligations: Where portion as federal business

### Continuation of Collective Agreement or Arbitral Award

Section 47(1)(a) directly addresses the question, stating:
"Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business, (a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This passage clarifies that a collective agreement or arbitral award that was in force for employees in the portion of the federal public administration that is being established as or becoming a part of a corporation or business *continues in force* until its term expires. This ensures that existing labor arrangements are not disrupted by the organizational change.

### Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act

Section 47(1)(b) further elaborates on the continuation of the agreement by adding:
"...and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award."

This means that the entire legal framework governing the collective agreement or arbitral award is maintained. The Act's rules and procedures continue to apply, providing a consistent and predictable environment for both employers and employees.

### Section 47(3) - Application for Order Determining Bargaining Units

Section 47(3) outlines the process for determining appropriate bargaining units when a portion of the federal public administration is being restructured. It states:
"Where the employees in a portion of the federal public administration that is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies are bound by a collective agreement or arbitral award, the corporation or business, as employer of the employees, or any bargaining agent affected by the change in employment, may, during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date on which the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of the corporation or business, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters referred to in subsection (4)."

This indicates that the corporation or business, or its bargaining agent, can apply to the Board for an order to determine the appropriate bargaining units for the employees covered by the existing collective agreement or arbitral award. This ensures that the agreement remains relevant and applicable to the correct groups of workers.

### Section 47(4) - Determination of Board

Section 47(4) details the Board's role in determining bargaining units. It states:
"Where an application is made under subsection (3) by a corporation or business or bargaining agent, the Board, by order, shall (a) determine whether the employees of the corporation or business who are bound by any collective agreement or arbitral award constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining; (b) determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; and (c) in respect of each collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to employees of the corporation or business, (i) determine whether the collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, and (ii) if the collective agreement or arbitral award is to remain in force, determine whether it shall remain in force until the expiration of its term or expire on such earlier date as the Board may fix."

This passage highlights the Board's authority to not only determine bargaining units but also to decide whether the existing collective agreement or arbitral award will continue in force and, if so, until when. This provides flexibility to adapt the agreement to the new organizational structure.

### Section 47(8) - Arbitral Award Deemed Part of Collective Agreement

Section 47(8) provides a crucial clarification regarding arbitral awards. It states:
"An arbitral award that is continued in force by virtue of subsection (1) is deemed to be (a) part of the collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates, or (b) where there is no collective agreement for the bargaining unit, a collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates for the purposes of section 49, and this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of the renewal or revision of the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This passage is particularly important because it treats arbitral awards that are carried over into the new corporate structure as if they were part of a collective agreement. This ensures that the outcomes of past arbitrations continue to be respected and applied. It also clarifies that the entire Part of the Canada Labour Code, excluding section 80, applies to the interpretation and application of these arbitral awards, including any future renewals or revisions.

Section 47(8) is crucial as it treats arbitral awards that are carried over with the transfer to a corporation or business as if they were part of a collective agreement. It states that
"An arbitral award that is continued in force by virtue of subsection (1) is deemed to be (a) part of the collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates, or (b) where there is no collective agreement for the bargaining unit, a collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates for the purposes of section 49, and this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of the renewal or revision of the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement." individual_results.answer:
## Governor in Council Exclusion of Federal Public Administration from Sections 47 and 47.1

### Section 47.2: General Circumstances for Exclusion

Section 47.2 outlines the broad circumstances under which the Governor in Council can exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1. It states:
"The Governor in Council may, by order, exclude from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1) where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so."

This passage is crucial as it establishes the core condition for exclusion: a determination by the Governor in Council, informed by the Minister's recommendation and consultation with relevant ministers and the Treasury Board, that the exclusion is "in the public interest." The exclusion applies to any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1). This indicates a flexible power granted to the Governor in Council, subject to a rigorous process of deliberation and justification.

### Section 47: Exclusion Related to Nuclear Safety and Control Act

Section 47 provides a more specific circumstance for exclusion, linking it to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It states:
"(1) The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This passage clarifies that the Governor in Council can exclude certain employment or classes of employment from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 through a regulation. The exclusion is limited to work or undertakings regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This suggests a recognition of the unique regulatory environment surrounding nuclear safety and control and the need for flexibility in applying these sections within that context.

### Section 47.1: Exclusion Related to Successor Rights and Obligations

Section 47.1 also outlines a circumstance for exclusion, specifically related to successor rights and obligations. It states:
"Section 47.1 Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration, (a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise; (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a); (c) on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; (d) where the Board makes the determinations under paragraph (c), the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the other to commence collective bargaining under this Act for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement; and (e) this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d)."

While Section 47.1 discusses successor rights and obligations, it does not explicitly state a circumstance under which the Governor in Council can exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1. However, it does mention that
"...this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d)." This suggests that the exclusion, if it exists, would be related to the application of this Part to successor relationships.



### Conclusion

The Governor in Council can exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 under several circumstances. The most general circumstance is when the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister and after consultation with relevant ministers and the Treasury Board, is of the opinion that the exclusion is "in the public interest." This exclusion can apply to any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1). A more specific circumstance is when the exclusion is related to work or undertakings regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act, which can be achieved through a regulation. Finally, Section 47.1 suggests that the exclusion, if it exists, would be related to the application of this Part to successor relationships.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement?

## Successive Contracts for Services - Section 47.3

### Remuneration Requirements

Section 47.3(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes a clear requirement for an employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services. It states:
"An employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services, in accordance with a contract or other arrangement, must pay to the employees providing the services under that contract or arrangement remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."

This quotation is central to the question as it directly addresses the financial obligation of the succeeding employer. It mandates that the new employer must maintain, and not reduce, the wages and benefits of the employees who were previously employed by the outgoing contractor. The reference to a "collective agreement" is important, as it indicates that the successor employer is bound by any existing agreement that was in place when the change occurred. This provision aims to protect the employees' hard-earned entitlements during a transition of service provision.

### Application to Dual Jurisdiction Employers

While Section 47.3 outlines the general requirements, IPG-087 provides context on how this applies to dual jurisdiction employers. It mentions that the successor employer must pay remuneration
"...not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied." This confirms that the successor employer's obligation is not diminished by the fact that the employer is subject to both federal and provincial employment equity legislation. The interpretation ensures that the successor employer adheres to all applicable labour standards, including those related to wages and benefits.

individual_results.question: What can a certified bargaining agent or an employer do to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force?
individual_results.answer:
## Initiating Collective Bargaining When No Collective Agreement is in Force

### Section 36 (1) - Effect of Certification: Exclusive Bargaining Authority
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

Section 36(1)(a) directly addresses the question by establishing the fundamental right of a certified bargaining agent to
"...bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..." This means that once certification is granted, the union is the sole entity authorized to engage in negotiations with the employer regarding terms and conditions of employment. The employer, in this scenario, is obligated to bargain with the certified union.

### Section 24 (1) - Application for Certification: Time of Application
"A trade union seeking to be certified as the bargaining agent for a unit that the trade union considers constitutes a unit appropriate for collective bargaining may, subject to this section and any regulations made by the Board under paragraph 15(e), apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the unit."

Section 24(1) outlines the timeframe within which a trade union can apply for certification. It states that the application can be made "at any time" if no collective agreement is in force and no other union has been certified. This indicates that the union can initiate the certification process even before formal bargaining has commenced.

### Section 36 (2) - Notice to Bargain
"Where, pursuant to paragraph (1)(c), a trade union is substituted as a party to a collective agreement, the trade union may, within three months after the date on which it is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit affected by the collective agreement, require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

Section 36(2) details the union's power to formally request the employer to begin collective bargaining. It specifies that the union can
"...require the employer who is a party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining..." within three months of receiving certification. This is a direct mechanism for the union to initiate the bargaining process when no existing agreement is in place.

### Section 33 (1) - Designation of Employers’ Organization
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

Section 33(1) provides a scenario where an employers' organization can be designated as the employer for certification purposes. If the employers' organization has received proper authorization from each member employer, the Board can make this designation. This allows the union to bargain with the designated employers' organization, effectively initiating collective bargaining even without a prior collective agreement.

### Section 35 (1) - Board May Declare Single Employer
"Where, on application by an affected trade union or employer, associated or related federal works, undertakings or businesses are, in the opinion of the Board, operated by two or more employers having common control or direction, the Board may, by order, declare that for all purposes of this Part the employers and the federal works, undertakings and businesses operated by them that are specified in the order are, respectively, a single employer and a single federal work, undertaking or business."

Section 35(1) allows the Board to declare a single employer when multiple employers have common control or direction over associated businesses. This declaration enables the union to bargain with the single declared employer, effectively initiating collective bargaining even without an existing agreement. The Board must provide an opportunity for the affected employers and trade unions to make representations before making such a declaration.

individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Initiating Collective Bargaining for Renewal, Revision, or New Agreement

### Section 48: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Notice to bargain to enter into a collective agreement
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

This section outlines the primary mechanism for initiating collective bargaining. It states that either the bargaining agent or the employer can issue a notice to the other party to commence negotiations. This notice is triggered by two conditions: first, the Board must have certified a bargaining agent for the unit, and second, there must not be an existing collective agreement in effect. The notice is specifically for the purpose of "entering into a collective agreement," indicating its applicability to all types of collective bargaining – renewal, revision, or a new agreement. The use of "by notice" highlights the formal and deliberate nature of this initiation process.

### Section 49: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Notice to bargain to renew or revise a collective agreement or enter a new collective agreement
"Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section further elaborates on the notice-to-bargain requirement, specifically addressing the renewal, revision, or entry into a new collective agreement. It specifies a timeframe within which either party can issue such a notice:
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..." This timeframe provides a clear window for initiating the bargaining process before the existing agreement expires. The notice is also explicitly for the purpose of
"...renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement." reinforcing its broad applicability.

### Section 36: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Effect of certification
"(2) Where a collective agreement provides that any provision of the collective agreement may be revised during the term of the collective agreement, a party entitled to do so by the collective agreement may, by notice, require the other party to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of revising the provision."

While this section focuses on the effect of certification, it also touches upon the notice-to-bargain requirement. It states that if a collective agreement contains a provision for revision during its term, a party with the right to revise that provision can issue a notice to commence bargaining for that specific revision. This demonstrates that the notice-to-bargain mechanism is not limited to the overall renewal or revision of the entire agreement; it can be used for targeted revisions as well.

### Section 50: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Duty to bargain and not to change terms and conditions
"(b) the employer shall not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the bargaining agent consents to the alteration of such a term or condition, or such a right or privilege."

This section provides a crucial constraint on employers. It prohibits employers from unilaterally changing terms and conditions of employment once a bargaining agent has been certified and there is no existing collective agreement. The employer can only make such changes if the bargaining agent consents or if the collective agreement itself allows for such revisions. This ensures that the bargaining process is not undermined by employer actions taken outside of the formal negotiation.
