## Obligations of Bargaining Agent and Employer After Notice to Bargain Collectively

### Section 50: Duty to Bargain Collectively

Section 50 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the immediate obligations of the bargaining agent and the employer following the issuance of notice to bargain collectively.
"Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, (a) the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

This passage establishes a strict timeline for the commencement of collective bargaining. It states that the bargaining agent and the employer
"...without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..." This highlights the imperative to engage in good faith bargaining and to exert a sincere effort to reach a new collective agreement. The twenty-day timeframe is a crucial element, preventing undue delays in the negotiation process.

### Section 48: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Notice to Bargain to Enter into a Collective Agreement

Section 48 further elaborates on the bargaining obligations, particularly when no existing collective agreement is in force.
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

This section clarifies that either party can initiate collective bargaining by providing notice to the other. The bargaining agent can direct the employer to begin negotiations, or the employer can direct the bargaining agent to do so. The stated purpose of this notice is
"...for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement." reinforcing the ultimate goal of reaching a mutually acceptable agreement.

### Section 47.1: Successor Rights and Obligations: Where notice to bargain collectively given prior to deletion

Section 47.1 addresses the obligations that continue after a deletion or severance of a collective agreement.
"(a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise..."

This passage is particularly relevant as it details the obligations that persist even after a change in the employer's structure. It states that the terms and conditions of employment from the previous collective agreement or arbitral award continue in force until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent mutually agree otherwise. This ensures stability for the employees during the transition period.

### Section 36: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Effect of certification

Section 36 outlines the consequences of a trade union being certified as the bargaining agent.
"(a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

This passage is fundamental as it establishes the bargaining agent's exclusive right to negotiate on behalf of the employees. Once certified, the union is the sole entity authorized to engage in collective bargaining. This prevents multiple parties from attempting to negotiate simultaneously and ensures a unified voice for the employees.

### Section 49: Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Notice to Bargain to Renew or Revise a Collective Agreement or Enter a New Collective Agreement

Section 49 reinforces the obligation to bargain collectively, specifically when a current collective agreement is nearing its expiration.
"(1) Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This section provides a mechanism for either party to initiate renewal or revision of an existing collective agreement. The notice must be given within a specified timeframe, either four months before the expiration date or a longer period outlined in the current agreement. This proactive approach to renewal or revision helps to avoid disruptions to the employment relationship.

individual_results.answer:
## Conditions Where Sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code Do Not Apply

### Section 51(2) - Collective Agreement Provisions

Section 51(2) of the Canada Labour Code outlines several conditions under which sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change. One such condition is when the collective agreement contains provisions that
"...specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement..."
"...the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement..."

This indicates that if the existing collective agreement already has a framework for addressing the potential impacts of technological change, the requirements of sections 52, 54, and 55 are waived. The parties are obligated to utilize this established process rather than being compelled to initiate new collective bargaining solely due to the technological change.

### Section 51(2)(c) - Collective Agreement Exclusions

Another condition is when the collective agreement contains provisions that
"...are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent."
"...the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent."

This provision allows the collective agreement itself to explicitly exclude the application of sections 52, 54, and 55 for the duration of its term. This is a mechanism for the parties to manage technological change internally, without the external intervention of the Board. The agreement must also include provisions to support employees through the transition.

### Section 55 - Conditions Precedent to Technological Change

Section 55 further clarifies the conditions under which sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply. It states that the employer cannot effect the technological change until either the Board has refused to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining, or the Board has granted leave and an agreement has been reached or the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met.
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This section essentially says that if the bargaining agent initiates the process under section 54, the employer is not obligated to proceed with the technological change until a certain point in the collective bargaining process is reached. This provides a pause in the implementation of the change while the parties attempt to negotiate a resolution.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Requirements for Technological Change Implementation by Collective Agreement Employers

### Section 52: Notice of Technological Change

Section 52 outlines the initial obligation of an employer bound by a collective agreement to inform the bargaining agent about an impending technological change.
"An employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who proposes to effect a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of the employer’s employees to whom the collective agreement applies shall give notice of the technological change to the bargaining agent bound by the collective agreement at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected."
This quote establishes the timeframe for providing notice: at least 120 days before the change is implemented. It also specifies the threshold for "significant number" of employees, which is determined by regulations made pursuant to subsection (4).

### Section 52: Contents of Notice

Section 52 further details the mandatory information that must be included in the notice.
"The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)."
This list is comprehensive, covering the type of change, the implementation date, the number and type of affected employees, the anticipated impact on employment terms and conditions, and any additional information mandated by regulations. The inclusion of
"(e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)." indicates that the notice may need to include further details depending on the specifics of the technological change.

### Section 53: Application for Order Respecting Technological Change

Section 53 addresses the bargaining agent's ability to apply to the Board for an order to commence collective bargaining if the employer has failed to comply with section 52.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."
This passage highlights the 30-day window the bargaining agent has to file the application after becoming aware of the employer's non-compliance with section 52.

### Section 54: Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain

Section 54 details the bargaining agent's ability to apply to the Board for an order to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. This application can be made within 30 days after receiving the notice of technological change.
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."
This quote emphasizes the bargaining agent's proactive role in initiating collective bargaining to address the potential impact of the technological change on employees. The application is made within 30 days of receiving the notice of technological change.

### Section 55: Conditions Precedent to Technological Change

Section 55 outlines the conditions that must be met before the employer can implement the technological change.
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."
This passage clearly states that the employer is prohibited from implementing the technological change until either the Board denies the bargaining agent's request for leave to serve a notice to commence bargaining, or the Board grants leave and one of two conditions is satisfied: an agreement has been reached through collective bargaining, or the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met. This ensures that the technological change is implemented only after a good-faith effort has been made to address the potential impact on employees through bargaining.

individual_results.question: What can a bargaining agent do if they allege that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, and what are the potential outcomes of such an action?
individual_results.answer:
## Bargaining Agent Actions Upon Alleged Technological Change Compliance Failure

### Section 53: Application for Order Determining Technological Change Compliance

Section 53 outlines the process a bargaining agent can undertake if they believe an employer has failed to comply with the technological change notification requirements outlined in sections 52, 54, and 55.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."
This indicates that the bargaining agent has a specific timeframe – thirty days – from becoming aware of the alleged failure to comply with section 52 to formally request an order from the Board. The application is directed at the Board to make a determination on whether the employer indeed failed to comply with section 52.

### Section 53: Potential Outcomes of Board Order

Section 53 further details the potential outcomes of the Board's order.
"(a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change; or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change."
The Board's order can go in two directions: it can either dismiss the bargaining agent's allegations and find that sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply to the employer's technological change, or it can uphold the allegations and find that the employer did indeed fail to comply with section 52.

### Section 53: Additional Directives from the Board

Section 53 also grants the Board broader powers within its order.
"(a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate; (b) require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change; and (c) where an employee is reinstated pursuant to paragraph (b), require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement."
If the Board determines that the employer failed to comply with section 52, it can issue a directive to halt the technological change for up to 120 days. It can also order the reinstatement of any employees who were displaced by the change and require the employer to compensate them for any lost wages.

### Section 54: Application for Order Respecting Technological Change

Section 54 provides a more proactive approach for the bargaining agent.
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."
This section allows the bargaining agent to immediately request an order to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. This notice can be used to either revise the existing collective agreement or add new provisions to address the impact of the technological change on employees' terms and conditions of employment. The thirty-day timeframe for this application is also specified.

### Section 54: Board Granting Leave for Collective Bargaining

Section 54 further elaborates on the Board's power to grant leave for collective bargaining.
"...an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."
The Board's decision to grant leave for collective bargaining is based on its assessment of whether the technological change is likely to have a significant and adverse impact on employees' employment terms and conditions. If the Board finds this to be the case, it can issue an order allowing the bargaining agent to serve the notice to commence collective bargaining.

individual_results.question: What recourse does a bargaining agent have when it receives notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Recourse for Bargaining Agent Upon Receiving Notice of Technological Change

### Section 54: Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain

Section 54 outlines the immediate recourse a bargaining agent has upon receiving notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52. It states:
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This passage is crucial because it directly answers the question. It specifies that the bargaining agent has a
"...for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining..." This application must be made within thirty days of receiving the technological change notice. The purpose of this notice to commence collective bargaining is twofold: either to revise existing collective agreement provisions or to add new ones that address the potential adverse effects of the technological change on employees' terms and conditions of employment or security.

### Section 53: Application for Order Respecting Technological Change

Section 53 provides further context regarding the Board's role in addressing technological change. It details the Board's ability to determine whether sections 52, 54, and 55 apply to an employer and whether the employer has failed to comply with section 52. It also mentions that the Board can direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change for a period not exceeding one hundred and twenty days.

While Section 53 doesn't directly address the bargaining agent's recourse *upon* receiving notice, it highlights the Board's power to intervene and potentially halt or modify the technological change if it is deemed likely to adversely affect employees. This intervention complements the bargaining agent's ability to initiate collective bargaining to proactively address these potential impacts.

### Section 51: Application of Sections 52, 54 and 55

Section 51 clarifies the conditions under which sections 52, 54, and 55 *do not* apply to an employer and a bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement. It lists several scenarios, including when the notice of technological change was given substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2)(i) or (ii), or when the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures for negotiating and settling matters related to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change.

This section is relevant because it explains that the bargaining agent's recourse under section 54 is available even if the employer has provided notice of the technological change in a manner that would otherwise fall outside the scope of those sections. It emphasizes that the bargaining agent's right to initiate collective bargaining is not automatically negated by the employer's compliance with section 52.

In summary, a bargaining agent, upon receiving notice of a technological change that may adversely affect employees, has the immediate recourse of applying to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining. This notice is intended to facilitate the revision or addition of collective agreement provisions to mitigate the potential negative impacts of the technological change. The Board retains the power to intervene further by directing the employer to halt the technological change or to reimburse employees for lost wages.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employer's ability to effect a technological change when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1)?
individual_results.answer:
## Technological Change and Board Orders under Subsection 54(1)

### Conditions Precedent to Technological Change

Section 55 outlines the conditions that must be met before an employer can effect a technological change when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1). It states:
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This passage is crucial because it establishes a pause on the employer's ability to implement the technological change. The employer is legally obligated to wait until either the Board denies the bargaining agent permission to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining, or the Board grants that permission and one of the specified conditions is fulfilled – either an agreement is reached through bargaining, or the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) are met. This waiting period is a safeguard to ensure that the technological change does not negatively impact employees without proper consultation and negotiation.

### Board Orders and Technological Change

Section 54(1) details the Board's power to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. It specifies:
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This section explains that the Board's order granting leave to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining is a significant step in the process. It allows the bargaining agent to initiate discussions about how the technological change will affect the employees' terms and conditions of employment. The Board's decision to grant or deny this leave directly impacts the employer's timeline for implementing the change.

Section 53 further elaborates on the Board's powers in response to a bargaining agent's application for an order determining the alleged technological change. It states:
"On receipt of an application for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection (1) and after affording an opportunity for the parties to make representations, the Board may, by order, (a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change; or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change."

This passage highlights the Board's ability to intervene and determine whether the technological change falls within the scope of sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code. If the Board finds that these sections do apply and the employer has failed to comply with section 52, it can issue an order directing the employer not to proceed with the technological change for a specified period. It can also order the reinstatement of any displaced employees and reimburse them for any lost wages.

Section 53(4) is particularly relevant as it clarifies that an order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is
"...deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1)." This means that the Board's order effectively acts as if the employer had already provided the required notice of technological change, and it simultaneously allows the bargaining agent to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining. This accelerates the process of negotiation and potential agreement on the impact of the technological change on employees.

In summary, when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer's ability to effect a technological change is significantly restricted. The employer must wait until the Board either denies the bargaining agent permission to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining, or grants that permission and one of the specified conditions is met. The Board's orders can also directly impact the employer's timeline by directing it not to proceed with the change, ordering reinstatement and reimbursement of displaced employees, or effectively deeming the employer to have already provided the required notice and allowing the bargaining agent to serve a notice to commence collective bargaining.

Section 56 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses who is bound by a collective agreement. It states:

This quotation is crucial because it explicitly identifies the three parties obligated to adhere to the terms and conditions outlined in a collective agreement. The bargaining agent, representing the employees, is bound. Every employee within the bargaining unit is also bound. Finally, the employer, the other party to the agreement, is equally bound. The phrase
"...subject to and for the purposes of this Part..." indicates that the collective agreement operates within the framework of the entire Canada Labour Code, and its interpretation and application are guided by its provisions. Therefore, a collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit has a comprehensive scope of obligation, extending to all involved parties.

individual_results.question: What is required to be included in a collective agreement in Canada regarding the resolution of differences between parties, and what happens if the parties are unable to agree on an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson?
individual_results.answer:
## Collective Agreements and Dispute Resolution in Canada

### Section 57: Final Settlement Without Stoppage of Work

Section 57 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states a mandatory provision for final settlement of differences between the parties to or employees bound by a collective agreement.
"Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or employees bound by the collective agreement, concerning its interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention."
This provision is fundamental, ensuring that disagreements are resolved through a structured process that avoids work stoppages. It allows for resolution through arbitration or other agreed-upon methods.

### Section 57: Appointment of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Chairperson

Section 57 further details the process when the parties cannot agree on an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson. It outlines a series of steps, starting with the Minister's appointment.
"Where any difference arises between parties to a collective agreement that does not contain a provision for final settlement of the difference as required by subsection (1), the difference shall, notwithstanding any provision of the collective agreement, be submitted by the parties for final settlement (a) to an arbitrator selected by the parties; or (b) where the parties are unable to agree on the selection of an arbitrator and either party makes a written request to the Minister to appoint an arbitrator, to an arbitrator appointed by the Minister after such inquiry, if any, as the Minister considers necessary."
This indicates that if the parties fail to reach a consensus, either party can request the Minister to make the appointment.
"Where any difference arises between parties to a collective agreement that contains a provision for final settlement of the difference by an arbitration board and either party fails to name its nominee to the board in accordance with the collective agreement, the difference shall, notwithstanding any provision in the collective agreement, be submitted by the parties for final settlement to an arbitrator in accordance with paragraphs (2)(a) and (b)."
This provides a fallback mechanism even if the parties miss their deadline for nominating an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson.
"On receipt of a written request under subsection (4), the Minister shall, after such inquiry, if any, as the Minister considers necessary, appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be."
This confirms the Minister's role in intervening when the parties are deadlocked.

### Section 63: Arbitration Costs, Fees and Expenses

Section 63 addresses the financial aspects of arbitration proceedings.
"Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted by the parties to an arbitrator or arbitration board, the costs, fees and expenses with respect to the arbitration proceedings shall, unless the collective agreement otherwise provides or the parties otherwise agree, be borne as follows: (a) each party shall bear its own costs and shall pay the fees and expenses of any member of the arbitration board who is nominated by it; and (b) the fees and expenses of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, whether the arbitrator or chairperson is selected by the parties or their nominees or appointed by the Minister under this Part, shall be borne equally by the parties."
This clarifies that each party is responsible for their own expenses and the fees of their nominee on the board. However, the fees and expenses of the arbitrator or chairperson are shared equally between the parties.

### Section 62: Decision of Arbitration Board

Section 62 outlines how an arbitration board reaches a decision.
"Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted to an arbitration board, the decision of a majority of those comprising the board is the decision of the board, but if a majority of those comprising the board cannot agree on a decision, the decision of the chairperson of the board is the decision of the board."
This establishes that a simple majority vote constitutes the board's decision. If the board is deadlocked, the chairperson's decision prevails. This ensures that a resolution is ultimately reached, even in the face of disagreement among the board members.

individual_results.question: What is the status of an arbitrator or arbitration board's decision under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Status of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Decisions Under the Canada Labour Code

### Finality and Non-Review by Court

Section 58(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of arbitrator or arbitration board decisions, stating,
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This quote is central to understanding the status of such decisions. It unequivocally declares that courts have no jurisdiction to overturn or second-guess the rulings made by these bodies. 

Section 58(2) reinforces this point by prohibiting any court action, including injunctions, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto, or other means, to question, review, prohibit, or restrain an arbitrator or arbitration board in their proceedings. This comprehensive prohibition ensures the sanctity and stability of the arbitration process.

### Judicial Review in Limited Circumstances

While arbitrator and arbitration board decisions are generally final and non-reviewable by court, Section 60(1) acknowledges a limited exception: judicial review. It states,
"An arbitrator or arbitration board has (a) the powers conferred on the Board by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c) and (f.1); (a.1) the power to interpret, apply and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement; (a.2) the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate; (a.3) the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree; (a.4) the power to expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes..." This section details the broad powers of an arbitrator or arbitration board, which implicitly support the finality of their decisions. 

However, judicial review is only available in "limited circumstances," specifically when the referee has made an

Furthermore, it details what happens if the employer refuses to comply with the order.
"If the referee’s decision orders the employer to pay  additional sums to the employee, the employer must comply with the order as  soon as possible, or within the time period ordered by the referee. If the employer refuses to comply with the referee’s order,  the employee can ask the Labour Program inspector in their case to file the  referee’s decision in the Federal Court of Canada." individual_results.question: What are the general powers and authorities granted to an arbitrator or arbitration board in the context of labor disputes and collective agreements under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Powers and Authorities of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board

### Section 60: Powers of Arbitrator, etc.

Section 60 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad powers vested in an arbitrator or arbitration board. It states that
"An arbitrator or arbitration board has (a) the powers conferred on the Board by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c) and (f.1); (a.1) the power to interpret, apply and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement; (a.2) the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate; (a.3) the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree; (a.4) the power to expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes; and (b) power to determine any question as to whether a matter referred to the arbitrator or arbitration board is arbitrable."

This section establishes a comprehensive toolkit for arbitrators and boards. They possess the
"...powers conferred on the Board by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c) and (f.1)..." which are not explicitly detailed within this excerpt but likely encompass procedural and evidentiary aspects of arbitration. Crucially, they have the power to
"(a.1) the power to interpret, apply and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement..." This demonstrates their ability to consider and apply both the terms of the collective agreement and relevant employment legislation. Furthermore, they can issue
"...interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate..." and
"...expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process..."

### Section 15.1: General Power to Assist Parties

Section 15.1 further elaborates on the Board's, its members', and external adjudicators' powers to assist parties in resolving disputes. It states that
"The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."

This provision highlights the Board's role in facilitating settlement. They can offer assistance
"...at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate..." provided the parties consent. This can include mediation, conciliation, or other problem-solving techniques. The assistance is offered
"...without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled." ensuring that the Board retains its authority to make final decisions on unresolved matters.

### Section 60 (1.2): Power to Mediate

Section 60 (1.2) specifically grants the arbitrator or arbitration board the power to
"At any stage of a proceeding before an arbitrator or arbitration board, the arbitrator or arbitration board may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving the difference at issue without prejudice to the power of the arbitrator or arbitration board to continue the arbitration with respect to the issues that have not been resolved."

This reiterates the Board's ability to mediate, emphasizing that this assistance is contingent upon the parties' agreement and does not limit their authority to proceed with arbitration on remaining issues.

### Section 60 (1.1): Power to Extend Time

Section 60 (1.1) details the Board's power to extend timeframes. It states that
"The arbitrator or arbitration board may extend the time for taking any step in the grievance process or arbitration procedure set out in a collective agreement, even after the expiration of the time, if the arbitrator or arbitration board is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for the extension and that the other party would not be unduly prejudiced by the extension."

This power is intended to ensure that the arbitration process can proceed effectively, even if the parties require additional time to prepare their submissions or consider the arbitrator's preliminary views. The extension must be reasonable and not unfairly disadvantage the other party.

### Section 60 (2): Power to Substitute Penalties

Section 60 (2) grants the arbitrator or arbitration board the power to
"Where an arbitrator or arbitration board determines that an employee has been discharged or disciplined by an employer for cause and the collective agreement does not contain a specific penalty for the infraction that is the subject of the arbitration, the arbitrator or arbitration board has power to substitute for the discharge or discipline such other penalty as to the arbitrator or arbitration board seems just and reasonable in the circumstances."

This provision allows the arbitrator or board to fashion a penalty that is proportionate to the employee's misconduct, even if the collective agreement lacks a specific one. The substituted penalty must be "just and reasonable in the circumstances."

In summary, arbitrators and arbitration boards in Canada possess a wide range of powers and authorities under the Canada Labour Code. These powers encompass interpretation and application of statutes and collective agreements, issuing interim orders, expediting proceedings, assisting parties in settlement through mediation, extending timeframes, and substituting penalties for employer actions. These powers are designed to ensure that arbitration is a fair, efficient, and effective means of resolving labor disputes.

individual_results.answer:
## Key Responsibilities of an Arbitrator or Arbitration Board in Procedure and Fairness

### Procedural Responsibilities

#### Power to Determine Procedure
"...arbitrator or arbitration board may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving the difference at issue without prejudice to the power of the arbitrator or arbitration board to continue the arbitration with respect to the issues that have not been resolved." This passage highlights the arbitrator's flexibility in managing the proceedings. They can facilitate direct negotiation between the parties if they wish, but retain the authority to proceed with a more formal hearing if necessary. This adaptability ensures the process is tailored to the needs of the dispute.

#### Power to Expedite Proceedings
"...expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes..." This power is crucial for ensuring the arbitration is timely and efficient. The arbitrator can issue orders to manage the pace of the hearing, prevent unnecessary delays, and address any attempts to obstruct the process.

#### Power to Consider Submissions
"...the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate; (a.3) the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree..." This demonstrates the arbitrator's ability to adapt to the parties' preferred methods of presenting their cases. They can set a standard format for submissions or allow the parties to use their own, as long as it is manageable for the arbitration.

#### Power to Extend Time
"The arbitrator or arbitration board may extend the time for taking any step in the grievance process or arbitration procedure set out in a collective agreement, even after the expiration of the time, if the arbitrator or arbitration board is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for the extension and that the other party would not be unduly prejudiced by the extension." This power provides a safety net for complex cases that may require more time to resolve. The arbitrator can grant extensions if there is a valid reason and the other party is not unfairly disadvantaged.

#### Power to Determine Arbitrability
"...power to determine any question as to whether a matter referred to the arbitrator or arbitration board is arbitrable." This is a fundamental procedural responsibility. The arbitrator must first determine if the dispute falls within the scope of the agreement or law that allows for arbitration.

#### Power to Make Interim Orders
"(a.2) the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate..." This power allows the arbitrator to provide temporary solutions while the full arbitration is underway. Interim orders can address urgent issues, such as reinstatement or payment of wages, to prevent further harm.

### Fairness Responsibilities

#### Impartiality
"...is an independent, neutral person who is not connected to, or associated with, either party to the appeal." This passage explicitly states the arbitrator's obligation to be unbiased. They must make their decision based solely on the evidence presented, without any personal stake in the outcome.

#### Opportunity to Present Evidence and Arguments
"Administrative fairness:   These are principles of fairness, such as: having an unbiased referee; being given an opportunity to present evidence and arguments; receiving a referee’s decision in a timely manner; and having the reasons for a decision be clearly explained." This quote from Labour-Reports-12_9 outlines key principles of fairness in an appeal hearing, including the right to present evidence and arguments. The arbitrator must ensure that both sides have a fair chance to make their case.

#### Timely Decision
"Administrative fairness:   receiving a referee’s decision in a timely manner." (no source found for the quotation) This principle emphasizes the importance of a prompt resolution to the dispute. The arbitrator should strive to make a decision within a reasonable timeframe, without unnecessary delays.

#### Clear Reasons for Decision
"...having the reasons for a decision be clearly explained." This ensures transparency and allows the parties to understand the basis for the arbitrator's ruling. The arbitrator must provide a detailed explanation of how they reached their decision, citing the relevant evidence and legal principles.

#### Power to Review and Correct Errors
"Judicial review:   A review of the referee’s decision by a court of law." While not a direct responsibility *during* the proceeding, the existence of judicial review acts as a check on the arbitrator's power and ensures that decisions are legally sound. It provides a mechanism for correcting any errors or misinterpretations of the law.

## Decision-Making Process of an Arbitration Board under the Canada Labour Code

### Majority Decision
"Section 62 Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted to an arbitration board, the decision of a majority of those comprising the board is the decision of the board, but if a majority of those comprising the board cannot agree on a decision, the decision of the chairperson of the board is the decision of the board."

This section of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the process for reaching a decision by an arbitration board. It states that if a majority of the board members can agree on a decision, that majority's decision stands as the board's decision. However, it also addresses the scenario where the board cannot reach a majority consensus. In such cases, the chairperson of the board has the authority to make the final decision, and that decision is considered the board's decision. This ensures that the arbitration process can continue even when the board members are divided.

### Chairperson's Decision in Case of Impasse
"Section 62 Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted to an arbitration board, the decision of a majority of those comprising the board is the decision of the board, but if a majority of those comprising the board cannot agree on a decision, the decision of the chairperson of the board is the decision of the board."

This quote further elaborates on the chairperson's role in the arbitration process. It clarifies that if the board is deadlocked and cannot achieve a majority agreement, the chairperson's decision becomes the board's decision. This prevents the arbitration from being stalled by a lack of consensus among the board members. The chairperson's decision is binding and represents the final outcome of the arbitration.

### Time Limit for Decision
"(2) If a decision is to be made under this Part, the panel shall make it and give notice of it to the parties no later than 90 days after the day on which the panel reserved the decision or within any further period that may be determined by the Chairperson."

While this section pertains to decisions made by a panel formed under subsection 14(1), it is relevant to the arbitration board process as well. It establishes a time limit for the board to issue a decision. The board must make its decision and provide notice to the parties involved no later than 90 days after the panel reserved the decision, or within any further period set by the chairperson. This ensures that the arbitration process is timely and does not drag on indefinitely.

individual_results.question: In the event of a labour dispute being submitted to an arbitrator or arbitration board under the Canada Labour Code, who bears the costs, fees, and expenses associated with the arbitration proceedings?
individual_results.answer:
## Arbitration Costs, Fees, and Expenses under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 63: Arbitration Costs, Fees and Expenses

Section 63 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the allocation of costs, fees, and expenses in arbitration proceedings. It states:
"Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted by the parties to an arbitrator or arbitration board, the costs, fees and expenses with respect to the arbitration proceedings shall, unless the collective agreement otherwise provides or the parties otherwise agree, be borne as follows: (a) each party shall bear its own costs and shall pay the fees and expenses of any member of the arbitration board who is nominated by it; and (b) the fees and expenses of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, whether the arbitrator or chairperson is selected by the parties or their nominees or appointed by the Minister under this Part, shall be borne equally by the parties."

This passage is crucial because it clearly outlines the cost-sharing arrangement in arbitration. It specifies that each party is responsible for their own expenses and the fees of their nominated arbitration board member. Furthermore, it mandates that the fees and expenses of the arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson will be divided equally between the two parties involved in the dispute, unless a collective agreement or the parties themselves have agreed to a different arrangement. This ensures a balanced financial burden for both sides when arbitration is pursued.

### Section 116: Remuneration and Expenses for Industrial Inquiry Commission, Conciliation Board, and Commissioner Members

Section 116 provides context regarding the remuneration and expenses of individuals who act in various conciliation and inquiry capacities under the Part of the Canada Labour Code. While it doesn't directly address arbitration costs, it establishes a precedent for compensating individuals involved in dispute resolution processes.
"The members of an Industrial Inquiry Commission, the members of a conciliation board and every person not employed in the federal public administration who acts as a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner or who functions under this Part in any other capacity at the request of the Minister, except as an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, shall be paid such remuneration and expenses as may be fixed by the Governor in Council by regulation or by order."

This indicates that those who serve as arbitrators or arbitration board chairpersons are also entitled to remuneration and expenses, which are determined by the Governor in Council. This aligns with Section 63, which states that the fees and expenses of the arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson will be borne equally by the parties.

### Section 118: Witness Fees and Expenses

Section 118 outlines the compensation for individuals summoned by the Board to attend as witnesses. While not directly related to arbitration costs, it reinforces the principle of compensating individuals for their time and expenses in the context of labour disputes.
"A person who is summoned by the Board, a conciliation board, a conciliation commissioner or an Industrial Inquiry Commission to attend as a witness in any proceeding taken under this Part, and who so attends, is entitled to be paid an allowance for expenses and a witness fee, determined in accordance with the scale for the time being in force with respect to witnesses in civil suits in the superior court of the province in which the proceeding is being taken."

This provision ensures that witnesses are not financially penalized for providing testimony during labour dispute proceedings, including arbitration.

In summary, Section 63 is the most direct and comprehensive source of information regarding the allocation of arbitration costs, fees, and expenses. It clearly states that each party bears its own costs and pays the fees of its nominated arbitration board member, while the fees and expenses of the arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson are shared equally between the parties, unless otherwise agreed upon.

individual_results.question: What are the rules and exceptions surrounding the timeframe for an arbitrator or arbitration board to make or give an order or decision in a labour dispute?
individual_results.answer:
## Timeframe for Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Orders and Decisions

### Section 64: Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements: Order or decision within sixty days

Section 64(1) establishes the general timeframe for an arbitrator or arbitration board to issue an order or decision. It states:
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board shall be made or given within sixty days after, in the case of an arbitrator, their appointment as arbitrator, and, in the case of an arbitration board, the appointment of the arbitration board chairperson, unless (a) the collective agreement otherwise provides or the parties otherwise agree; or (b) owing to circumstances beyond the control of the arbitrator or arbitration board, it is not practicable to make or give the order or decision within those sixty days."

This passage is central to understanding the timeframe. It mandates that the order or decision must be made within sixty days of the arbitrator's appointment or the chairperson's appointment of the arbitration board. However, it also outlines two exceptions to this rule. The first exception is if the collective agreement or the parties themselves have agreed on a different timeframe. The second exception is if circumstances beyond the arbitrator's or board's control make it impossible to meet the sixty-day deadline.

### Section 224: Division IX-Group Termination of Employment: Appointment of arbitrator

Section 224(4) further elaborates on the arbitrator's duty and the timeframe for their decision. It specifies:
"An arbitrator shall assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and the arbitrator, if sent a statement pursuant to subsection (2), shall, within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify, (a) consider the matters set out in the statement; (b) render a decision thereon; and (c) send a copy of the decision with the reasons therefor to the joint planning committee and to the Minister."

This section indicates that the arbitrator has four weeks, or a longer period as designated by the Minister, to consider the statement of matters in dispute and render a decision. This timeframe is set *after* receiving the statement from the joint planning committee. This provides a more specific timeframe within the broader sixty-day rule, particularly for cases involving adjustment programs.

### Section 223: Division IX-Group Termination of Employment: Application to Minister for arbitrator

Section 223(1) details the process for applying to the Minister for an arbitrator's appointment. It mentions that the committee members can apply jointly after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, if either of the following conditions are met:
"(a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This section does not directly address the timeframe for the arbitrator's order or decision. However, it sets the stage for the sixty-day rule by outlining when the Minister will appoint the arbitrator, which is the starting point for the arbitrator's work and the sixty-day deadline.

### Section 14.1: Continuation of proceeding | Decision of panel

Section 14.1(1) addresses the situation where a panel member dies or becomes incapacitated. It states:
"In the event of the death or incapacity of a member of a panel formed under subsection 14(1) who represents either employees or employers, the chairperson of the panel may determine any matter that was before the panel and the chairperson’s decision is deemed to be the decision of the panel."

This section is not relevant to the timeframe for an arbitrator's order or decision. It deals with the continuity of a panel's work in the event of a member's absence.

### Section 14.2: Decision of panel

Section 14.2(2) clarifies that a decision made by a majority of the panel members or, where there is no majority, by the chairperson, is the decision of the Board. It also includes a time limit:
"(2) If a decision is to be made under this Part, the panel shall make it and give notice of it to the parties no later than 90 days after the day on which the panel reserved the decision or within any further period that may be determined by the Chairperson."

This passage provides a more extended timeframe of ninety days for the panel to make a decision, with the chairperson having the authority to extend this period. However, it is not directly applicable to the arbitrator's order or decision, which is set at sixty days.

### Section 251.05(1)(b) and (c): Complaint Suspension and Rejection

Sections 251.05(1)(b) and (c) discuss the suspension or rejection of a complaint. While these sections do not directly address the arbitrator's timeframe, they highlight the possibility of a complaint being dealt with within a specific timeframe, or being rejected if the complainant fails to take required measures within that timeframe. This indirectly supports the concept of time limits in labour dispute resolution.

### Referral to the Board
"Where any question arises in connection with a matter that has been referred to an arbitrator or arbitration board, relating to the existence of a collective agreement or the identification of the parties or employees bound by a collective agreement, the arbitrator or arbitration board, the Minister or any alleged party may refer the question to the Board for determination."

The referral can be initiated by the arbitrator or arbitration board itself, the Minister, or any party claiming to be bound by a collective agreement. The Board is then tasked with providing a determination on the matter.

### Effect on the Proceeding
"(2) The referral of any question to the Board pursuant to subsection (1) shall not operate to suspend any proceeding before an arbitrator or arbitration board unless the arbitrator or arbitration board decides that the nature of the question warrants a suspension of the proceeding or the Board directs the suspension of the proceeding."

This subsection clarifies the impact of the referral on the ongoing arbitration proceeding. It states that the referral itself does not automatically halt the arbitration. However, the arbitrator or arbitration board has the discretion to suspend the proceeding if the question is deemed significant enough to warrant it, or the Board itself can issue a direction for suspension. This ensures that the arbitration can continue unless the referral necessitates a temporary pause. The referral is a mechanism for obtaining clarification on a foundational issue (collective agreement existence or party identification) without necessarily disrupting the core dispute resolution process.

individual_results.question: How can an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board be enforced in the Federal Court?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Orders and Decisions in the Federal Court

### Filing in the Federal Court

Section 66(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board to be enforced in the Federal Court.
"Any person or organization affected by any order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board may, after fourteen days from the date on which the order or decision is made or given, or from the date provided in it for compliance, whichever is the later date, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of the reasons therefor." This indicates that any party impacted by the decision has a window of fourteen days from the date it was issued or the compliance date to file a copy of the order or decision with the Federal Court. The filing must be of the order or decision itself, excluding the reasoning behind it.

Section 66(2) further clarifies the effect of this filing.
"On filing an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board in the Federal Court under subsection (1), the order or decision shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order or decision were a judgment obtained in the Court." This is a crucial point, as it establishes that once the order or decision is registered in the Federal Court, it gains the full legal weight of a judgment.
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court." This reiterates the equivalence of the registered order or decision to a judgment, allowing for all standard court enforcement mechanisms to be utilized.

### Filing in Provincial Superior Court

Section 23(1) of the Canada Labour Code provides an alternative method for enforcement, which is filing in the superior court of a province.
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose." While this section primarily addresses filing in the Federal Court, it also mentions the possibility of filing in provincial superior court under Section 23.1.
"Section 23 applies, with any modifications that the circumstances require, to an order or decision filed in such a superior court." This indicates that the procedures and consequences of filing in provincial superior court are largely the same as those for filing in the Federal Court, with minor adjustments made to accommodate the different court systems.

### After a Decision is Issued

Section 18 of the Labour Program's Wage Recovery Guide details what happens after a decision is issued.
"Once a decision is filed with the Court, the Labour Program  has no statutory authority to proceed beyond this point. The party may now seek  enforcement of the order through other avenues as with any judgment of the  Federal Court." This confirms that once the order or decision is filed with the Federal Court, the Labour Program's direct enforcement powers are exhausted, and the affected party must pursue enforcement through the standard court system.
"If the employer refuses to comply with the referee’s order,  the employee can ask the Labour Program inspector in their case to file the  referee’s decision in the Federal Court of Canada. This may be done 15 days  after the date of the referee’s decision or after the date by which the  employer is required to comply with the order (whichever is the latest). Once a decision is filed with the Court, the Labour Program  has no statutory authority to proceed beyond this point. The party may now seek  enforcement of the order through other avenues as with any judgment of the  Federal Court." This passage further emphasizes the Federal Court's role in enabling enforcement, stating that the Labour Program's authority ends upon filing the decision with the Court, and the party must then seek enforcement through the court system.

individual_results.question: What are the implications for a collective agreement that contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year, and how can its term be altered or revised?
individual_results.answer:
## Implications of a Collective Agreement with No Term or Less Than One Year

### Section 67(1) - Deemed Term of One Year
"Where a collective agreement contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year, the collective agreement shall be deemed to be for a term of one year from the date on which it comes into force and shall not, except as provided by subsection 36(2) or with the consent of the Board, be terminated by the parties thereto within that term of one year."

Section 67(1) directly addresses the scenario of a collective agreement lacking a specified term or having a term shorter than one year. It establishes a default term of one year for such agreements. This means that unless the parties mutually agree to a revision or the Board orders an alteration, the agreement will automatically expire after one year from its effective date. This provision provides stability and predictability for both employers and employees, preventing frequent renegotiations of short-term agreements.

### Section 67(2) - Revision of Collective Agreement
"Nothing in this Part prohibits the parties to a collective agreement from agreeing to a revision of any provision of the collective agreement other than a provision relating to the term of the collective agreement."

Section 67(2) clarifies that while the default term is one year, the parties retain the freedom to negotiate and agree to a revision of *any* other provision of the collective agreement, with the exception of the term itself. This allows for adjustments to wages, benefits, working conditions, and other aspects of the agreement without needing Board intervention. However, any attempt to change the term would require a separate agreement between the parties or an order from the Board.

### Section 67(3) - Board Order Altering Termination Date
"The Board may, on application made jointly by both parties to a collective agreement, order that the termination date of the collective agreement be altered for the purpose of establishing a common termination date for two or more collective agreements binding a single employer."

Section 67(3) grants the Board the authority to modify the termination date of a collective agreement. This power is exercised upon a joint application from both the employer and the union. The Board can adjust the date to create a unified end date for multiple agreements covering the same employer. This can streamline the bargaining process and avoid overlapping or conflicting agreements.

### Section 67(4) - Provision for Settlement of Differences Remains in Force
"Notwithstanding anything contained in a collective agreement, the provision required to be contained therein by subsection 57(1) shall remain in force after the termination of the collective agreement and until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

Section 67(4) ensures that the provisions for the settlement of differences, as outlined in subsection 57(1), continue to be applicable even after the collective agreement expires. This provides a mechanism for resolving disputes that may arise during the transition period between agreements. The provision remains in effect until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) are satisfied, which likely relate to the negotiation and ratification of a new or revised agreement.

### Section 67(5) - Arbitrator Powers During Term of Collective Agreement
"Where a difference between the parties to a collective agreement relating to a provision contained in the collective agreement arises during the period from the date of its termination to the date the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, (a) an arbitrator or arbitration board may hear and determine the difference; and (b) sections 57 to 66 apply to the hearing and determination."

Section 67(5) outlines the arbitrator's powers when a difference arises during the term of a collective agreement that is about to expire. It states that an arbitrator or arbitration board *can* hear and determine the difference, and that sections 57 to 66 of the Canada Labour Code govern the hearing and determination process. This ensures that disputes are resolved efficiently and consistently, even as the agreement nears its end.

### Section 67(7) - Revision of Term Despite Notice to Bargain
"Despite subsection (2), if a notice to bargain referred to in subsection 65.12(1) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act has been served, the parties may agree to revise the term of the collective agreement without approval of the Board."

Section 67(7) provides an exception to the general rule that Board approval is required for revising the term of a collective agreement when a notice to bargain has been served under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act. This allows for a quick adjustment to the term if the employer is in financial distress and the parties agree on a new one.

### Section 67(8) - Revision of Term Despite Notice to Bargain
"Despite subsection (2), if a notice to bargain referred to in subsection 33(2) of the Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act has been served, the parties may agree to revise the term of the collective agreement without approval of the Board."

Section 67(8) mirrors Section 67(7), providing a similar exception for a notice to bargain served under the Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act. This allows for a swift term revision if the employer is undergoing a restructuring process and the parties reach an agreement.

In summary, a collective agreement with no term or a term shorter than one year is deemed to be for a one-year term. The parties can agree to revise the term, the Board can order an alteration to the termination date, and the arbitrator retains jurisdiction to hear and determine disputes during the term of the agreement, even if a notice to bargain has been served under certain insolvency acts. These provisions offer flexibility and stability to collective bargaining relationships.

individual_results.question: Can a collective agreement include provisions that require employees to be members of a specific trade union or give preference to union members for employment?
individual_results.answer:
## Collective Agreements and Trade Union Membership Requirements

### Section 68: Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements: Collective agreement may contain certain provisions

Section 68 directly addresses the question, stating:
"Nothing in this Part prohibits the parties to a collective agreement from including in the collective agreement a provision (a) requiring, as a condition of employment, membership in a specified trade union; or (b) granting a preference of employment to members of a specified trade union."

This passage is a clear and unambiguous answer to the question. It explicitly permits collective agreements to contain provisions that mandate trade union membership as a condition of employment or to provide preferential treatment to union members in hiring and promotions. The use of the phrase "Nothing in this Part prohibits" is a strong statement of permission, leaving no room for interpretation that such provisions would be invalid under the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 69: Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements: Collective agreement may contain certain provisions

Section 69 further supports the permissibility of trade union membership requirements in collective agreements by including a provision about the operation of hiring halls. While not directly addressing membership requirements as a condition of employment or preference, it acknowledges the potential for trade unions to manage their own hiring processes, which could involve prioritizing union members.
"Where, pursuant to a collective agreement, a trade union is engaged in the referral of persons to employment, it shall establish rules for the purpose of making such referrals and apply those rules fairly and without discrimination."

This indicates that trade unions can establish rules for their hiring halls, which could inherently favor union members. While the section emphasizes fairness and non-discrimination, it does not prohibit the union from having rules that give preference to its members.

### Section 25: Application for Certification: Where certification prohibited

Section 25, which discusses situations where a trade union cannot be certified as the bargaining agent, does not provide any limitations on the types of provisions that can be included in a collective agreement. It focuses on situations where the union is dominated by an employer or denies membership to employees based on arbitrary policies. Therefore, it does not contradict the permissibility of trade union membership requirements in collective agreements.

### Section 29: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Representation vote

Section 29, which outlines the process for certification of bargaining agents, also does not place any restrictions on the content of a collective agreement that might include trade union membership requirements. It focuses solely on whether employees in a unit want a particular trade union to represent them. The certification process itself does not dictate what provisions can be included in a resulting collective agreement.
