individual_results.question: What are the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees in the bargaining unit during a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code, and what role does the Board play in ensuring public safety and health?
individual_results.answer:
## Obligations During a Strike or Lockout

### Section 87.4: Maintenance of Activities

Section 87.4 outlines the primary obligation of employers, trade unions, and employees during a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part:
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."

This obligation is further detailed in subsection (2), which mandates that an employer and a trade union must enter into an agreement within 15 days of receiving notice to bargain collectively. This agreement must specify
"...the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose."

### Section 87.1: Strike Notice

Section 87.1 defines "employer" and "trade union" for the purposes of this Division. It also establishes the notice requirements for a strike or lockout.
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

These notices are only permissible if an agreement has been filed with the Minister and the Board, or if the Board has determined an application made by either party.

### Section 87.6: Reinstatement of Employees After Strike or Lockout

Section 87.6 specifies the obligation of the employer after a strike or lockout that is not prohibited by this Part:
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person." This ensures that employees who participated in the industrial action are restored to their former positions.

### Section 87.7: Services to Grain Vessels

Section 87.7 addresses the specific obligations of employers in the long-shoring industry during a strike or lockout.
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, an employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, its employees and their bargaining agent shall continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port."

This provision highlights the importance of maintaining essential services, particularly those related to grain vessels, even during a labor dispute.

## The Board's Role in Ensuring Public Safety and Health

The Board plays a crucial role in overseeing the maintenance of essential services during a strike or lockout and ensuring public safety and health.

### Section 87.4: Board Order for Public Safety

Section 87.4(6) details the Board's power to issue an order if it determines that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public.
"If, in determining an application made under subsection (4) or referral made under subsection (5), the Board is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section."

This Board order can mandate the continuation of specific services and operations, as well as impose other measures to mitigate potential risks to the public.

### Section 87.4: Review of Agreement

Section 87.4(7) allows the Board to review and confirm, amend, or cancel an agreement entered into under this section.
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances."

This Board review power ensures that any agreement reached during a strike or lockout is adequate to maintain essential services and protect public safety.

### Section 87.4: Referral to the Board

Section 87.4(5) allows the Minister to refer any question with respect to the application of subsection (1) to the Board.
"The Minister may refer to the Board any question with respect to whether an agreement entered into by the employer and the trade union is sufficient to ensure that subsection (1) is complied with."

This referral mechanism enables the Board to provide expert guidance and make orders to ensure that essential services are maintained.

### Section 87.4: Time Limit for Board Action

Section 87.4(6.1) sets a time limit for the Board to act on an application or referral.
"Despite subsection 14.2(2), the Board must determine an application made under subsection (4) or a referral made under subsection (5), make any order under subsection (6) and send a copy of its decision and any order to the parties no later than 82 days after the day on which it received the application or referral."

This time limit ensures that the Board responds promptly to issues that arise during a strike or lockout.

individual_results.answer:
## Restrictions Imposed on Employers During Dispute Resolution and After a Strike or Lockout

### Restrictions During Dispute Resolution

#### Section 87.4: Maintenance of Activities
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."
This section establishes a fundamental restriction on employers during a strike or lockout. It mandates that they must maintain essential services, operations, and production to avoid posing an immediate and serious danger to public safety or health. This obligation is not absolute and is limited to what is "necessary" to prevent such a danger.

#### Section 87.4(2): Agreement on Compliance
"An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose."
This subsection further details the employer's obligation under Section 87.4 by requiring them to enter into an agreement with the trade union within 15 days of receiving notice to bargain collectively. This agreement must specify the level of essential services, operations, or production that will be maintained and the methods for doing so. This agreement has the same effect as an order from the Board once filed.

#### Section 87.4(3): Filing with Minister and Board
"Immediately after entering into the agreement, the employer and the trade union must file a copy of it with the Minister and the Board."
This provision emphasizes the importance of formalizing the agreement by filing it with the relevant authorities. This filing triggers the agreement's legal effect, making it binding on all parties.

#### Section 87.4(4): Board Determination if No Agreement
"If the employer and the trade union do not enter into an agreement within the period referred to in subsection (2), the Board must, on application made by either of them, determine any question with respect to the application of subsection (1)."
This section outlines the Board's role if the employer and trade union fail to reach an agreement within the stipulated timeframe. The Board will then make a determination on any outstanding questions related to maintaining essential services.

#### Section 87.4(5): Referral to Board
"The Minister may refer to the Board any question with respect to whether an agreement entered into by the employer and the trade union is sufficient to ensure that subsection (1) is complied with."
This allows the Minister to escalate a dispute to the Board for review if they have concerns about the adequacy of the agreement in maintaining essential services.

#### Section 87.4(6): Board Order
"If, in determining an application made under subsection (4) or referral made under subsection (5), the Board is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section."
This section grants the Board broad powers to issue an order if it determines that a strike or lockout could endanger public safety. The order can specify essential services, methods of continuation, and any other measures deemed necessary.

### Restrictions After a Strike or Lockout

#### Section 87.5(1): Reinstatement of Employees
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."
This section places a restriction on employers immediately following a strike or lockout. They cannot unilaterally change employees' wages or other terms of employment without the bargaining agent's consent until the Board has made a determination and the requirements of Section 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met.

#### Section 87.5(2): Continuation of Strike or Lockout
"Unless the parties otherwise agree, the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment, and any rights, duties or privileges of the employees, the employer or the trade union in effect before the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) were met, continue to apply with respect to employees who are members of the bargaining unit and who have been assigned to maintain services, facilities and production pursuant to section 87.4."
This subsection clarifies that, absent a new agreement, the terms of employment in effect before the strike or lockout began continue to apply to employees assigned to maintain essential services.

#### Section 87.5(6): Board Review of Agreement
"On application by the employer or the trade union, or on referral by the Minister, during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the Board may, where in the Board’s opinion the circumstances warrant, review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under this section and make any orders that it considers appropriate in the circumstances."
This section allows the Board to revisit and potentially modify or overturn an agreement reached during the strike or lockout if it deems the circumstances warrant such action.

#### Section 87.5(8): Binding Method of Resolving Issues
"Where the Board is satisfied that the level of activity to be continued in compliance with subsection (1) renders ineffective the exercise of the right to strike or lockout, the Board may, on application by the employer or the trade union, direct a binding method of resolving the issues in dispute between the parties for the purpose of ensuring settlement of a dispute."
This section provides the Board with the power to impose a binding dispute resolution method if the essential services level maintained during the strike or lockout negates the effectiveness of the strike or lockout itself.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions are strikes and lockouts allowed to occur during the term of a collective agreement?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Strikes and Lockouts During a Collective Agreement Term

### Section 88.1: Strikes and Lockouts Prohibited During Term of Collective Agreement

Section 88.1 of the Canada Labour Code establishes the general prohibition on strikes and lockouts during the term of a collective agreement. It states:
"Strikes and lockouts are prohibited during the term of a collective agreement except if (a) a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, other than subsection 49(1); and (b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met."

This passage directly answers the question by outlining the two specific conditions under which strikes and lockouts are *not* prohibited during the term of a collective agreement. 

The first condition is that a notice to bargain collectively must have been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, excluding subsection 49(1). This indicates that the collective agreement must have been negotiated and ratified *after* a notice to bargain collectively had been served. 

The second condition is that the requirements of subsection 89(1) must have been met. Subsection 89(1) details the conditions that must be satisfied before an employer can declare a lockout or a trade union can authorize a strike. These conditions include that the employer or trade union must have given notice to bargain collectively, failed to bargain collectively within the specified period, bargained collectively but failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement, the Minister has taken action under subsection 72(2), twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or commissioner, or the Board has determined any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), and sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with. Therefore, even during a collective agreement term, a strike or lockout is only permissible if these overarching requirements have also been fulfilled.



### Section 87.4(2): Agreement on Maintenance of Activities

Section 87.4(2) further elaborates on the conditions for strikes and lockouts during a collective agreement term by requiring an agreement on the maintenance of activities. It states:
"An employer and a trade union must, no later than 15 days after the day on which notice to bargain collectively has been given, enter into an agreement with respect to compliance with subsection (1) that sets out (a) the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that they consider necessary to continue in the event of a strike or a lockout; and (b) the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production, including the approximate number of those employees that, in the opinion of the employer and the trade union, would be required for that purpose."

This passage highlights that even with a notice to bargain collectively and the requirements of subsection 89(1) met, a strike or lockout during a collective agreement term is still subject to an agreement on the maintenance of activities. This agreement must detail the essential services, facilities, or goods that must be maintained during the disruption, and the manner and extent to which this will be achieved. The agreement must also specify the approximate number of employees needed for this maintenance. The filing of this agreement with the Minister and Board has the same effect as an order of the Board, providing a framework for minimizing disruption to the public.



### Section 87.4(6): Board Order on Compliance

Section 87.4(6) outlines the Board's power to make an order on compliance with subsection (1) of section 87.4. It states:
"If, in determining an application made under subsection (4) or referral made under subsection (5), the Board is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, may, by order (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; (b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production; and (c) impose any measure that it considers appropriate for carrying out the requirements of this section."

This passage indicates that the Board has the authority to issue an order on compliance with subsection (1) of section 87.4, particularly if a strike or lockout could pose a danger to public safety. This order can designate essential services, facilities, or goods to be maintained, specify how this will be done, and impose any other measures deemed necessary. This Board order would be binding on the parties, ensuring that the minimum level of essential services is maintained during the disruption, even while a strike or lockout is in effect.



In summary, strikes and lockouts are generally prohibited during the term of a collective agreement. However, they are permissible only if a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part (excluding subsection 49(1)), and the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met. Furthermore, even with these conditions satisfied, an agreement on the maintenance of activities must be entered into within 15 days of the notice to bargain collectively, and the Board may issue an order on compliance if a strike or lockout could pose a danger to public safety.

## Conditions Preceding a Lockout or Strike

### Section 89: No Strike or Lockout Until Certain Requirements Met

Section 89 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the conditions that must be satisfied by an employer or a trade union before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike. It states,
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement; (c) the Minister has (i) received a notice, given under section 71 by either party to the dispute, informing the Minister of the failure of the parties to enter into or revise a collective agreement, or (ii) taken action under subsection 72(2); (d) twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister (i) notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board under subsection 72(1), (ii) notified the parties that a conciliation officer appointed under subsection 72(1) has reported, (iii) released a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a), or (iv) is deemed to have been reported to pursuant to subsection 75(2) or to have received the report pursuant to subsection 75(3); (e) the Board has determined any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5); and (f) sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with."

This section details a multi-step process. First, a notice to bargain collectively must have been given. Second, either bargaining has failed within the specified timeframe, or bargaining has occurred but a new or revised collective agreement has not been reached. Third, the Minister must have taken action, such as receiving a notice of failure to reach an agreement or releasing a conciliation report. Fourth, the Board must have determined any referral made under subsection 87.4(5). Finally, sections 87.2 and 87.3 must have been complied with. These cumulative conditions ensure that all avenues for peaceful resolution have been exhausted before a lockout or strike can be initiated.

### Section 91: Employer May Apply for Declaration that Strike Unlawful

Section 91 addresses the employer's right to seek a declaration from the Board that a strike is unlawful. It states,
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

This passage clarifies that an employer can apply to the Board for such a declaration if they believe a strike is in violation of the Canada Labour Code. The Board will then consider the employer's allegations and provide a declaration. If the Board declares the strike unlawful, it can issue an order, including requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration and give notice to the employees, enjoining any employee from participating in the strike, requiring any employee participating in the strike to perform their duties, and requiring the trade union to give notice of any order made against it to any employee to whom it applies. This provides a mechanism for an employer to seek judicial intervention to prevent an unlawful strike.

### Section 92: Declaration that Lockout Unlawful and Prohibition of Lockout

Section 92 outlines the conditions under which a trade union can apply to the Board for a declaration that a lockout is unlawful and a prohibition of the lockout. It states,
"Where a trade union alleges that an employer has declared or caused or is about to declare or cause a lockout of employees in contravention of this Part, the trade union may apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout was, is or would be unlawful and the Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the trade union so requests, may make an order (a) enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout; (b) requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment; and (c) requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee..."

This section mirrors the employer's right to seek a declaration of an unlawful strike, but in reverse. The trade union can apply to the Board for such a declaration and an order prohibiting the lockout. If the Board issues such an order, it can enjoin the employer from carrying out the lockout, enjoin any employee from participating in it, require any employee participating in it to perform their duties, and require the trade union to notify any employee to whom an order is made under paragraphs (b) or (c) of the Board's declaration. This provides a remedy for a trade union to prevent an unlawful lockout.

## Governor in Council Intervention to Defer Strikes or Lockouts

### Circumstances for Intervention

The Governor in Council can intervene to defer a strike or lockout
"...during the time commencing on the date of a dissolution of Parliament and ending on the date fixed for the return of the writs at the next following general election..." if, in their opinion, it
"...adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest..." This is outlined in Section 90(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

### Purpose of Intervention

The purpose of such intervention is to
"...the strike or lockout during the period commencing on the day the order is made and ending on the twenty-first day following the date fixed for the return of the writs." This deferral is intended to mitigate the potential negative impacts on the national interest that the strike or lockout might cause during the period between Parliaments.

Section 90(2) further clarifies this purpose by stating that the Minister must lay before Parliament a report stating the reasons for making the order
"...on any of the first ten sitting days of the first session of Parliament next following that time..." This report ensures transparency and accountability for the Governor in Council's decision to defer the strike or lockout, highlighting the consideration of the national interest as the primary driver.

individual_results.question: What recourse does an employer have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe a trade union has called or authorized a strike, or employees are participating in a strike, that contravenes the Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Recourse Against an Unlawful Strike

### Section 91: Employer Application for Declaration of Unlawful Strike

Section 91 outlines the primary recourse an employer has when they believe a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or employees are participating in one that violates the Canada Labour Code.
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

This passage directly answers the question by stating that an employer can apply to the Board for a declaration that a strike is unlawful. The employer must make an allegation that the strike contravenes the Code.

### Section 87.4: Maintenance of Activities During a Strike or Lockout

Section 87.4 details the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees to maintain essential services during a strike or lockout. While not a direct recourse against an unlawful strike, it provides a mechanism for the employer to mitigate the negative impacts of a strike that is deemed unlawful by the Board.
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."

This section emphasizes the ongoing responsibility to maintain essential services, which can help the employer minimize losses associated with an unlawful strike.

### Section 87.3: Secret Ballot Vote Requirements for Strikes and Lockouts

Section 87.3 establishes secret ballot vote requirements for both trade unions to declare a strike and employers to declare a lockout. This provision can be used by an employer to challenge a strike if they can demonstrate that the union failed to meet these requirements.
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union may not declare or authorize a strike unless it has, within the previous sixty days, or any longer period that may be agreed to in writing by the trade union and the employer, held a secret ballot vote among the employees in the unit and received the approval of the majority of the employees who voted."

An employer can argue that a strike is unlawful if they can prove that the union did not conduct the secret ballot vote as required by this section.

### Section 94: Unfair Practices: Employer Interference in Trade Union

Section 94 prohibits employers from interfering with the formation or administration of a trade union or contributing financial support to one. An employer can use this section to challenge a strike if they can demonstrate that the union was formed or administered through unfair practices, including employer interference.
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..."

This passage highlights the employer's ability to challenge a strike if they can show that the union's formation or administration involved employer interference.

### Section 95: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

Section 95 lists numerous prohibitions relating to trade unions, including attempting to compel an employer to bargain collectively if the union is not the bargaining agent, bargaining collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit if another trade union is the bargaining agent, and expelling or suspending an employee from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay dues. An employer can use this section to challenge a strike if they can demonstrate that the union engaged in any of these prohibited practices.
"No trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall (a) seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer..."

This passage provides a broad range of prohibitions that an employer can use to challenge a strike if they can show that the union violated one of them.

## Recourse for a Trade Union Alleging an Unlawful Lockout

### Section 92: Declaration that Lockout Unlawful and Prohibition of Lockout

Section 92 outlines the specific recourse a trade union has when it alleges an employer has declared or caused an lockout in contravention of Part I of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where a trade union alleges that an employer has declared or caused or is about to declare or cause a lockout of employees in contravention of this Part, the trade union may apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout was, is or would be unlawful and the Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the trade union so requests, may make an order (a) enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout; (b) requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment; and (c) requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout."

This passage clearly states that the trade union can apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout is unlawful. If the Board issues such a declaration, it has a range of orders it can make against the employer. These orders include
"...enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout..."
"...requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment..." and
"...requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout." These actions are designed to immediately halt the lockout and restore employees to their jobs.

### Section 91: Declaration that Strike Unlawful and Prohibition of Strike

Section 91, while addressing unlawful strikes, also provides a framework that can be applied to unlawful lockouts. It details the process by which an employer can apply to the Board for a declaration that a strike is unlawful. The Board, after affording the trade union an opportunity to make representations, can issue such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, make an order.
"Where an employer applies to the Board under subsection (1) for a declaration that a strike was, is or would be unlawful, the Board may, after affording the trade union or employees referred to in subsection (1) an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, may make an order (a) requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and to give notice of such revocation forthwith to the employees to whom it was directed; (b) enjoining any employee from participating in the strike; (c) requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment; and (d) requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, forthwith to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies."

This order can be adapted to an unlawful lockout scenario. For instance, it could
"...enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout..." It could also
"...requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment..." Furthermore, it could
"...requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout." This demonstrates that the Board has the power to issue orders that directly address the unlawful lockout, including its immediate cessation and the restoration of employees' jobs.

individual_results.question: What are the considerations and procedures involved when the Board makes an order, and how can the order be adjusted over time?
individual_results.answer:
## Finality of Board Orders

### Section 156: Decision Final
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This section establishes the fundamental principle of finality for Board orders and decisions. It unequivocally states that such orders are not subject to judicial review. This means that once issued, they are binding and cannot be challenged in the courts. This finality is a cornerstone of the Board's decision-making process, providing certainty and closure to disputes.

### Section 22: Finality and Exceptions
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act."
Section 22 reinforces the finality of Board orders, mirroring the language of Section 156. However, it introduces a narrow exception. It specifies that judicial review is only permissible in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on very limited grounds, namely those related to the Board's jurisdiction or exceeding its authority. This exception is crucial as it acknowledges the possibility of judicial oversight in exceptional circumstances, while maintaining the overall principle of finality.

### Section 247.991: No Review by Certiorari, etc.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 247.99."
This section further emphasizes the lack of judicial review for Board orders issued under section 247.99, which pertains to genetic testing. It explicitly prohibits any court action aimed at questioning, reviewing, prohibiting, or restraining the Board's proceedings in this area. This strong prohibition underscores the Board's autonomy in making decisions related to genetic testing and its immunity from external judicial interference.

## Adjusting Board Orders Over Time

"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal; (c) award costs in the proceedings; and (d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board."

"For the purposes of this Division, the Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing circumstances for the purposes of paragraph 247.99(3)(b); (b) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 247.99(6); (c) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1); and (d) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1)."

## Restrictions on Employers' Interactions with Trade Unions and Employees' Union Activities

### Section 94: Unfair Practices: Employer Interference in Trade Unions

Section 94 of the Canada Labour Code outlines numerous restrictions on employers regarding their interactions with trade unions and their employees' union activities. These prohibitions aim to prevent employers from intimidating, coercing, or retaliating against employees for their union involvement.

#### Section 94(1)(a): Prohibiting Employer Participation in Trade Union Formation or Administration
"No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..." This section establishes a fundamental restriction on employers from actively influencing the creation or operation of a trade union or its ability to represent employees. It prohibits any form of involvement, whether positive or negative.

#### Section 94(1)(b): Prohibiting Financial or Other Support to Trade Unions
"(b) contribute financial or other support to a trade union." This prohibition extends to any form of financial or material assistance an employer provides to a trade union. This is intended to maintain a level playing field and prevent employers from unduly influencing union activities through funding.

#### Section 94(1)(c): Prohibiting Employer Expression of Personal Political Views
"(c) express a personal point of view, so long as the employer does not use coercion, intimidation, threats, promises or undue influence." While employers are generally allowed to express their personal political views, this section clarifies that they cannot do so in a way that coerces or unduly influences employees' union decisions.

#### Section 94(1)(d): Prohibiting Employer Conditions on Employment
"...impose any condition in a contract of employment that restrains, or has the effect of restraining, an employee from exercising any right conferred on them by this Part..." This section prohibits employers from including clauses in employment contracts that limit employees' ability to engage in union activities, such as speaking with union representatives during work hours.

#### Section 94(1)(e): Prohibiting Employer Retaliation Against Union Activities
"(e) seek, by intimidation, threat of dismissal or any other kind of threat, by the imposition of a financial or other penalty or by any other means, to compel a person to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member, officer or representative of a trade union or to refrain from (i) testifying or otherwise participating in a proceeding under this Part, (ii) making a disclosure that the person may be required to make in a proceeding under this Part, or (iii) making an application or filing a complaint under this Part..." This section is a strong prohibition against employers using threats or penalties to discourage employees from unionizing or participating in union activities.

#### Section 94(1)(f): Prohibiting Employer Disciplinary Action Against Union Activities
"(f) suspend, discharge or impose any financial or other penalty on a person employed by them, or take any other disciplinary action against such a person, by reason of that person having refused to perform an act that is prohibited by this Part..." This section prevents employers from disciplining employees for exercising their union rights, such as refusing to participate in a strike that is not prohibited by the Code.

#### Section 94(1)(g): Prohibiting Employer Bargaining Collectively with a Trade Union That is Not the Bargaining Agent
"(g) bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with a trade union in respect of a bargaining unit, if another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit." This section prevents employers from engaging in collective bargaining with a trade union that is not the recognized bargaining agent for the employees in the unit.

### Section 95: Unfair Practices: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

Section 95 further details prohibitions against unfair practices related to trade unions.

#### Section 95(a): Prohibiting Employer Compulsion of Collective Bargaining
"No trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall (a) seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer..." This section mirrors the prohibition in Section 94(1)(g), preventing a trade union from pressuring an employer to bargain when another union is already the bargaining agent.

#### Section 95(b): Prohibiting Employer Bargaining Collectively with a Trade Union That is Not the Bargaining Agent
"(b) bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit, if that trade union or person knows or, in the opinion of the Board, ought to know that another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit..." This section reinforces the prohibition against bargaining collectively with a trade union that is not the bargaining agent, emphasizing the employer's right to choose their bargaining representative.

#### Section 95(c): Prohibiting Employer Interference in Trade Union Formation or Administration
"(c) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employers’ organization..." This section prohibits trade unions from meddling in the internal affairs of employers' organizations.

#### Section 95(d): Prohibiting Employer Attempts to Persuade Employees to Leave a Trade Union
"...except with the consent of the employer of an employee, attempt, at an employee’s place of employment during the working hours of the employee, to persuade the employee to become, to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union..." This section prohibits trade unions from attempting to pressure employees to leave their union during work hours without the employer's permission.

#### Section 95(e): Prohibiting Employer Requirements for Trade Union Membership
"...require an employer to terminate the employment of an employee because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union..." This section prevents employers from firing employees solely because they have been expelled or suspended from their union for reasons other than financial obligations.

#### Section 95(f): Prohibiting Employer Discriminatory Trade Union Membership Rules
"...expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or deny membership in the trade union to an employee by applying to the employee in a discriminatory manner the membership rules of the trade union..." This section prohibits trade unions from applying discriminatory membership rules.

"...take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by applying to that employee in a discriminatory manner the standards of discipline of the trade union..." This section prevents trade unions from imposing discriminatory disciplinary actions on employees for their union activities.

"...expel or suspend an employee from membership in the trade union or take disciplinary action against or impose any form of penalty on an employee by reason of that employee having refused to perform an act that is contrary to this Part..." ## Consequences for Employers or Individuals Using Intimidation or Coercion Regarding Trade Union Membership or Employment Status

### Section 94(e) - General Prohibition on Intimidation

Section 94(e) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly prohibits employers or individuals acting on their behalf from using intimidation, threat of dismissal, or any other kind of threat to compel a person to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member, officer, or representative of a trade union, or to refrain from activities related to trade union promotion, formation, or administration.
"...seek, by intimidation, threat of dismissal or any other kind of threat, by the imposition of a financial or other penalty or by any other means, to compel a person to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member, officer or representative of a trade union or to refrain from (i) testifying or otherwise participating in a proceeding under this Part, (ii) making a disclosure that the person may be required to make in a proceeding under this Part, or (iii) making an application or filing a complaint under this Part..."

This passage directly addresses the question by outlining the prohibited conduct. It details the various forms of intimidation that are forbidden, including threats of dismissal, financial penalties, and other coercive tactics. The section further specifies that this prohibition extends to actions that aim to prevent individuals from exercising their trade union rights, such as testifying in proceedings, making disclosures, or filing complaints.

### Section 147 - Abuse of Rights

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the issue of employers taking disciplinary action against employees for exercising their rights under the Part. It states that an employer cannot
"...impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

While Section 147 does not explicitly mention intimidation or coercion, it underscores the prohibition against retaliatory actions against employees for exercising their trade union rights. This retaliation can manifest as disciplinary measures, including financial penalties or termination of employment, which are all forms of pressure and coercion.

### Section 95 - Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

Section 95 of the Canada Labour Code contains a comprehensive list of prohibitions relating to trade unions and employers' interactions with them. Subsection (4) specifically prohibits employers from using the services of replacement workers during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part. This prohibition is linked to the concern that replacement workers can be used to pressure employees to abandon their union membership or strike.
"Subject to subsection (7), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, no employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall use the services of any of the following persons to perform all or part of the duties of an employee who is in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out: (a) any employee or any person who performs management functions or who is employed in a confidential capacity in matters related to industrial relations, if that employee or person is hired after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (b) any contractor, other than a dependent contractor, or any employee of another employer; (c) any employee whose normal workplace is a workplace other than that at which the strike or lockout is taking place or who was transferred to the workplace at which the strike or lockout is taking place after the day on which notice to bargain collectively is given; (d) any volunteer, student or member of the public."

This subsection highlights the employer's obligation to refrain from using replacement workers as a tactic to undermine union efforts. The prohibition is designed to prevent employers from circumventing the legal framework designed to protect employees' rights to strike and bargain collectively.

### Section 94(d) - Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

Section 94(d) of the Canada Labour Code prohibits employers from imposing conditions in a contract of employment that restrain, or have the effect of restraining, an employee from exercising any right conferred on them by this Part. This prohibition is relevant to the question because it prevents employers from using employment contracts to pressure employees to abandon their union membership or strike.
"...impose any condition in a contract of employment that restrains, or has the effect of restraining, an employee from exercising any right conferred on them by this Part..."

This subsection ensures that employees are not penalized for exercising their trade union rights, such as participating in a strike or filing a complaint. Employers cannot use employment contracts to create a chilling effect on union activity.

In conclusion, the Canada Labour Code contains numerous provisions that prohibit employers and individuals from using intimidation or coercion to influence an individual's decision regarding trade union membership or their employment status. These prohibitions are designed to protect employees' rights to organize, bargain collectively, and exercise their trade union rights without fear of retaliation.

## Filing a Labour Standards Complaint with the Labour Program

### Before You File a Complaint

The Labour Program outlines several crucial steps to take *before* formally submitting a complaint.
"If you are a unionized employee covered by a collective agreement, which provides for third party resolution provisions, you must first contact your union representative to discuss: the issue, and how it might be addressed In most instances, the Labour Program is not authorized to handle your complaint which may be rejected." This indicates that unionized employees are obligated to exhaust internal dispute resolution mechanisms with their union before approaching the Labour Program. The Program's limited authority to handle such complaints is explicitly stated.

### Eligibility and Timelines

Strict eligibility criteria and deadlines apply to all types of labour standards complaints.
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you." This sets a firm time limit for pursuing unpaid wages or other financial entitlements.
"You must file your non-monetary complaint within 6 months from the day you were aware of the issue." This provides a slightly longer window for complaints not involving direct monetary loss, such as denied flexible work arrangements.
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal." This is the most stringent deadline, emphasizing the urgency of addressing wrongful termination. Furthermore, specific eligibility requirements must be met for an unjust dismissal complaint to be accepted, including at least 12 consecutive months of employment without a collective agreement and not being a manager.

### Complete the Complaint Form

The Labour Program requires a comprehensive complaint form to be filled out. While the exact form is not provided in the documents, the section "Complete the complaint form" clearly indicates its necessity. This form will likely request detailed information about the alleged violation, including dates, times, individuals involved, and any supporting documentation.

### Provide Records

Submitting relevant documentation is a critical requirement for a strong complaint.
"If relevant to your complaint allegations, you should provide:  pay stubs  employment contracts, and  employee records or receipts..." This lists the primary types of records that should be included.
"For complaints related to wages or other amounts owed, you should only provide documents covering a period of 24 months prior to the complaint." This provides a specific timeframe for wage-related documentation.
"If your employer provided the reasons for your  dismissal in writing, you should provide a copy of that letter.  Do  not submit genetic test results to the Labour Program." This clarifies the type of dismissal letter required and explicitly prohibits the submission of genetic test results.

### Submit Your Complaint

The final step is formally submitting the completed complaint form and supporting records.
"Submit your complaint" is a clear heading indicating this action. The documents do not detail the specific submission method (e.g., online portal, mail), but this section signifies the culmination of the preparation process.

### After You File a Complaint

The Labour Program outlines the actions it will take following the submission of a complaint.
"The Labour Program will accept and investigate your complaint if filed within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you..." This reiterates the monetary complaint timeframe.
"After you file a complaint, the Labour Program may write to you about  your complaint asking for you to provide information or answer questions within certain timelines. As such, during this  time it is important that you keep the Labour Program updated as to any changes in your contact information. If you do not respond  to the Labour Program correspondence within noted timelines, the Labour Program will consider your complaint abandoned and issue a Notice of Complaint Rejection." This highlights the interactive nature of the investigation, involving requests for further information and the potential for the complaint to be dismissed if the complainant is unresponsive.
"If an agreement is not reached, at your request, the Labour Program may refer the complaint to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (the “Board”)." This outlines the escalation path if the Labour Program's initial efforts at settlement fail.

individual_results.answer:
## Process for Handling a Complaint Made Under Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 97: Making a Complaint to the Board

Section 97(1) outlines the general process for making a complaint to the Board. It states that
"...any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96." This indicates a broad scope of potential violations that can be brought before the Board.

Section 97(2) specifies the time limit for making a complaint. It mandates that
"...a complaint pursuant to subsection (1) must be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint." This deadline is crucial for ensuring the Board has timely information to address the issue.

### Section 98: Duty and Power of the Board

Section 98(1) details the Board's initial approach upon receiving a complaint. It states that
"Subject to subsection (3), on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint." This highlights the Board's primary role as a facilitator of settlement. However, if settlement is not achieved, the Board has the authority to make a decision on the merits of the complaint.

Section 98(3) outlines a limitation on the Board's ability to determine a complaint. It states that
"The Board may refuse to determine any complaint made pursuant to section 97 in respect of a matter that, in the opinion of the Board, could be referred by the complainant pursuant to a collective agreement to an arbitrator or arbitration board." This provision recognizes the role of internal dispute resolution mechanisms established through collective agreements.

Section 98(4) establishes the burden of proof when a complaint is made in writing pursuant to section 97 in respect of an alleged failure by an employer or any person acting on behalf of an employer to comply with subsection 94(3). It states that
"Where a complaint is made in writing pursuant to section 97 in respect of an alleged failure by an employer or any person acting on behalf of an employer to comply with subsection 94(3), the written complaint is itself evidence that such failure actually occurred and, if any party to the complaint proceedings alleges that such failure did not occur, the burden of proof thereof is on that party." This rule simplifies the process by treating the written complaint as prima facie evidence of the violation.

## Factors Influencing the Board's Decision to Assist Parties or Determine the Complaint

### Section 98(1): Board's Approach

Section 98(1) indicates that the Board's decision to assist parties or determine the complaint is influenced by whether settlement can be achieved. It states that the Board
"...may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint." This suggests a preference for facilitating a mutually agreeable solution before issuing a formal decision.

### Section 98(3): Referral to Arbitration

Section 98(3) highlights a factor that can influence the Board's decision. It states that
"The Board may refuse to determine any complaint made pursuant to section 97 in respect of a matter that, in the opinion of the Board, could be referred by the complainant pursuant to a collective agreement to an arbitrator or arbitration board." This means that if the collective agreement provides for arbitration on the specific issue, the Board may decline to make a determination itself.

### Section 98(4): Burden of Proof

Section 98(4) outlines a factor that can affect the Board's decision by shifting the burden of proof. It states that
"Where a complaint is made in writing pursuant to section 97 in respect of an alleged failure by an employer or any person acting on behalf of an employer to comply with subsection 94(3), the written complaint is itself evidence that such failure actually occurred and, if any party to the complaint proceedings alleges that such failure did not occur, the burden of proof thereof is on that party." This rule can expedite the process by requiring the party denying the violation to prove it.

### Section 97(4): Limitation on Complaints Against Trade Unions

Section 97(4) introduces a limitation on complaints against trade unions. It states that
"Subject to subsection (5), no complaint shall be made to the Board under subsection (1) on the ground that a trade union or any person acting on behalf of a trade union has failed to comply with paragraph 95(f) or (g) unless (a) the complainant has presented a grievance or appeal in accordance with any procedure that has been established by the trade union and to which the complainant has been given ready access; (b) the trade union (i) has dealt with the grievance or appeal of the complainant in a manner unsatisfactory to the complainant, or (ii) has not, within six months after the date on which the complainant first presented their grievance or appeal pursuant to paragraph (a), dealt with the grievance or appeal; and (c) the complaint is made to the Board not later than ninety days after the first day on which the complainant could, in accordance with paragraphs (a) and (b), make the complaint." This provision ensures that complaints against trade unions are only pursued after a proper grievance procedure has been followed and the union has failed to address the complaint adequately.

## Section 134: Board Orders for Contraventions

### Enforcement of Orders

Section 134(1) outlines the Board's power to issue orders when it determines an employer has contravened section 147. It states,
"...the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This passage is crucial because it directly answers the question. It details the range of actions the Board can order an employer to take to rectify a contravention of section 147. These orders are comprehensive, addressing reinstatement, compensation, rescinding disciplinary action, and ensuring affected employees can return to their jobs. The Board's power extends beyond simply finding a contravention; it can compel the employer to implement specific corrective measures.

### Additional Board Powers under Section 98

Section 98(1) further elaborates on the Board's ability to act upon a complaint. It states,
"Subject to subsection (3), on receipt of a complaint made under section 97, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint."

This indicates that the Board's response to a complaint is not limited to issuing orders. It has the power to facilitate settlement between the parties. However, if settlement is not achieved, the Board can formally determine the complaint. This determination can take various forms, including orders similar to those outlined in Section 134(1), or other remedies deemed appropriate by the Board.

### Section 133: Complaint to Board and Board Orders

Section 133(5) also highlights the Board's power to issue orders. It states,
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This passage reinforces the Board's ability to issue orders after a complaint is received. It emphasizes the Board's role in both facilitating settlement and, if that fails, formally determining the complaint and issuing orders to address the contravention.

### Section 246.3: Rejection of Complaint

While Section 246.3 discusses the Board's power to reject a complaint, it does not detail what the Board can do if it determines a party has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code. It focuses on the Board's grounds for rejection, such as the complaint being frivolous or not made in good faith, or the matter being adequately dealt with through other means. Therefore, this section is not directly relevant to the question.

### Section 134(2): Notice of Rejection

Section 134(2) states,
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons." This passage is also not directly relevant to the question, as it describes the Board's action when it *rejects* a complaint, not what it does when it *determines* a complaint and issues orders.

### Section 97: Complaints to the Board

Section 97(1) outlines the types of complaints that can be made to the Board. It states,
"Subject to subsections (2) to (5), any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96."

This section is relevant because it establishes the Board's role as a forum for receiving complaints about contraventions of various provisions of the Canada Labour Code. However, it does not detail the Board's subsequent actions once a complaint is received and determined.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board certify a trade union even if there is no evidence that it has the support of a majority of employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Certification of Bargaining Agents Without Majority Support

### Section 25: Application for Certification: Where certification prohibited

Section 25 outlines specific circumstances where the Board is prohibited from certifying a trade union, even if it appears to have majority support. It states,
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for any unit comprised of employees of the employer and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer that applies to any such employees shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part." This indicates that if the Board determines a union is excessively controlled by an employer, it will not be certified, regardless of its membership numbers.

Furthermore, Section 25 addresses situations where a union denies membership to employees based on qualifications. It specifies,
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union denies membership in the trade union to any employee or class of employees in a bargaining unit by virtue of a policy or practice that the trade union applies relating to qualifications for membership in the trade union, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer of the employees in the bargaining unit that applies to the bargaining unit shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part." This provision reinforces the Board's power to deny certification if a union's membership practices are discriminatory or violate its own charter.

### Section 29: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters: Representation vote

Section 29 details the Board's authority to order a representation vote to determine employee support for a union. It states,
"The Board may, in any case, for the purpose of satisfying itself as to whether employees in a unit wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This highlights that the Board can initiate a vote even if it lacks initial evidence of majority support.

Section 29(2) further elaborates on this,
"If a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit in respect of which no other trade union is the bargaining agent, and the Board is satisfied that not less than 35% and not more than 50% of the employees in the unit are members of the trade union, the Board shall order that a representation vote be taken among the employees in the unit." This sets a threshold for the Board to order a vote. While a union needs at least 35% membership to trigger a vote, the Board can still order one if it has reason to believe the union has significant support.

### Section 30: Conduct of Vote

Section 30 outlines the Board's responsibilities in conducting a representation vote. It states,
"Where the Board orders that a representation vote be taken among employees in a unit, the Board shall (a) determine the employees that are eligible to vote; and (b) make such arrangements and give such directions as the Board considers necessary for the proper conduct of the representation vote, including the preparation of ballots, the method of casting and counting ballots and the custody and sealing of ballot boxes." This ensures the vote is conducted fairly and according to established procedures.

Section 30(3) addresses situations where a union receives more than 50% of the ballots cast but does not secure a majority. It clarifies,
"Notwithstanding subsection (2), where the employees in a unit have cast ballots in favour of all trade unions involved in a representation vote totalling more than fifty per cent of all the ballots cast but have not given majority support to one trade union in that vote and, as a result, a second or subsequent representation vote is required, the Board shall not be required to include the choice referred to in subsection (2) in the ballots for the second or subsequent vote." This provision prevents the Board from including a "no preference" option in subsequent votes if no single union wins a majority in the first.

In summary, the Board can certify a trade union even without evidence of a majority of employee support under specific circumstances. These include when the union is excessively dominated by an employer, when its membership practices are discriminatory, or when a first vote does not produce a majority, but the Board has reason to believe the union has significant support (between 35% and 50% membership). The Board also has the power to order a representation vote itself to satisfy itself about employee preferences.
