## Primary Responsibilities of a Health and Safety Representative in a Workplace with Fewer Than 20 Employees

### Section 136: Appointment of Health and Safety Representative

Section 136 outlines the process for appointing a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than twenty employees or one where a workplace committee is not required. It states:
"(2) The health and safety representative for a work place shall be selected as follows: (a) the employees at the work place who do not exercise managerial functions shall select from among those employees the person to be appointed; or (b) if those employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union shall select the person to be appointed, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented, and subject to any regulations made under subsection (11)."

This indicates that the selection of the health and safety representative is either done by the non-managerial employees at the workplace or by the trade union representing those employees, in consultation with any non-unionized employees. The employer is responsible for performing the functions of the representative until a person is selected.

### Section 136: Duties of Representative

Section 136(5) details the comprehensive duties of a health and safety representative. These duties are extensive and cover a wide range of aspects related to occupational health and safety.
"(a) shall consider and expeditiously dispose of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees; (b) shall ensure that adequate records are maintained pertaining to work accidents, injuries, health hazards and the disposition of complaints related to the health and safety of employees and regularly monitor data relating to those accidents, injuries, hazards and complaints; (c) shall meet with the employer as necessary to address health and safety matters; (d) shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c); (e) where the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c) does not cover certain hazards unique to that work place, shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of those hazards that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters related to those hazards; (f) where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the work place that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters; (g) shall participate in all of the inquiries, investigations, studies and inspections pertaining to the health and safety of employees, including any consultations that may be necessary with persons who are professionally or technically qualified to advise the representative on those matters; (h) shall cooperate with the Head; (i) shall participate in the implementation of changes that may affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures and, where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the planning of the implementation of those changes; (j) shall inspect each month all or part of the work place, so that every part of the work place is inspected at least once each year; (k) shall participate in the development of health and safety policies and programs; (l) shall assist the employer in investigating and assessing the exposure of employees to hazardous substances; and (m) shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials and, where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the development of the program."

These duties demonstrate that the health and safety representative is a key figure in promoting and maintaining a safe working environment. They are responsible for addressing employee concerns, tracking safety data, collaborating with management, participating in investigations, conducting inspections, and contributing to the development of safety policies and programs.

### Section 136: Time Required for Duties and Payment of Wages

Section 136(8) and (9) address the time commitment and compensation for the representative's duties.
"(8) A health and safety representative is entitled to take the time required, during their regular working hours, (a) to perform any of the representative’s functions; and (b) for the purposes of preparation and travel, as authorized by both chairpersons of the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, as authorized by the employer."
"(9) A health and safety representative shall be compensated by the employer for the functions described in paragraphs (8)(a) and (b), whether performed during or outside the representative’s regular working hours, at the representative’s regular rate of pay or premium rate of pay, as specified in the collective agreement or, if there is no collective agreement, in accordance with the employer’s policy."

These sections ensure that the representative is adequately compensated for the significant time and effort required to fulfill their responsibilities. They are entitled to use their regular working hours for their duties and will be paid their regular or premium rate of pay for any time spent on these tasks, even outside of their scheduled hours, with proper authorization.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident be revealed to a health and safety representative?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Revealing Identity to a Health and Safety Representative

### General Rule: Consent is Required

Section 136.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes a clear principle:
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place." This indicates that, as a general rule, the identity of a person involved in a workplace harassment and violence incident cannot be disclosed to a health and safety representative without their explicit consent.

### Exceptions to the Consent Requirement

Section 136.1(1) also outlines two exceptions to this consent rule.
"Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to (a) information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections; or (b) a decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2)." These exceptions pertain to information shared under specific sections of the Canada Labour Code or those related to decisions and directions made under subsection 146.1(2). However, these exceptions do not directly address the general rule of requiring consent for any information likely to reveal identity.

### Employer's Obligation to Obtain Consent

Section 943-1-IPG-081_11 elaborates on the employer's responsibility to obtain consent.
"For each person involved, the employer may obtain consent  for all disclosures at the same time, as long as this is made clear to the  person involved, or may obtain each consent separately so that the person  involved can pick and choose which consent to grant. Before a person involved makes a decision with regard to  consent, the employer should ensure the employee can make an informed decision.  The person should receive all necessary information about the regulatory  requirements (for example, the role of the CP), and be informed about the  consequences of giving consent or not (for example, there is the chance the CP  may discover their identity through other means). The employer must be able to demonstrate the required  consent was obtained from the persons involved. Therefore, it is recommended  the employer obtain consent in writing; a template “consent form” is found at Appendix B." This passage emphasizes the employer's duty to provide sufficient information to the individual involved so they can make an informed decision about whether or not to grant consent. It also recommends obtaining consent in writing for documentation purposes.

### Information Likely to Reveal Identity

Section 136.1(1) specifies that the information disclosed to a health and safety representative cannot be
"...likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place." This highlights the importance of carefully considering the content of any information shared with the representative to avoid compromising the individual's privacy.

### Health and Safety Representatives' Access

Section 136.1(1) also states that a health and safety representative
"...shall not have access to that information without the person’s consent." This reinforces the principle that access to information about individuals involved in workplace harassment and violence incidents is strictly limited to those who have given their permission.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances may an employer need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Requiring Multiple Workplace Health and Safety Committees or Representatives

### Section 135: Mandatory Workplace Health and Safety Committees

Section 135 outlines the general requirement for employers to establish workplace health and safety committees for each workplace where twenty or more employees are normally employed. However, it also includes an exception.
"An employer is not required to establish a committee under subsection (1) for a work place that is on board a ship in respect of employees whose base is the ship." This exception pertains to workplaces located on ships.

### Section 137: Multiple Workplace Health and Safety Committees or Representatives

Section 137 directly addresses the scenario where an employer may need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives. It states:
"Despite sections 135 and 136, if an employer controls more than one work place or the size or nature of the operations of the employer or those of the work place precludes the effective functioning of a single work place committee or health and safety representative, as the case may be, for those work places, the employer shall, subject to the approval or in accordance with the direction of the Head, establish or appoint in accordance with section 135 or 136, as the case may be, a work place committee or health and safety representative for the work places that are specified in the approval or direction."

This section clearly indicates that an employer may need multiple committees or representatives when they control more than one workplace, or when the size or nature of their operations makes a single committee or representative ineffective. The establishment of these multiple bodies is subject to approval or direction from the Head.

### Section 136: Duties of Health and Safety Representatives

Section 136 details the duties of health and safety representatives. While it doesn't explicitly state circumstances requiring multiple representatives, it does mention that a health and safety representative is appointed for each workplace.
"Every employer shall, for each work place controlled by the employer at which fewer than twenty employees are normally employed or for which an employer is not required to establish a work place committee, appoint the person selected in accordance with subsection (2) as the health and safety representative for that work place." This confirms that a health and safety representative is appointed per workplace, implying the potential for multiple representatives if an employer controls multiple workplaces.

### Section 134.1: Policy Health and Safety Committees

Section 134.1 discusses policy health and safety committees, which are mandatory for employers who normally employ directly three hundred or more employees. It also allows employers with fewer than three hundred employees to establish such a committee, subject to certain conditions.
"For the purposes of addressing health and safety matters that apply to the work, undertaking or business of an employer, every employer who normally employs directly three hundred or more employees shall establish a policy health and safety committee and, subject to section 135.1, select and appoint its members." This establishes a mandatory policy committee for larger employers. The section further allows for the establishment of multiple policy committees with the agreement of the trade union and/or the employees.
"An employer may establish more than one policy committee with the agreement of (a) the trade union, if any, representing the employees; and (b) the employees, in the case of employees not represented by a trade union." This directly answers the question by stating that an employer may establish multiple policy committees under specific circumstances.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission and how is it structured?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

### Section 137.1: Establishment of Commission
"There is hereby established a Coal Mining Safety Commission, in this section referred to as the “Commission” consisting of, subject to subsection (2.1), not more than five members to be appointed by the Minister to hold office during pleasure."

This section explicitly states the purpose of the Commission: its establishment. It details the Commission's composition, which is a maximum of five members appointed by the Minister. The term of office is "during pleasure," indicating the Minister has the discretion to remove members at any time.

### Section 137.2: Approval of plans, procedures
"The Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)."

This section outlines a key function of the Commission: the approval of plans and procedures related to coal mining methods, machinery, and equipment. It states that the Commission or designated persons can approve these plans in writing, with or without changes. This approval is contingent upon the Commission's opinion that it will not diminish the health and safety of employees.

### Section 137.1: Members of Commission
"One member of the Commission shall be designated chairperson of the Commission by the Minister and the others shall be equally representative of the non-supervisory employees employed in coal mines and of the employers of those employees."

This section elaborates on the Commission's structure by describing its membership. It specifies that there will be a chairperson, appointed by the Minister, and the remaining members will be equally divided between non-supervisory employees and employers in the coal mines. This ensures a balanced perspective in the Commission's decision-making process.

### Section 137.1: Alternate Chairperson
"The Minister may appoint, by order, and under the terms and conditions specified in the order, any person as an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the chairperson. An alternate chairperson, while acting as chairperson, has all of the powers, duties and immunity of the chairperson."

This section details the provision for an alternate chairperson. The Minister can appoint an alternate chairperson to step in if the chairperson is unavailable. The alternate chairperson has all the same powers, duties, and immunity as the regular chairperson while performing those duties. This ensures continuity in the Commission's operations.

### Section 137.1: Quorum
"A quorum of the Commission consists of the chairperson or alternate chairperson, one member representative of non-supervisory employees and one member representative of employers."

This section defines the minimum number of members required for the Commission to conduct business. A quorum is formed by the chairperson or alternate chairperson, one member representing non-supervisory employees, and one member representing employers. This ensures that there is sufficient representation from all stakeholders to make informed decisions.

## Structure of the Coal Mining Safety Commission

### Section 137.1: Membership
"One member of the Commission shall be designated chairperson of the Commission by the Minister and the others shall be equally representative of the non-supervisory employees employed in coal mines and of the employers of those employees."

As mentioned above, the Commission is structured with a chairperson appointed by the Minister and the remaining members equally representing non-supervisory employees and employers.

### Section 137.1: Chairperson and Alternate Chairperson
"The Minister may appoint, by order, and under the terms and conditions specified in the order, any person as an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the chairperson. An alternate chairperson, while acting as chairperson, has all of the powers, duties and immunity of the chairperson."

The Commission also has an alternate chairperson who can assume the responsibilities of the chairperson if needed. This provides a backup plan for leadership.

### Section 137.1: By-laws
"The Commission may, subject to the approval of the Minister, make by-laws for the conduct of its activities."

The Commission has the authority to create its own internal rules and procedures, subject to the Minister's approval. This allows the Commission to adapt its operations to its specific needs.

### Section 137.1: Staff and other assistance
"The Minister may, at the request of the Commission, make available to the Commission such staff and other assistance as are necessary for the proper conduct of its activities."

The Commission can request support from the Minister, including staff and other resources, to effectively carry out its functions.

### Section 137.1: Annual Report
"The Commission shall, within sixty days following the end of each calendar year, submit a report to the Minister of its activities during the year."

The Commission is required to submit an annual report to the Minister detailing its accomplishments and activities during the past year. This promotes transparency and accountability.

individual_results.question: What is the primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions?
individual_results.answer:
## Primary Goal of the Commission in Approving Plans, Procedures, Methods, Machinery, and Equipment

### Section 137.2(1) - General Approval Standard
"The Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may approve in writing, with or without modification, plans or procedures submitted in accordance with paragraph 125.3(1)(d)."

This section establishes the Commission's fundamental principle when reviewing plans and procedures. It states that approval is granted "in writing, with or without modification," provided the plans and procedures are submitted according to the specified requirements. This indicates a willingness to work with employers to develop safe practices, rather than simply rejecting proposals outright. The Commission's role is to assess the plans and procedures and determine if they meet the safety standards, potentially suggesting changes to enhance those standards.

### Section 137.2(2) - Health and Safety as Paramount
"On the application of an employer, the Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..."

This subsection explicitly identifies "protection of the health and safety of employees" as the Commission's primary consideration when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions. The phrase
"...if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..." is crucial. It highlights that the Commission will only approve such changes if it is confident that the overall safety level will not be compromised. This demonstrates a cautious and safety-focused approach to regulatory flexibility.

### Section 137.2(2)(a) - Approving Non-Prescribed Safety Standards
"...or (b) approve in writing, notwithstanding anything in this Part, the use by the employer in coal mines, for a specified time and subject to specified conditions, of any mining method, machinery or equipment that does not meet prescribed safety standards applicable in respect of it."

This subsection provides a specific example of how the Commission applies its health and safety standard. It states that the Commission can approve the use of mining methods, machinery, or equipment that do not meet prescribed safety standards, but only
"...for a specified time and subject to specified conditions..." This indicates that the Commission is willing to allow for the use of newer or less-established technologies, but only if there are safeguards in place to prevent harm to employees. The conditionality is key, ensuring that the approval is not a blanket endorsement of unsafe practices.

### Section 137.2(3) - Exemptions and Substitutions
"On the application of an employer, the Commission may, if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, by order, (a) exempt the employer from compliance with any provision of the regulations in the operation of coal mines controlled by the employer, subject to any conditions contained in the order; or (b) substitute for any provision of the regulations, so far as it applies to coal mines controlled by the employer, another provision having substantially the same purpose and effect."

This subsection further reinforces the Commission's commitment to health and safety by allowing for exemptions and substitutions of regulatory provisions. The Commission can either exempt an employer from a specific provision or substitute it with another provision that serves the same purpose. However, this is only done
"...if in its opinion protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished..." This reiterates the central goal of prioritizing employee well-being in all its decisions.

In conclusion, the Commission's primary goal when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions, is unequivocally the "protection of the health and safety of employees." This principle is consistently emphasized throughout Section 137.2, guiding its decision-making process and ensuring that any changes to safety standards are made with the utmost caution and a clear understanding of their potential impact on worker well-being.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Minister take to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Actions to Promote and Ensure Occupational Health and Safety

### Section 138: Administration: Special Committees

The Minister possesses several direct actions to promote and ensure occupational health and safety.
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies." This indicates the Minister can establish specialized groups to provide expertise and support in addressing specific health and safety challenges. These committees can focus on a wide range of issues, from research to program development.

Furthermore, the Minister can initiate investigations into occupational health and safety concerns.
"The Minister may cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning occupational health and safety in any employment to which this Part applies and may appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This power allows the Minister to delve into specific incidents or systemic problems to understand their root causes and recommend solutions.

The Minister can also undertake research into the causes of employment injury and occupational illness.
"The Minister may undertake research into the cause of and the means of preventing employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake such research in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or with any organization undertaking similar research." This proactive approach to knowledge generation is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies.

The Minister has the authority to publish the results of this research and disseminate relevant data.
"The Minister may publish the results of any research undertaken under subsection (4) and compile, prepare and disseminate data or information bearing on health or safety of employees obtained from that research or otherwise." This ensures that the latest scientific understanding of workplace hazards is shared with employers and employees.

Finally, the Minister can undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness.
"The Minister may undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs." This demonstrates the Minister's commitment to implementing practical solutions to improve workplace safety.

### Section 122.1: Purpose of Part: Prevention of accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment to which this Part applies.

While Section 122.1 outlines the overarching goal of the Part, it also implicitly highlights the Minister's role. The Minister, as the head of compliance and enforcement, is responsible for ensuring that the Part's preventive measures are implemented effectively.
"The purpose of this Part is to prevent accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment to which this Part applies." This statement underscores the Minister's responsibility to create a workplace environment free from these hazards.

### Section 122.2: Preventive measures

Section 122.2 details the hierarchy of preventive measures, which the Minister oversees.
"Preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, all with the goal of ensuring the health and safety of employees." The Minister must ensure that these measures are prioritized and implemented across all federally regulated workplaces.

### Section 122.21: Head of Compliance and Enforcement

Section 122.21 formally designates a person as the Head of Compliance and Enforcement, who is responsible for overseeing the Minister's powers and duties in relation to occupational health and safety.
"(1) The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement." This ensures a dedicated individual is accountable for driving the Minister's efforts in this area.
"(2) If no Head is designated under subsection (1), the Minister shall exercise the powers and perform the duties and functions of the Head." This provides a mechanism for the Minister to continue exercising these powers even if a formal designation is not made.

individual_results.question: What is the role of the Minister in relation to medical surveillance, examination programs, and reporting on harassment and violence in workplaces under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## The Minister's Role in Medical Surveillance, Examination Programs, and Reporting on Harassment and Violence

### Medical Surveillance and Examination Programs

The Minister holds a significant role in overseeing medical surveillance and examination programs within federally regulated workplaces. Section 139(1) explicitly states,
"The Minister may undertake medical surveillance and examination programs with respect to occupational health and safety and may, if the Minister considers it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all of the provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs." This indicates the Minister's authority to initiate such programs independently or collaboratively.

Furthermore, Section 139(2) details the Minister's power to appoint medical practitioners qualified in occupational medicine to carry out these programs.
"The Minister may appoint any medical practitioner qualified in occupational medicine to undertake the medical surveillance and examination programs." This appointment is crucial for ensuring the programs are conducted by professionals with the necessary expertise.

### Annual Report on Harassment and Violence

The Minister is mandated to produce an annual report on harassment and violence in workplaces covered by the Canada Labour Code. Section 139.1(1) specifies,
"The Minister shall prepare and publish an annual report that contains statistical data relating to harassment and violence in work places to which this Part applies. The report shall not contain any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence." This annual report serves as a vital source of data for understanding the prevalence of these issues and tracking progress in prevention efforts.

Section 139.1(2) further elaborates on the content of the report, stating that the statistical data must be
"...categorized according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act..." This ensures the report provides a nuanced understanding of harassment and violence, considering the various forms of discrimination that can contribute to these problems.

### Five-Year Review of Harassment and Violence Provisions

The Minister is also responsible for conducting a five-year review of the harassment and violence provisions within the Canada Labour Code. Section 139.2(1) outlines this process:
"Five years after the day on which this section comes into force and every five years after that, the Minister shall commence a review of the provisions of this Part relating to harassment and violence. At the conclusion of the review, the Minister shall prepare a report on the review." This review allows for the evaluation of the effectiveness of the existing provisions and the identification of areas for improvement.

Section 139.2(2) mandates that the Minister must
"...cause the report to be tabled in each House of Parliament on any of the first 15 days on which that House is sitting after the day on which the report is completed." This ensures that the findings of the review are made public and can inform future policy decisions.

individual_results.question: Who can the Minister and the Head delegate their powers, duties, or functions to, and under what conditions?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 249: Delegation of Powers, Duties, and Functions by the Head

### Who Can the Head Delegate Powers To?

Section 249(1) of the Canada Labour Code states:
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This indicates that the Head has broad authority to delegate their powers to "any qualified person or class of persons." The qualification is that this delegation is subject to any terms and conditions that the Head deems appropriate.

### Conditions Governing Delegation by the Head

Section 249(1) further elaborates on the conditions under which the Head can make a delegation:
"The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate." This highlights the Head's discretion in setting the parameters of the delegation. These terms and conditions could relate to the scope of the delegated powers, the individuals or groups to whom they can be delegated, or any other relevant limitations.

### Delegation by the Minister

Section 140(1) of the Canada Labour Code mirrors the Head's delegation powers, stating:
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Minister may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers, duties or functions the Minister is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part." This confirms that the Minister also possesses the ability to delegate their own powers, duties, and functions to qualified individuals or groups, again with the possibility of attaching terms and conditions.

### Delegation by the Head with Certificate of Authority

Section 249(1.1) provides a specific condition for delegation by the Head:
"The Head shall furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated under subsection (1) a certificate of authority and, when entering any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business the person, shall, when requested, show the certificate to the person in charge of that place." This mandates that the Head must issue a certificate of authority to each person or class of persons to whom they delegate powers, duties, or functions. This certificate serves as proof of the delegated authority and must be presented upon request.

## Section 272: Delegation of Powers by the Head

Section 272 of the Canada Labour Code reiterates the Head's delegation powers, stating:
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate." This section is virtually identical to Section 249(1), reinforcing the Head's broad delegation authority subject to ministerial terms and conditions.

individual_results.question: What are the powers and responsibilities of the Head in carrying out duties related to workplace health and safety, particularly in terms of entering workplaces, conducting examinations, and issuing directions?
individual_results.answer:
## Powers and Responsibilities of the Head in Workplace Health and Safety

### Entering Workplaces and Conducting Examinations

Section 141 outlines the Head's extensive powers to enter workplaces and conduct examinations.
"Subject to section 143.2, the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them; (b) take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent..."

This passage establishes that the Head has the authority to
"...enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them..." This is a broad power allowing for proactive monitoring and investigation of workplace conditions. Furthermore, the Head can
"...take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent..." indicating the ability to gather evidence for further analysis.

Section 141.1 further elaborates on these examination powers.
"If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer."

This subsection details the Head's obligation to conduct inspections with appropriate representation present.
"The Head may proceed with an inspection in the absence of any person mentioned in subsection (1) if that person chooses not to be present."

This provides flexibility, allowing the Head to proceed with an inspection even if the required representatives are unavailable.

### Issuing Directions

Section 141 grants the Head the power to issue directions.
"The Head may issue a direction under subsection (1) whether or not the Head is in the work place at the time the direction is issued."

This is a crucial power, allowing the Head to mandate specific actions to be taken to improve workplace health and safety.
"...direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing..."

This direction can halt potentially hazardous activities while the Head conducts an investigation.
"...direct any person not to disturb any place or thing specified by the Head for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing..."

This direction extends the no-disturbance order to individuals, ensuring the integrity of the Head's work.

### Other Powers and Responsibilities

Section 141 also outlines several other significant powers and responsibilities of the Head.
"The Head shall investigate every death of an employee that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working, or that was the result of an injury that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working."

This mandates a thorough investigation into all workplace fatalities.
"The Head shall investigate every death of an employee that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working, or that was the result of an injury that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working."

This reinforces the Head's commitment to understanding the causes of workplace deaths.
"...direct the employer or an employee or a person designated by either of them to accompany the Head while the Head, is in the work place..."

This direction ensures the Head has support and assistance while conducting inspections or investigations.
"The Head may issue a direction under subsection (1) whether or not the Head is in the work place at the time the direction is issued."

This reiterates the Head's ability to issue directions remotely.

Furthermore, it includes assistance to individuals to whom powers, duties, or functions have been delegated. The phrase "all reasonable assistance" is significant, indicating a commitment to providing whatever support is necessary to facilitate the exercise of powers or the performance of duties.

### Analysis of the Quote

The quote directly addresses the question by explicitly stating who is required to give reasonable assistance. It covers a wide range of individuals, from the person in charge of the workplace to external adjudicators and Board members, as well as those to whom powers have been delegated. The use of "all reasonable assistance" underscores the importance of a proactive and supportive approach to enabling the Code's provisions to be carried out effectively. This provision is essential for ensuring that the Labour Code can be enforced and its objectives achieved in the workplace.

individual_results.question: What are the consequences and prohibitions related to interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and providing information to authorities?
individual_results.answer:
## Consequences and Prohibitions Related to Interfering with Occupational Health and Safety Powers and Duties and Providing Information

### Section 143: Obstruction and False Statements | Provision of Information

#### Prohibition Against Obstruction and False Statements
"No person shall obstruct or hinder, or make a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions, under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This section establishes a broad prohibition against interfering with the exercise of occupational health and safety powers and duties. It explicitly states that no one can "obstruct or hinder" the Head in their work under Part II. Furthermore, it forbids making
"...a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing..." to various individuals and bodies involved in occupational health and safety, including the Head, external adjudicators, Board members, and delegated authorities. This prohibition aims to ensure the integrity of investigations, inspections, and other activities undertaken to protect employee health and safety.

#### Provision of Information
"Section 143.1 No person shall prevent an employee from providing information to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions under this Part; (a.1) an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsection 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part; or (b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This subsection reinforces the obligation to facilitate the provision of information to occupational health and safety authorities. It prohibits any action that would "prevent an employee from providing information" to the Head, external adjudicators, Board members, or delegated authorities. This provision is crucial for ensuring that authorities have access to the necessary information to identify and address workplace hazards effectively. The inclusion of information provision to legal counsel or union representatives further protects employees' rights to be informed and to seek support.

### Section 141: Exercise of Powers in Relation to Health and Safety: Inspections

#### Inspection Procedures
"(1) If the Head conducts an inspection of the work place at the work place, it shall be done in the presence of (a) an employee member and an employer member of the work place committee; or (b) the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer. Marginal note: Inspection not to be delayed (2) The Head may proceed with an inspection in the absence of any person mentioned in subsection (1) if that person chooses not to be present."

This section details the requirements for conducting workplace inspections. It mandates that inspections be conducted in the presence of either an employee and an employer member of the workplace committee, or the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer. This ensures transparency and allows for immediate feedback and clarification during the inspection process. However, it also allows the Head to proceed with an inspection if the designated person chooses not to be present, preventing unnecessary delays.

#### Powers During Inspections
"Section 141 (1) Subject to section 143.2, the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer and, in respect of any work place, may (a) conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them; (b) take or remove for analysis, samples of any material or substance or any biological, chemical or physical agent; (c) be accompanied or assisted by any person and bring any equipment that the Head deems necessary to carry out the Head’s duties; (d) take or remove, for testing, material or equipment if there is no reasonable alternative to doing so; (e) take photographs and make sketches; (f) direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (g) direct any person not to disturb any place or thing specified by the Head for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing; (h) direct the employer to produce documents and information relating to the health and safety of the employer’s employees or the safety of the work place and to permit the Head to examine and make copies of or take extracts from those documents and that information; (i) direct the employer or an employee to make or provide statements, in the form and manner that the Head may specify, respecting working conditions and material and equipment that affect the health or safety of employees; (j) direct the employer or an employee or a person designated by either of them to accompany the Head while the Head, is in the work place; and (k) meet with any person in private or, at the request of the person, in the presence of the person’s legal counsel or union representative."

This section grants the Head extensive powers during workplace inspections. These powers include conducting examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations, and inspections, and directing the employer to do so. The Head can also take samples for analysis, bring necessary equipment, take photographs and sketches, direct the employer to maintain undisturbed access to areas under inspection, and direct the employer to produce documents and information. Furthermore, the Head can compel employees to provide statements and meet with individuals in private or with legal counsel present. These powers are designed to facilitate thorough and effective investigations into workplace hazards.

### Section 143.1: Provision of Information (Repeated)

This section is a repetition of Section 143.1, which reiterates the prohibition against preventing employees from providing information to occupational health and safety authorities. It emphasizes the importance of facilitating the flow of information to ensure that authorities have the necessary data to protect employee health and safety.

individual_results.question: What are the general rules regarding the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals, such as the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and others, in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Rules Regarding Disclosure of Information Obtained in the Exercise of Powers or Performance of Duties

### Section 144 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 144 of the Canada Labour Code establishes comprehensive rules governing the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties. It broadly states that
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), and no person who has accompanied or assisted that person in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions may be required to give testimony in civil or administrative proceedings, other than proceedings under this Part, with regard to information obtained in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, except with the written permission of the Head, in which case subsection (5) does not apply to restrict the disclosure of the information."

This section is foundational, creating a strong presumption of non-disclosure for individuals acting under delegated authority. It protects the integrity of investigations and proceedings by preventing witnesses from being compelled to reveal confidential information. The exception to this rule is when the Head grants written permission, in which case subsection (5) of the same section does not apply to restrict disclosure.

### Non-Disclosure of Information Obtained in the Workplace

Section 144(3) further elaborates on this principle by stating that
"Subject to subsection (4), the Head, an external adjudicator or a member of the Board who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 — or a person who is admitted to a work place under the powers conferred by section 141 that are delegated to them under subsection 140(1.1) or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2) — and any person accompanying them, shall not disclose to any person any information obtained in the work place by the Head, external adjudicator or member or person with regard to any secret process or trade secret, except for the purposes of this Part or as required by law."

This provision specifically protects information obtained in the workplace by the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and those admitted to a workplace under delegated authority. It extends the non-disclosure rule to include "secret process or trade secret," ensuring that sensitive business information remains confidential. The exception is for purposes related to this Part of the Canada Labour Code or as required by law.

### Privileged Information

Section 144(4) declares that
"All information that, under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , an employer is exempt from disclosing under this Act or the Hazardous Products Act and that is obtained in a work place under section 141 is privileged and, notwithstanding the Access to Information Act or any other Act or law, shall not be disclosed to any other person except for the purposes of this Part."

This section establishes a specific category of privileged information – that which is exempt from disclosure under the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act and obtained in the workplace under section 141. It reinforces the protection of confidential information, even against broader disclosure laws like the Access to Information Act.

### Factors the Head May Consider in Disclosure

Section 144(5.01) outlines situations in which the Head may be satisfied that publication or disclosure is in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest. These include
"...situations in which the publication or disclosure is for the purposes of a coroner’s inquiry, the administration or enforcement of a federal or provincial law or the administration of a foreign law or international agreement."

This provision provides a limited exception to the general rule of non-disclosure, allowing for disclosure when it serves a greater public good, such as investigating a death or enforcing a law.

### Confidential Communication

Section 144(6) addresses the confidentiality of information obtained under section 141, stating that
"No person to whom information obtained under section 141 is communicated in confidence shall divulge the name of the informant to any person except for the purposes of this Part, and no such person is competent or compellable to divulge the name of the informant before any court or other tribunal."

This provision protects the identity of informants, ensuring that they are not exposed to potential retaliation for providing information. It establishes a strong obligation of confidentiality on those who receive information under section 141.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Head take if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened, and what are the requirements for documenting and communicating these actions?
individual_results.answer:
## Head's Powers Regarding Notices of Violation

### Establishing Form and Designating Issuers

Section 271 outlines the Head's authority to
"...establish the form of notices of violation; (b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation; and (c) establish a short-form description for each violation to be used in notices of violation." This indicates that the Head has significant control over the creation and distribution of these notices. They can standardize their appearance, specify who is permitted to send them, and create concise labels for each type of violation. This ensures consistency and clarity in the communication of contraventions.

### Actions the Head Can Take Upon Belief of Contravention

Section 271(a) further clarifies the Head's actions by stating they
"...may (a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee; (b) take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a); (c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment; (c.1) require any employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan that must be insured in accordance with subsection 239.2(1) to furnish proof that the plan is insured in accordance with that subsection; (d) require an employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment; and (e) require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made." This demonstrates a wide range of investigative powers. The Head can conduct audits, request documentation, compel statements, and demand information from both employers and employees. These actions are all designed to gather evidence to support the belief that a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened.

### Requirements for Documenting and Communicating These Actions

Section 286(1) mandates that
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This highlights the importance of documenting appeals. The Board is obligated to keep the Head informed of any challenges to their decisions.

Section 286(3) states that
"The Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This reinforces the need for thorough documentation. When the Board reviews an appeal, it can request the Head to provide the evidence they used to reach their initial conclusion.

Section 286(4) allows
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This indicates that the Head can actively participate in the appeal process by providing additional information and arguments.

Section 271(a) also mentions the Head's power to "establish the form of notices of violation." This suggests that the Head will likely use these notices to communicate their findings of contravention to the relevant parties. The standardized form ensures that the notices are clear, consistent, and legally sound.

### Delegation of Powers

Section 249(1) allows the Head to
"...delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This means the Head can empower others to carry out their enforcement responsibilities.

Section 249(1.1) requires the Head to
"...furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated under subsection (1) a certificate of authority and, when entering any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business the person, shall, when requested, show the certificate to the person in charge of that place." This outlines the documentation required when delegating powers. The certificate of authority provides clear evidence of the Head's delegation.

Section 249(3) grants the Head the
"...enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer." This is a significant power for gathering information.

Section 249(4) mandates that
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations." This ensures that the Head's enforcement efforts are not obstructed.

Section 249(5) states that
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary." This allows the Head to bring in experts or support staff as needed.

Section 249(6) provides immunity from testimony in civil suits or proceedings related to information obtained during inspections. This protects the Head and their delegated agents from being compelled to testify about evidence they gathered while enforcing the Part.

Section 249(7) extends this immunity to anyone to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated, or who accompanied or assisted the Head. This ensures that the entire enforcement team is protected from being called upon to testify about evidence they gathered.

Section 249(8) states that
"Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part." This provides a layer of protection against personal liability for actions taken in good faith while enforcing the Part.

## Powers, Duties, and Functions of the Board in Relation to Canada Labour Code Sections

### Section 84: Powers of Board

#### Procedural Authority
"A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board (a) may determine their own procedure..."
This passage establishes the Board's inherent authority to establish its own methods for conducting conciliation proceedings. This is a fundamental power that allows the Board to adapt its approach to the specific needs of each case.

#### Powers Conferred on the Board
"...has, in relation to any proceeding before them, the powers conferred on the Board, in relation to any proceeding before the Board, by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), (f) and (h)..."
This quote is crucial as it explicitly states that the Board's conciliation commissioners and boards possess all the powers that are already granted to the Board in general. These powers are detailed in paragraphs 16(a) through (h) of Section 16. This means the Board can perform a wide range of functions, including summoning witnesses, compelling testimony, examining documents, administering oaths, and entering on premises for inspections.

#### Authorization of Others
"(c) may authorize any person to do anything described in paragraph 16(b) or (f) that the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board may do and to report to the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board thereon."
This passage highlights the Board's ability to delegate its powers. It can authorize individuals to perform tasks that the Board itself is authorized to do, and these individuals are required to report back to the Board on their activities. This allows the Board to manage its workload effectively and to leverage the expertise of others.

### Section 15.1: General Power to Assist Parties

#### Assistance in Resolving Issues
"(1) The Board, any member of the Board or any external adjudicator — or an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada who is authorized by the Board — may, if the parties agree, assist the parties in resolving any issues in dispute at any stage of a proceeding and by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled."
This section outlines the Board's broad power to assist parties in reaching a settlement. It states that the Board, its members, external adjudicators, and authorized support service employees can provide assistance
"...by any means that the Board considers appropriate, without prejudice to the Board’s power to determine issues that have not been settled." This demonstrates a commitment to facilitating amicable resolutions.

#### Declaratory Opinions
"(2) The Board, on application by an employer or a trade union, may give declaratory opinions."
This passage specifies another function of the Board: the ability to issue declaratory opinions. These opinions can clarify the legal status of certain issues or questions that are in dispute between the parties. This can help to narrow the scope of the proceedings and to facilitate settlement.

### Section 15: Regulations

#### General Power to Make Regulations
"The Board may make regulations of general application respecting (a) the establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings; (a.1) the use of means of telecommunication that permit the parties and the Board or its members to communicate simultaneously for pre-hearing conferences, hearings and Board meetings; (b) the determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining; (c) the certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units; (d) the conduct of representation votes; (e) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application from the trade union for certification in respect of the same or substantially the same unit; (f) the specification of the period of time after which the Board may receive an application from an employee for revocation of a trade union’s certification as the bargaining agent for a unit where the Board has refused an application for revocation in respect of the same unit; (g) the hearing or determination of any application, complaint, question, dispute, difference or appeal that may be made or referred to the Board; (g.1) an expeditious procedure and matters that may be determined under that procedure; (h) the forms to be used in respect of any proceeding that may come before the Board; (i) the time within which and the circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18; (j) any inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2); (k) the form in which and the period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board in connection with any proceeding that may come before it; (l) the specification of the time within which and the parties or persons to whom notices and other documents shall be sent and the circumstances in which such notices or other documents shall be deemed to have been given or received by the Board or any party or person; (m) the determination of the form in which and the period during which evidence as to (i) the membership of any employees in a trade union, (ii) any objection by employees to the certification of a trade union, or (iii) any signification by employees that they no longer wish to be represented by a trade union shall be presented to the Board on an application made to it pursuant to this Part; (n) the criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union; (o) the circumstances in which evidence referred to in paragraph (m) may be received by the Board as evidence that any employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them as their bargaining agent, including the circumstances in which the evidence so received by the Board may not be made public by the Board; (o.1) the conditions for valid strike or lockout votes; (p) the authority of any person to act on behalf of the Board and the matters and things to be done and the action to be taken by that person, including the authority of an employee of the Administrative Tribunals Support Service of Canada to make decisions on uncontested applications or questions; (p.1) the manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators; and (q) any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act."
This section is a comprehensive list of the Board's rulemaking authority. It allows the Board to create detailed rules and procedures for all aspects of its work, from pre-hearing processes to the conduct of representation votes. This ensures consistency and efficiency in its operations. The sheer number of topics covered demonstrates the Board's capacity to adapt its procedures to the evolving needs of industrial relations.

### Section 16: Determination Without Oral Hearing

#### Deciding Questions Arising in Proceedings
"(p) to decide for all purposes of this Part any question that may arise in the proceeding, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any question as to whether (i) a person is an employer or an employee, (ii) a person performs management functions or is employed in a confidential capacity in matters relating to industrial relations, (iii) a person is a member of a trade union, (iv) an organization or association is an employers’ organization, a trade union or a council of trade unions, (v) a group of employees is a unit appropriate for collective bargaining, (vi) a collective agreement has been entered into, (vii) any person or organization is a party to or bound by a collective agreement, and (viii) a collective agreement is in operation; and (q) to decide any question that may arise in a proceeding under Part II, III or IV."
This passage explicitly states the Board's power to decide any question that may arise in a proceeding under Part II, III, or IV of the Canada Labour Code. This is a broad power that ensures the Board can resolve all issues that come before it, regardless of their complexity. The list of questions it can decide is extensive, covering fundamental aspects of employment relationships and collective bargaining.

individual_results.question: What happens to a direction issued by the Head when an appeal is made, and what are the requirements for making the appeal?
individual_results.answer:
## Appeal of a Direction Issued by the Head

### Status of the Direction During Appeal

Section 146(1) of the Canada Labour Code states:
"An employer, employee or trade union that feels aggrieved by a direction issued by the Head under this Part may appeal the direction to the Board, in writing, within 30 days after the day on which the direction was issued or confirmed in writing." This indicates that the direction issued by the Head remains in effect until the Board makes a decision on the appeal. The appeal is a process to challenge the validity of the direction, not to suspend its application.

Section 286(1) further clarifies this by stating:
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This ensures the Head is aware of the appeal and has access to the grounds for the challenge.

### Requirements for Making an Appeal

Section 146(1) outlines the formal requirements for making an appeal:
"An employer, employee or trade union that feels aggrieved by a direction issued by the Head under this Part may appeal the direction to the Board, in writing, within 30 days after the day on which the direction was issued or confirmed in writing." This means the appeal must be submitted in writing within 30 days of the direction being issued or confirmed.

Section 251.111(1) provides a similar requirement:
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 251.11(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This reinforces the need for a written appeal within the specified timeframe.

Section 146.01(1) also confirms this:
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146 and provide him or her with a copy of the request for appeal." This is a reiteration of the notification requirement and the provision of a copy of the request to the Head.

Section 146(4) details the Head's rights during the appeal process:
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This allows the Head to respond to the arguments made by the appellant and to provide their own perspective on the direction.

Section 146.01(2) specifies the documents the Head must provide to the Board upon request:
"The Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision or issuing the direction being appealed." This ensures the Board has access to the information the Head considered when issuing the direction.

Section 146.01(3) states the Board will provide the Head with a copy of any document filed with the Board in the appeal:

This ensures the Head is immediately aware of the challenge to their decision or direction and has the necessary documentation to prepare their response.

#### Section 146.1

#### Section 146.1 (1)
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)."

It states that the Board will conduct a "summary way and without delay" inquiry into the appeal's merits, including the decision or direction in question and the rationale behind it. The Board's potential actions are broad, encompassing the ability to "vary, rescind or confirm" the original decision or direction. Furthermore, it empowers the Board to issue new directions deemed appropriate under specific sections of the Canada Labour Code. This demonstrates the Board's significant authority in the appeal process, allowing it to correct errors, adjust outcomes, or provide further guidance.

#### Section 146.2, 146.3, 146.4

These sections are repealed and therefore do not contribute to the answer.

### Section 145.1

#### Section 145.1
"For the purposes of sections 146 to 146.‍5, the Board has all of the powers, duties and functions of the Minister and the Head under this Part, except for those referred to in section 130, subsections 135(6), 137.‍1(1) to (2.‍1) and (7) to (9), 137.‍2(4), 138(1) to (2) and (4) to (6), section 139, subsections 140(1) to (2) and (4) and 144(1), section 146.‍01, subsection 149(1), sections 152 and 155 and subsections 156.‍1(1), 157(3) and 159(2)."
This section clarifies the Board's expanded powers during an appeal. It grants the Board
"...all of the powers, duties and functions of the Minister and the Head under this Part..." with a specific list of exceptions. individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's pay if they attend a proceeding under a specific subsection of the Canada Labour Code, or are summoned by the Board to attend such a proceeding?
individual_results.answer:
## Employee Pay for Attending a Proceeding under the Canada Labour Code

### General Entitlement to Regular Wages

Section 288 of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses an employee's pay when attending a proceeding under this Part. It states:
"An employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at an appeal proceeding under this Part and who attends is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This quote is fundamental to understanding an employee's pay rights. It clearly establishes that an employee summoned by the Board to attend an appeal proceeding is entitled to be paid their regular rate of wages for the time spent there. The phrase
"...time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." is crucial, as it ensures the employee is compensated for their lost regular work hours due to their attendance at the proceeding.

### Further Support from CLC-146.5

CLC-146.5 provides additional support for this entitlement, stating:
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This section reinforces the principle established in Section 288, explicitly mentioning employees who are "a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1)" as well as those who are
"...summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding..." The identical wording regarding lost regular work hours further solidifies the employee's right to be paid their regular rate of wages for their time at the proceeding.

### Application to Wage Recovery Appeals

LABOUR-REPORTS-12_2 also confirms this entitlement in the context of wage recovery appeals. It mentions:
"As an employee, if you are summoned by the Canada Industrial Relations Board to attend at an appeal proceeding, you are entitled to be paid at your regular rate of wages. Your employer must pay you your regular rate of wages for time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time spent at work."

This quote directly links the employee's pay entitlement to being summoned by the Board to attend an appeal proceeding, specifically those related to wage recovery. It reiterates the obligation of the employer to pay the employee their regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding.

### Application to Appeal Hearings at the Canada Industrial Relations Board

LABOUR-STANDARDS-6_7 further clarifies this by stating:
"As an employee, if you are summoned by the Canada Industrial Relations Board to attend at an appeal proceeding, you are entitled to be paid at your regular rate of wages. Your employer must pay you your regular rate of wages for time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time spent at work. This applies to appeal proceedings related to:  payment orders compliance orders notices of unfounded complaint, or notices of voluntary compliance..."

This section mirrors the information provided in LABOUR-REPORTS-12_2 and CLC-146.5, explicitly stating that an employee summoned to attend an appeal proceeding at the Canada Industrial Relations Board is entitled to be paid their regular rate of wages for that time.

In summary, an employee attending a proceeding under a specific subsection of the Canada Labour Code, or being summoned by the Board to attend such a proceeding, is legally entitled to be paid their regular rate of wages for the time spent there. This entitlement is consistently affirmed across multiple documents, including Section 288 of the Canada Labour Code, CLC-146.5, LABOUR-REPORTS-12_2, and LABOUR-STANDARDS-6_7.
