individual_results.question: What protection does the Canada Labour Code offer to employees who exercise their rights or provide information related to workplace health and safety?
individual_results.answer:
## Protection for Employees Exercising Health and Safety Rights

### Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

The Canada Labour Code explicitly grants employees the right to refuse to work if they have
"...reasonable cause to believe that:  your workplace presents a danger to you the use or operation of a machine or apparatus presents a danger to you or to another employee, and  the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to you or to another employee..." This right is protected by requiring employees to follow the proper procedure when exercising it.
"In order for you to be protected by the Code when exercising your right to refuse to do dangerous work, you must follow the proper procedure."

### Right to Report Hazards and Concerns

The Canada Labour Code mandates several employee reporting obligations related to workplace health and safety. Employees are required to
"...report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer..." This reporting extends to
"...all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury to you or any other person..." Furthermore, employees have the right to
"...report to the employer any situation you believe to be a contravention of Part II of the Code by the employer, another employee, or any other person..." These reporting duties are designed to proactively identify and address potential hazards.

### Right to Participate in Health and Safety Committees

The Canada Labour Code provides employees with the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns through health and safety representatives or workplace health and safety committees. Employers with 300 or more employees are required to establish a policy health and safety committee to handle issues that are organization-wide in nature.
"As health and safety representatives or workplace health and safety committee or policy health and safety committee members, employees have the right to participate in identifying and correcting work-related health and safety concerns."

### Protection Against Retaliation

While not explicitly stated as a standalone "protection" in the provided documents, the broader context of the Canada Labour Code and its emphasis on employee rights implies protection against retaliation for exercising those rights. The Code aims to create a safe environment where employees feel comfortable reporting hazards and participating in health and safety initiatives without fear of negative consequences. The emphasis on employer responsibilities to ensure safe workplaces and the right to refuse dangerous work would likely be reinforced by provisions against retaliation.

individual_results.question: What are the potential consequences for a person who contravenes a provision of Part of the Canada Labour Code related to health and safety, and how do these consequences vary depending on the circumstances of the contravention?
individual_results.answer:
## Consequences for Contravening Health and Safety Provisions of Part of the Canada Labour Code

### General Offences

Section 101(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the general offences and potential penalties for persons who contravene a provision of Part of the Code, excluding sections 50, 94, or 95. It states:
"Subject to section 100, every person other than an employer or a trade union who contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars." This indicates that a general contravention can result in a fine of up to one thousand dollars upon summary conviction.

Section 101(2) specifies the consequences for employers or trade unions who commit such contraventions:
"Subject to section 100, every employer or trade union who or that contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars." This significantly increases the potential fine for these entities, reaching ten thousand dollars upon summary conviction.

### Offences Resulting in Death or Serious Injury

Section 148(1) provides a more severe penalty for contraventions that directly result in death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee:
"Every person who contravenes a provision of this Part the direct result of which is the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000." This establishes a potential fine of up to one million dollars or imprisonment for a term of up to two years on indictment, or a fine of up to one million dollars on summary conviction for such a contravention.

Section 148(2) further elaborates on the offences related to contraventions that are the direct result of wilful contravention knowing it is likely to cause death, serious illness, or serious injury:
"Every person who wilfully contravenes a provision of this Part knowing that the contravention is likely to cause the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000." This penalty is identical to that for contraventions resulting in death, serious illness, or serious injury, but with the added element of wilful contravention and knowledge of the likely outcome.

### Offences Related to the Right to Refuse Dangerous Work

Section 274 outlines the liability of parties to a violation, including those who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in, or participated in its commission. While not directly tied to a contravention of a specific health and safety provision, it is relevant to the right to refuse dangerous work. It states:
"If a corporation or a department commits a violation, any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department." This indicates that individuals within a corporation or department who played a role in a violation, including those exercising managerial or supervisory functions, can be held liable.

### Offences Related to Due Care and Diligence

Section 148(4) provides a defence for a person who exercised due care and diligence to avoid a contravention, but it does not apply to offences resulting in death or serious injury. It states:
"On a prosecution of a person for a contravention of any provision of this Part, except paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11), it is a defence for the person to prove that the person exercised due care and diligence to avoid the contravention. However, no person is liable to imprisonment on conviction for an offence under any of paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11)." This means that if a person took reasonable steps to prevent a contravention, they may avoid a conviction on summary conviction. However, this defence is not available for offences resulting in death or serious injury, where the penalties are much more severe.

### Offences Related to Regulations

Section 148(5) clarifies that regulations made under subsection 157(1.1) in relation to health or safety matters are deemed to be prescribed within the meaning of a paragraph of any of sections 125 to 126. This ensures that offences related to contraventions of health and safety regulations are treated consistently with other offences under Part of the Canada Labour Code.

individual_results.question: Who can be held liable and prosecuted for an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and what are the conditions for instituting proceedings?
individual_results.answer:
## Liability and Prosecution for Offences under Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 148: General Offence and Conditions for Instituting Proceedings

Section 148(1) establishes the general offence for contravening a provision of Part II of the Canada Labour Code. It states:
"Subject to this section, every person who contravenes a provision of this Part is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000."
This indicates that any individual found to have broken a rule in Part II can be charged with an offence and face either a substantial fine or a prison sentence, depending on the severity of the violation.

Section 148(2) specifies the liability for contraventions that result in death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee. It amplifies the penalties:
"Every person who contravenes a provision of this Part the direct result of which is the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000."
This means that those whose actions directly lead to harm to an employee face the maximum penalties available for an indictment, regardless of the specific provision violated.

Section 148(3) addresses the wilful contravention of a provision of Part II with knowledge that it is likely to cause death, serious illness, or serious injury to an employee. It further increases the penalties:
"Every person who wilfully contravenes a provision of this Part knowing that the contravention is likely to cause the death of, serious illness of or serious injury to an employee is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or to both; or (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000."
This provision highlights the seriousness with which the law views intentional and reckless disregard for employee safety, imposing the highest possible penalties.

Section 148(4) outlines a defence for those who exercised due care and diligence to avoid a contravention, but excludes imprisonment for certain specific contraventions. It states:
"On a prosecution of a person for a contravention of any provision of this Part, except paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11), it is a defence for the person to prove that the person exercised due care and diligence to avoid the contravention. However, no person is liable to imprisonment on conviction for an offence under any of paragraphs 125(1)(c), (z.10) and (z.11)."
This defence acknowledges that mistakes can happen, but it is not a shield against prosecution for wilful or reckless behaviour. It also specifies that imprisonment is not a possible outcome for certain contraventions related to first-aid or emergency measures.

### Section 274: Liability of Parties to a Violation

Section 274 broadens the scope of liability to include those who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in, or participated in the commission of a violation by a corporation or department. It lists the individuals who can be held liable:
"(a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."
This means that even if a corporation or department commits an offence, the individuals within that entity who were responsible for the actions that led to the offence can also be prosecuted and fined.

### Section 126: Duties of Employees - Reporting Hazardous Circumstances

Section 126(g) specifically addresses the duty of employees to report hazardous situations:
"(g) report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer..."
This passage directly answers the question by stating that employees are legally obligated to inform their employer of any potential dangers in the workplace. Failure to do so can result in prosecution.

### Section 126(h): Reporting Accidents and Hazardous Occurrences

Section 126(h) further details employee reporting duties by requiring them to report all work-related accidents, occupational diseases, or other hazardous occurrences that have caused injury:
"(h) report in the prescribed manner every accident or other occurrence arising in the course of or in connection with the employee’s work that has caused injury to the employee or to any other person..."
This passage reinforces the importance of employee vigilance and reporting. It specifies that such incidents must be reported using the method prescribed by the employer.

### Section 126(j): Reporting Contraventions by Others

Section 126(j) extends employee reporting duties to include situations where they believe the employer, another employee, or any other person is violating Part II of the Code:
"(j) report to the employer any situation that the employee believes to be a contravention of this Part by the employer, another employee or any other person."
This passage highlights the role of employees as watchdogs, empowered to report any actions that undermine workplace safety.

In summary, Section 148 establishes the general offence and the escalating penalties for different levels of culpability, including wilful contravention. Section 274 extends liability to those who facilitated violations by corporations or departments. Crucially, Section 126(g), (h), and (j) explicitly outline the mandatory reporting duties of employees regarding hazardous conditions, accidents, and contraventions by others, all of which can lead to prosecution.

individual_results.question: What can the Head do to prevent or address contraventions of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety)?
individual_results.answer:
## Preventing and Addressing Contraventions of Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 122.2: Preventive Measures
"Preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, all with the goal of ensuring the health and safety of employees."

This section establishes the fundamental approach of Part II to occupational health and safety: a hierarchy of controls. The Head can prevent contraventions by prioritizing the removal of hazards altogether. When elimination is not feasible, the Head can focus on reducing the severity or likelihood of harm. Finally, the Head can provide personal protective equipment as a last line of defense. This proactive stance is crucial for preventing violations of the Part.

### Section 145: Special Safety Measures: Direction to Terminate Contravention
"If the Head is of the opinion that a provision of this Part is being contravened or has recently been contravened, the Head may direct the employer or employee concerned, or both, to (a) terminate the contravention within the time that the officer may specify; and (b) take steps, as specified by the Head and within the time that the Head may specify, to ensure that the contravention does not continue or re-occur."

This section outlines the Head's power to issue directions to stop ongoing or recently completed contraventions. The Head can order the immediate cessation of the violation and require the employer or employee to implement corrective measures to prevent recurrence. This is a direct intervention to address existing problems and ensure compliance with the Part.

### Section 145 (2): Dangerous Situations — Direction to Employer
"If the Head considers that the use or operation of a machine or thing, a condition in a place or the performance of an activity constitutes a danger to an employee while at work, (a) the Head shall notify the employer of the danger and issue directions in writing to the employer directing the employer, immediately or within the period that the Head specifies, to take measures to (i) correct the hazard or condition or alter the activity that constitutes the danger, or (ii) protect any person from the danger; and (b) the Head may, if the Head considers that the danger or the hazard, condition or activity that constitutes the danger cannot otherwise be corrected, altered or protected against immediately, issue a direction in writing to the employer directing that the place, machine, thing or activity in respect of which the direction is issued not be used, operated or performed, as the case may be, until the Head’s directions are complied with, but nothing in this paragraph prevents the doing of anything necessary for the proper compliance with the direction."

This subsection details the Head's ability to issue a direction to an employer to address an immediate danger. The Head must first notify the employer of the danger and order them to take corrective actions. If the danger cannot be addressed quickly, the Head can order the immediate cessation of the dangerous activity or the use of the machine or thing until the necessary measures are in place. This is a powerful tool for preventing accidents and injuries.

### Section 145 (2.1): Dangerous Situations — Direction to Employee
"If the Head considers that the use or operation of a machine or thing by an employee, a condition in a place or the performance of an activity by an employee constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, the Head shall, in addition to the directions issued under paragraph (2)(a), issue a direction in writing to the employee to discontinue the use, operation or activity or cease to work in that place until the employer has complied with the directions issued under that paragraph."

This subsection extends the Head's ability to issue directions to employees when they are engaging in a dangerous activity. In addition to directing the employer to take corrective actions, the Head can order the employee to stop the dangerous activity until the employer has complied with the directions. This ensures that the employee is also protected from harm.

### Section 145 (3): Posting Notice of Danger
"If the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(a), the Head shall affix or cause to be affixed to or near the place, machine or thing in respect of which the direction is issued, or in the area in which the activity in respect of which the direction is issued is performed, a notice of danger in the form and containing the information that the Head may specify, and no person shall remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Head."

This section mandates the posting of a danger notice when a direction is issued to an employer to correct a hazard. This serves as a visible reminder of the danger and prevents anyone from resuming the dangerous activity until the necessary measures have been taken.

### Section 145 (4): Cessation of Use
"If the Head issues a direction under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of a place, machine, thing or activity, the employer shall cause the use of the place, the use or operation of the machine or thing or the performance of the activity to be discontinued, and no person shall use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place or perform the activity until the measures directed by the Head have been taken."

This subsection reinforces the Head's power to order the immediate cessation of a dangerous activity or the use of a machine or thing. It prohibits anyone from resuming the activity until the Head's directions have been followed.

### Section 145 (5): Copies of Directions and Reports
"If the Head issues a direction in writing under subsection (1) or (2) or makes a report in writing to an employer on any matter under this Part, the employer shall without delay (a) cause a copy or copies of the direction or report to be posted in a conspicuous place accessible to every employee; (b) give a copy of the direction or report to the policy committee and a copy to the work place committee or the health and safety representative."

This section ensures that all employees are informed of any directions issued or reports made by the Head. The employer is required to post the direction or report in a visible location and to distribute it to relevant committees. This promotes transparency and allows employees to be aware of the safety measures being implemented.

### Section 145 (6): Copy to Person Who Made Complaint
"If the Head issues a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (2.1) or makes a report referred to in subsection (5) in respect of an investigation made by the Head following a complaint, the Head shall immediately provide a copy of the direction or report to each person, if any, whose complaint led to the investigation."

This section ensures that individuals who initially raised a safety concern are kept informed of the Head's actions in response to their complaint. This demonstrates accountability and provides closure for those who reported the hazard.

### Section 145 (7): Copy to Employer
"If the Head issues a direction to an employee under subsection (1) or (2.1), the Head shall immediately provide a copy of the direction to the employee’s employer."

This section ensures that the employer of an employee who has been directed to cease a dangerous activity is also informed. This allows the employer to take appropriate steps to support the employee and prevent future occurrences.

### Section 145 (8): Response to Direction or Report
"If the Head issues a direction under subsection (1), (2) or (2.1) or makes a report referred to in subsection (5), the Head may require the employer or the employee to whom the direction is issued or to whom the report relates to respond in writing to the direction or report, within the time that the Head may specify. The employer or employee shall provide a copy of the response to the policy committee and a copy to the work place committee or the health and safety representative."

This section allows the Head to request a written response to a direction or report. This can help to clarify understanding, track progress on corrective actions, and ensure that the Head's recommendations are being implemented. The Head requires the employer or employee to share the response with relevant committees for broader awareness.

individual_results.question: What discretion does a judge have when an application under section 152 is made, and how can the resulting order be handled?
individual_results.answer:
## Judge's Discretion in Injunction Proceedings (Section 152)

### Section 152: Application to a Superior Court

Section 152 outlines the Head's ability to apply to a superior court for an order enjoining someone from violating a provision of the Part. It states,
"The Head may apply or cause an application to be made to a judge of a superior court for an order enjoining any person from contravening a provision of this Part, whether or not a prosecution has been instituted for an offence under this Part, or enjoining any person from continuing any act or default for which the person was convicted of an offence under this Part."
This indicates that the judge's discretion is primarily focused on whether to grant the injunction based on the evidence presented. The judge will consider whether the Head has demonstrated a likelihood of irreparable harm if the contravention continues. The judge's discretion extends to the scope and terms of the injunction itself, as the judge can tailor the order to address the specific violation.

### Section 153: Finality of Orders and Directions

Section 153 emphasizes the finality of orders and directions made by the Board under this Part. It declares,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This means that once the Board issues an injunction under section 152, the judge's discretion is effectively concluded. The resulting order is binding and cannot be challenged in higher courts.

### Section 145.1: Powers, Duties and Functions of the Board

Section 145.1 clarifies that the Board has all the powers, duties, and functions of the Minister and the Head under this Part, with certain exceptions. This is relevant to the judge's discretion because it confirms that the Board is the entity that makes the injunctions under section 152. The judge's discretion is exercised *upon* receiving the Board's application and recommendation for an injunction.

### Section 146.1: Inquiry into Decisions and Directions

Section 146.1 details the Board's process when an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146. It states,
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)."
This highlights the Board's discretion to modify, overturn, or uphold its own injunction. The judge's discretion is limited to whether to grant the Board's initial injunction request. If the Board later issues a direction, the judge's discretion is again limited to whether to enforce that direction.

### Section 156: Finality of Orders and Directions (Reiteration)

Section 156 reiterates the finality of Board orders and directions, stating,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
This reinforces the point that the judge's discretion is exhausted once the Board issues an injunction under section 152. The resulting order is not subject to judicial review.

### Section 152: Handling the Resulting Order

Section 152 explains how the resulting order can be handled. It states,
"The Head may apply or cause an application to be made to a judge of a superior court for an order enjoining any person from contravening a provision of this Part, whether or not a prosecution has been instituted for an offence under this Part, or enjoining any person from continuing any act or default for which the person was convicted of an offence under this Part."
This indicates that the Head, acting on the Board's injunction, can seek a formal court order to enforce it. The court will then handle the enforcement of the injunction, potentially including issuing warrants for arrest or seizure of property if the injunction is violated.

## Consequences of Failing to Pay a Fine Imposed for an Offence under Part II of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 154(1) - Imprisonment Precluded in Certain Cases
"If a person is convicted of an offence under this Part on proceedings by way of summary conviction, no imprisonment may be imposed in default of payment of any fine imposed as punishment."

This section directly addresses the consequence of failing to pay a fine imposed for an offence under Part II of the Canada Labour Code when convicted by summary conviction. It explicitly states that imprisonment is not an option in such cases. This provision aims to ensure that fines serve their intended purpose of deterring violations and compensating for harm, rather than leading to incarceration for inability to pay.

### Section 289 - Payment Considered as Admission of Violation
"If a person or a department pays the penalty set out in a notice of violation, the person or the department is considered to have committed the violation and proceedings in respect of it are ended."

This section outlines the legal effect of paying a fine. It declares that making the payment is treated as an admission of guilt.
"Section 289 If a person or a department pays the penalty set out in a notice of violation, the person or the department is considered to have committed the violation and proceedings in respect of it are ended."
This means that the prosecution is satisfied, and the matter is closed. The person or department is legally considered to have committed the violation, and no further action will be taken.

### Section 290 - Failure to Act Considered as Admission of Violation
"Section 290 A person or a department that neither pays a penalty imposed under this Part nor requests a review or an appeal in the specified time is considered to have committed the violation and is liable for the penalty."

This section provides a consequence for not taking action on a notice of violation. It states that failing to either pay the penalty or request a review or appeal within the specified timeframe is treated as an admission of guilt.
"Section 290 A person or a department that neither pays a penalty imposed under this Part nor requests a review or an appeal in the specified time is considered to have committed the violation and is liable for the penalty."

individual_results.question: How can the Head require a person to provide information for the purposes of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and what type of evidence can be used to prove that the information was not provided?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 155: Providing of Information: Notice to provide information

### How the Head can require information
"Section 155 (1) If a person is required to provide information for the purposes of this Part, the Head may require the information to be provided by a notice to that effect served personally or sent by registered mail addressed to the latest known address of the person, and the person shall comply with the notice within such reasonable time as is specified in it."

This section outlines the method by which the Head can formally request information from an individual. It specifies that the Head can issue a notice, either served in person or via registered mail to the person's latest known address. The notice will also include a timeframe within which the information must be provided. This ensures that the individual is officially informed of the request and has a defined period to comply.

### Type of Evidence to Prove Non-Provision of Information
"(2) A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head or by a person authorized by the Head, (a) certifying that a notice was sent by registered mail to the person to whom it was addressed, accompanied by an identified post office certificate of the registration and a true copy of the notice, and (b) certifying that the information has not been provided as requested in the notice sent by the Head, is evidence of the facts set out therein without proof of the signature or official character of the person by whom the certificate purports to be signed."

This section details the type of evidence that can be used to demonstrate that the requested information was not provided. It states that a certificate, either from the Head or an authorized person, is sufficient proof. This certificate must include two key elements: first, a confirmation that the notice was sent by registered mail with a post office certificate of registration and a true copy of the notice, and second, a certification that the information was not received as requested. Importantly, this certificate is admissible as evidence
"...without proof of the signature or official character of the person by whom the certificate purports to be signed." This simplifies the process of proving non-provision, as it avoids the need for extensive verification of the certificate's authenticity.

### Section 156.1(1) - Authority to Fix Fees

This section establishes the legal basis for the Governor in Council to determine the fees charged for services, facilities, and products offered by the Minister. ### Section 156.1(2) - Limitation on Fee Amount
"Fees fixed under subsection (1) may not exceed the costs to Her Majesty in right of Canada in respect of those items or matters."

This subsection places a clear cap on the fees that can be established. It states that the fees
"...may not exceed the costs to Her Majesty in right of Canada in respect of those items or matters." This means that the fees are intended to recover the actual expenses incurred by the Minister in providing the services, facilities, and products. ### Section 116 - Scope of Remuneration and Expenses
"R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 116 1998, c. 26, s. 59(E) 2003, c. 22, s. 224(E) Previous Version Marginal note: Persons deemed not to be employed in public service..."

This marginal note clarifies the individuals covered by Section 116. It explicitly states
"Persons deemed not to be employed in public service..." which is a specific category of individuals who can receive remuneration and expenses for their work under this Part. This broadens the scope of compensation beyond traditional federal public administration employees.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the regulations that can be made under section 157 of the Canada Labour Code, and who is responsible for making them?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Regulations under Section 157 of the Canada Labour Code

### General Authority for Making Regulations

Section 157 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad authority to make regulations.
"Subject to this section, the Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing anything that by this Part is to be prescribed; (a.01) defining the expressions “harassment” and “violence” for the purposes of this Part; (a.1) restricting or prohibiting any activity or thing that any provision of this Part contemplates being the subject of regulations; (a.2) prescribing the method for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages for the purpose of section 146.5; and (b) respecting such other matters or things as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Part."

This opening sentence establishes that the regulations can cover
"...anything that by this Part is to be prescribed..." indicating a wide scope. It also specifically mentions defining terms like "harassment" and "violence," restricting activities, prescribing wage calculation methods, and addressing "such other matters or things as are necessary." This demonstrates the regulations' potential to clarify, expand upon, and detail the provisions of the main Labour Code text.

### Specific Areas of Regulation

Section 157 further elaborates on the types of regulations that can be made.
"(a.01) defining the expressions “harassment” and “violence” for the purposes of this Part; (a.1) restricting or prohibiting any activity or thing that any provision of this Part contemplates being the subject of regulations; (a.2) prescribing the method for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages for the purpose of section 146.5; and (b) respecting such other matters or things as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Part."

This list includes the ability to define key terms, prohibit specific activities, establish wage calculation methods, and address "other matters" deemed necessary for the Labour Code's implementation. This highlights the regulations' role in providing practical guidance and addressing specific issues that arise in the workplace.

### Ministerial Recommendations for Specific Areas

Section 157 also specifies that regulations concerning occupational safety and health of employees employed on ships, trains, or aircraft in operation, or those relating to oil and gas exploration and production in frontier lands, shall be made on the recommendation of specific Ministers.
"(3) Regulations of the Governor in Council under subsection (1) or (1.1) in respect of occupational safety and health of employees employed (a) on ships, trains or aircraft, while in operation, shall be made on the recommendation of the Minister and the Minister of Transport; or (b) on or in connection with exploration or drilling for or the production, conservation, processing or transportation of oil or gas in frontier lands, as defined in the Canada Petroleum Resources Act , shall be made on the recommendation of (i) the Minister and the Minister of Indigenous Services, and (ii) the Minister of Natural Resources, taking into consideration any recommendations made by the Canadian Energy Regulator in relation to the regulations."

This indicates that the Ministers of Transport and Indigenous Services, along with the Minister of Natural Resources and the Canadian Energy Regulator, have a role in advising the Governor in Council on the content of these specific safety and health regulations. This ensures that these regulations are informed by expertise and relevant industry considerations.

## Responsibility for Making Regulations

The primary responsibility for making regulations under section 157 of the Canada Labour Code lies with the Governor in Council.
"Subject to this section, the Governor in Council may make regulations..."

This opening phrase clearly assigns the legislative power to create these regulations to the Governor in Council. However, as noted above, the Ministers of Transport, Indigenous Services, and Natural Resources, along with the Canadian Energy Regulator, can provide recommendations to the Governor in Council on regulations concerning occupational safety and health in specific industries. This collaborative process ensures that the regulations are comprehensive and reflect the needs of the various sectors covered by the Labour Code.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council direct that a part of the Canada Labour Code applies to certain federal works, undertakings, or businesses?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for the Governor in Council to Direct Application of Part of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 4: General Application

Section 4 of the Canada Labour Code establishes the broad initial application of Part of the Code. It states:
"This Part applies in respect of employees who are employed on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with those employees and in respect of trade unions and employers’ organizations composed of those employees or employers."
This indicates that Part of the Code applies to all federal works, undertakings, and businesses, encompassing the relationships between employers and employees, as well as trade unions and employers' organizations.

### Section 158: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 158 of the Canada Labour Code provides a specific circumstance where the Governor in Council can direct the application of Part. It specifies:
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This section clarifies that Part of the Code can be applied to employment within provincial Crown corporations that are agents of Her Majesty and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This is a targeted application based on the specific nature of these corporations and their regulatory oversight.

### Section 121.1: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations (Similar to Section 158)

Section 121.1 mirrors the provisions of Section 158, further solidifying the Governor in Council's power to direct the application of Part to provincial Crown corporations regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It states:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This repetition emphasizes the importance of this specific category of federal works, undertakings, and businesses in the context of the Governor in Council's regulatory authority.

### Section 265: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations (Similar to Section 158 and 121.1)

Section 265 also provides a similar circumstance to Sections 158 and 121.1, allowing the Governor in Council to direct the application of Part to provincial Crown corporations regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It reads:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This further reinforces the Governor in Council's ability to tailor the application of Part to the unique circumstances of these Crown corporations.

### Section 266: Exclusion from Application

Section 266, while discussing exclusion from application, indirectly supports the Governor in Council's power to direct application. It states:
"Section 266 (1) The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."
This indicates that the Governor in Council has the opposite power to *exclude* Part from certain provincial Crown corporations regulated by the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This power to both direct and exclude application demonstrates the Governor in Council's comprehensive control over the scope of Part's operation.

In summary, the Governor in Council can direct the application of Part of the Canada Labour Code to certain federal works, undertakings, or businesses under the following circumstances:
1.  The Part applies to employees employed on or in connection with the operation of such federal works, undertakings, or businesses, and to the employers and trade unions and employers' organizations involved in those relationships. (Section 4)
2.  The Part applies to employment within provincial Crown corporations that are agents of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. (Sections 158, 121.1, 265)
3.  The Part can be excluded from application to certain provincial Crown corporations regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. (Section 266)

## Exclusion of Employment Types from Part Application and Occupational Safety and Health Regulations

### Section 266(1) and (2) - General Exclusion by Regulation

Section 266(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the broad power of the Governor in Council to exclude certain employment types from the application of Part. It states:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote is central to understanding the circumstances under which employment can be excluded. The exclusion can be "in whole or in part," indicating a flexible approach. The exclusion applies to employment
"...on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." This specifies a particular category of employment – those related to nuclear safety and control activities.

Section 266(2) further elaborates on this power by allowing the Governor in Council to make regulations relating to occupational safety and health in relation to employment subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1). It says:
"On the recommendation of the Minister, the Governor in Council may make regulations relating to labour standards in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This passage highlights a process for creating occupational safety and health regulations for excluded employment. The regulation excluding the nuclear safety and control activities is the prerequisite. Then, upon the Minister's recommendation and consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the Governor in Council can enact regulations specifically for that excluded employment.

### Section 159(1) and (2) - Similar Exclusion and Occupational Safety and Health Regulations

Section 159(1) of the Canada Labour Code mirrors the provisions of Section 266(1), reiterating the Governor in Council's power to exclude employment from Part's application by regulation. It reads:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote directly supports the idea that nuclear safety and control employment can be excluded from Part's application through regulation.

Section 159(2) is identical to Section 266(2), outlining the process for creating occupational safety and health regulations for excluded employment. It states:
"On the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the Governor in Council may make regulations relating to occupational safety and health in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This passage confirms that occupational safety and health regulations for excluded employment (those related to nuclear safety and control) are made following a recommendation from the Minister and consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and are based on a prior regulation excluding that employment from Part's application.

### Section 158 - Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 158 of the Canada Labour Code provides another circumstance where Part's application can be directed by regulation. It states:
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote indicates that Part's application can be directed to employment within federal Crown corporations that are agents of a province and whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This is a specific application of Part, not an exclusion. However, it demonstrates the Governor in Council's power to direct Part's application to certain employment types.

### Section 159(1) and (2) - Exclusion from Application for Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 159(1) is identical to Section 158, stating the Governor in Council's power to exclude employment from Part's application by regulation. It reads:
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This quote directly supports the idea that employment within federal Crown corporations regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act can be excluded from Part's application through regulation.

Section 159(2) is also identical to Section 158, outlining the process for creating occupational safety and health regulations for excluded employment within these Crown corporations. It states:
"On the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the Governor in Council may make regulations relating to occupational safety and health in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This passage confirms that occupational safety and health regulations for excluded employment within these Crown corporations are made following a recommendation from the Minister and consultation with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, and are based on a prior regulation excluding that employment from Part's application.

### Section 3 - Exclusion from Application for Certain Professions

Section 3 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations provides an exclusion from Part's application for members of certain professions. It states:
"Division I of the Act does not apply to members of the architectural, dental, engineering, legal or medical professions."

This quote is not directly related to the circumstances under which employment types can be excluded from Part's application and have their own occupational safety and health regulations made. It deals with an exclusion from the *entire* Part, not a specific provision within it.

### Section 123(1) - Application to Federal Public Administration

Section 123(1) of the Canada Labour Code specifies that Part applies to employment on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut. It also applies to employment by a corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada and by a Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act, that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province.

This quote is relevant because it establishes the broad scope of Part's application to federal public administration and related entities. However, it does not detail the specific circumstances under which employment types can be excluded from Part's application and have their own occupational safety and health regulations made.

### Section 123(2) - Application to Federal Public Administration and Persons Employed There

Section 123(2) further clarifies Part's application to the federal public administration, stating:
"This Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act..."

This quote reinforces Part's application to the federal public administration but does not address the exclusion of specific employment types.

### Section 123(2.1) - Persons Appointed Under Public Service Employment Act

Section 123(2.1) specifies that Part applies to persons appointed under subsection 128(1) of the Public Service Employment Act, other than those appointed by a person holding the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the Senate or Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and to their employer.

### Section 123(3) - Persons Not Employees but Performing Activities for an Employer

Section 123(3) addresses persons who are not employees but perform activities for an employer to which Part applies. It states:
"This Part applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer, and every provision of this Part must be read accordingly."

This quote is not directly related to the exclusion of specific employment types from Part's application and having their own occupational safety and health regulations made. It deals with a specific relationship between a person and an employer.

In summary, the Governor in Council has the power to exclude certain employment types from the application of Part by regulation. ## Section 167 of the Canada Labour Code: Purpose

### Application of Part

Section 167 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the scope of its application. It begins with a broad statement:
"This Part applies (a) to employment in or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut; (b) to and in respect of employees who are employed in or in connection with any federal work, undertaking or business described in paragraph (a); (c) to and in respect of any employers of the employees described in paragraph (b); (d) to and in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada other than a department as defined in the Financial Administration Act ; and (e) to or in respect of any Canadian carrier, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act , that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province."

This indicates that Part 167 applies to a wide range of federal activities, including "federal work, undertaking or business." It extends to the employees working in these activities, their employers, and any corporations established to carry out government functions. Furthermore, it covers Canadian carriers acting as agents of the Crown. This comprehensive application ensures that the penalties outlined in Part 167 are relevant to the vast number of individuals and entities involved in federal operations.

### Application to Other Persons

Section 167(1.1) further clarifies the Part's reach by stating:
"Subject to subsection (1.2), this Part applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer, and every provision of this Part must be read accordingly."

This provision broadens the Part's applicability to individuals who are not formally employed but are providing services to an employer covered by the Part. It treats these individuals as if they were employees for the purposes of the penalties outlined in Part 167. This is a significant extension, ensuring that those gaining experience through short-term or contract work are also subject to the Part's provisions.

### Exception

Section 167(1.2) provides a specific exception to the Part's application:
"Except to the extent provided for in the regulations, this Part does not apply to a person referred to in subsection (1.1) or, in relation to the person, the employer, if the person performs the activities to fulfil the requirements of a program that is offered by a secondary or post-secondary educational institution, vocational school, or equivalent educational institution outside Canada, specified or described in the regulations."

This exception excludes individuals performing activities to meet educational program requirements from the Part's penalties, provided the program is offered outside of Canada and is specified in the regulations. This ensures that legitimate educational pursuits are not inadvertently caught by the Part.

### Non-application to Certain Employees

Section 167(2) specifies that Division I of the Part does not apply to employees who are managers or superintendents or exercise management functions, or those members of professions designated by regulation as professions to which Division I does not apply. Similarly, Division XIV of the Part does not apply to employees who are managers. These exclusions recognize the distinct responsibilities and regulatory frameworks that govern certain types of employees.

### Non-application to Federal Public Administration

Section 123(2) states:
"This Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act..."

This indicates that Part 167 applies to the federal public administration, but with a limitation. It only applies to those employed within the public administration to the extent specified in Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act. This ensures that the Part's penalties are tailored to the specific regulatory environment of the federal public administration.

### Application to Persons Appointed Under the Public Service Employment Act

Section 123(2.1) further clarifies the Part's application to federal public administration employees, stating:
"This Part applies to persons appointed under subsection 128(1) of the Public Service Employment Act , other than persons appointed by a person holding the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the Senate or Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and to their employer."

This provision explicitly includes individuals appointed under the Public Service Employment Act, with a specific exception for those appointed by the Leaders of the Opposition. This ensures that the Part's penalties are applicable to the vast majority of federal public administration employees.

### Application to Other Persons (Repeated)

Section 123(3) reiterates the Part's application to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer, and every provision of this Part must be read accordingly. This is a repetition of a provision found in Section 167(1.1), emphasizing the Part's broad reach to those providing services to covered employers.

### Purpose of Part 269

Section 269 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states the Part's purpose:
"The purpose of this Part is to establish, as an alternative to the existing penal system and as a supplement to existing enforcement measures, a fair and efficient penalty system to promote compliance with Parts II and III of this Act."

This passage directly answers the question about the Part's purpose. It is designed to provide a "fair and efficient penalty system" to encourage adherence to the provisions of Parts II and III of the Act. This system is intended to be both a replacement for the current penal system and a reinforcement of existing enforcement methods. The emphasis on fairness and efficiency highlights the Part's commitment to achieving compliance in a just and effective manner.

## Burden of Proof When Employer Alleges Non-Employment

### Section 123.3 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 123.3 directly addresses the question of who bears the burden of proof when an employer alleges that a person receiving remuneration is not their employee. It states:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This passage is a clear and unambiguous answer to the question. It establishes a rule that, in specific types of proceedings under the Canada Labour Code (those not involving a prosecution and those related to violations under Part IV), the employer has the responsibility to prove that the person is *not* their employee. This is a significant allocation of burden, shifting it from the applicant or appellant to the one making the negative assertion.

### Section 167.01(2) and 167.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Sections 167.01(2) and 167.2 of the Canada Labour Code reinforce the presumption of employment and the burden of proof on the employer when they deny it. Section 167.01(2) states:
"The presumption does not apply for the purposes of a prosecution under this Part." This clarifies that the presumption of employment, which is established in other sections, does *not* apply when the employer is prosecuting the person for a violation. However, it is the employer who still bears the burden of proving non-employment in those prosecution scenarios.

Section 167.2 mirrors this, stating:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This is a repetition of the rule found in Section 123.3, further solidifying it as the applicable rule in the specified types of proceedings.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code also confirms the employer's burden of proof when they deny employment. It says:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This is another instance of the rule being reiterated, providing additional support for the answer.

### Section 167.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 167.1, while not directly addressing the burden of proof in the employer's denial of employment, is relevant because it prohibits employers from treating an employee as if they were not their employee. This reinforces the legal framework that supports the presumption of employment and the employer's burden to disprove it.

### Section 123.1 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 123.1 provides a general statement that nothing in this Part shall abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act. While not directly answering the burden of proof question, it is a principle that underpins the broader legal context in which the presumption of employment and the employer's burden of proof operate.

### Section 294 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 294 outlines the general burden of proof in proceedings under this Part. It states:
"If the facts of a violation are reviewed or appealed, the person who issued the notice of violation shall establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the applicant or the appellant committed the violation." This passage is not directly relevant to the employer's denial of employment, as it concerns the applicant's burden of proof when a violation is reviewed or appealed.

### Section 275 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 275 deals with the sufficiency of proof in proceedings against a person or department in relation to a violation. It states:
"In any proceedings under this Part against a person or a department in relation to a violation, it is sufficient proof of the violation to establish that it was committed by an employee or agent or mandatary of the person or of the department, whether or not the employee or agent or mandatary has been identified or proceeded against in accordance with this Part." This passage is not directly relevant to the employer's denial of employment, as it concerns the proof of a violation, not the employer's assertion of non-employment.

## Canada Labour Code and Interaction with Other Laws, Customs, Contracts, and Collective Agreements

### Section 168: Saving More Favourable Benefits

Section 168 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a principle of "saving more favourable benefits." It states:
"This Part and all regulations made under this Part apply notwithstanding any other law or any custom, contract or arrangement, but nothing in this Part shall be construed as affecting any rights or benefits of an employee under any law, custom, contract or arrangement that are more favourable to the employee than his rights or benefits under this Part."

This section is fundamental to understanding how the Labour Code interacts with other sources of employee rights. It clarifies that the Labour Code takes precedence over any conflicting provisions found elsewhere. However, it also provides a crucial exception: if an employee has rights or benefits under another law, custom, contract, or arrangement that are *more* favourable than those offered by the Labour Code, those more favourable rights and benefits are *not* affected by the Labour Code. This ensures that employees are not disadvantaged by the Labour Code if they already have better terms and conditions elsewhere.

### Section 69: Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements

Section 69 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the scope and interpretation of collective agreements. It mentions that collective agreements "may contain certain provisions." This indicates that collective agreements can supplement, but not contradict, the provisions of the Labour Code.

Furthermore, Section 69 details the operation of hiring halls, where trade unions may establish rules for the referral of persons to employment. It emphasizes that these rules must be applied "fairly and without discrimination" and must be "kept posted in a conspicuous place." This demonstrates how collective agreements can govern specific aspects of employment relationships, such as recruitment and placement.

### Labour-Reports-24_14: Benefits: Access and Portability - Issue Paper

This issue paper provides a broad overview of various approaches to enhancing access to and portability of benefits for workers in non-standard work arrangements. It highlights the role of multi-employer benefit plans, group insurance plans, and industry-specific benefit schemes.

The paper notes that
"...employers in this industry have formed large employer associations  that provide centralized payroll processes and allow members to collectively  manage benefits for employees." This illustrates how collective agreements, often facilitated by employer associations, can be used to create comprehensive benefit plans that follow employees from job to job.

It also discusses the use of "scale agreements" in Quebec, which set out minimum terms and conditions for the provision of artists' services and related matters. These agreements are binding on all employers and employees in a specified sector. This demonstrates how collective agreements can be used to establish industry-wide benefit standards.

### Labour-Reports-25_14: Collective Voice for Non-Unionized Workers: Issue Paper

This issue paper further explores sector-based approaches to collective voice and benefits. It discusses the Status of the Artist Act, which allows artists' associations to be recognized and certified by the Canada Industrial Relations Board to represent their members in collective bargaining with producers.

The paper also mentions that Quebec's Act Respecting Collective Agreement Decrees provides the government with the power to order that a collective agreement respecting any trade, industry, commerce or occupation shall also bind all the employees and professional employers in Quebec or in a stated region of Quebec. This demonstrates how collective agreements can be extended by decree to cover entire sectors of the economy.

### CLC-166: Interpretation: Definitions

Section 166 of the Canada Labour Code provides definitions for key terms used throughout the Part. It defines "collective agreement" as
"...an agreement in writing containing terms or conditions of employment of employees, including provisions with reference to rates of pay, hours of work and settlement by a third party of disagreements arising in the application of the agreement, between (a) an employer or an employers’ organization acting on behalf of an employer, and (b) a trade union acting on behalf of the employees in collective bargaining or as a party to an agreement with the employer or employers’ organization..."

This definition is crucial for understanding the scope of the Labour Code's application to collective agreements. It clarifies that a collective agreement must be in writing and must address a range of employment terms, including wages, hours, and dispute resolution. It also specifies the parties involved in the collective bargaining process.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code interacts with other laws, customs, contracts, and collective agreements in a nuanced way. Section 168 establishes a principle of saving more favourable benefits, while Section 69 allows collective agreements to supplement the Labour Code's provisions. The issue papers highlight the role of collective agreements, often facilitated by employer associations or sectoral legislation, in creating comprehensive benefit plans that follow employees from job to job. Section 166 provides the essential definition of a collective agreement for understanding the Labour Code's application to these arrangements.

individual_results.question: What are the standard hours of work for an employee under the Canada Labour Code, and are there any exceptions or alternative arrangements that can be made?

## Standard Hours of Work Under the Canada Labour Code

### General Standard Hours
"Section 169 (1) Except as otherwise provided by or under this Division (a) the standard hours of work of an employee shall not exceed eight hours in a day and forty hours in a week; and (b) no employer shall cause or permit an employee to work longer hours than eight hours in any day or forty hours in any week."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the baseline for standard hours of work. It clearly states that an employee's standard hours cannot exceed eight hours per day or forty hours per week. This is the fundamental rule that applies to most employees in federally regulated workplaces.

### Exceptions and Alternative Arrangements

#### Averaging Hours
"Where the nature of the work in an industrial establishment necessitates irregular distribution of the hours of work of an employee, the hours of work in a day and the hours of work in a week may be calculated, in such manner and in such circumstances as may be prescribed by the regulations, as an average for a period of two or more weeks."

This exception addresses situations where employees have varying work schedules. It allows for the calculation of standard hours as an average over a period of two or more weeks. This is particularly relevant for employees whose hours fluctuate due to the nature of their job.

#### Modified Work Schedules
"Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work. Examples of modified work schedules include:   compressed work weeks flexible hours of work   Note: you can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements. For more information, please consult the Flexible Work Arrangements web page.  If you have a modified work schedule:   your standard hours of work for a period of 2 or more weeks cannot exceed an average of 40 hours in a week  the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed an average of 48 hours in a week your employer must pay overtime when  your daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule. Overtime must also be paid when your hours exceed an average of 40 hours in a week where the schedule consists of 2 or more weeks  If you are a student intern, your employer may establish a modified work schedule with your approval. This schedule can exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. However, it cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks."

Modified work schedules offer a way to deviate from the standard hours. They can include compressed work weeks or flexible hours. However, there are limitations. The standard hours for a period of two or more weeks cannot exceed 40 hours on average, and the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed 48 hours on average. Overtime must be paid when these averages are exceeded. Student interns may have modified work schedules exceeding 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week, but these cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks.

#### Maximum Hours of Work
"In most cases, the maximum hours of work allowable in a week is 48. If you are a person doing both an unpaid student internship to fulfill the requirements of your educational program and paid employment with the same employer, your total hours of work must not exceed:   10 hours in a day, or 48 hours in a week  The maximum hours of work in a week can be exceeded in exceptional circumstances. For example, the maximum hours of work can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work under an averaging plan under a modified work schedule..."

While the standard hours are 40 per week, the maximum hours are generally 48 per week. However, this can be exceeded in "exceptional circumstances," such as under an excess hour permit or for emergency work under an averaging plan or modified work schedule.

#### Specific Employee Classes

The documents also mention specific employee classes with their own maximum hour rules. For example,
"Motor vehicle operators, including all employees normally referred to as truck drivers and bus drivers, may work the maximum hours permitted by the Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations (administered by Transport Canada)." This indicates that truck and bus drivers have different maximum hour limits governed by separate regulations.

#### Non-Driving Personnel in Trucking Industry
"If you are a shunt driver or non-driving personnel in the trucking industry, your maximum number of hours in a week is 48. Your employer may require or permit you to work more than 48 hours in a week:   in exceptional circumstances (excess hours permit) to do emergency work, or where averaging is permitted..."

Non-driving personnel in the trucking industry have a maximum of 48 hours per week, but their employer may allow them to work more in "exceptional circumstances" or where averaging is permitted.

#### Bus Operators, Shunt Drivers, and Non-Driving Personnel
"The working hours of a highway or city motor vehicle operator cannot be averaged. Under certain circumstances, the standards hours of bus operators, shunt drivers and non-driving personnel may be average over a period of 2 or more weeks. The rules of averaging are the same as for other eligible employees under Part III of the Canada Labour Code."

The working hours of highway or city motor vehicle operators cannot be averaged. However, under certain circumstances, the standard hours of bus operators, shunt drivers, and non-driving personnel may be averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks, following the same rules as other eligible employees.
