individual_results.question: What conditions must an employer meet in order to employ a person under the age of 18?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Employing a Person Under the Age of 18

### General Age of Employment

Section 179 of the Canada Labour Code states:
"An employer may employ a person under the age of 18 years only (a) in an occupation specified by the regulations; and (b) subject to the conditions fixed by the regulations for employment in that occupation." This establishes the fundamental principle that employing someone under 18 is not a blanket permission. It is contingent upon the specific occupation and the conditions outlined in the relevant regulations.

### Specific Conditions for Employment Under 18

Section 10 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations elaborates on these general conditions, providing a detailed list of requirements an employer must meet.
"An employer may employ a person under the age of 18 years in any office or plant, in any transportation, communication, maintenance or repair service, or in any construction work or other employment in a federal work, undertaking or business if (a) the person is not required, under the law of the province in which they are ordinarily resident, to be in attendance at school; and (b) the work in which the person is to be employed (i) is not carried on underground in a mine, (ii) would not cause them to be employed in or enter a place that they are prohibited from entering under the Explosives Regulations, 2013 , (iii) is not work as a nuclear energy worker as defined in the Nuclear Safety and Control Act , (iv) is not work that they are prohibited from doing under the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 by reason of their age, and (v) is not likely to be injurious to their health or to endanger their safety."

This section outlines several key restrictions. First, the person under 18 must not be legally required to attend school. Second, the work they are employed in must not pose specific dangers, such as being underground in a mine, entering prohibited places, working as a nuclear energy worker, or being prohibited from doing so by the Canada Shipping Act. Finally, the work must not be likely to harm their health or safety.

### Additional Considerations for Student Interns

Section 3.3 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations provides additional conditions specifically for student interns under 18.
"Student interns under 18 years of age may only perform  activities in the workplace if they meet the following conditions:   they are not required by provincial law to attend school their work is not likely to endanger their health or safety they are not required to work underground in a mine or in employment prohibited for young workers under the Explosives Regulations, 2013, the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and General Nuclear Safety and Control Regulations, or the Canada Shipping Act, 2001, and  they are not required to work between 11 pm on one day and 6 am on the following day..."

This section reiterates several of the conditions mentioned in Section 10, including not being required to attend school and the work not being likely to endanger their health or safety. It also adds a restriction on working between 11 pm and 6 am.

### Leave Entitlements for Student Interns

Section 3.3 also details the leave entitlements for student interns under 18.
"Student interns are not entitled to pay while  on leave." This is a crucial point to note, as it clarifies that student interns do not receive compensation while taking any of the protected leaves of absence.

### Modifying Activities for Student Interns

Section 3.3 further addresses the situation where a student intern is pregnant or nursing.
"A student intern who is pregnant or nursing has the right to make a request that you modify their activities. They must provide a certificate from a health care practitioner stating their duties cause a risk to their health or that of the foetus or child. You must either accept to modify their activities or else provide reason in writing explaining why this is not reasonably practicable. The student intern is entitled to leave while awaiting your response. However, unlike for an employee, you are not required to provide an additional leave of absence if they cannot continue to perform their activities, including situations in which you are unable to modify them. You are required to provide student interns, with the following  leaves of absence:  Personal leave Leave for victims of family violence Leave for traditional Aboriginal practices Bereavement leave Medical leave Leave for work-related illness or injury..."

This section emphasizes the student intern's right to request a modification of their activities due to pregnancy or nursing, supported by a medical certificate. It also confirms that they are entitled to the same leaves of absence as other employees, but without the additional leave provision if modifications are not possible.

individual_results.question: What types of regulations can the Governor in Council make to carry out the purposes and provisions of this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations Made by the Governor in Council

### Section 264: General Regulatory Powers

Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad range of regulations the Governor in Council can enact to achieve the Division's objectives. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (a.1) requiring employers to keep records relevant to the purposes of this Part in respect of persons who are excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of all or any of this Part; (a.2) respecting the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it; (a.3) specifying the circumstances in which a person who performs activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) must provide to an employer the information referred to in paragraph (a.2); (a.4) for the purpose of subsection 167(1.2), specifying or describing secondary or post-secondary educational institutions, vocational schools, or equivalent educational institutions outside Canada; (b) designating any branch, section or other division of any federal work, undertaking or business as an industrial establishment for the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (b.1) extending the application of this Part, in the manner and to the extent provided for in the regulations, to any class of persons; (c) governing the production and inspection of records required to be kept by employers; (d) for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees; (e) for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages, on an hourly basis, of employees who are paid on any basis of time other than hourly or who are not paid solely on a basis of time; (e.1) respecting the calculation and payment of the wages and other amounts to which an employee whose wages are paid on a commission basis, on a salary plus commission basis or on any other basis other than time is entitled to under Divisions V, VII, VIII, X and XI; (f) prescribing the maximum number of hours that may elapse between the commencement and termination of the working day of any employee; (g) [Repealed, 2018, c. 27, s. 505] (h) requiring an employer in any industrial establishment to notify employees, by the publication of such notices, in such manner as may be prescribed, of (i) the provisions of this Part or any regulation or order made under this Part, (ii) the particulars of hours of work, including the hours at which shifts change, (iii) the particulars of rest periods and meal periods, and (iv) other matters related to hours and conditions of work of employees; (i) providing for the payment of any wages of an employee to the Head or to another person in the event that the employee cannot be found or in any other case; (i.1) providing for the application of any provisions of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part to persons and, in relation to those persons, employers who are otherwise excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of this Part and adapting those provisions for the purpose of applying them to those persons and those employers; (j) providing for the establishment of consultative or advisory committees to advise the Minister on any matters arising in relation to the administration of this Part; (j.1) prescribing the circumstances and conditions for the purposes of subsection 251.01(3); (j.2) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be rejected under paragraph 251.05(1)(c); (j.3) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be rejected under paragraph 251.05(1)(c); (j.4) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 251.05(1.1); and (j.5) [Repealed, 2020, c. 12, s. 4] (k) for any other matter or purpose that under this Part is required or permitted to be prescribed by regulation."

This section is crucial as it explicitly states the Governor in Council's power to make regulations "for carrying out the purposes of this Part." The list within section 264 is extensive, covering a wide array of topics from record-keeping requirements to the calculation of wages and the notification of employees about their working conditions. The inclusion of regulations
"...extending the application of this Part, in the manner and to the extent provided for in the regulations, to any class of persons..." highlights the flexibility of this regulatory power. Furthermore, it allows for the creation of "consultative or advisory committees" to assist the Minister in administering the Division.

### Section 111: Administrative and Procedural Regulations

Section 111 focuses on the administrative and procedural aspects of the Division. It grants the Governor in Council the power to make regulations concerning
"...any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received; (b) prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent..."

This indicates that regulations can be made to standardize the communication processes between the Minister and various bodies involved in dispute resolution. Section 111 also covers the form and content of specific notices, such as those to commence collective bargaining or under section 87.2. The power to set
"...a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit..." demonstrates the ability to create rules for the functioning of the Industrial Inquiry Commission.

### Section 121.1 and Section 265: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Sections 121.1 and 265 address the application of this Division to employment within provincial Crown corporations. Both sections state that the Governor in Council can by regulation direct that this Part applies to employment on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This provision allows for a targeted application of the Division's regulations to a specific category of employers – those operating under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. It highlights the Governor in Council's ability to tailor the regulatory framework to the unique circumstances of provincial Crown corporations involved in nuclear safety.

individual_results.question: What are the entitlements of employees under the Canada Labour Code regarding breaks for medical reasons and nursing breaks?
individual_results.answer:
## Medical Breaks for Medical Reasons

### Entitlement to Unpaid Breaks
"Subject to the regulations, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted any unpaid breaks that are necessary for medical reasons."

This section establishes the fundamental right of employees to take unpaid breaks for medical needs. It is a broad entitlement, applicable to all employees, with the specifics of the break length and frequency potentially subject to further regulation. The phrase
"...any unpaid breaks that are necessary for medical reasons." is key, indicating that the breaks are not mandated but are provided to accommodate the employee's health.

### Medical Certificate Requirement
"On written request by the employer, the employee must provide a certificate issued by a health care practitioner setting out the length and frequency of the breaks needed for medical reasons and any additional information that may be prescribed by regulation."

This passage details the documentation required when an employee needs medical breaks. The employer can request a certificate from a healthcare practitioner. This certificate must specify the duration and frequency of the breaks required, as well as any other information deemed necessary by regulation. This certificate serves as proof to the employer of the medical necessity of the breaks.

## Nursing Breaks

### Entitlement to Unpaid Nursing Breaks
"...every employee who is nursing is entitled to and shall be granted any unpaid breaks necessary for them to nurse or to express breast milk."

This section specifically addresses the needs of nursing mothers. It grants them the right to take unpaid breaks for nursing or expressing breast milk. This entitlement is explicitly stated, ensuring that nursing mothers have the necessary time to care for their infants.

### Medical Certificate Requirement for Nursing Breaks
"Subject to the regulations, every employee who is nursing is entitled to and shall be granted any unpaid breaks necessary for them to nurse or to express breast milk."

This passage reiterates the entitlement to nursing breaks and also mentions that a medical certificate may be required, subject to further regulation. While not as explicitly stated as for medical breaks, the possibility of a certificate suggests that the nursing breaks may need to be documented for administrative purposes.

### Regulations Governing Nursing Breaks
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) modifying the provisions of sections 181.1 or 181.2 for the purpose of the application of this Division to any class of employees; (b) exempting any class of employees from the application of section 181.1 or 181.2; (c) respecting the breaks set out in subsection 181.1(1) and section 181.2, including circumstances in which those breaks cannot be taken; and (d) respecting additional information to be included in a certificate required under subsection 181.1(2)."

This section highlights the flexibility of the regulations in addressing the specific needs of nursing mothers. The Governor in Council can create regulations to modify or exempt certain classes of employees from the nursing break provisions. These regulations can also clarify circumstances under which nursing breaks cannot be taken and specify additional information that may be required on a nursing break certificate.

individual_results.question: What is the process for addressing discriminatory practices under the Canadian Human Rights Act according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Addressing Discriminatory Practices under the Canadian Human Rights Act: The Canada Labour Code Process

### Section 182: Head's Authority to Notify the Canadian Human Rights Commission

Section 182 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process by which the Head of the Labour Program can address discriminatory practices under the Canadian Human Rights Act.
"If the Head has reasonable grounds at any time for believing that an employer is engaging or has engaged in a discriminatory practice described in subsection (1), the Head may notify the Canadian Human Rights Commission or file a complaint with that Commission under section 40 of the Canadian Human Rights Act..."

This passage is crucial because it establishes the Head's proactive role in identifying and reporting discriminatory practices. The Head's "reasonable grounds for believing" a practice is occurring triggers a formal notification to the Canadian Human Rights Commission or a direct complaint filing. This demonstrates a mechanism for escalating concerns about discrimination to the appropriate legal body. The reference to "section 40 of the Canadian Human Rights Act" explicitly links the Labour Program's authority to the broader framework of human rights law in Canada.

### Section 125: Time Limits for Reporting Harassment and Violence

Section 125 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the question of time limits for reporting harassment and violence. It clarifies that there is no strict time limit for an employee to notify their employer of an occurrence.
"No, there is no time limit for you to submit a notice of an  occurrence of harassment and violence to your employer. However, lapse of time  may impact the employer’s ability to properly assess the situation. You are  therefore encouraged to submit your notice as soon as you are able to. If the  responding party identified in the notice of an occurrence is no longer in the  workplace, the employer will not be required to pursue an investigation.  Instead, the employer will have to conduct a review and update of the workplace assessment, as required by paragraph 6(1)(b) of the Regulations."

This section is important because it acknowledges the employee's right to report an incident without delay. However, it also provides a caveat: a significant delay in reporting could potentially hinder the employer's ability to conduct a thorough investigation. The recommendation to
"...submit your notice as soon as you are able to." is a practical one. Furthermore, it addresses a specific scenario where the responding party is no longer in the workplace, outlining an alternative course of action for the employer.

### Section 123.1: Pursuing Multiple Concurrent Proceedings

Section 123.1 of the Canada Labour Code confirms that an employee can pursue multiple concurrent proceedings under the Code/Regulations, the Canadian Human Rights Act, and grievances under their collective agreement.
"Yes, you can pursue multiple concurrent proceedings under the Code/Regulations, the Canadian  Human Rights Act and grievances under your collective agreement."

This passage is directly relevant to addressing discriminatory practices. It empowers employees to utilize all available avenues for redress. If they have filed a complaint under the Canadian Human Rights Act, they are not barred from also pursuing a resolution process under the Regulations or a grievance under their collective agreement. This provides a layered approach to seeking justice for discriminatory treatment.

### Section 95: Prohibitions Relating to Trade Unions

While Section 95 of the Canada Labour Code primarily focuses on prohibitions against trade unions, it indirectly relates to addressing discriminatory practices. It includes prohibitions against employers terminating employment
"...because the employee has been expelled or suspended from membership in the trade union for a reason other than a failure to pay the periodic dues, assessments and initiation fees uniformly required to be paid by all members of the trade union as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership in the trade union..."

This prohibition is significant because it safeguards employees from being penalized for exercising their right to unionize, which can be a crucial tool in combating discrimination. It ensures that union membership is not used as a pretext for unfair treatment or termination.

### Section 125(5): Extension to Notify Employer After Employment Ends

Section 125(5) of the Canada Labour Code addresses the question of a time limit for a former employee to apply to the Labour Program for an extension to the 3-month period after their employment ended to notify their employer of an occurrence.
"No, there is no time limit for you to submit an application to the Labour Program to extend the time period for notifying your employer of an occurrence. However, you are required to demonstrate in your request for an extension that:  you incurred trauma as a result of the  occurrence, or you have a health condition that prevented you from notifying your employer within the prescribed 3 month time period..."

This section clarifies that there is no absolute time limit for a former employee to seek an extension to the 3-month notification period. However, the extension request must be supported by evidence, such as trauma or a health condition that prevented timely notification. This ensures that extensions are granted only in exceptional circumstances.

individual_results.question: What constitutes a year of employment for an employee in terms of continuous employment with one employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Defining a Year of Employment for Continuous Employment

### Continuous Employment and Year of Employment

The Canada Labour Code, specifically Division IV on Annual Vacations, addresses the concept of continuous employment and its relation to a year of employment. Section 189(1) states:
"Despite the lease or transfer of a work, undertaking or business, or any part of a work, undertaking or business, from one employer to another employer by sale, merger or otherwise, the employment of the employee, before and after the lease or transfer, who is employed in or in connection with the operation of that work, undertaking or business, is, for the purposes of this Division, deemed to be continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking or business (a) is a federal work, undertaking or business; or (b) becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to the lease or transfer."

This section is crucial because it clarifies that continuous employment is maintained even when there is a lease or transfer of a work, undertaking, or business. For the purposes of annual vacations, the employment before and after the transfer is treated as continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking, or business is either a federal one or becomes so due to the transfer.

### Calculation of Continuous Employment

Section 189(1.3) further elaborates on the calculation of continuous employment:
"For greater certainty, if an employer’s work, undertaking or business becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to a change in its activities, for the purposes of this Division, an employee’s period of continuous employment by the employer includes any period in which the work, undertaking or business in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed was not a federal work, undertaking or business."

This means that even if an employer's work becomes federal due to a change in activities, the employee's continuous employment with that employer includes any period where the work was *not* federal. This ensures a more accurate reflection of the total time spent employed by a single employer.

### Exceptions to Continuous Employment

Section 189(1.5) outlines exceptions to the continuous employment rule. It states:
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of the employee’s entitlement under section 230 if the first employer complied with that section in respect of their employment by that employer."

This exception applies if the first employer complied with the severance pay requirements of Section 230. In such cases, the continuous employment calculation for the second employer does not include the period of employment with the first employer.

### Vacation Entitlement and Year of Employment

Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code connects a year of employment to vacation entitlement. It states:
"When an employee ceases to be employed, the employer shall pay to the employee within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed (a) any vacation pay then owing by the employer to the employee under this Division in respect of any prior completed year of employment; and (b) the applicable percentage, under section 184.01, of the wages of the employee during any part of the completed portion of their year of employment in respect of which vacation pay has not been paid to them."

This indicates that vacation pay is earned based on completed years of employment with a single employer. Therefore, a year of employment is defined as a period of continuous employment with one employer where the employee has earned vacation pay.

### Lay-off Becoming Termination

Section 188 also addresses the scenario where a lay-off becomes a termination of employment. It states:
"When an employee ceases to be employed, the employer shall pay to the employee within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed (a) any vacation pay then owing by the employer to the employee under this Division in respect of any prior completed year of employment; and (b) the applicable percentage, under section 184.01, of the wages of the employee during any part of the completed portion of their year of employment in respect of which vacation pay has not been paid to them."

This passage is relevant because it confirms that vacation pay is accrued based on completed years of employment, regardless of whether the initial period was a lay-off that later became a termination.

individual_results.question: What are the minimum vacation entitlements for employees in Canada under the Labour Code, and how is vacation pay calculated?
individual_results.answer:
## Minimum Vacation Entitlements in Canada

### Entitlement Based on Years of Employment

The Canada Labour Code outlines minimum vacation entitlements based on the number of consecutive years of employment with the same employer. Section 184(a) states:
"Except as otherwise provided by or under this Division, in respect of every year of employment by an employer, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a vacation with vacation pay of (a) at least two weeks if they have completed at least one year of employment..."
This indicates that after completing just one year of continuous employment, an employee is legally entitled to a minimum of two weeks of paid vacation.

Section 184(b) further specifies the entitlement for employees with more experience:
"(b) at least three weeks if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer..."
This increases the minimum vacation to three weeks after five consecutive years of service.

Finally, Section 184(c) details the maximum entitlement for long-term employees:
"(c) at least four weeks if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."
Employees who have dedicated ten or more years to the same employer are entitled to a minimum of four weeks of paid vacation.

### Vacation Pay Calculation

Vacation pay is calculated as a percentage of the gross wages earned during the "year of employment" for which the vacation is being taken. Section 184.01 explains this:
"An employee is entitled to vacation pay equal to: (a) 4% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation; (b) 6% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer; and (c) 8% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."
This demonstrates a tiered calculation, with the percentage increasing with the number of consecutive years of employment. For example, an employee with at least five years of service receives 6% of their wages in vacation pay, while an employee with at least ten years receives 8%.

Section 184.02 provides a more detailed breakdown:
"Your vacation pay is calculated as a percentage of the gross wages that you earn during your “year of employment”. When your vacation is:  2 weeks; vacation pay is 4% of earnings 3 weeks; vacation pay is 6% of earnings, and 4 weeks; vacation pay is 8% of earnings..."
This directly links the vacation entitlement (in weeks) to the vacation pay percentage.

### Defining Wages

The definition of "wages" for vacation pay purposes is crucial. Section 184.01 clarifies:
"For the purpose of vacation, “wages” include every form of payment for work performed. However, it does not include tips and other gratuities."
This means that all forms of compensation received during the "year of employment" are included in the vacation pay calculation, excluding tips.

### Taking Vacation in One or More Periods

Section 184.1 addresses the flexibility of taking vacation:
"A vacation granted to an employee under this Division is to be taken only in one period or, if the employee makes a request in writing and the employer approves it in writing, in more than one period."
This allows employees and employers to agree on a single vacation block or to split the vacation into multiple periods, subject to written agreement.

individual_results.question: What are the key responsibilities of an employer towards an employee who has become entitled to a vacation with vacation pay under this Division?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Towards an Employee Entitled to Vacation with Pay

### Granting Vacation

Section 185(a) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the primary responsibility of an employer towards an employee who has become entitled to a vacation with vacation pay.
"The employer of an employee who under this Division has become entitled to a vacation with vacation pay (a) shall grant to the employee the vacation to which the employee is entitled, which shall begin not later than ten months immediately following the completion of the year of employment for which the employee became entitled to the vacation..."

This indicates that the employer must provide the employee with the full vacation time to which they are legally entitled. The employer has a timeframe within which to grant this vacation, which is
"...not later than ten months immediately following the completion of the year of employment for which the employee became entitled to the vacation..." This ensures that the employee receives their earned vacation in a timely manner.

### Paying Vacation Pay

Section 185(b) further details the employer's obligation regarding vacation pay.
"(b) shall, at any time that is prescribed by the regulations, pay to the employee (i) if the vacation is taken in one period, the vacation pay to which the employee is entitled in respect of that vacation, or (ii) if the vacation is taken in more than one period, for each period, the proportion of the vacation pay that the vacation taken is of the annual vacation to which the employee is entitled."

This passage clarifies that the employer must pay the employee their full vacation pay entitlement. The timing of this payment is regulated by the government, but it must occur
"...at any time that is prescribed by the regulations..." If the vacation is taken in multiple periods, the employer must pay the vacation pay proportionally to each period. This comprehensive provision ensures that the employee receives all the financial benefits associated with their earned vacation.

### Providing Notice

Section 185(b)(iii) also addresses the employer's responsibility to provide adequate notice.
"...the vacation pay to which the employee is entitled in respect of that vacation, or (ii) if the vacation is taken in more than one period, for each period, the proportion of the vacation pay that the vacation taken is of the annual vacation to which the employee is entitled."

While this subsection primarily focuses on the timing of vacation pay, it implicitly supports the employer's responsibility to provide notice. The employer must pay the vacation pay either in one lump sum or proportionally for each period of vacation taken. This payment must occur within the timeframe specified by the regulations, which would likely include providing the employee with sufficient notice of the vacation period.

### Handling Terminations During the Year

Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's obligations when an employee's year of employment is terminated during the year.
"When an employee ceases to be employed, the employer shall pay to the employee within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed (a) any vacation pay then owing by the employer to the employee under this Division in respect of any prior completed year of employment; and (b) the applicable percentage, under section 184.01, of the wages of the employee during any part of the completed portion of their year of employment in respect of which vacation pay has not been paid to them."

This section mandates that the employer must pay any outstanding vacation pay owed to the employee within 30 days of their termination. It also requires the employer to pay the applicable percentage of the employee's wages for any completed portion of their year of employment for which vacation pay had not yet been provided. This ensures that the employee receives all their earned vacation pay, even if their employment is terminated before the end of the year.

individual_results.question: How is vacation pay treated in terms of its status and implications under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Vacation Pay: Status and Implications under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 186: Vacation Pay Defined as Wages
"Section 186 Vacation pay shall for all purposes be deemed to be wages."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental status of vacation pay. It unequivocally states that
"Vacation pay shall for all purposes be deemed to be wages." This means that vacation pay is subject to all the provisions, entitlements, and protections afforded to regular wages under the Code. It is not treated as a separate or distinct form of compensation. This broad categorization has significant implications for how vacation pay is calculated, accrued, and paid to employees.

### Section 183: Vacation Pay - Year of Employment Definition
"In this Division, vacation pay means the amount an employee is entitled to under section 184.01; ( indemnité de congé annuel ) year of employment year of employment means continuous employment of an employee by one employer (a) for a period of twelve consecutive months beginning with the date the employment began or any subsequent anniversary date thereafter, or (b) for a calendar year or other year determined by the employer, in accordance with the regulations, in relation to an industrial establishment."

Section 183 clarifies the definition of "year of employment," which is crucial for calculating vacation pay. It defines a year of employment as
"...continuous employment of an employee by one employer (a) for a period of twelve consecutive months beginning with the date the employment began or any subsequent anniversary date thereafter, or (b) for a calendar year or other year determined by the employer, in accordance with the regulations, in relation to an industrial establishment." This definition ensures that vacation pay accrues based on the total period of uninterrupted service with a single employer.

### Section 184: Vacation Pay Entitlement Based on Years of Employment
"Section 184 Except as otherwise provided by or under this Division, in respect of every year of employment by an employer, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a vacation with vacation pay of (a) at least two weeks if they have completed at least one year of employment; (b) at least three weeks if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer; and (c) at least four weeks if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."

Section 184 details the minimum vacation entitlement with vacation pay based on the number of consecutive years of employment with the same employer. It specifies that an employee is entitled to at least two weeks of vacation pay after one year of employment, at least three weeks after five years, and at least four weeks after ten years. This progressive increase in vacation entitlement incentivizes long-term employment.

### Section 184.01: Vacation Pay Calculation Based on Wages
"Section 184.01 An employee is entitled to vacation pay equal to: (a) 4% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation; (b) 6% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least five consecutive years of employment with the same employer; and (c) 8% of their wages during the year of employment in respect of which they are entitled to the vacation, if they have completed at least 10 consecutive years of employment with the same employer."

Section 184.01 provides the specific formula for calculating vacation pay. It states that an employee is entitled to vacation pay equal to 4% of their wages during the year of employment for every year of service, increasing to 6% for every five years of service, and further to 8% for every ten years of service. This wage-based calculation ensures that vacation pay is directly linked to an employee's contribution to the company over time.

### Section 185: Vacation Pay Payment Timing
"14 days before the day on which a vacation period begins; or (b) on the regular pay day during or immediately following a vacation period if it is not practicable to comply with paragraph (a) or if it is an established practice in the industrial establishment in which the employee is employed to pay vacation pay or a proportion of that vacation pay on the regular pay day during or immediately following a vacation period."

Section 185 outlines the permissible timing for vacation pay payments. It mandates that vacation pay must be paid to an employee at least 14 days before the start of their vacation, or on their regular pay day during or immediately following their vacation if the former is not feasible. This ensures that employees receive their vacation pay in a timely manner to enjoy their time off without financial concerns.

### Section 183: Vacation Pay for Interns
"Section 183 In this Division, vacation pay means the amount an employee is entitled to under section 184.01; ( indemnité de congé annuel ) year of employment year of employment means continuous employment of an employee by one employer (a) for a period of twelve consecutive months beginning with the date the employment began or any subsequent anniversary date thereafter, or (b) for a calendar year or other year determined by the employer, in accordance with the regulations, in relation to an industrial establishment."

While Section 183 defines vacation pay, it also includes a crucial distinction: "Student interns are not entitled to vacation pay." This clarifies that vacation pay is a benefit specifically for employees, not for individuals undertaking internships for educational purposes.

### Section 183: Vacation Pay for Employees on Leave
"Section 183 In this Division, vacation pay means the amount an employee is entitled to under section 184.01; ( indemnité de congé annuel ) year of employment year of employment means continuous employment of an employee by one employer (a) for a period of twelve consecutive months beginning with the date the employment began or any subsequent anniversary date thereafter, or (b) for a calendar year or other year determined by the employer, in accordance with the regulations, in relation to an industrial establishment."

Section 183 further clarifies that vacation pay is also considered wages for employees who are on leave awaiting an employer's decision regarding maternity-related reassignment and leave, as well as those required to remain available at the workplace during a 30-minute unpaid break. This reinforces its comprehensive status as compensation for work performed.

In summary, vacation pay is treated as wages under the Canada Labour Code, with its entitlement, calculation, and payment timing all directly linked to an employee's continuous employment with a single employer. It is a benefit earned over time and is subject to all the legal protections afforded to regular wages. However, it is specifically excluded for student interns.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's vacation time and pay if one or more general holidays occur during their vacation?
individual_results.answer:
## General Holidays During Vacation Time

### Vacation Pay Entitlement During General Holidays
"You are entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday takes place while you are on 1 of the following leaves:  personal leave leave for victims of family violence, or bereavement leave medical leave..." This passage directly addresses the scenario of general holidays occurring during vacation time. It clarifies that an employee on any of these leaves is still entitled to general holiday pay for that specific day.

### Postponing or Interrupting Vacation to Take Another Leave
"You may postpone or interrupt your vacation in order to take 1 of the following leaves:  maternity-related reassignment maternity parental compassionate care critical illness death or disappearance of a child personal victims of family violence traditional aboriginal practices court or jury duty bereavement medical work-related illness or injury, and leave of absence for members of the reserve force..." This section outlines the flexibility employees have regarding their vacation. It states that they can postpone or interrupt their vacation to take another leave, and their vacation time will not be affected by the general holidays that may fall during this period.

### Calculating General Holiday Pay When on Leave Provided for Under the Code
"If a general holiday occurs while you are on a leave with pay, you will only be paid general holiday pay for that day. Your leave with pay may continue the next regular working day without interruption. In this case, because you were only paid for the general holiday and not for the leave with pay, a day of leave with pay will not be subtracted from your entitlement. To calculate your general holiday pay, if you are paid on a basis other than time, or if your hours of work differ from day to day, your employer will need to determine your regular rate of wages. Your regular rate of wages is equal to:  the average daily earnings, excluding overtime pay, for the 20 days you worked immediately before the general holiday, or an amount calculated by a method agreed on in your collective agreement, if applicable..." This passage further elaborates on general holiday pay when an employee is already on a leave with pay. It specifies that they will only receive general holiday pay for that day, and their leave with pay will continue uninterrupted. It also details how general holiday pay is calculated for employees paid on a basis other than time.

### Continuous Operations and General Holiday Pay
"When you work on a general holiday in a “continuous operation” business or sector, you are entitled to:  1.5 times your regular rate of pay for the actual hours worked on the general holiday, in addition to general holiday pay (for information on the general holiday pay entitlement, refer to Calculating general holiday pay), or be paid for the actual hours worked on the general holiday at your regular rate of wages. You must also be provided a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to your annual vacation or on another day that is convenient to both you and your employer, or be paid holiday pay for the first day on which you do not work after the general holiday, if permitted by your collective agreement..." This section addresses employees working on general holidays within continuous operations. It states they are entitled to either 1.5 times their regular rate of pay plus general holiday pay, or their regular rate of pay plus a holiday with pay at a later date.

### Vacation Time and Pay When General Holidays Occur
"Generally, you may take vacation at a time that:  you have mutually agreed upon with your employer, or your employer scheduled with at least two weeks notice  However, your vacation must begin no later than 10 months after you have completed each “year of employment”." This passage explains the general rules around vacation time, which are not directly impacted by general holidays occurring during that period. It highlights the need for mutual agreement or employer scheduling with at least two weeks' notice, and that vacation must begin no later than 10 months after completing a year of employment.

### Vacation Pay Calculation and General Holiday Pay
"Your vacation pay is calculated as a percentage of the gross wages that you earn during your “year of employment”. When your vacation is:  2 weeks; vacation pay is 4% of earnings 3 weeks; vacation pay is 6% of earnings, and 4 weeks; vacation pay is 8% of earnings  A vacation pay calculator is available to assist you in determining vacation entitlements." This section details how vacation pay is calculated, which is based on the gross wages earned during the year of employment. It also mentions a vacation pay calculator for assistance. General holiday pay is a separate calculation, as outlined in other sections, and is added to vacation pay when general holidays fall during vacation time.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions and implications for an employee who needs to interrupt their vacation for reasons such as taking a leave of absence or being absent due to specific reasons?
individual_results.answer:
## Interrupting Vacation for Various Reasons

### Conditions for Interrupting Vacation

Section 187.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the initial condition for interrupting vacation:
"An employee may interrupt a vacation granted to them under this Division in order to permit them to take a leave of absence under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5 or to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1)." This indicates that an interruption is permissible when it is necessary to take another type of leave or due to a reason specified in the Canada Labour Code.

Section 207.02(1) further elaborates on this, stating:
"An employee may interrupt a leave of absence referred to in any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1)." While this section refers to leaves of absence rather than vacation, it reinforces the principle that interruptions are allowed for specific reasons.

### Implications of Interrupting Vacation

#### Resumption of Vacation

Section 187.1(1) and Section 207.02(2) both address the resumption of vacation after an interruption. Section 187.1(1) says:
"The interrupted leave resumes immediately after the interruption ends." Section 207.02(2) mirrors this, stating:
"The interrupted leave resumes immediately after the interruption ends." This means that the vacation is not lost and continues without further disruption.

#### Notice to Employer

Section 187.1(6) and Section 207.02(1) both mandate that the employee provide written notice to their employer before or as soon as possible after the interruption begins. Section 187.1(6) specifies:
"An employee who intends to interrupt their vacation shall provide the employer with written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after the interruption begins." Section 207.02(1) is similar:
"An employee who intends to interrupt their leave under subsection 206.1(2.4) or 207.02(1) shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins." This ensures the employer is aware of the change in plans and can make necessary adjustments.

#### Impact on Vacation Entitlements

Section 187.1(2) and Section 207.02(3) discuss the application of other sections of the Canada Labour Code to interrupted vacations. Section 187.1(2) states:
"If an employee interrupts a vacation to take leave under any of sections 205.1, 206, 206.1 and 206.3 to 206.9 and resumes the vacation immediately at the end of that leave, section 209.1 applies to them as if they did not resume the vacation before returning to work." Section 207.02(3) provides a similar provision for absences due to reasons referred to in subsection 239(1). These sections ensure that vacation entitlements are not negatively affected by the interruption, provided the vacation is resumed immediately after the other leave ends.

#### Postponing or Interrupting Vacation to Take Another Leave

Section 187.1(5) and Section 207.02(4) address the possibility of postponing or interrupting vacation to take another type of leave. Section 187.1(5) says:
"If an employee interrupts a vacation to take leave under section 247.5 and resumes the vacation immediately at the end of that leave, sections 247.93 to 247.95 apply to that employee as if they did not resume the vacation before returning to work." Section 207.02(4) provides a similar rule for absences due to reasons referred to in subsection 239.1(1). These sections clarify that if vacation is interrupted to take another leave, the rules governing that other leave still apply, and the vacation is resumed immediately afterward.

individual_results.question: Can an employee postpone their vacation under the Canada Labour Code, and if so, what are the conditions surrounding this postponement?
individual_results.answer:
## Postponing Annual Vacation Under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 187.2: General Postponement Conditions

Section 187.2 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly addresses the possibility of postponing annual vacation. It states:
"Despite paragraph 185(a) or any term or condition of employment, an employee may postpone their vacation until after the day on which a leave of absence taken under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5, or an absence due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1), ends."
This passage is fundamental to answering the question. It establishes that an employee *can* postpone their vacation, even if their leave of absence or absence is related to another reason outlined in the Canada Labour Code. The condition attached to this postponement is that it can occur
"...until after the day on which a leave of absence taken under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5, or an absence due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1), ends." This indicates that the postponement is directly linked to the completion of the other leave or absence.

### Section 187.2: Notice to Employer

Section 187.2 further clarifies the employer's notification requirements regarding vacation postponement. It mandates:
"An employee who intends to postpone their vacation shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with prior written notice of the postponement."
This highlights the importance of timely communication. The employee must inform their employer of their intention to postpone their vacation in writing, and "as soon as possible" before the postponement takes effect. This allows the employer to make necessary adjustments to their staffing and scheduling.

### Section 14: Postponement by Written Agreement

Section 14 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations also confirms the possibility of postponement, but with a specific condition: it must be done "by written agreement with the employer."
"An employee may, by written agreement with the employer, postpone or waive the employee’s entitlement to an annual vacation for a specified year of employment."
This passage emphasizes that the postponement is not automatic; it requires a mutual understanding and written confirmation from both the employee and the employer. The agreement should clearly state the year of employment for which the vacation is being postponed or waived.

### Section 12: Employer Notification of Vacation Year

Section 12 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations outlines the employer's obligation to notify affected employees about their year of employment, including the start and end dates and the method of vacation calculation. While not directly about postponement, it provides context for the overall vacation process and the employer's communication responsibilities.
"An employer shall, at least 30 days prior to determining a year of employment under paragraph (b) of the definition in section 183 of the Act, notify in writing the affected employees of (a) the dates of commencement and expiry of the year of employment; and (b) the method of calculating the length of vacation and the vacation pay for a period of employment of less than 12 consecutive months."
This ensures that employees are aware of their vacation year in advance, which is relevant when considering a postponement.

In summary, an employee *can* postpone their annual vacation under the Canada Labour Code, provided they do so through a written agreement with their employer (Section 14) and provide the employer with prior written notice of the postponement (Section 187.2). The postponement is also contingent on it occurring after the end of any other leave of absence or absence due to a reason listed in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1) (Section 187.2).

individual_results.question: What are the obligations of an employer regarding vacation pay when an employee ceases to be employed?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Obligations Regarding Vacation Pay Upon Employee Cessation of Employment

### Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the employer's obligation to pay accrued vacation pay to an employee upon their termination of employment.
"Section 188 When an employee ceases to be employed, the employer shall pay to the employee within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed (a) any vacation pay then owing by the employer to the employee under this Division in respect of any prior completed year of employment; and (b) the applicable percentage, under section 184.01, of the wages of the employee during any part of the completed portion of their year of employment in respect of which vacation pay has not been paid to them."

This passage clearly states that the employer must pay any outstanding vacation pay within 30 days of the employee's last day of work. It further specifies that this payment includes vacation pay earned in prior completed years and any accrued vacation pay for the current year that has not yet been paid. This provision ensures that employees receive all their earned vacation pay when their employment ends.

### Section 3_3 of WORKPLACE-3

WORKPLACE-3_3 reinforces the vacation pay obligation, stating that employers must provide affected employees with a statement of benefits, which includes
"...information on the employee’s:             wages vacation pay severance pay, if applicable, and any other benefits and pay arising from employment..." This indicates that vacation pay is a key component of the benefits statement provided to employees upon termination.

### Section 6 of WORKPLACE-3

WORKPLACE-3 also reiterates the vacation pay obligation, stating that severance pay is the greater of
"2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..." While severance pay is not solely vacation pay, it is a related form of compensation provided upon termination, and vacation pay is included within the broader context of benefits provided.

### Section 5 of WORKPLACE-3

WORKPLACE-3 further elaborates on vacation pay, mentioning that severance pay is not required when
"...the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..." This clarifies that vacation pay is still owed even in lay-off situations where the employment contract has an end date.

### Section 4 of WORKPLACE-3

WORKPLACE-3 also addresses the timing of vacation pay. It states that severance pay is provided
"...within 30 days after the day on which the employee ceases to be employed..." This aligns with Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code, which also specifies a 30-day timeframe for vacation pay.

### Section 23 of CLSR-23

CLSR-23 details the process for paying wages, including vacation pay, when an employee cannot be found. It states that the employer must pay the wages to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement within six months of becoming due and payable. It also mandates that the employer must inform the employee of the wages owed within two months of becoming due. This ensures that vacation pay is ultimately paid to the employee, even if they are unreachable.

In summary, employers have a clear legal obligation to pay accrued vacation pay to employees within 30 days of their employment termination, as outlined in Section 188 of the Canada Labour Code and reinforced by WORKPLACE-3_3, WORKPLACE-3, and CLSR-23. Vacation pay is a crucial element of the benefits statement provided to employees upon termination, and it is paid in a timely manner, even in lay-off situations with an end date to the employment contract.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's employment status when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased from one employer to another, according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Definitions

### Section 44: Business Definition and Successor Rights

Section 44(1) of the Canada Labour Code defines "business" broadly as
"...any federal work, undertaking or business and any part thereof..." This broad definition is crucial for understanding the successor rights and obligations outlined in subsequent sections.

### Section 47: Successor Obligations and Collective Agreements

Section 47(1) addresses the obligations of a successor employer when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased. It states that
"Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business, (a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires; and (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award." This passage is directly relevant to the question as it clarifies that a collective agreement or arbitral award remains in force when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased, subject to certain conditions.

### Section 47(1.1): Successor Employer Continuity of Employment

Section 47(1.1) further elaborates on the continuity of employment for employees when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased. It states that
"If, due to a contract being awarded through a retendering process, a second employer becomes responsible for carrying out any particular federal work, undertaking or business, or part of one, that was previously carried out by a first employer, an employee who is employed in or in connection with the its operation before and after the retendering, is, for the purposes of this Division, deemed to be continuously employed with one employer." This passage is a key provision for understanding how an employee's employment status is maintained during a retendering process. It establishes that an employee is considered continuously employed with the first employer if they are employed before and after the retendering, and the second employer becomes responsible for the work.

### Section 47(1.2): Non-Application of Continuity of Employment for Specific Circumstances

Section 47(1.2) specifies that the continuity of employment provisions in Section 47(1) and (1.1) do not apply in certain situations. It states that
"Subsections (1) and (1.1) do not apply if the employee’s first day of employment by the second employer is more than 13 weeks after the day that is the earlier of (a) the employee’s last day of employment by the first employer; and (b) the day on which the federal work, undertaking or business is transferred or the first day the second employer carries out the federal work, undertaking or business, as the case may be." This passage clarifies that the continuity of employment provisions do not apply if there is a significant gap between the employee's first day of employment by the second employer and the transfer or retendering of the work.

### Section 47(1.3): Inclusion of Provincial Business

Section 47(1.3) clarifies that for the purposes of continuity of employment, a provincial business becomes federal business due to a change in its activities or sale to an employer subject to this Part. It states that
"Where, as a result of a change of activity, a provincial business becomes subject to this Part, or such a business is sold to an employer who is subject to this Part, (a) the trade union that, pursuant to the laws of the province, is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the provincial business continues to be their bargaining agent for the purposes of this Part; (b) a collective agreement that applied to employees employed in the provincial business at the time of the change or sale continues to apply to them and is binding on the employer or on the person to whom the business is sold; (c) any proceeding that at the time of the change or sale was before the labour relations board or other person or authority that, under the laws of the province, is competent to decide the matter, continues as a proceeding under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party; and (d) any grievance that at the time of the change or sale was before an arbitrator or arbitration board continues to be processed under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party." This passage is relevant because it ensures that the existing bargaining unit and collective agreement are maintained when a provincial business is transferred or leased to an employer subject to this Part.

### Section 47(1.4): Calculation of Period of Continuous Employment

Section 47(1.4) provides guidance on how the period of continuous employment is calculated when a work, undertaking, or business is transferred or leased. It states that
"For greater certainty, if an employer’s work, undertaking or business becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to a change in its activities, for the purposes of this Division, an employee’s period of continuous employment by the employer includes any period in which the work, undertaking or business in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed was not a federal work, undertaking or business." This passage clarifies that the period of continuous employment includes any period in which the work, undertaking, or business was not federal business.

### Section 47(1.5): Exception for Severance Pay

Section 47(1.5) provides an exception to the continuity of employment rule for severance pay. It states that
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of the employee’s entitlement under section 230 if the first employer complied with that section in respect of their employment by that employer." This passage is relevant because it ensures that an employee is still entitled to severance pay from the first employer if the first employer complied with the severance pay requirements in Section 230.

### Section 47(1.6): Exception for Severance Pay

Section 47(1.6) provides another exception to the continuity of employment rule for severance pay. It states that
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of their entitlement to severance pay under section 235 if the first employer paid them severance pay in respect of their employment by that employer." This passage is similar to Section 47(1.5) and ensures that an employee is still entitled to severance pay from the first employer if the first employer paid them severance pay.

## Regulations Regarding Employee Vacation Rights and Pay

### Section 190: General Regulations for Annual Vacations

Section 190 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad scope of regulations that the Governor in Council can enact to achieve the purposes of Division IV, which deals with annual vacations. It states:
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of this Division and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) defining the circumstances and conditions under which the rights of an employee under this Division may be waived or the enjoyment thereof postponed; (b) prescribing the notices to be given to employees of the times when vacations may be taken; (c) prescribing the time when vacation pay shall be paid; (d) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment; (e) respecting the determination by the employer of a year of employment in relation to any industrial establishment; (f) for the calculation and determination of vacation and vacation pay in the case of seasonal or temporary employees or in other suitable cases; (g) providing for the granting of vacation or the payment of vacation pay in the event of temporary cessation of employment; and (h) providing for the application of this Division where, owing to illness or other unavoidable absence, an employee has been absent from his employment."

This section provides a comprehensive list of specific areas where the Governor in Council can create detailed rules. These regulations cover aspects such as:
*   **Waivers and Postponements:
"...defining the circumstances and conditions under which the rights of an employee under this Division may be waived or the enjoyment thereof postponed..."
*   **Notice to Employees:

*   **Vacation Pay Timing:
"...prescribing the time when vacation pay shall be paid..."

"...defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment..."
*   **Year of Employment:
"...respecting the determination by the employer of a year of employment in relation to any industrial establishment..."
*   **Vacation Pay Calculation:
"...for the calculation and determination of vacation and vacation pay in the case of seasonal or temporary employees or in other suitable cases..."

"...providing for the granting of vacation or the payment of vacation pay in the event of temporary cessation of employment..."
*   **Application During Absence:
"...providing for the application of this Division where, owing to illness or other unavoidable absence, an employee has been absent from his employment."

### Section 264: Regulations for Carrying Out the Purposes of This Part

Section 264 further elaborates on the types of regulations the Governor in Council can make, stating:
"(1) The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations (a) requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (a.1) requiring employers to keep records relevant to the purposes of this Part in respect of persons who are excluded under subsection 167(1.2) from the application of all or any of this Part; (a.2) respecting the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it; (a.3) specifying the circumstances in which a person who performs activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) must provide to an employer the information referred to in paragraph (a.2); (a.4) for the purpose of subsection 167(1.2), specifying or describing secondary or post-secondary educational institutions, vocational schools, or equivalent educational institutions outside Canada; (b) designating any branch, section or other division of any federal work, undertaking or business as an industrial establishment for the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof; (b.1) extending the application of this Part, in the manner and to the extent provided for in the regulations, to any class of persons; (c) governing the production and inspection of records required to be kept by employers; (d) for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees; (e) for calculating and determining the regular rate of wages, on an hourly basis, of employees who are paid on any basis of time other than hourly or who are not paid solely on a basis of time; (e.1) respecting the calculation and payment of the wages and other amounts to which an employee whose wages are paid on a commission basis, on a salary plus commission basis or on any other basis other than time is entitled to under Divisions V, VII, VIII, X and XI; (f) prescribing the maximum number of hours that may elapse between the commencement and termination of the working day of any employee; (g) [Repealed, 2018, c. 27, s. 505] (h) requiring an employer in any industrial establishment to notify employees, by the publication of such notices, in such manner as may be prescribed, of (i) the provisions of this Part or any regulation or order made under this Part, (ii) the particulars of hours of work, including the hours at which shifts change, (iii) the particulars of rest periods and meal periods, and (iv) other matters related to hours and conditions of work of employees; (i) providing for the payment of..."

This section reiterates and expands upon the regulatory powers of the Governor in Council, including the ability to create regulations on record-keeping, extending the application of the vacation rules to specific classes of people, and prescribing the maximum number of hours between the start and end of a workday. It also mentions regulations for vacation pay during temporary cessation of employment and when an employee has been absent due to illness.

### Section 190: Specific Vacation Regulations

Section 190 provides a more concise list of specific vacation regulations that the Governor in Council can make. It states:
"(a) defining the circumstances and conditions under which the rights of an employee under this Division may be waived or the enjoyment thereof postponed; (b) prescribing the notices to be given to employees of the times when vacations may be taken; (c) prescribing the time when vacation pay shall be paid; (d) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment; (e) respecting the determination by the employer of a year of employment in relation to any industrial establishment; (f) for the calculation and determination of vacation and vacation pay in the case of seasonal or temporary employees or in other suitable cases; (g) providing for the granting of vacation or the payment of vacation pay in the event of temporary cessation of employment; and (h) providing for the application of this Division where, owing to illness or other unavoidable absence, an employee has been absent from his employment."

This section is very similar to Section 264(a), essentially providing a slightly different phrasing of the same set of regulatory possibilities. It covers the same key areas, including waivers, vacation pay timing, continuity of employment, vacation pay calculation for specific employees, vacation granting during temporary cessation, and application during illness.

In summary, the Governor in Council has extensive regulatory power over employee vacation rights and pay under the Canada Labour Code. These regulations can cover a wide range of aspects, from defining vacation years and pay calculation methods to specifying notice requirements and how absences from work are treated for continuity of employment purposes. The sections collectively paint a picture of a flexible regulatory framework that can be adapted to the needs of different employers and employees.
