individual_results.question: What types of work operations are considered continuous operations for the purpose of determining holiday entitlement under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Continuous Operations for Holiday Entitlement

### Section 191: Definitions

Section 191 of the Canada Labour Code provides the definition of "employed in a continuous operation" which is crucial for understanding holiday entitlement for employees working in such environments.
"...employed in a continuous operation means, in respect of an employee, employment in (a) any industrial establishment in which, in each seven-day period, operations once begun normally continue without cessation until the completion of the regularly scheduled operations for that period; (b) any operations or services concerned with the running of trains, planes, ships, trucks or other vehicles, whether in scheduled or non-scheduled operations; (c) any telephone, radio, television, telegraph or other communication or broadcasting operations or services; or (d) any operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays."

This definition is comprehensive, encompassing a wide range of work operations. It includes
"...any industrial establishment in which, in each seven-day period, operations once begun normally continue without cessation until the completion of the regularly scheduled operations for that period..." This covers traditional manufacturing and production settings. It also extends to essential services like
"...any operations or services concerned with the running of trains, planes, ships, trucks or other vehicles, whether in scheduled or non-scheduled operations..." This explicitly includes transportation. Furthermore, it includes
"...any telephone, radio, television, telegraph or other communication or broadcasting operations or services..." highlighting the inclusion of media. Finally, it covers
"...any operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays." which captures businesses that operate 24/7, such as hospitals and emergency services.

### Section 7: Annual Vacations and General Holidays for Employees Working for Federally Regulated Employers

Section 7 of the Canada Labour Code elaborates on the holiday entitlement for employees working in continuous operations.
"**Continuous operations** A continuous operation is any:  business, whose operations, in each 7-day period, continue without interruption until the completion of the regularly scheduled operations for that period operation or service concerned with the running of trains, planes, ships, trucks and other vehicles whether in scheduled or non-scheduled operations telephone, radio, television telegraph or other communication or broadcasting operation or service, or operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays  As an employee working in the continuous operations, there are separate general holiday entitlements."

This section directly reiterates the definition of continuous operations provided in Section 191, emphasizing that it is a distinct category with its own holiday entitlements. It further clarifies that continuous operations include not only the businesses listed in Section 191 but also
"...operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays." This reinforces the broad scope of continuous operations as defined by the Code.

### Section 196: Holiday pay

Section 196 of the Canada Labour Code details the holiday pay entitlement for employees in continuous operations.
"(4) An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable."

This section specifies that employees in continuous operations are *not* entitled to holiday pay if they do not report for work or make themselves unavailable when required. This is a key distinction from employees in non-continuous operations who are generally entitled to holiday pay. The condition that employees must be "available to work" when conditions of employment require it is important.

### Section 199: Holiday work for managers, etc.

Section 199 of the Canada Labour Code addresses holiday work for managers and other excluded employees.
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

While this section deals with holiday work for excluded employees, it indirectly supports the understanding of continuous operations. It ensures that even excluded employees in continuous operations who are required to work on a general holiday receive holiday pay at a later date. This reinforces the idea that continuous operations have a distinct approach to holiday pay, including provisions for holiday pay even when employees are required to work.

individual_results.question: What is the general entitlement of employees regarding holidays with pay under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Holiday Entitlement for Employees under the Canada Labour Code

### Entitlement to General Holidays with Pay

The Canada Labour Code establishes a general entitlement to a day off with pay for the following 10 days, which are called general holidays:
"New Year’s Day Good Friday Victoria Day Canada Day Labour Day National Day for Truth and Reconciliation  Thanksgiving Day Remembrance Day Christmas Day Boxing Day..." This entitlement applies to all employees working for federally regulated employers, unless otherwise specified in their collective agreement.

### Holiday Pay Calculation

The Code outlines specific holiday pay calculations based on an employee's earnings.
"Section 196 (1) Subject to subsections (2) and (4), an employer shall, for each general holiday, pay an employee holiday pay equal to at least one twentieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that the employee earned with the employer in the four-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This indicates that holiday pay is at least one-twentieth of the wages earned in the preceding four weeks.
"An employee whose wages are paid in whole or in part on a commission basis and who has completed at least 12 weeks of continuous employment with an employer shall, for each general holiday, be paid holiday pay equal to at least one sixtieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that they earned in the 12-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This provides a different calculation for employees whose wages are commission-based.
"For the road transportation sector, the mileage rate cannot be inclusive of general holiday pay. The general holiday entitlement must be calculated and recorded separately." This clarifies a specific provision for the road transportation sector.

### Holiday Pay for Continuous Operations Employees

Employees working in continuous operations have a different holiday pay entitlement.
"When you work on a general holiday in a “continuous operation” business or sector, you are entitled to:  1.5 times your regular rate of pay for the actual hours worked on the general holiday, in addition to general holiday pay (for information on the general holiday pay entitlement, refer to Calculating general holiday pay), or be paid for the actual hours worked on the general holiday at your regular rate of wages. You must also be provided a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to your annual vacation or on another day that is convenient to both you and your employer, or be paid holiday pay for the first day on which you do not work after the general holiday, if permitted by your collective agreement   Note: If you do not work on a general holiday, but you were available to work, you are still entitled to holiday pay." This states that continuous operations employees are entitled to either 1.5 times their regular rate of pay for the hours worked on the holiday, plus general holiday pay, or their regular rate of pay for the hours worked, plus general holiday pay, and an additional holiday with pay at a later date.
"An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable." This clarifies that continuous operations employees are not entitled to holiday pay if they are not scheduled to work or make themselves unavailable to work when required.

### Holiday Pay During Leave

Employees on leave provided for under the Canada Labour Code are still entitled to general holiday pay.
"You are entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday takes place while you are on 1 of the following leaves:  personal leave leave for victims of family violence, or bereavement leave medical leave  If a general holiday occurs while you are on a leave with pay, you will only be paid general holiday pay for that day. Your leave with pay may continue the next regular working day without interruption. In this case, because you were only paid for the general holiday and not for the leave with pay, a day of leave with pay will not be subtracted from your entitlement. To calculate your general holiday pay, if you are paid on a basis other than time, or if your hours of work differ from day to day, your employer will need to determine your regular rate of wages. Your regular rate of wages is equal to:  the average daily earnings, excluding overtime pay, for the 20 days you worked immediately before the general holiday, or an amount calculated by a method agreed on in your collective agreement, if applicable..." This explains that general holiday pay is paid for the day the holiday occurs while the employee is on leave with pay, and the regular rate of wages is calculated based on the 20 days worked immediately before the holiday.

## General Holiday Falling on a Non-Working Day: Employee Entitlements

### Section 193(1) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 193(1) directly addresses the scenario where a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee. It states:
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This passage is crucial because it clearly outlines the employee's right to an additional holiday with pay when a general holiday coincides with a non-working day. The employee has the flexibility to take this holiday either as an addition to their annual vacation or at a mutually agreeable time with their employer. This provision ensures that the employee is not disadvantaged by the holiday falling on a day they would normally not be working.

### Section 192 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 192 reinforces the general entitlement to a holiday with pay on each general holiday within an employee's period of employment. While not specifically addressing the non-working day scenario, it establishes the fundamental principle that such a holiday must be provided.
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on each of the general holidays falling within any period of his employment."

This statement supports the interpretation of Section 193(1), as it confirms that a general holiday *must* be provided, even if it falls on a non-working day for the employee. The "except as otherwise provided by this Division" clause acknowledges the specific provision in Section 193(1) for this situation.

### Section 193(2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 193(2) provides a specific rule for general holidays that fall on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day. It states:
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division, when New Year’s Day, Canada Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Remembrance Day, Christmas Day or Boxing Day falls on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on the working day immediately preceding or following the general holiday."

This subsection offers a tailored solution for these particular general holidays. If a general holiday falls on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day, the employee is entitled to a holiday with pay on the working day either before or after the general holiday. This ensures that the employee still receives the holiday, even if it is not their usual day off.

individual_results.question: Are there any exceptions to the application of Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code regarding holidays with pay for employees?

## Exceptions to Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 193: General Holiday Falling on Day Off

Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the entitlement to a holiday with pay when a general holiday falls on a day that is normally a non-working day for an employee. It states:
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This section establishes a general rule for employees whose scheduled day off coincides with a general holiday. However, it also includes a crucial exception found in subsection (2).

### Subsection (2): Exemption Under Collective Agreement

Subsection (2) of Section 193 provides a specific exemption for employees covered by a collective agreement that guarantees at least nine paid holidays per year, in addition to their annual vacation. It clarifies:
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This subsection explicitly states that the entitlement to a holiday with pay on a normally non-working day is *not* applicable to employees under a collective agreement with a higher paid holiday entitlement. This means that if an employee's scheduled day off is a general holiday, and their collective agreement provides for at least nine paid holidays annually, they are not entitled to an additional paid holiday on the following or preceding working day.

### Section 194: Exemption for Employees Employed in Continuous Operation

Section 194 offers another exception, specifically for employees employed in a continuous operation. It states:
"Section 193 does not apply in respect of any employees who are employed under the terms of a collective agreement that entitles those employees to at least nine holidays with pay, exclusive of any annual vacation, in each year."

This section reiterates the exemption found in subsection (2) of Section 193, but applies it more broadly. It clarifies that the entitlement to a holiday with pay on a normally non-working day does not apply to employees in continuous operation who are covered by a collective agreement with a higher paid holiday entitlement. This reinforces the idea that the holiday with pay on a normally non-working day rule is not universal.

### Section 199: Holiday Work for Managers, etc.

Section 199 addresses employees excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who are required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay. It states:
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

While this section deals with holiday work, it does not present an exception to the application of Section 193. It simply provides an alternative arrangement for employees who are otherwise excluded from certain holiday pay provisions.

In summary, there are several exceptions to the application of Section 193 of the Canada Labour Code. The most significant exception is found in subsection (2), which exempts employees covered by a collective agreement with at least nine paid holidays per year. Section 194 reiterates this exemption more broadly, applying it to employees in continuous operation with higher paid holiday entitlements.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can an employer substitute a different day for a general holiday for their employees according to the Canada Labour Code?

## Employer Substitution of General Holidays

### Section 195: General Conditions for Substitution

Section 195 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the primary conditions under which an employer can substitute a different day for a general holiday for their employees. It distinguishes between employees subject to a collective agreement and those not.

#### Substitution for Employees Subject to Collective Agreement
"An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, substitute any other day for a general holiday if the substitution is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union, and the substituted day shall, for that employee or those employees, be deemed to be a general holiday for the purposes of this Part."

This passage establishes that substitution for employees covered by a collective agreement requires a mutual written agreement between the employer and the trade union. The agreement must explicitly state that the substituted day will be treated as a general holiday for those employees. This ensures that the change is not unilateral and has the support of the relevant employee representatives.

#### Substitution for Employees Not Subject to Collective Agreement
"Subject to subsection (3), an employer may, in respect of one or more employees not subject to a collective agreement, substitute any other day for a general holiday and the substituted day shall, for that employee or those employees, be deemed to be a general holiday for the purposes of this Part, if the substitution has been approved (a) in the case of a substitution that affects one employee, by that employee in writing; or (b) in the case of a substitution that affects more than one employee, by at least 70% of the affected employees."

For employees without a collective agreement, the employer needs approval from a significant portion of the affected workforce. This approval can be obtained either individually in writing from each employee if only one employee is affected, or from at least 70% of the employees affected by the substitution if more than one employee is impacted. This threshold ensures that the change has broad acceptance among the employees.

### Section 195.1: Voting and Duration of Substitution

Section 195.1 clarifies the application of voting procedures outlined in Section 195 to the substitution of a general holiday. It states that
"Sections 172.1 and 172.2 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of the substitution of a general holiday pursuant to this Division." This means that the voting procedures detailed in Sections 172.1 and 172.2, which govern the approval of changes to work schedules, are also applicable to the substitution of a general holiday.

### Section 195(3): Posting of Notice
"If any other day is to be substituted for a general holiday under subsection (2), the employer shall post a notice of the substitution in readily accessible places where it is likely to be seen by the affected employees, for at least 30 days before the substitution takes effect."

This section mandates that the employer must provide ample notice of the substitution to the affected employees. The notice must be posted in easily accessible locations for at least 30 days before the substituted day becomes a general holiday. This ensures that employees are aware of the change in advance and can make necessary arrangements.

### Section 195(4): Exception to Posting
"Subsection (3) does not apply to a substitution in respect of one employee following a request made under subsection 177.1(1)."

This provides a limited exception to the posting requirement. If an employee makes a specific request for a substitution under subsection 177.1(1), the employer is not required to post a notice. This allows for individual, less formal substitutions in certain circumstances.

## Holiday Pay Calculation under the Canada Labour Code

### General Holiday Pay Entitlement

The Canada Labour Code outlines the minimum holiday pay an employee is entitled to for a general holiday. Section 196(1) states:
"Subject to subsections (2) and (4), an employer shall, for each general holiday, pay an employee holiday pay equal to at least one twentieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that the employee earned with the employer in the four-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This indicates that the base holiday pay is calculated as a fraction of the employee's earnings in the preceding four weeks.

### Holiday Pay for Continuous Operations Employees

Employees working in "continuous operations" have separate general holiday entitlements. Section 196(4) clarifies this:

This means that if a continuous operations employee is scheduled to work on a general holiday but does not report for duty or makes themselves unavailable, they are not entitled to holiday pay.

### Holiday Pay for Employees on Leave

Employees on leave provided for under the Code are still entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday falls during their leave. Section 196(4) addresses this:
"An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable." This section, while seemingly contradictory to the previous one, is likely a misinterpretation or a section that has been amended. The context of continuous operations suggests that holiday pay is still provided for continuous operations employees on leave. However, for other types of leave, the entitlement is clarified in Workplace-2_6:
"You are entitled to general holiday pay if a general holiday takes place while you are on 1 of the following leaves:  personal leave leave for victims of family violence, or bereavement leave medical leave..." This states that general holiday pay is provided for leave with pay.

### Holiday Pay for Employees Paid on Commission

Employees paid on commission have a different holiday pay calculation. Section 196(2) specifies:
"An employee whose wages are paid in whole or in part on a commission basis and who has completed at least 12 weeks of continuous employment with an employer shall, for each general holiday, be paid holiday pay equal to at least one sixtieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that they earned in the 12-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." For employees who have not completed 12 weeks of continuous employment, the holiday pay is at least one-twentieth (1/20th) of their wages earned in the 4-week period immediately before the holiday.

### Holiday Pay for Employees in the Longshoring Sector

Employees in the longshoring sector have a more complex holiday pay calculation. Section 196(5) details this:
"Working in the longshoring sector can mean working for several different employers (an employer’s association and/or multi-employer unit) during a pay period. As an employee working in the longshoring sector, your general holiday pay is your basic rate of wages multiplied by at least one-twentieth (1/20th) of the total number of hours worked, excluding overtime hours, during the 4-week period before the week in which the holiday occurs." However, if they work for an employers’ association and perform work for another employer who is not a member of the association, a different calculation applies:
"In this case, instead of general holiday pay, the other employer must also pay you, on each payday, an amount equal to 3.5% of your basic rate of wages, multiplied by the number of hours you worked during that pay period. In addition to any amounts received, if your employer requires you to work on a general holiday, your employer must pay you at least 1.5 times your basic rate of wages for the time worked on that day." This indicates that holiday pay for longshoring employees varies depending on their employment structure.

### Holiday Pay for Part-Time Employees

Part-time employees are entitled to holiday pay for the same 10 general holidays as full-time employees, but their holiday pay is adjusted to reflect their hours worked. Section 196(5) mentions this:
"As a part-time employee, you are entitled to receive pay for the same 10 general holidays as full-time employees. Your holiday pay is adjusted to the number of hours you work." This confirms that holiday pay for part-time employees is proportional to their hours worked.

individual_results.answer:
## Holiday Pay Requirements for Employees Required to Work on a General Holiday

### General Holiday Pay Entitlement

Section 197(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the minimum holiday pay an employee working on a general holiday is entitled to:
"An employee who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be paid, in addition to the holiday pay for that day, wages at a rate equal to at least one and one-half times their regular rate of wages for the time that they work on that day." This indicates that holiday pay is not a fixed amount, but rather an additional amount calculated as 1.5 times the employee's regular rate of pay for the hours worked on the holiday.

Section 196(1) further clarifies the holiday pay calculation for employees whose wages are paid on a commission basis:
"Subject to subsections (2) and (4), an employer shall, for each general holiday, pay an employee holiday pay equal to at least one twentieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that the employee earned with the employer in the four-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This provides a formula for commission-based employees, calculating holiday pay as one-twentieth of their earnings in the preceding four weeks.

### Additional Holiday with Pay

Section 197(2)(b) specifies that an employee working on a general holiday is also entitled to:
"...be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer." This means that in addition to the 1.5 times regular rate of pay, the employee receives an extra paid day off.

Section 197(2)(c) provides an alternative to the additional paid day off:
"...or (c) be paid holiday pay for the first day on which they do not work after that day, if a collective agreement that is binding on the employer and the employee so provides." This allows for holiday pay to be paid for the first day after the holiday if the collective agreement allows for it.

### Continuous Operations

Section 2_7 defines "continuous operations" and outlines separate general holiday entitlements for employees working in these sectors:
"A continuous operation is any:  business, whose operations, in each 7-day period, continue without interruption until the completion of the regularly scheduled operations for that period operation or service concerned with the running of trains, planes, ships, trucks and other vehicles whether in scheduled or non-scheduled operations telephone, radio, television telegraph or other communication or broadcasting operation or service, or operation or service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or general holidays  As an employee working in the continuous operations, there are separate general holiday entitlements." This highlights that continuous operations employees have different holiday pay rules than those in standard businesses.

### Employees Not Reporting for Work

Section 196(4) addresses the situation where an employee is scheduled to work on a general holiday but does not report for duty:
"An employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday (a) on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day..." This clearly states that continuous operations employees are not entitled to holiday pay if they do not report for work after being called to do so.

### Managers and Professionals

Section 199 clarifies the holiday pay entitlement for managers and professionals who are required to work on a general holiday:
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer." This indicates that managers and professionals who work on a general holiday receive a holiday with pay at a later date, even though they are excluded from the 1.5 times regular rate of pay provision of section 197.

## Holiday Work for Managers and Others: Status under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 199: Holiday Pay for Managers and Others

Section 199 of Division V of the Canada Labour Code explicitly addresses the status of holiday work for managers and others who are excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2).
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This passage is crucial because it clarifies that even if an employee is excluded from the additional pay provisions of Section 197 for holiday work, they are still entitled to a holiday with pay at a later date. The section provides flexibility, allowing the employer and employee to determine the most suitable time for the holiday. This ensures that managers and others who are not eligible for the 1.5 times regular rate pay for holiday work are not disadvantaged.

### Section 197: Additional Pay for Holiday Work - Exclusion of Managers, etc.

Section 197 of Division V details the additional pay an employee receives for working on a general holiday. However, it also includes an exclusion.
"An employee employed in a continuous operation who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall (a) be paid in accordance with subsection (1); (b) be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer; or (c) be paid holiday pay for the first day on which they do not work after that day, if a collective agreement that is binding on the employer and the employee so provides."

While Section 197 outlines the additional pay for holiday work, it does not explicitly exclude managers or others from this provision. However, Section 199 clarifies that such excluded employees will still receive a holiday with pay at a later date, as outlined in Section 197(b) and (c). This suggests that the exclusion in Section 167(2) does not negate the entitlement to a holiday with pay for holiday work, but rather modifies the compensation structure.

### Section 168: Saving More Favourable Benefits

Section 168 of the Canada Labour Code provides a general principle regarding the application of the Part and its regulations.
"This Part and all regulations made under this Part apply notwithstanding any other law or any custom, contract or arrangement, but nothing in this Part shall be construed as affecting any rights or benefits of an employee under any law, custom, contract or arrangement that are more favourable to the employee than his rights or benefits under this Part."

This section is relevant because it ensures that any holiday pay provisions under Division V are not diminished by other agreements or laws that offer employees better terms. It reinforces the idea that holiday pay, as defined in Division V, is the minimum standard and employees can still benefit from more generous holiday pay arrangements in their collective agreements or other agreements.

individual_results.answer:
## Holiday Pay for Managers and Exempt Employees

### Section 199: Holiday Work for Managers, Etc.

Section 199 directly addresses the scenario posed in the question. It states:
"Despite section 197, an employee excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This passage is crucial because it explicitly outlines the entitlement of employees excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) to a holiday with pay when they are required to work on a general holiday. The "despite section 197" indicates that this provision overrides the general rule in section 197, which provides additional pay for holiday work. Instead of the additional pay outlined in section 197, these excluded employees receive a holiday with pay at a later date. The flexibility in how this holiday is provided – either added to their annual vacation or granted at a mutually convenient time – is also noteworthy.

### Section 197: Additional Pay for Holiday Work

While Section 197 discusses holiday pay for employees *not* excluded from Division I, it is relevant for understanding the contrast with Section 199. Section 197(1) states:
"An employee who is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay shall be paid, in addition to the holiday pay for that day, wages at a rate equal to at least one and one-half times their regular rate of wages for the time that they work on that day."

This passage details the additional pay that non-excluded employees receive for holiday work. Section 197(2) further elaborates on this, mentioning that employees in continuous operation receive this additional pay in accordance with subsection (1), or are given a holiday with pay at some other time, or are paid holiday pay for the first day on which they do not work after that day, if a collective agreement so provides.

### Section 167.01: Presumption of Employee Status

Section 167.01 establishes a presumption that an employee is their employer's employee unless the contrary is proven. This presumption is important because it informs the application of Division I to various employment relationships. However, it does not directly address the specific situation of managers and exempt employees under subsection 167(2).

### Section 167: Application of Part

Section 167 outlines the scope of application of Division I. It states that Division I applies to employment in or in connection with federal work, undertakings, or businesses, and to employers of those employees. It also specifies that Division I applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs activities for an employer to which this Part applies, as if that person were an employee.

### Section 167(2): Exclusion from Division I

Section 167(2) is the key provision that clarifies the treatment of managers and superintendents. It states:
"Division I does not apply to or in respect of employees who (a) are managers or superintendents or exercise management functions; or (b) are members of such professions as may be designated by regulation as professions to which Division I does not apply."

This exclusion from Division I is what makes Section 199 relevant. Since managers and superintendents are excluded from Division I, they are not entitled to the additional pay outlined in Section 197 for holiday work. Instead, Section 199 provides them with a holiday with pay at a later date.

In summary, when an employee who is excluded from the application of Division I under subsection 167(2) is required to work on a day on which they are entitled to holiday pay, they are given a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer, as stated in Section 199. This provision overrides the additional pay outlined in Section 197, which applies to employees *not* excluded from Division I.

## Holiday Pay Under the Canada Labour Code

### General Holiday Pay Entitlement

The Canada Labour Code establishes a clear entitlement to holiday pay for eligible employees. Section 196(1) states that an employer shall, for each general holiday, pay an employee holiday pay equal to
"...at least one twentieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that the employee earned with the employer in the four-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This indicates a base level of holiday pay tied to recent earnings.

Section 196(2) further elaborates on this entitlement for employees whose wages are paid on a commission basis. It specifies that such employees are entitled to holiday pay equal to
"...at least one sixtieth of the wages, excluding overtime pay, that they earned in the 12-week period immediately preceding the week in which the general holiday occurs." This provides a different calculation for commission-based employees, reflecting their potentially more variable earnings.

Section 197(1) details the additional pay an employee required to work on a general holiday shall receive. It states they will be paid
"...wages at a rate equal to at least one and one-half times their regular rate of wages for the time that they work on that day." This is a significant premium on top of the base holiday pay.

### Holiday Pay for Employees on Leave

The Canada Labour Code also addresses holiday pay for employees on leave provided for under the Code. Section 196(4) clarifies that an employee who is employed in a continuous operation is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday
"...on which they do not report for work after having been called to work on that day; or (b) for which they make themselves unavailable to work when the conditions of employment in the industrial establishment in which they are employed (i) require them to be available, or (ii) allow them to make themselves unavailable." This provision ensures that employees on leave are not penalized for missing a general holiday.

Section 196(5) repeals a previous provision related to continuous operation employees not reporting for work.

### Holiday Pay for Managers and Professionals

Section 199 addresses the specific situation of managers and professionals who are required to work on a general holiday. It states that such employees are entitled to
"...a holiday with pay at some other time, either by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer..." This ensures they receive the benefit of the holiday even if they are working.

### Holiday Pay for Employees Working on a General Holiday

Section 200 explicitly states that
"Holiday pay granted to an employee is for all purposes deemed to be wages." This is a fundamental aspect of holiday pay under the Code, ensuring it is included in the calculation of an employee's total earnings.

Section 200 also details the specific holiday pay requirements when an employee works on a general holiday. It states that they must be paid
"...no less than 1.5 times your regular rate of wages for the time worked on that day, and general holiday pay for that day..." This combines the premium pay for holiday work with the standard holiday pay entitlement.

Furthermore, Section 200 clarifies that if an employee is entitled to holiday pay and their employer requires them to work on a general holiday, the employer must pay them this premium pay, along with general holiday pay. It also specifies that if a general holiday occurs while an employee is on leave with pay, they will only be paid general holiday pay for that day, and their leave with pay may continue the next regular working day without interruption.

## Section 189's Application to Section 201

### General Application of Section 189

Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code has a broad application, as explicitly stated in multiple documents.
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This phrase appears in CLC-237, CLC-234, CLC-201, CLC-209.5, and CLC-201.1, indicating a consistent rule across several divisions of the Code. This means that the provisions of Section 189 are relevant when interpreting and applying the rules outlined in Section 201, which deals with General Holidays.

### Section 189's Specific Application to Section 201

Section 189's application to Section 201 is further clarified in CLC-237.
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division." This statement directly answers the question, confirming that Section 189 is in effect when considering the application of Section 201.

### Section 189's Impact on Continuous Employment for General Holidays

Section 189's effect on continuous employment is relevant to Section 201 because it determines how an employee's prior employment is counted towards their eligibility for general holidays.
"For greater certainty, if an employer’s work, undertaking or business becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to a change in its activities, for the purposes of this Division, an employee’s period of continuous employment by the employer includes any period in which the work, undertaking or business in or in connection with the operation of which the employee is employed was not a federal work, undertaking or business." This passage from CLC-209.5 explains that Section 189 accounts for changes in federal status of an employer's work. This is important for Section 201 because it ensures that an employee's continuous employment with a non-federal employer is included when calculating their general holiday entitlement after the employer becomes federal.

### Section 189's Exclusion for Severance Pay and Exceptions

Section 189 also includes specific exclusions that might be relevant to Section 201 in certain circumstances.
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of the employee’s entitlement under section 230 if the first employer complied with that section in respect of their employment by that employer." and
"For the purposes of an employee’s employment by the second employer, this section does not apply in respect of the calculation of their entitlement to severance pay under section 235 if the first employer paid them severance pay in respect of their employment by that employer." These exclusions mean that Section 189 will not affect the calculation of general holiday entitlement if the first employer complied with Section 230 (severance pay) or Section 235 (severance pay upon termination).

In summary, Section 189 applies to Section 201 by providing a framework for determining continuous employment for general holidays, taking into account changes in federal status of an employer's work and specific exclusions related to severance pay.

## Main Purpose of Section 203 Regulations

### Defining Multi-Employer Employment

Section 203 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the power to make regulations that further define "multi-employer employment." This is a foundational aspect of the section's purpose.
"In this Division, , as more particularly defined by the regulations, means employment in any occupation or trade in which, by custom of that occupation or trade, any or all employees would in the usual course of a working month be ordinarily employed by more than one employer." This quote directly states the core concept that the regulations aim to refine. By providing a more detailed definition, the regulations ensure clarity and consistency in applying the provisions of Division VI to various employment arrangements.

### Ensuring Equivalent Rights and Benefits

The regulations also aim to ensure that employees engaged in multi-employer employment receive the same rights and benefits as those employed by a single employer,
"...so that, as far as practicable, employees engaged in multi-employer employment will be entitled to the same rights and benefits under that Division as employees employed by one employer." This is a central objective.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) defining more particularly the expression “multi-employer employment”; and (b) modifying, to the extent that the Governor in Council considers necessary, the provisions of Division I.1, IV, V, VII, VIII, X, XI, XIII or XIV so that, as far as practicable, employees engaged in multi-employer employment will be entitled to the same rights and benefits under that Division as employees employed by one employer." This passage explicitly outlines the scope of the regulations, which includes modifying provisions from other Divisions of the Code to achieve this parity.

### Application to Federal Works and Undertakings

Furthermore, the regulations can be made applicable to all federal works, undertakings, or businesses, or to specific ones. This broad applicability ensures that the provisions of Division VI extend to a wide range of employment situations.
"(3) Any regulation made pursuant to subsection (2) may be made applicable to all federal works, undertakings or businesses or particularly to one or more such works, undertakings or businesses or such classes thereof or classes of employees thereof as may be specified in the regulations." This quote highlights the potential for the regulations to have a widespread impact on federal employment standards.

### Addressing Shared Employer Obligations

Section 203 regulations are particularly relevant to addressing the challenges of shared employer obligations in multi-employer employment. As discussed in the Labour Reports, determining who is ultimately responsible for wages and other entitlements can be complex when work is subcontracted or involves multiple entities. The regulations can provide tools to clarify these responsibilities.
"Section 203 (1) In this Division, , as more particularly defined by the regulations, means employment in any occupation or trade in which, by custom of that occupation or trade, any or all employees would in the usual course of a working month be ordinarily employed by more than one employer." This definition is crucial for applying the regulations to situations where employees work for multiple employers. The subsequent regulations can then address how to allocate those obligations fairly.

individual_results.question: What accommodations can an employee who is pregnant or nursing request from their employer, and what documentation is required to support such a request?
individual_results.answer:
## Maternity-Related Reassignment and Leave: Accommodations and Documentation

### Section 204: Reassignment and Job Modification

Section 204 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific accommodations an employee who is pregnant or nursing can request from their employer.
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing may, during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, request the employer to modify her job functions or reassign her to another job if, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."
This indicates that the employee has the right to ask for either a change to their existing job duties or a transfer to a different role that is safer for her and her child. The timeframe for this request is clearly defined as from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week after birth.

### Section 204(2): Required Documentation

To support this request, the employee must provide their employer with a certificate from a health care practitioner of their choice.
"(2) An employee's request under subsection (1) must be accompanied by a certificate from a health care practitioner of the employee's choice indicating the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk."
This certificate is crucial as it details the medical reasons why the current job functions pose a risk and specifies what the employee needs to avoid to mitigate that risk. This allows the employer to properly assess the request and determine if a modification or reassignment is reasonably practicable.

### Section 205: Employer Obligations

Section 205 details the employer's responsibilities when an employee makes such a request.
"(1) An employer to whom a request has been made under subsection 204(1) shall examine the request in consultation with the employee and, where reasonably practicable, shall modify the employee's job functions or reassign her."
This highlights that the employer is obligated to seriously consider the request and make a reasonable effort to accommodate the employee's needs.
"(3) The onus is on the employer to show that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate issued under subsection 204(2) is not reasonably practicable."
This places the burden of proof on the employer to justify why a reasonable accommodation cannot be made.
"(4) If the employer concludes that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate is not reasonably practicable, the employer shall inform the employee in writing."
If the employer determines that a reasonable accommodation is not possible, they must communicate this decision to the employee in writing.

### Section 205.2: Employee Duty to Inform Employer of Changes

Section 205.2 outlines the employee's responsibility to inform their employer of any changes to the duration of the risk or inability to work.
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate."
This ensures that the employer has up-to-date information to continue planning for the employee's needs.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of an employer when an employee requests a job modification or reassignment due to a risk indicated in a certificate issued under subsection 204(2), and what are the rights of the employee during this process?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Regarding Maternity-Related Reassignment and Job Modification

### Section 204: Employee's Right to Request Job Modification or Reassignment

Section 204(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the initial obligation of an employer when an employee makes such a request. It states:
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing may, during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, request the employer to modify her job functions or reassign her to another job if, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child." This passage is fundamental as it establishes the employee's right to make the request. The timeframe for the request is clearly defined, from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week postpartum.

### Section 204(2): Certificate Requirement

Section 204(2) specifies the documentation the employee must provide with the request:
"An employee’s request under subsection (1) must be accompanied by a certificate from a health care practitioner of the employee’s choice indicating the expected duration of the potential risk and the activities or conditions to avoid in order to eliminate the risk." This certificate is crucial because it provides the medical basis for the request. It details the specific risks associated with continuing the employee's current job functions and the necessary adjustments to mitigate those risks. The employer relies on this certificate to assess the reasonableness of the request.

### Section 204(3): Onus of Proof

Section 204(3) clarifies the burden of proof in the employer's assessment:
"The onus is on the employer to show that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate issued under subsection 204(2) is not reasonably practicable." This is a significant point. The employer cannot simply deny the request; they must actively demonstrate that such a change is not feasible. This places a responsibility on the employer to explore all possible solutions.

### Section 204(4): Employer's Written Response

Section 204(4) details the employer's obligation to inform the employee in writing if they conclude that a modification or reassignment is not reasonably practicable:
"If the employer concludes that a modification of job functions or a reassignment that would avoid the activities or conditions indicated in the certificate is not reasonably practicable, the employer shall so inform the employee in writing." This ensures transparency and allows the employee to understand the employer's position and explore other options.

### Section 204(5): Status of Employee

Section 204(5) addresses the employee's job security during the process:
"An employee whose job functions are modified or who is reassigned shall be deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time of making the request under subsection 204(1), and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job." This guarantees the employee's continuity in terms of their position, pay, and benefits, providing reassurance during a potentially disruptive period.

### Section 204(6): Employee's Entitlement to Leave

Section 204(6) confirms the employee's right to a leave of absence for the duration of the identified risk:
"An employee referred to in subsection (4) is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence for the duration of the risk as indicated in the certificate." This leave is essential to protect the employee's health and the health of their developing child. It is granted automatically upon the employer's determination that a modification or reassignment is not reasonably practicable.

## Employee Rights During the Process

### Entitlement to Continue in Current Job While Employer Examines Request

Section 204(2) also states:
"An employee who has made a request under subsection 204(1) is entitled to continue in her current job while the employer examines her request, but, if the risk posed by continuing any of her job functions so requires, she is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence with pay at her regular rate of wages until the employer (a) modifies her job functions or reassigns her, or (b) informs her in writing that it is not reasonably practicable to modify her job functions or reassign her, and that pay shall for all purposes be deemed to be wages." This highlights the employee's right to continue in their current role while the employer reviews the request. However, it also includes a provision for a leave of absence with pay if the risk associated with continuing the job functions necessitates it.

### Right to Be Represented

Section 204(5) mentions the employee's right to be represented during the resolution process:
"An employee whose job functions are modified or who is reassigned shall be deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time of making the request under subsection 204(1), and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job." While not explicitly stating the right to be represented, this passage implies that the employee will have a voice in the process and will not be disadvantaged by the changes made.

### Right to Information

Section 204(4) mandates that the employer must inform the employee in writing if they conclude that a modification or reassignment is not reasonably practicable. This ensures the employee is kept informed of the employer's decision and can explore other avenues if necessary.

## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Leave of Absence Notification and Documentation

### Section 205.1: Entitlement to Leave and Employee's Duty to Inform Employer

This section outlines an employee's entitlement to maternity-related reassignment and leave, as well as their crucial responsibility to inform their employer.
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability."
This quote directly addresses the employee's initial obligation. It states that the employee must provide their employer with a certificate from a healthcare practitioner. This certificate must detail the inability to work due to pregnancy or nursing and the expected duration of that inability. This notification is the first step in securing the leave entitlement.

### Section 205.2: Employee's Duty to Inform Employer of Changes in Leave Duration

This section further elaborates on the employee's notification responsibilities, specifically concerning changes in the leave duration.
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate."
This passage emphasizes the ongoing duty to inform the employer. It specifies that the employee must provide at least two weeks' written notice of any change in the leave duration, as indicated in the healthcare practitioner's certificate. However, it also acknowledges that a valid reason for not providing this notice may exist, and in such cases, a new certificate must accompany the explanation. This ensures the employer is always up-to-date on the employee's leave status and any potential adjustments.

### Section 207.2: Notification to Employer — Interruption for Child’s Hospitalization

While not directly about maternity-related leave, this section provides a related obligation for employees who intend to interrupt their maternity or parental leave.
"An employee who intends to interrupt their maternity or parental leave in order to return to work as a result of the hospitalization of his or her child shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption as soon as possible."
This quote highlights the employee's responsibility to promptly notify their employer of any planned interruptions to their leave due to a child's hospitalization. This allows the employer to plan accordingly and ensure a smooth transition back to work.

### Section 132: Cease to Perform Job

This section addresses the employee's right to cease performing their job if they believe it poses a risk to their health or that of their fetus or child.
"In addition to the rights conferred by section 128 and subject to this section, an employee who is pregnant or nursing may cease to perform her job if she believes that, by reason of the pregnancy or nursing, continuing any of her current job functions may pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."
This passage explicitly states the employee's right to stop working if they have a medical certificate confirming a risk. It also mentions the employer's obligation to notify the workplace committee or health and safety representative with the employee's consent. This ensures transparency and allows for appropriate support and adjustments to the employee's work situation.

## Maternity Leave Entitlements and Extensions for Pregnant Employees

### Entitlement to Maternity Leave

Section 206 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the entitlement to maternity leave for pregnant employees. It states:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 17 weeks, which leave may begin not earlier than 13 weeks prior to the estimated date of her confinement and end not later than 17 weeks following the actual date of her confinement, if the employee provides her employer with a certificate of a health care practitioner certifying that she is pregnant."
This indicates that a pregnant employee is generally entitled to up to 17 weeks of unpaid maternity leave, with specific start and end dates tied to the estimated and actual date of confinement. The condition for taking this leave is providing a certificate from a health care practitioner confirming the pregnancy and the inability to work due to it.

Section 205.1 further elaborates on this entitlement, emphasizing the requirement for a certificate:
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability."
This reinforces the importance of the health care practitioner's certificate as the foundational requirement for taking maternity leave.

### Extension of Maternity Leave

Section 206.1 details the circumstances under which maternity leave can be extended. It states:
"(2) The leave of absence granted under this section may only be taken during the 78-week period beginning (a) in the case of a new-born child of the employee, at the option of the employee, on the day the child is born or comes into the actual care of the employee; and (b) in the case of an adoption, on the day the child comes into the actual care of the employee."
This establishes a primary 78-week period during which maternity leave can be taken.

Section 206.1 further explains how this period can be extended. It mentions:
"(2.1) The period referred to in subsection (2) is extended by the number of weeks during which the employee is on leave under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9, is absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1) or is on leave under any of paragraphs 247.5(1)(a), (b) and (d) to (g)."
This indicates that the 78-week period can be extended by the amount of time the employee is on leave for other reasons, such as parental leave or absence due to a medical condition.

Section 206.1 also addresses extensions related to the child's hospitalization:
"(2.2) If the child referred to in subsection (1) is hospitalized during the period referred to in subsection (2), the period is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized."
This provides a specific extension for the period the child is hospitalized after birth.

Section 206.1 includes a limitation on these extensions:
"(2.3) An extension under subsection (2.1) or (2.2) must not result in the period being longer than 104 weeks."
This sets a maximum total maternity leave duration of 104 weeks, including all extensions.

### Employee's Duty to Inform Employer of Changes

Section 205.2 outlines the employee's responsibility to inform their employer of any changes to the duration of their leave, as indicated in their health care practitioner's certificate:
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate."
This emphasizes the importance of proactive communication with the employer regarding any adjustments to the leave period, ensuring the employer is aware of the updated information.

individual_results.question: What is the purpose of the leave provided under section 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code, and what life events qualify an employee for this leave?
individual_results.answer:
## Purpose of Parental Leave under Section 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code

### Entitlement to Leave

Section 206.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes that
"Subject to subsections (2) and (3), every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 63 weeks to care for a newborn child of the employee or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides." This clearly states the primary purpose of parental leave: to provide time off work for employees to bond with and care for a new child, either their own or one they have adopted.

### Life Events Qualifying for Parental Leave

Several life events qualify an employee for parental leave under section 206.1. These are explicitly listed in subsection (1):
"(1) Subject to subsections (2) and (3), every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 63 weeks to care for a newborn child of the employee or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides." This indicates that parental leave is available for:
"...a newborn child of the employee or a child who is in the care of the employee for the purpose of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the employee resides."

### Extension of Parental Leave

Section 206.1(2) further clarifies the parental leave entitlement by stating that
"The leave of absence granted under this section may only be taken during the 78-week period beginning (a) in the case of a new-born child of the employee, at the option of the employee, on the day the child is born or comes into the actual care of the employee; and (b) in the case of an adoption, on the day the child comes into the actual care of the employee." This 78-week period is extended by the number of weeks the employee is on leave under other sections of the Canada Labour Code, is absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1), or is on leave under any of paragraphs 247.5(1)(a), (b) and (d) to (g). This provision acknowledges that employees may take parental leave in conjunction with other types of leave, resulting in a longer overall period of time off work.

### Aggregate Leave Limit

Section 206.1(3) sets an aggregate limit on the amount of parental leave that can be taken by multiple employees under the same birth or adoption:
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by more than one employee under this section in respect of the same birth or adoption shall not exceed 71 weeks, but the amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under this section in respect of the same birth or adoption shall not exceed 63 weeks." This ensures that parental leave is distributed fairly among the parents of a new child.

individual_results.question: What are the maximum aggregate leave limits for multiple employees and for a single employee in respect of the same birth?
individual_results.answer:
## Aggregate Parental and Maternity Leave Limits

### Aggregate Leave Limits for Multiple Employees

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) establishes aggregate leave limits for more than one employee taking leave in respect of the same birth. Section 206.2 states:
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by more than one employee under sections 206 and 206.1 in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 86 weeks, but the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under those sections in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 78 weeks."

This indicates that for a single birth, the total leave taken by all parents combined cannot exceed 86 weeks. However, for a single parent taking leave, the maximum leave duration is 78 weeks.

### Aggregate Leave Limits for a Single Employee

For a single employee taking leave in respect of the same birth, the CLC sets a maximum aggregate leave duration of 78 weeks. Section 206.2 reiterates this:
"...the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under those sections in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 78 weeks."

This means that even if a single parent takes multiple periods of leave, the total leave they can take for the same birth is capped at 78 weeks.

### Combining Maternity and Parental Leave

CLC-206.2 also addresses the combination of maternity and parental leave. It specifies that the aggregate amount of leave taken by one employee under these sections cannot exceed 78 weeks.
"...the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under those sections in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 78 weeks."

This means that if a parent takes both maternity and parental leave, the total leave they can take for the same birth is 78 weeks, regardless of how they choose to divide the leave between the two types.

### Parental Leave Sharing

LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_11 further clarifies parental leave sharing. It states:
"If both parents share the parental benefits, only 1, 1-week waiting period applies."

This means that if both parents take parental leave, they can share the leave duration up to a maximum of 86 weeks combined, with only a 1-week waiting period applying to the first parent's leave.

### Additional Considerations for Multiple Children

LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_11 also addresses situations with multiple children. It specifies that if an employee has two or more children under 25 years of age who have disappeared or are murdered as a result of the same event, they are eligible for a maximum of 156 weeks of leave for each affected child.
"If you are an employee who has 2 or more children under 25 years of age, who have disappeared or are murdered as a result of the same event, you are eligible for:  only 1 leave of 156 weeks, if they have disappeared, and only 1 leave of 156 weeks, if they are murdered..."

This demonstrates that the aggregate leave limits can be extended in exceptional circumstances involving multiple children.

## Purpose of Leave of Absence in the Canada Labour Code

### General Entitlement

Section 239(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental purpose of medical leave of absence:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d)..." This broad definition encompasses a wide array of health-related and personal circumstances that necessitate time away from work.

### Conditions for Taking Medical Leave

Section 239(1) also outlines the conditions an employee must meet to be eligible for medical leave. The employee must have completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, unless a shorter period is prescribed for their class of employees. This ensures that the leave is available to employees who have established a stable working relationship with their employer.

Section 206.6(2) further details the conditions for leave related to family responsibilities:
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This indicates that leave for family care can be taken with pay after three months of continuous employment.

Section 247.5(1) specifies the leave of absence provided for members of the reserve force:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This leave is specifically for reserve force members called upon for military operations, training, or civil support.

### Leave for Other Reasons

Section 206.6(1)(b) mentions leave for
"...carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members..." Section 206.6(1)(c) mentions leave for
"...carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age..." Section 206.6(1)(d) mentions leave for
"...addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members..." Section 206.6(1)(e) mentions leave for "attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act." Section 206.6(1)(f) allows for leave for "any other reason prescribed by regulation." These provisions demonstrate that leave can also be taken for a variety of other personal or family-related needs.

### Leave for Personal Reasons

Section 206.6(1)(a) states that an employee is entitled to leave of absence for "any other reason prescribed by regulation." This is a catch-all provision that allows for leave for reasons not explicitly listed elsewhere in the CLC, as long as they are specified in a regulation.

### Leave for Five Days

Section 206.6(1) also grants every employee a leave of absence of up to five days in every calendar year for various reasons, including family care, education, urgent matters, citizenship ceremonies, and other reasons prescribed by regulation. This leave is typically unpaid, unless the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, in which case the first three days are paid at their regular rate of wages.
