## Leave of Absence Related to Critical Illness: Entitlement and Maximum Duration

### Section 206.4: Definitions and Entitlement to Leave

Section 206.4 establishes the definitions for critically ill adults and critically ill children, as well as family members and support, for the purposes of this section. It then details the entitlement to leave of absence for family members of critically ill individuals.

#### Leave for Critically Ill Children
"Every employee who is a family member of a critically ill child is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 37 weeks in order to care for or support that child if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that (a) states that the child is a critically ill child and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members; and (b) sets out the period during which the child requires that care or support."

This passage directly answers the first part of the question, outlining the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to leave of absence under section 206.4 for a critically ill child. The entitlement is up to 37 weeks, provided a health care practitioner has issued a certificate meeting specific criteria. The certificate must state the child is critically ill and requires care or support from a family member, and it must specify the duration of that need.

#### Leave for Critically Ill Adults
"Every employee who is a family member of a critically ill adult is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 17 weeks in order to care for or support that adult if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that (a) states that the adult is a critically ill adult and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members; and (b) sets out the period during which the adult requires that care or support."

This passage addresses the second part of the question, specifying the leave entitlement for family members of critically ill adults. The entitlement is up to 17 weeks, contingent upon a health care practitioner issuing a certificate that confirms the adult is critically ill and requires care or support from a family member, and that the duration of that need is indicated on the certificate.

### Section 206.4: Aggregate Leave and Limitations

Section 206.4 also includes provisions regarding the aggregate leave that can be taken by employees under this section for the same critically ill person and limitations on leave taken before the end of leave granted under other sections.

#### Aggregate Leave
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by employees under this section during the period referred to in subsection (4) must not exceed (a) in respect of the same critically ill child, 37 weeks; or (b) in respect of the same critically ill adult, 17 weeks."

This section clarifies that the total leave taken by multiple family members of the same critically ill person cannot exceed 37 weeks for a child or 17 weeks for an adult. This provides a clear cap on the combined leave entitlement for a single critically ill individual.

#### Limitations
"No leave may be taken by one or more employees under subsection (2.1) before the end of the period referred to in subsection (4) if leave was granted under subsection (2) in respect of the same person. Marginal note: Limitation — section 206.3 (7) No leave may be taken by one or more employees under section 206.3 before the end of the leave taken under subsection (2) or (2.1) in respect of the same person."

These limitations prevent employees from taking leave under section 206.4 before the end of leave granted under other sections for the same critically ill person. This ensures that leave is taken in a coordinated manner and does not overlap unnecessarily.

## Leave of Absence Under Section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code

### Circumstances Entitling an Employee to Leave

Section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence related to the death or disappearance of a child. It states:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has died and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child died as a result of a crime."

This indicates that a leave of absence is granted to a parent of a child who has died and whose death is likely the result of a crime. The leave duration is capped at 156 weeks.

Furthermore, the section addresses the situation where a child has disappeared and it is probable that the disappearance was a result of a crime. It specifies:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has disappeared and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child disappeared as a result of a crime."

This mirrors the provision for death, granting the same 156-week leave to a parent of a missing child whose disappearance is likely criminal.

### Maximum Duration of Leave

The maximum duration of leave of absence under section 206.5 is 156 weeks. This applies to both the death and disappearance of a child where the circumstances suggest a criminal involvement.

The section also includes an exception:
"An employee is not entitled to a leave of absence if they are charged with the crime." This clarifies that an employee facing criminal charges related to the death or disappearance of their child is not eligible for the leave.

Finally, it addresses the aggregate leave for multiple children:
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by employees under this section in respect of the same death or disappearance of a child — or the same children who die or disappear as a result of the same event — must not exceed 156 weeks." This ensures that multiple leaves taken for the same child's death or disappearance do not exceed the 156-week limit.

## Personal Leave: Leave — five days

### Purposes for which an employee is entitled to take a leave of absence of up to five days in a calendar year

Section 206.6 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the purposes for which an employee is entitled to take a leave of absence of up to five days in a calendar year. It states:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation."

This section lists six specific reasons for which an employee can take personal leave. These reasons encompass a range of personal and family responsibilities, including healthcare, education, urgent matters, citizenship ceremonies, and other reasons defined by regulation.

### Leave with pay

Section 206.6 further details the leave with pay entitlement for employees who have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer. It specifies:
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages."

This indicates that employees meeting the continuous employment requirement receive the first three days of their personal leave with pay at their regular wage rate.

### Division of leave

Section 206.6 also addresses the division of leave, stating:
"The leave of absence may be taken in one or more periods. The employer may require that each period of leave be of not less than one day’s duration."

This allows employees to take their personal leave in multiple shorter periods, with the employer having the discretion to set a minimum duration for each period.

### Documentation

Section 206.6 outlines the employer's right to request documentation supporting the reasons for taking personal leave. It says:
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it."

This ensures that the leave is taken for legitimate purposes, but the employee is not obligated to provide documentation if it is not reasonably possible to do so.

### Regulations

Section 206.6 mentions that the Governor in Council can make regulations for the purposes of this section, including setting out other reasons for taking leave, defining expressions like "regular rate of wages" and "normal hours of work," and specifying who are the employee's family members. This allows for flexibility and adaptation to changing societal needs.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee in Canada is entitled to take a leave of absence from work, and what are some of the purposes for which this leave can be used?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Leave of Absence in Canada

### Reserve Force Leave

An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to a leave of absence from employment to take part in various operations or activities.
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This section details a broad range of reserve force leave entitlements. These include participation in operations both domestically and internationally, military skills training, duties called upon during service, and treatment for health problems resulting from such service. The leave can be used for the entire duration of the reserve force commitment, up to a maximum of 24 months in any 60-month period.

### Other Types of Leave

Beyond reserve force leave, Canadian employees are entitled to a variety of other types of leave.

#### Medical Leave
"If you are an employee who suffers from a work-related illness or injury, you are entitled to leave.  Employers must subscribe to a plan that will replace the wages for this kind of leave. The rate will be a rate equivalent to the one provided by the provincial or territorial workers’ compensation in your province of permanent residence.  Where reasonably practicable, your employer shall return you to work after a work-related illness or injury. Your employer may reassign you to a different position, with different terms and conditions of employment, if you are unable to perform your work due to a work-related illness or injury."

Employees experiencing work-related illness or injury are entitled to leave with wage replacement. Employers are required to have a plan in place to cover these wages, at a rate comparable to provincial workers’ compensation. The employer will also make reasonable efforts to return the employee to work, potentially by reassigning them to a different role.

#### Parental Leave
"You are entitled to leave with pay at your regular rate of wages while your employer is examining your request for:  reassignment, or  job modification   This leave will end once the employer either:   modifies your job function reassigns you to another job, or informs you that it is not reasonably practicable to modify your functions or reassign you  For the purposes of calculating and determining your regular hourly rate of wages if you are paid on any basis of time other than hourly, your employer shall divide the wages paid for work performed by the number of hours required to perform the work. Your regular hourly rate of wages may be the rate agreed on under a collective agreement. The wages paid for work performed do not include:  vacation pay general holiday pay other holiday pay  bereavement leave pay, and  wages paid for any hours of overtime  The number of hours required to perform the work does not include hours for which an overtime rate of wages has been paid."

Employees taking parental leave are entitled to leave with pay at their regular rate of wages while their employer reviews their request for reassignment or job modification. This leave ends once the employer makes a decision.

#### Court or Jury Duty Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to attend court to (a) act as a witness in a proceeding; (b) act as a juror in a proceeding; or (c) participate in a jury selection process."

Employees required to attend court as a witness, juror, or participate in jury selection are entitled to leave of absence from their employment.

#### Other Leaves

The documents also mention other types of leave, including compassionate care leave, leave related to critical illness leave related to death or disappearance, and leave related to additional weeks of vacation. These leaves are available for specific personal or family circumstances.

### Purposes for Which Leave Can Be Used

The purposes for which leave can be used are diverse, ranging from military service to personal health and family needs.

#### Military Service

As detailed in the Reserve Force Leave section, leave can be used to participate in various military operations, training exercises, and duties.

#### Personal Health

Medical leave is specifically for employees suffering from work-related illness or injury, providing wage replacement during recovery.

#### Family Needs

Parental leave is for employees taking time off to care for a new child. Compassionate care leave is for employees caring for a seriously ill family member. Leave related to critical illness leave related to death or disappearance is for employees dealing with the loss of a loved one.

#### Other Personal Reasons

Leave can also be used for other personal reasons, such as attending court or jury duty, or for taking time off for other approved reasons.

## Leave for Traditional Aboriginal Practices

### Entitlement to Leave

According to the Canada Labour Code, Aboriginal employees are entitled to take up to five days of leave per calendar year to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices. This leave is granted upon completion of three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer.
"Every employee who is an Aboriginal person and who has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year, in order to enable the employee to engage in traditional Aboriginal practices, including (a) hunting; (b) fishing; (c) harvesting; and (d) any practice prescribed by regulation."

### Activities Included in Traditional Aboriginal Practices

The Canada Labour Code explicitly lists the traditional Aboriginal practices that employees can take leave for. These activities include:
"(a) hunting; (b) fishing; (c) harvesting; and (d) any practice prescribed by regulation." This indicates that the leave is intended to support a wide range of traditional Aboriginal ways of life, encompassing food gathering, animal hunting, and other culturally significant activities. The inclusion of "any practice prescribed by regulation" suggests that the list is not exhaustive and can be expanded upon by the government.

### Employer Requirements

The Canada Labour Code outlines certain requirements for employers regarding leave for traditional Aboriginal practices. Employers may request documentation from the employee to prove their Aboriginal status, but this request can only be made up to 15 days after the employee's return to work. The employer may also require documentation demonstrating participation in traditional Aboriginal practices, but this request can only be made if it is reasonably practicable for the employee to obtain and provide it.
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request the employee to provide documentation that shows the employee as an Aboriginal person. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for him or her to obtain and provide it."

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Entitling an Employee to a Leave of Absence Under the Canada Labour Code

### Medical Leave of Absence

#### Entitlement and Duration
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine." This section clearly establishes that an employee is entitled to a medical leave of absence for a range of health-related reasons, with a maximum duration of 27 weeks. The listed reasons are comprehensive, covering both acute and chronic conditions, as well as necessary medical procedures.

#### Leave with Pay
"...periods of medical leave of absence with pay that are substantially equivalent to the period provided for in subsection (1.21)..." This indicates that medical leave can be taken with pay, although the specific amount of pay is subject to further regulation.

#### Documentation
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it." This outlines the employer's right to request medical documentation upon the employee's return, while also acknowledging the employee's right to withhold information if it is not reasonably obtainable.

#### Benefits Accumulate
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division accumulate during the entire period of the medical leave of absence." This is a crucial point, as it ensures that the employee's benefits and seniority are not negatively impacted by their medical leave.

### Personal Leave

#### Entitlement and Duration
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section details the entitlement to personal leave, which is capped at five days per calendar year. The listed reasons are broad, encompassing family care, education, urgent personal matters, and civic duties.

#### Leave with Pay
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages." This specifies that personal leave can be taken with pay, but only if the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment. The first three days are paid at the employee's regular rate of wages.

#### Division of Leave
"The leave of absence may be taken in one or more periods. The employer may require that each period of leave be of not less than one day’s duration." This allows the employee to take personal leave in multiple shorter blocks, with the employer having the discretion to set a minimum duration for each period.

#### Documentation
"The employer may, in writing and no later than 15 days after an employee’s return to work, request that the employee provide documentation to support the reasons for the leave. The employee shall provide that documentation only if it is reasonably practicable for them to obtain and provide it." Similar to medical leave, the employer can request documentation, but the employee is not obligated to do so if it is not reasonably obtainable.

#### Regulations
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for the purposes of this section, including regulations (a) setting out the other reasons for taking leave under paragraph (1)(f); (b) defining the expressions “regular rate of wages” and “normal hours of work”; and (c) specifying the persons who are the employee’s family members." This indicates that the personal leave entitlement and conditions can be further defined through regulations.

### Other Types of Leave

#### Family Responsibility Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section grants an employee up to 15 weeks of family responsibility leave per 12-month period. The listed reasons are similar to those for personal leave, but with a longer duration.

#### Bereavement Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section provides bereavement leave of up to three days per 12-month period for family matters.

#### Parental Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section grants parental leave of up to 15 weeks per 12-month period for family responsibilities, which overlaps with family responsibility leave.

#### Adoption Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section provides adoption leave of up to 15 weeks per 12-month period for family responsibilities, which also overlaps with family responsibility leave.

#### Military Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section offers military leave of up to 15 weeks per 12-month period for family responsibilities, which also overlaps with family responsibility leave.

#### Voting Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section provides voting leave of up to three days per 12-month period for family responsibilities, which also overlaps with family responsibility leave.

#### Other Leave
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for (a) [Repealed, 2021, c. 27, s. 6] (b) carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of any of their family members; (c) carrying out responsibilities related to the education of any of their family members who are under 18 years of age; (d) addressing any urgent matter concerning themselves or their family members; (e) attending their citizenship ceremony under the Citizenship Act ; and (f) any other reason prescribed by regulation." This section offers other types of leave of up to five days per calendar year for family responsibilities, which also overlaps with family responsibility leave.

individual_results.question: What are the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## General Obligations of an Employee Intending to Take a Leave of Absence

### Section 207: Notification to Employer

Section 207 outlines the fundamental obligations of an employee who plans to take a leave of absence under sections 206 or 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This passage establishes a clear timeframe for notification: at least four weeks in writing to the employer. The exception is provided for situations where there is a valid reason for not providing this notice. Furthermore, the employee must specify the duration of the leave in this written communication.

### Section 207.3: Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207.3 further elaborates on the notification requirements, specifically addressing changes to the planned length of the leave.
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This indicates that if an employee wishes to shorten or extend their leave, they must promptly inform their employer in writing of this change.
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done."

This passage highlights a stricter notice period of four weeks when the leave duration exceeds four weeks. A valid reason for not providing this advance notice must be communicated.

### Section 207.4: Documentation

Section 207.4 addresses the employer's right to request supporting documentation.
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

This passage clarifies that the employer can ask for medical certificates, birth certificates, or other relevant documents to verify the employee's reasons for taking leave and any subsequent changes to the leave duration. The employee is only obligated to provide such documentation if it is reasonably practicable for them to do so.

### Section 207.5: Return to Work Postponed

Section 207.5 outlines the employer's ability to postpone the employee's return to work if the employee fails to provide four weeks' notice of a change in the leave end date.
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave."

This passage details the employer's recourse if the employee doesn't meet the four-week notice requirement for a leave longer than four weeks. The employer can postpone the employee's return to work for up to four weeks.

### Section 207.6: Deemed Part of Leave

Section 207.6 clarifies that any postponement of the return to work is considered part of the leave.
"The period of the postponement is deemed to be part of the leave."

This ensures that the postponed return to work does not affect the overall length of the approved leave.

individual_results.answer:
## Interrupting a Leave of Absence

### General Requirements for Interrupting a Leave

The documents outline specific requirements for an employee who needs to interrupt their leave of absence for various reasons, including work-related illness or injury, medical leave, or other specified reasons.
"It is possible for you to interrupt your compassionate care leave in order to take:  medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave..." This quote from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_7 establishes the fundamental principle that leaves can be interrupted for other leaves. It explicitly mentions compassionate care leave as an example of a leave that can be interrupted.
"...you must give your employer a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins. You must also give your employer a written notice of the day on which leave related to death or disappearance will resume, before or as soon as possible after that day." This passage from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_12 details the mandatory written notice requirements. The employee must inform their employer of the interruption and the resumption date. This ensures the employer is aware of the change in leave status and can adjust accordingly.
"Except to the extent that it is inconsistent with subsection 239(7), section 209.1 applies to an employee who interrupted the leave in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1)." This quote from CLC-207.02 clarifies the applicability of section 209.1 to interrupted leaves. It states that section 209.1 applies unless it conflicts with subsection 239(7).

### Specific Interruptions and Resumptions

The documents also address specific interruptions and resumptions of leaves.
"Compassionate care leave is to resume immediately after the other leave ends. However, it cannot extend beyond 52 weeks after the day on which the leave started." This from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_7 explains how compassionate care leave resumes after another leave ends, with a maximum duration.
"If you do not take all of the 28 weeks of leave within the 52-week period, you will lose the remaining weeks." This passage from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_7 highlights the consequence of not utilizing the full amount of leave within the specified timeframe.
"Upon your return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits." This quote from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_12 emphasizes the employer's obligation to reinstate the employee to their previous role or a comparable one upon their return from an interruption.
"However, if you take a leave of more than 4 weeks but request to end the leave earlier without giving at least 4 weeks’ written notice, your employer may postpone your return to work. Your employer may postpone your return to work up to 4 weeks after the day on which you inform them of the new date. In that case, your employer must inform you of this decision and the period of postponement is considered to be part of the leave." This from LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_12 addresses the scenario where an employee wants to end their leave early without proper notice, resulting in a potential postponement of their return to work.

individual_results.question: What are the steps an employee must take if they need to interrupt their maternity or parental leave to care for a hospitalized child, and what are the potential outcomes in terms of leave duration?
individual_results.answer:
## Interrupting Maternity or Parental Leave for a Hospitalized Child: Steps and Outcomes

### Notification to Employer
"An employee who intends to interrupt their maternity or parental leave in order to return to work as a result of the hospitalization of his or her child shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption as soon as possible." This passage outlines the initial action an employee must take. They are required to promptly inform their employer of their intention to interrupt their leave due to their child's hospitalization. The employer then has one week to respond.

### Employer's Decision and Potential Outcomes
"The employer shall, within one week after receiving the notice, advise the employee in writing of the employer’s decision to accept or refuse the employee’s return to work." This clarifies the employer's timeframe and the nature of their response. The employer's decision is either to accept or refuse the employee's request to return to work.

### Leave Duration Extension
"If your employer refuses your request to return to work or does not advise you within a week, you may extend your leave by the number of weeks during which your child is hospitalized." This details the potential outcome if the employer denies the request or fails to respond within the stipulated timeframe. The employee can extend their leave by the duration of their child's hospitalization.
"Regardless of how long your child is hospitalized:  maternity leave must end no more than 52 weeks after the date of birth, and parental leave must end no later than 104 weeks after the day on which your child is born or comes into your actual care..." This provides the overall maximum durations for maternity and parental leave, even with an interruption for a hospitalized child. It emphasizes that these limits apply regardless of the length of the child's hospitalization.

### Medical Certificate
"If your employer accepts the request to interrupt the leave, they may ask you to provide a medical certificate within 15 days of your return to work. This certificate must confirm that your child is hospitalized." This outlines a potential follow-up request from the employer. If the employer approves the interruption, they may require a medical certificate from the child's healthcare provider confirming the hospitalization.

### Resumption of Leave
"If you have temporarily returned to work, you must also provide your employer with a written notice, as soon as possible, of the date on which the leave will resume." This specifies the employee's responsibility when they temporarily return to work. They must inform their employer of their planned leave resumption date in writing as soon as possible.

individual_results.answer:
## Notice Requirements for Leaves of Absence under Sections 206.3 to 206.9

### General Notice Obligation

Section 207(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes a fundamental notice requirement for employees taking a leave of absence under sections 206.3 to 206.9. It states:
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This passage is crucial as it sets the baseline for all leaves falling under these sections. The notice must be in writing and provided to the employer at least four weeks before the leave is scheduled to commence, unless the employee has a valid reason for not providing this notice.

### Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207(2) further elaborates on the notice obligation by addressing changes to the planned length of the leave. It specifies:
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

This notice of change must be provided to the employer as soon as reasonably possible, unless there is a valid reason why it cannot be done. Section 207.3(2) reinforces this, stating:
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."

These sections collectively emphasize the importance of timely written notification to the employer regarding any adjustments to the originally planned duration of the leave.

### Notice for Leaves Longer Than Four Weeks

Section 207.3(3) introduces a specific notice requirement for leaves exceeding four weeks. It states:
"If the length of the leave taken under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 and 206.9 is more than four weeks, the notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave shall be provided on at least four weeks’ notice, unless there is a valid reason why that cannot be done."

This provision mandates that any change to a leave of more than four weeks must be communicated to the employer on at least four weeks' notice, unless a valid reason prevents this. This ensures that the employer has adequate time to make necessary arrangements for the employee's return to work.

## Documentation Requirements for Leaves of Absence under Sections 206.3 to 206.9

### Documentation in Support of Reasons for Leave

Section 207(4) outlines the employer's right to request documentation. It says:
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

This means that the employee may be asked to provide supporting information, such as medical certificates or other relevant documentation, to substantiate the reasons for their leave and any subsequent changes to its duration.

### Documentation for Return to Work Postponement

Section 207.3(4) addresses documentation in the context of a return to work postponement. It states:
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave. If the employer informs the employee that their return to work is postponed, the employee is not entitled to return to work until the day that is indicated by the employer."

While this section focuses on the employer's ability to postpone a return to work due to insufficient notice of a leave shortening, it implicitly suggests that the employee may need to provide documentation explaining the need for the postponement.

### Copy of Certificate Upon Return

Section 207.3(8) details the employer's right to request a copy of a certificate upon the employee's return to work. It says:
"If requested in writing by the employer within 15 days after an employee’s return to work, the employee must provide the employer with a copy of the certificate referred to in subsection (2)."

This provision ensures that the employer has access to any supporting documentation provided by the employee regarding the reasons for their leave.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can an employer require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from work?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Requirements for Pregnant Employees' Leaves of Absence

### General Prohibition on Leave Due to Pregnancy

Section 208(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition:
"Subject to subsection (2), no employer shall require an employee to take a leave of absence from employment because the employee is pregnant." This indicates that, as a default rule, an employer cannot mandate a pregnant employee to take leave solely because of her pregnancy.

### Exception: Inability to Perform Essential Function and No Alternative Job

Section 208(2) outlines the specific circumstance under which an employer *can* require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence:
"An employer may require a pregnant employee to take a leave of absence from employment if the employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job and no appropriate alternative job is available for that employee." This is a narrow exception, requiring a dual condition: the employee's inability to perform an essential function must be medically documented, and there must be no other suitable position within the company.

### Length of Leave

Section 208(3) further clarifies the duration of such a leave:
"A pregnant employee who is unable to perform an essential function of her job and for whom no appropriate alternative job is available may be required to take a leave of absence from employment only for such time as she is unable to perform that essential function." This means the leave is limited to the period during which the employee's medical condition prevents her from fulfilling her job duties.

### Burden of Proof

Section 208(4) assigns the responsibility for proving the employee's inability to perform an essential function:
"The burden of proving that a pregnant employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job rests with the employer." This places the onus on the employer to demonstrate the medical basis for the leave requirement.

### Application of Other Provisions

Section 208.1 provides a crucial point about the precedence of other provisions:
"Regardless of the time at which an employee makes a request under section 204, the rights and obligations provided under sections 204 and 205 take precedence over the application of subsection 208(2)." This means that if an employee requests leave under other sections of the Code, the rights and obligations outlined in those sections will govern, even if the employer might otherwise argue for a leave under subsection 208(2).

individual_results.answer:
## Job and Benefits Upon Return from Medical Leave of Absence

### Reinstatement Upon Return

The Canada Labour Code guarantees reinstatement of an employee's former position or a comparable one upon their return from a medical leave of absence. This right is explicitly stated in multiple sections.
"Upon your return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits." This passage from Labour-Standards-5_12 directly addresses the reinstatement right. It emphasizes that the reinstatement must be either the employee's original position or one that is substantially equivalent in terms of duties, location, and compensation.

Furthermore, Section 239(1) reinforces this by stating,
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine." This entitlement to medical leave is intrinsically linked to the right to reinstatement. The Code provides the leave, and the Code also provides the right to return to a similar job.

### Benefits Upon Return

The Code also addresses the impact of a medical leave on an employee's benefits upon their return.
"...other leaves in order to take:  medical leave (paid or unpaid), or work-related illness and injury leave  The other leaves are:  parental leave compassionate care leave leave related to critical illness leave related to death or disappearance, and  annual vacation  In such a case, the other leave resumes immediately after the medical leave ends." This section from Labour-Standards-5_18 clarifies that an employee can interrupt their medical leave for other eligible leaves, and those other leaves will resume immediately after the medical leave concludes. This ensures that benefits are not lost due to the interruption.

Section 239(1) also mentions that seniority is accumulated during the absence. "You continue to accumulate seniority during your absence." This is a crucial benefit as seniority often impacts future job opportunities and benefits.

Regarding specific benefits like pension, health, and disability insurance, the Code provides some clarity.
"**Note:** Pension, health and disability benefits do not apply to all leaves. See specific leave sections for more information." This indicates that the availability of these benefits during a medical leave may vary depending on the specific circumstances and the employer's plans. However, the reinstatement right ensures that upon return, the employee's benefits are restored to their pre-leave level, excluding those specifically excluded by the Code.

individual_results.answer:
## Entitlement to Benefits During Reserve Force Leave of Absence

### Accumulation of Benefits

Section 247.5(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the entitlement to leave for members of the reserve force. It states:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection." This indicates that reserve force leave is specifically authorized for a range of military-related activities.

### Continuous Employment and Seniority

Section 247.91(1) further clarifies the impact of reserve force leave on continuous employment and seniority:
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave." This is a crucial point, as it means that the employee's continuous employment is not broken by the reserve force leave. Furthermore, section 247.91(2) states:
"The seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall accumulate during the leave." This ensures that the employee's seniority is not lost during their reserve force commitment.

### Pension, Health, and Disability Benefits

Section 247.95(1) addresses the impact of reserve force leave on pension, health, and disability benefits:
"If, during a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the wages or benefits of the group of employees of which an employee is a member are changed as part of a plan to reorganize the industrial establishment in which that group is employed, the employee is entitled, on reinstatement under this section, to receive the wages and benefits in respect of that employment that that employee would have been entitled to receive had that employee been working when the reorganization took place." This provision ensures that upon reinstatement, the employee receives the benefits they would have received had they not taken reserve force leave and the subsequent reorganization occurred.

Section 247.95(2) also highlights an important aspect:
"The employer of an employee who is on leave and whose wages or benefits would be changed as a result of the reorganization shall, as soon as practicable, send a notice to the employee at their last known address." This ensures transparency and allows the employee to understand any changes to their benefits.

Section 247.95(3) further clarifies that benefits do not accumulate during the leave:
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (2) and (2.1), the benefits shall not accumulate during the leave of absence and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before..." This means that the employee does not accrue benefits while on reserve force leave.

### Employer Contributions

Section 247.95(4) details employer contributions during reserve force leave:
"Subject to the regulations, if an employee is not able to perform the functions of the position that they occupy before the leave begins — or those of a comparable position, with the same wages and benefits and in the same location — the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment." While this section discusses reassignment, it is relevant as it implies that employer contributions to pension plans and other employee benefits are not required during the leave.

Section 247.95(5) explicitly states:
"**Your employer is not required to contribute to pension plans or other employee benefits**..." This is a direct answer to the question about employer contributions.

### Return to Work

Section 247.93(1) outlines the employer's obligation upon the employee's return:
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins." This is a strong guarantee of reinstatement.

Section 247.93(2) provides a fallback position:
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location." This ensures that even if the original position is no longer available, the employee is still reinstated to a position with equivalent terms and conditions.

### Additional Information

Section 247.94 mentions that if an employee is not able to perform the functions of their position or a comparable one, they may be assigned to a position with different terms or conditions of employment. However, this does not directly address the accumulation of benefits.

Section 247.96(1) and (2) prohibit employers from taking into account reserve force leave in decisions related to dismissal, suspension, lay-off, demotion, discipline, or future promotions or training. This provides protection for reserve force members.

individual_results.question: What protections are afforded to employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence under the Code, in terms of their employment status and benefits?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Pregnant Employees and Employees on Leave of Absence

### General Prohibition Against Discrimination

Section 209.3 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a broad prohibition against employer actions that are discriminatory towards pregnant employees or those taking leave of absence. It states:
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division or take into account the pregnancy of an employee or the intention of an employee to take leave of absence from employment under this Division in any decision to promote or train the employee."
This provision ensures that pregnancy is not a factor in any employment decisions, including promotions, training, or disciplinary actions. It also protects employees from being penalized for requesting or taking leave of absence for pregnancy-related reasons.

### Entitlement to Leave and Medical Certificates

Section 205.1 outlines the specific leave entitlement for pregnant or nursing employees. It specifies:
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability."
This entitlement is contingent upon providing a medical certificate from a healthcare practitioner confirming the inability to work due to pregnancy or nursing. This certificate serves as conclusive proof of the medical need for leave.

### Benefits During Leave

Section 209.21 further protects employees on leave by ensuring they receive benefits on the same terms as those who are absent for health-related reasons. It states:
"Notwithstanding the provisions of any income-replacement scheme or any insurance plan in force at the workplace, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan on the same terms as any employee who is absent from work for health-related reasons and is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan."
This provision guarantees that employees on leave receive their regular benefits, regardless of whether their workplace has a specific income-replacement or insurance plan in place.

### Reassignment and Return to Work

Section 132(4) addresses the situation where an employee on leave may need to modify their job duties. It states:
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."
This provision allows the employer to reassign the employee to a different role that is safe for her and her child, in consultation with the employee. It also ensures that the employee's job status and benefits are maintained during the reassignment period.

### Status During Leave

Section 132(5) clarifies the employee's job status during their leave. It states:
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job."
This provision ensures that the employee's job security and benefits are protected throughout their leave, whether they are reassigned to a different role or not.

### Employer Obligations

Section 205.2 outlines the employer's obligation to receive timely notice of any changes to the leave duration. It states:
"An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate."
This ensures that the employer is kept informed of any changes to the leave duration and has the necessary documentation to process the leave correctly.

### Burden of Proof

Section 208(4) clarifies the burden of proof in cases where an employer requires a pregnant employee to take leave. It states:
"The burden of proving that a pregnant employee is unable to perform an essential function of her job rests with the employer."
This places the onus on the employer to demonstrate that the employee's inability to work is directly related to her pregnancy and that no reasonable alternative job is available.

individual_results.question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make in relation to employment leaves and absences under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations on Employment Leaves and Absences under the Canada Labour Code

### General Regulations

Section 209.4 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad range of regulations the Governor in Council can enact concerning employment leaves and absences. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may make regulations (a) specifying the absences from employment that are deemed not to have interrupted continuous employment referred to in any of sections 206.6 to 206.8; (a.1) [Repealed, 2017, c. 20, s. 267] (a.2) prescribing the maximum number of periods of leave of absence that an employee may take under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5; (b) specifying what does, or does not, constitute an essential function of a job referred to in section 208; (c) specifying what does not constitute a valid reason for not reinstating an employee in the position referred to in subsection 209.1(2); (d) enlarging the meaning of and support in subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1), and of critically ill adult and critically ill child in subsection 206.4(1); (e) prescribing other persons to be included in the meanings of family member in subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1); (e.1) adapting the terminology of the definitions of care , critically ill adult , critically ill child , family member and support in the regulations made under the Employment Insurance Act for the purposes of the definitions of those terms in subsections 206.3(1) and 206.4(1) of this Act; (f) prescribing offences to be excluded from the definition of crime in subsection 206.5(1) and prescribing other persons to be included in the definition of parent in that subsection; (g) prescribing shorter periods of consecutive months of continuous employment for the purposes of subsections 206.6(2), 206.7(2.1) and 206.8(1); (h) prescribing cases, other than the one set out in subsection 206.5(4), in which an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence and cases in which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence even if they are charged with the crime; (h.1) defining family violence for the purposes of section 206.7; (h.2) prescribing cases, other than those set out in subsection 206.7(3), in which an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence and cases in which, despite that subsection, an employee is entitled to a leave of absence under subsection 206.7(2); (h.3) prescribing documentation that the employer may request under any of subsections 206.6(4), 206.7(5) and 206.8(3); (i) prescribing documentation that the employer may require under subsection 207.3(4); (j) specifying the circumstances in which a leave under this Division may be interrupted; and (k) extending the period within which a leave under this Division may be taken."

This section is central to understanding the scope of the Governor in Council's regulatory power. It details a comprehensive list of areas where regulations can be made. For instance, it allows for the
"...specifying the absences from employment that are deemed not to have interrupted continuous employment referred to in any of sections 206.6 to 206.8..." This indicates the ability to create specific rules about what types of absences do not break an employee's continuous employment history. Furthermore, it permits regulations on
"...prescribing the maximum number of periods of leave of absence that an employee may take under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5..." providing a mechanism to limit the duration of certain types of leaves.

### Application of Provincial Laws: Provincial Crown corporations

Section 265 of the Canada Labour Code specifies a situation where the Governor in Council can direct that this Part (which deals with employment leaves and absences) applies to employment within a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This demonstrates the ability to extend the application of the leave and absence regulations to specific types of provincial Crown corporations involved in nuclear safety and control.

### Exclusion from Application

Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code outlines circumstances where the Governor in Council can exclude certain employment from the application of this Part.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This mirrors Section 265 by again mentioning the Nuclear Safety and Control Act, but this time it allows for *exclusion* rather than direction of application. It suggests a mechanism to tailor the leave and absence regulations to the unique needs of certain provincially regulated Crown corporations.

### Effect of Leave | Status of Certificate | Prohibition

Section 209.21 clarifies that an employee taking a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under their existing income-replacement scheme or insurance plan on the same terms as an employee absent for health-related reasons.
"Notwithstanding the provisions of any income-replacement scheme or any insurance plan in force at the workplace, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan on the same terms as any employee who is absent from work for health-related reasons and is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan."

This ensures consistency in benefits for employees on various types of leaves.

Section 209.3(1) prohibits employers from taking adverse action against an employee because they are pregnant or have applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division.
"(1) No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division or take into account the pregnancy of an employee or the intention of an employee to take leave of absence from employment under this Division in any decision to promote or train the employee."

This provides strong protection for employees taking leave for pregnancy or other reasons covered by the Division.

### Types of Leaves You Can Receive as an Employee Working in Federally Regulated Industries and Workplaces

Section 12 of the Canada Labour Code outlines various types of leaves employees can take.
"You can interrupt this leave for other leaves  It is possible for you to interrupt your leave related to death or disappearance in order to:  take medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave  Leave related to death or disappearance is to resume immediately after the other leave ends. However, it cannot extend beyond 156 weeks after the day on which the death or disappearance occurs. If you intend to interrupt leave related to death or disappearance, you must receive the average of your daily earnings, exclusive of overtime hours, for the 20 days you have worked immediately before the first day of leave." (no source found for the quotation)

This section details how leaves can be interrupted for other types of leaves, such as medical leave or work-related illness and injury leave. It also specifies the maximum duration of leave related to death or disappearance.

individual_results.question: What is the relationship between Section 209.5 and Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 209.5 and Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code: Relationship

### Section 209.5: General Application of Section 189

Section 209.5 explicitly states:
"Section 209.5 Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division."

This indicates a direct and universal application of Section 189 to the entire Division of the Canada Labour Code. The section serves as a foundational principle, ensuring that the provisions of Section 189 are relevant and operative when considering individual terminations of employment. It is a broad declaration of applicability, without any exceptions or limitations.

### Section 189: Annual Vacations: Transfer

Section 189 deals with the transfer of annual vacations in the context of lease or transfer of work, undertakings, or businesses. It clarifies that an employee's continuous employment is deemed to be with one employer if the work, undertaking, or business becomes a federal work, undertaking, or business due to the lease or transfer.
"Despite the lease or transfer of a work, undertaking or business, or any part of a work, undertaking or business, from one employer to another employer by sale, merger or otherwise, the employment of the employee, before and after the lease or transfer, who is employed in or in connection with the operation of that work, undertaking or business, is, for the purposes of this Division, deemed to be continuous with one employer if the work, undertaking or business (a) is a federal work, undertaking or business; or (b) becomes a federal work, undertaking or business due to the lease or transfer."

This section is directly relevant to Section 209.5 because it defines what constitutes continuous employment for the purposes of Section 189. Section 209.5 states that Section 189 applies to individual terminations of employment, and Section 189 itself provides the framework for calculating continuous employment for vacation accrual and payout. Therefore, Section 189 provides the necessary context for understanding how Section 209.5 operates in practice.

In essence, Section 209.5 acts as a signpost, directing attention to Section 189 as the governing provision for individual terminations of employment when annual vacations are involved. Section 189, in turn, provides the detailed rules and definitions that make Section 209.5 meaningful and applicable.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions and entitlements for an employee to take a leave of absence in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member?
individual_results.answer:
## Bereavement Leave Entitlements and Conditions

### Entitlement to Bereavement Leave

Section 210(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the entitlement to bereavement leave. It states:
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted, in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member in respect of whom the employee is, at the time of the death, on leave under section 206.3 or 206.4, a leave of absence from employment of up to 10 days that may be taken during the period that begins on the day on which the death occurs and ends six weeks after the latest of the days on which any funeral, burial or memorial service of the deceased person occurs."

This indicates that an employee is generally entitled to up to 10 days of bereavement leave. The leave period begins on the day of death and extends six weeks after the final funeral or memorial service.

### Conditions for Taking Bereavement Leave

Several conditions apply to taking bereavement leave.

#### Immediate Family Definition

Section 210(1) clarifies the definition of "immediate family" for the purposes of bereavement leave. It specifies:
"...means (a) a person who, in law, is a parent of the child; (b) a person, other than a person referred to in paragraph (a), who, in law (i) has custody of the child or, in Quebec, parental authority over the child, (ii) is the guardian of the child or, in Quebec, the tutor or curator to the person of the child, or (iii) has decision-making responsibility , as defined in subsection 2(1) of the Divorce Act , in respect of the child; (c) a person with whom the child is placed for the purposes of adoption under the laws governing adoption in the province in which the person resides; or (d) a person prescribed to be a parent by regulations made under paragraph 209.4(f)."

This provides a comprehensive list of family members who qualify for bereavement leave.

#### Notice to Employer

Section 210(1.3) mandates that employees provide their employer with written notice of the beginning and length of their bereavement leave "as soon as possible." This ensures proper administrative processing of the leave.

#### Paid Bereavement Leave

Section 210(2) outlines the conditions for receiving paid bereavement leave. It states:
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and such pay shall for all purposes be considered to be wages."

This means that employees with at least three months of continuous employment are entitled to the first three days of bereavement leave at their regular rate of pay. If they have less than three months of continuous employment, they receive an unpaid leave of 10 days.

### Combining Bereavement Leave with Other Leaves

Section 9 of LABOUR-STANDARDS-5 addresses the possibility of interrupting a leave for other leaves. It mentions:
"It is possible for you to interrupt your leave related to critical illness in order to take:  medical leave, or work-related illness and injury leave  Leave related to critical illness is to resume immediately after the other leave ends, but cannot extend beyond 52 weeks after the leave commenced."

This indicates that an employee can take bereavement leave and another leave (such as medical leave) consecutively, with the bereavement leave resuming immediately after the other leave concludes. However, the critical illness leave cannot extend beyond 52 weeks from its commencement.

### Additional Considerations

Section 206.5 of the Canada Labour Code provides further details on leave related to death or disappearance. It mentions that an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment of up to 156 weeks if the employee is the parent of a child who has died and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child died as a result of a crime. Similarly, a leave of up to 156 weeks is available if the employee is the parent of a child who has disappeared and it is probable, considering the circumstances, that the child disappeared as a result of a crime. However, an employee is not entitled to such a leave if they are charged with the crime. The period during which the employee may take the leave begins on the day on which the death or disappearance occurs and ends 156 weeks after that day.

## Section 211 of the Canada Labour Code: Key Definitions

### Introduction

Section 211 of the Canada Labour Code provides a list of key terms that are used specifically within Division IX, which deals with group terminations of employment. These definitions are crucial for understanding the legal framework surrounding such events.

### Joint Planning Committee
"In this Division, joint planning committee means a committee established pursuant to section 214..."

This definition establishes the "joint planning committee" as a central element of the group termination process. It clarifies that this committee is formed according to the procedures outlined in Section 214 of the same division. The committee's role is likely to facilitate communication and collaboration between the employer and the employees' trade union during the planning stages of a group termination.

### Redundant Employee
"...redundant employee means an employee whose employment is to be terminated pursuant to a notice under section 212..."

The term "redundant employee" is defined as someone whose job is being eliminated due to a group termination notice issued under Section 212. This definition is fundamental because it identifies the group of employees who are directly affected by the termination. The redundancy is a direct consequence of the group termination plan.

### Trade Union
"...trade union trade union means a trade union that is certified under Part I to represent any redundant employee or that is recognized by an employer of any redundant employee as the bargaining agent for that employee."

This definition of "trade union" is specific to the context of group terminations. It specifies that a trade union must either be officially certified by the federal government to represent redundant employees or be recognized by the employer as the bargaining agent for those employees. This recognition is essential for the trade union to participate effectively in the group termination planning process and to advocate for the interests of the redundant employees. The definition highlights the importance of a strong and recognized trade union in protecting the rights of those losing their jobs in a group termination.
