individual_results.question: What are the obligations of an employer who plans to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a certain timeframe, and what information must be provided to various parties?
individual_results.answer:
## Obligations of an Employer Planning a Group Termination of Employment

### Notice Requirements

An employer planning a group termination of employment of 50 or more employees within a particular industrial establishment has several crucial notice obligations.
"Section 212 (1) Any employer who terminates, either simultaneously or within any period not exceeding four weeks, the employment of a group of 50 or more employees employed by the employer within a particular industrial establishment, or of such lesser number of employees as prescribed by regulations applicable to the employer made under paragraph 227(b), shall, in addition to any notice required to be given under section 230, give notice to the Head, in writing, of his intention to so terminate at least 16 weeks before the date of termination of the employment of the employee in the group whose employment is first to be terminated." This section clearly outlines the initial notification requirement. The employer must inform the Head of Compliance and Enforcement in writing at least 16 weeks before the first group termination occurs. This notice must detail the employer's intention to terminate employment.

### Information to be Included in the Notice

The notice provided to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement must contain specific information.
"A notice referred to in subsection (1) shall set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations." This indicates that the notice must specify the termination dates, the projected number of layoffs within each job category, and any other details mandated by the regulations.

### Information to be Provided to Other Parties

Beyond the Head of Compliance and Enforcement, the employer is obligated to provide the notice to several other entities.
"(2) A copy of any notice given to the Head under subsection (1) must be given immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed." This passage details the immediate distribution of the notice. A copy must be sent to the Minister of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission (EI), as well as any trade union representing the redundant employees. If no union represents the redundant employees, a copy must be given to each affected employee or posted prominently within the workplace.

### Statement of Benefits

In addition to the initial notice, the employer must provide affected employees with a written statement of benefits.
"You must provide the statement of benefits not later than 2 weeks before the date of termination or earlier, if possible. You must also give your employees the following pay:   all outstanding wages, including overtime pay and general holiday pay owed  vacation pay  pay in lieu of notice of termination, if 2 weeks written notice was not provided, and  severance pay if they had more than 12 months of continuous service..." This statement must include comprehensive information about the employee's final pay, including outstanding wages, accrued vacation pay, and any severance pay they are entitled to. The statement must be provided to the employees no later than two weeks before the termination date, or earlier if feasible.

### Additional Requirements

The employer must also establish a joint planning committee with an employee representative and cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission.
"As an employer, when a group termination of employment occurs, you are required to:  establish a joint planning committee with an employee representative cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and  provide affected employees with a statement of benefits, which includes information on the employee’s:             wages vacation pay severance pay, if applicable, and any other benefits and pay arising from employment..." This section explicitly states these additional responsibilities. The joint planning committee will facilitate communication and collaboration between the employer and employees during the transition. Cooperation with the EI Commission will ensure that affected employees receive the unemployment benefits they are eligible for.

### Requests for Waivers

An employer may request that the Minister of Labour waive certain requirements.
"As an employer, you may request that the Minister of Labour waive certain requirements. Three types of waivers may be granted, including the requirement to:  give 16 weeks’ notice provide employees with a written statement of benefits, and/or establish a joint planning committee when you can show that:             it would be unduly prejudicial to your interests or of the affected employees it would be seriously detrimental to the operation of the industrial establishment similar measures are already in place..." This passage outlines the circumstances under which a waiver of the notice period, statement of benefits, or joint planning committee requirements may be granted. The employer must demonstrate that the waiver is necessary due to undue prejudice, serious detriment to operations, or the existence of similar measures. A waiver application can be submitted using the form
"“Notice to the Head of Compliance and Enforcement of a group termination of employment and Request for waiver under the Canada Labour Code - Part III (ESDC-LAB1197)”..." Any waiver granted will not exceed six months in duration.

individual_results.question: What are the key responsibilities of an employer who gives notice of termination to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code, particularly in relation to redundant employees and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Upon Group Termination Notice to the Head (Section 212)

### Section 212: Notice of Group Termination - Key Obligations

Section 212 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the employer's comprehensive responsibilities when providing notice of group termination to the Head. These obligations extend to redundant employees and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission.

#### Section 212(1): Content of the Notice
"A notice of termination given pursuant to subsection 212(1) of the Act shall, in addition to the information required by paragraphs 212(3)(a) and (b) of the Act, set out (a) the name of the employer; (b) the location at which the termination is to take place; (c) the nature of the industry of the employer; (d) the name of any trade union certified to represent any employee in the group of employees whose employment is to be terminated or recognized by the employer as bargaining agent for any such employees; and (e) the reason for the termination of employment."

This passage details the mandatory information that must be included in the notice to the Head. It goes beyond the basic requirements by specifying the inclusion of the name of any trade union representing the redundant employees. This ensures the Head is aware of the existing bargaining relationship and can coordinate accordingly. Furthermore, the notice must state the reason for the termination, providing context for the affected employees and the Commission.

#### Section 212(2): Copies of Notice and Information to the Commission
"A copy of any notice given to the Head under subsection (1) must be given immediately by the employer to the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission and any trade union representing a redundant employee, and if any redundant employee is not represented by a trade union, a copy of that notice must be given to the employee or immediately posted by the employer in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which that employee is employed."

This section emphasizes the employer's duty to disseminate the notice widely. It mandates that a copy be provided to the Minister, the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and any trade union representing the redundant employees. Crucially, it also requires a copy to be given to each redundant employee individually or posted prominently within the workplace if no union represents them. This ensures all stakeholders are informed promptly.

#### Section 212(3): Additional Information Required in the Notice
"A notice referred to in subsection (1) shall set out (a) the date or dates on which the employer intends to terminate the employment of any one or more employees; (b) the estimated number of employees in each occupational classification whose employment will be terminated; and (c) such other information as is prescribed by the regulations."

This passage specifies further information that the notice to the Head must contain. It requires the employer to provide the planned termination dates and the projected number of layoffs within each job category. This allows the Commission to anticipate the needs of the redundant employees and plan its services accordingly. It also allows the Head to prepare for the logistical aspects of the group termination.

#### Section 212(4): Employer Deemed to Terminate Employment
"Except where otherwise prescribed by regulation, an employer shall, for the purposes of this Division, be deemed to have terminated the employment of an employee where the employer lays off that employee."

This section clarifies how the employer is considered to have terminated an employee for the purposes of this Division. It states that a layoff is equivalent to a termination, simplifying the process and ensuring consistency.

### Section 213: Cooperation with the Commission

Section 213 further elaborates on the employer's responsibilities towards the Canada Employment Insurance Commission.

#### Section 213(1): Information and Cooperation
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee."

This passage highlights the employer's obligation to be proactive in assisting redundant employees through the Commission. It states they must provide any information the Commission requests and actively collaborate with them to help the employees find new jobs. This demonstrates a commitment to mitigating the negative impacts of the group termination.

#### Section 213(2): Statement of Benefits
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 shall give each redundant employee, as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

This section mandates that the employer provide each redundant employee with a written statement detailing their accrued benefits, final wages, severance pay, and any other entitlements at least two weeks before their termination date. This ensures transparency and allows the employees to understand their financial situation.

### Section 214(1) - Obligation to Establish the Committee
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217."

This section clearly establishes the employer's immediate obligation following the notice to the Head. It mandates the formation of a joint planning committee "as soon as possible after giving the notice." The composition of this committee is flexible, allowing for

### Section 214(2) - Minimum Number of Members
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members."

Building upon the requirement to establish the committee, this subsection specifies the minimum number of members it must have: four. This provides a foundational structure for the committee's operation and decision-making processes.

### Section 214(3) - Appointment of Members: Employee vs. Employer Representatives
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer."

This subsection details the crucial process of appointing members to the committee, ensuring a balanced representation of both the employees being terminated and the employer. It states that "at least half of the members" will be appointed by the redundant employees, following the procedures outlined in subsections 215(1), (2) and (3). The remaining "rest of the members" will be appointed by the employer, adhering to the procedures in subsection 215(5). This 50/50 split is a fundamental aspect of the joint planning committee's structure, designed to facilitate collaborative problem-solving and agreement on an adjustment program. The reference to subsections 215(1), (2) and (3) and 215(5) indicates that these sections provide the specific rules and processes for making these appointments.

individual_results.question: How are redundant employees represented on a joint planning committee, especially when some or all of them are represented by a trade union?
individual_results.answer:
## Redundant Employee Representation on a Joint Planning Committee

### Section 215: Employee Representatives

Section 215 of the Canada Labour Code details the process by which redundant employees are represented on a joint planning committee, particularly when some or all of them are represented by a trade union. It outlines three scenarios:

#### Scenario 1: All Redundant Employees Represented by a Trade Union
"Where all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of the joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents."
This passage directly addresses the question by stating that if all redundant employees are covered by one or more trade unions, each of those unions gets to nominate at least one member to the committee. This ensures that each union has a voice and can advocate for the interests of its members.

#### Scenario 2: No Redundant Employees Represented by a Trade Union
"Where no redundant employees are represented by a trade union, the employees are entitled to appoint all the members of a joint planning committee who are to be their representatives."
This scenario specifies that if no single trade union represents all the redundant employees, the redundant employees themselves have the authority to select all the members who will represent them on the committee. This provides a direct and unified voice for the affected workers.

#### Scenario 3: Some but Not All Redundant Employees Represented by a Trade Union
"(a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents; and (b) the employees that are not represented by a trade union are entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as their representative."
This scenario combines elements of the first two. It grants each union representation proportional to its membership among the redundant employees, while also ensuring that any redundant employees not covered by a union still have a voice on the committee. This approach aims for a balanced representation that considers both unionized and non-unionized workers.

#### Section 214: Establishment of Joint Planning Committee

Section 214 further clarifies the composition of the joint planning committee. It states that
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This confirms that the employee representation is a significant portion of the committee, with at least half of the seats dedicated to their interests.

### Section 219: Procedure

Section 219 outlines the procedures of the joint planning committee, including the election of co-chairpersons. It mentions that
"The members of a joint planning committee shall elect from among themselves two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees selected by their representatives and the other being a representative of the employer selected by his representatives." This ensures that the committee's leadership is also representative of both sides of the issue, further facilitating effective communication and decision-making.

individual_results.answer:
## Appointment of Joint Planning Committee Members

### Minimum Number of Members
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This section establishes the foundational requirement for the committee's size. It mandates that the committee must have a minimum of four individuals appointed to its membership.

### Appointment of Redundant Employee Representatives
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This passage details the proportional representation required on the committee. It specifies that at least half of the members must be chosen by the redundant employees, following the procedures outlined in subsections 215(1), (2), and (3). The remaining half must be chosen by the employer, following the procedures in subsection 215(5). This ensures a balanced representation of both sides in the planning process.

### Appointment of Employer Representatives
"An employer is entitled to appoint, as his representatives on a joint planning committee, a number of members not exceeding the number of members to be appointed to the committee pursuant to subsections (1), (2) and (3)." This section clarifies the employer's appointment process. It states that the employer can appoint a number of members equal to or less than the total number of members required for the committee, as determined by subsections 1, 2, and 3.

### Election of Joint Planning Committee Members
"Each person appointed as a member of a joint planning committee pursuant to subsection (2) or paragraph (3)(b) shall be elected by the redundant employees entitled to appoint the member." This passage addresses the election process for members appointed under subsections 215(2) and (3)(b). It mandates that each appointed member must be elected by the redundant employees who are entitled to make that appointment.

## Time for Appointment and First Sitting

### Time for Appointment
"The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212." This section sets a strict deadline for the appointment of committee members and their first meeting. It requires that the committee members must be appointed and convene for their first sitting within two weeks of the Head receiving the notice of group termination. This ensures a timely start to the planning process.

### Failure to Appoint
"If no person is selected under paragraph (1)(b), the employer shall perform the functions of the committee until a person is selected and the committee is established." This passage outlines the employer's responsibility if the employee representatives are not selected within the two-week timeframe. It states that the employer will continue to carry out the committee's functions until the employee representatives are selected and the committee is formally established.

### Vacancy in Membership
"Where any vacancy occurs in the membership of a joint planning committee before the committee has completed its work, the vacancy shall be filled forthwith in the manner provided in this Division for the selection of the person who vacated that membership." This section addresses what happens if a committee member resigns or is otherwise unable to continue their duties before the committee finishes its work. It mandates that the vacancy must be filled immediately using the same procedures used to select the original member.

### Quorum
"A majority of the members of a joint planning committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum, but the members shall not proceed in the absence of any member of the committee at any sitting unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting." This passage defines the minimum number of members required for a committee to conduct business. It states that a quorum is a majority of the members in office, with at least half of that majority being redundant employee representatives. However, the committee cannot proceed if any member is absent without reasonable notice.

individual_results.answer:
## Failure to Appoint a Joint Planning Committee Member

### Section 217: Head's Appointment in Lieu of Failure

Section 217 directly addresses the scenario where a trade union or redundant employees fail to appoint a required member to the joint planning committee. It states:
"If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

This passage is crucial because it outlines the mechanism for resolving the appointment failure. The Head has the authority to make an appointment
"...in lieu of that trade union or those employees..." but this appointment is specifically defined as a representative of either the redundant employees represented by the trade union or those redundant employees who did not make an appointment. The appointment is made upon application from any redundant employee. This ensures that the committee is still constituted with the required number of representatives from the redundant employees, even if the designated representatives fail to step forward.

### Section 214: Establishment of Joint Planning Committee

Section 214 provides context for the appointment process by detailing the employer's obligation to establish the committee "as soon as possible after giving the notice." It also specifies the minimum number of members:
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." Furthermore, it mandates that
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This framework highlights the importance of timely and balanced representation during the appointment process, which is directly relevant to the issue of a failure to make an appointment.

### Section 215: Employee Representatives

Section 215 elaborates on the process for appointing redundant employee representatives. It outlines scenarios based on whether redundant employees are represented by a trade union or not.
"...all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, (a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents..."
"Where no redundant employees are represented by a trade union, the employees are entitled to appoint all the members of a joint planning committee who are to be their representatives."
"Where some but not all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, (a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents; and (b) the employees that are not represented by a trade union are entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as their representative."

These subsections establish the entitlement of trade unions and redundant employees to appoint representatives, providing a clear pathway for these appointments to occur. The failure to make an appointment under these provisions would fall directly under the purview of Section 217, where the Head can intervene.

### Section 216: Time for Appointment

Section 216 sets a timeframe for the joint planning committee to convene:
"The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212."

While this section doesn't directly address the failure to make an appointment, it underscores the importance of adhering to the established process and timeline. A failure to make an appointment within two weeks would necessitate the Head's intervention as outlined in Section 217 to ensure the committee can commence its work.

### Section 218: Notice of Membership

Section 218 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states the employer's obligation regarding the names of the joint planning committee members.
"On completion of the appointment of the members of a joint planning committee, the employer shall post the names of those members in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment in which the redundant employees are employed."

This passage directly answers the question by outlining the specific action the employer must take. It mandates that the employer must publicly display the names of the committee members in a readily visible location within the workplace where the employees are being laid off. This ensures transparency and allows the redundant employees to know who will be involved in the group termination process. The phrase "conspicuous place" emphasizes the importance of making the information easily accessible.



### Section 216: Time for Appointment

While Section 216 details the timeframe for appointing the committee members, it does not address what is required of the employer *after* the appointment is complete. However, it provides context for when the employer would be in a position to fulfill the obligation outlined in Section 218.
"The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212."

This section indicates that the employer will have two weeks following the Head's notification to finalize the committee's membership and hold its first meeting. This timeframe is crucial because it sets the stage for the employer to then post the names of the members as required by Section 218.



### Section 214: Establishment of Joint Planning Committee

Section 214 outlines the employer's initial responsibility to establish the joint planning committee.
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217."

This passage confirms that the employer's first step is to form the committee. Once this is done, they are then obligated to post the members' names, as detailed in Section 218.



### Section 219: Procedure of Joint Planning Committee

Section 219 discusses the committee's internal procedures, including the election of co-chairpersons and the setting of meeting times. While it doesn't directly address the employer's actions *after* the committee is appointed, it highlights the committee's operational status, which would follow the employer's fulfillment of the posting requirement.
"The members of a joint planning committee shall elect from among themselves two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees selected by their representatives and the other being a representative of the employer selected by his representatives."

This section describes the committee's leadership structure, which would be in place after the employer completes the posting of the members' names.



In summary, Section 218 is the definitive source for what the employer is required to do with the names of the joint planning committee members after their appointment is complete. It mandates that the employer must post the names in a conspicuous place within the industrial establishment where the redundant employees are employed. The other sections provide context regarding the employer's initial responsibilities in establishing the committee and the timeframe for doing so, which would precede the posting requirement.

### Establishment of the Committee

Section 214 outlines the process for establishing a joint planning committee.
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This indicates that the employer is obligated to form the committee promptly after providing the initial notice of group termination.
"A joint planning committee established under subsection (1) shall consist of at least four members." This sets the minimum size for the committee, ensuring a sufficient number of voices and perspectives are represented.
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This is a crucial aspect of the committee's structure, mandating that employee representatives hold a majority of the seats. The appointment process for both employee and employer representatives is further detailed in sections 215, 216, and 217.

### Appointment of Co-Chairpersons

Section 219(2) details the appointment of co-chairpersons.
"The members of a joint planning committee shall elect from among themselves two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees selected by their representatives and the other being a representative of the employer selected by his representatives." This highlights the need for leadership within the committee, with co-chairpersons representing both sides of the issue. The selection process for each co-chairperson is also specified, ensuring that the employee and employer representatives have equal say in their appointment.

### Operational Aspects

Section 219(3) explains how the co-chairpersons manage the committee's schedule.
"The co-chairpersons of a joint planning committee may, after consultation with the other members of the committee, fix the time and place of its sittings and shall notify the members of the time and place so fixed." This indicates that the co-chairpersons are responsible for organizing the committee's meetings, taking into account the availability of all members.
"A majority of the members of a joint planning committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum, but the members shall not proceed in the absence of any member of the committee at any sitting unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting." This defines the minimum number of members required for a valid meeting.
"A decision or other act or thing taken or done by a majority of the members of a joint planning committee present at a sitting of the committee, if the members present constitute a quorum, shall be deemed to have been taken or done by the committee." This clarifies how the committee makes decisions, requiring a majority of the quorum to be present and agree.
"A member of a joint planning committee is entitled to such time from work as is necessary to attend sittings of the committee or to carry out any other functions as such a member, and any time spent by the member in carrying out any functions as a member shall, for the purpose of calculating wages owing to the member, be deemed to have been spent at his work." This section addresses the compensation of committee members, ensuring they are not penalized for dedicating time to their duties.

## Main Objective of a Joint Planning Committee in Adjustment Program Development

### Section 221(1) - Explicit Statement of Objective

Section 221(1) of the Canada Labour Code directly addresses the main objective of a joint planning committee. It states:
"It is the object of a joint planning committee to develop an adjustment program to (a) eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment."

This passage clearly outlines the dual-pronged approach of the committee. The primary goal is to avoid layoffs altogether, or if that is unavoidable, to soften the blow on those who lose their jobs. This assistance extends to helping them find new work. The phrase "eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment" highlights the committee's proactive stance, while "minimize the impact of the termination of employment" acknowledges the reality of potential job losses and focuses on mitigating their consequences.

### Section 221(2) - Scope of Matters Considered

Section 221(2) further clarifies the committee's scope by stating:
"In attaining its object under subsection (1), a joint planning committee may, unless the members of the committee agree otherwise, deal only with such matters as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to the termination of employment."

This passage indicates that the committee's work is generally confined to topics typically covered in collective agreements concerning layoffs, such as severance packages, outplacement services, and benefits continuation. This ensures that the committee's efforts are relevant and aligned with existing employment terms.

### Section 221(3) - Commitment to Expediency

Section 221(3) emphasizes the committee's dedication to efficiency:
"The members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible."

This passage underscores the committee's understanding of the urgency surrounding employment terminations. It highlights their commitment to working together and putting in the necessary effort to create a plan quickly.

### Section 221(4) - Cooperation and Assistance

Section 221(4) reinforces the collaborative nature of the committee's work:
"The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee shall cooperate with and assist the committee in developing an adjustment program."

This passage emphasizes that the committee's success hinges on the active participation and support of all stakeholders involved in the termination process. The requirement for cooperation and assistance ensures that the committee has the resources and information it needs to develop an effective adjustment program.

## Circumstances for Joint Planning Committee Application for Arbitrator

### Section 223(1) - Joint Application to Minister

Section 223(1) outlines the specific circumstances under which members of a joint planning committee can jointly apply to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator. It states:
"Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

This indicates that the application can be made by either the entire group of redundant employee representatives or the entire group of employer representatives, provided they all concur. Furthermore, the application can occur either if the committee has not yet finished developing an adjustment program, or if it has finished but the members present are dissatisfied with it. The six-week waiting period from the notice to the Minister under section 212 is a prerequisite for the joint application.

### Section 214(1) - Establishment of Joint Planning Committee

Section 214(1) provides context for the joint planning committee itself. It specifies that an employer giving notice to the Head under section 212 must establish a joint planning committee
"...as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This highlights that the joint planning committee is a formal body established to assist in the development of an adjustment program.

### Section 224(1) - Minister's Appointment of Arbitrator

Section 224(1) details the Minister's power to appoint an arbitrator. It states:

### Section 224(3): Restriction on Matters Included in Statement
"A statement referred to in subsection (2) shall be restricted to such of those matters set out in the application under subsection 223(1) as the Minister deems appropriate and as are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to termination of employment."

This ensures that the arbitrator's efforts are focused on issues typically addressed within the collective agreement, preventing them from delving into areas beyond their mandate.

### Section 224(4): Duty of Arbitrator
"An arbitrator shall assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and the arbitrator, if sent a statement pursuant to subsection (2), shall, within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify, (a) consider the matters set out in the statement; (b) render a decision thereon; and (c) send a copy of the decision with the reasons therefor to the joint planning committee and to the Minister."

individual_results.question: How do sections 58 and 66 apply to a decision made by an arbitrator under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code?

## Application of Sections 58 and 66 to Arbitrator Decisions under Section 224

### Section 58: Finality of Arbitrator Decisions

#### Core Principle
Section 58(1) establishes the finality of arbitrator and arbitration board orders and decisions, stating,
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This provision directly addresses the applicability of sections 58 and 66 to decisions made by an arbitrator under section 224.

#### Analysis
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This quote is central to understanding how sections 58 and 66 function in relation to decisions under section 224. It means that once an arbitrator is appointed under section 224 and renders a decision, that decision is not subject to judicial review. Therefore, the finality of arbitrator decisions, as outlined in section 58, applies without modification to decisions made under section 224.

### Section 66: Filing of Orders and Decisions in Federal Court

#### Core Principle
Section 66(1) outlines the process for filing an arbitrator or arbitration board order or decision in the Federal Court. It states,
"Any person or organization affected by any order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board may, after fourteen days from the date on which the order or decision is made or given, or from the date provided in it for compliance, whichever is the later date, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of the reasons therefor." Section 66(2) further clarifies that upon filing, the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Court.

#### Analysis
"On filing an order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board in the Federal Court under subsection (1), the order or decision shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order or decision were a judgment obtained in the Court." This quote from section 66(2) confirms that the filing of an arbitrator's decision under section 224 in the Federal Court results in its recognition and enforceability within the Federal Court system. This means that the decision can be used as a basis for further legal action, such as enforcement proceedings, just as a judgment obtained in the Court can. Therefore, section 66 applies to decisions made under section 224 without alteration.

### Section 225: Applicable Provisions for Group Termination Decisions

#### Core Principle
Section 225 explicitly states that sections 58 and 66 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of a decision of an arbitrator under section 224 as though it were a decision referred to in those sections.

#### Analysis
"Sections 58 and 66 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of a decision of an arbitrator under section 224 as though it were a decision referred to in those sections." This quote from section 225 directly answers the question by confirming that sections 58 and 66 are applicable to decisions made by an arbitrator under section 224. The phrase "with such modifications as the circumstances require" acknowledges that there might be minor adjustments needed due to the specific context of a group termination of employment adjustment program, but the core principles of finality (section 58) and enforcement through the Federal Court (section 66) remain intact.

## Employer and Other Parties' Responsibilities in Adjustment Program Implementation

### Section 226 of the Canada Labour Code

#### Implementation of the Program
"On completion of the development of an adjustment program, the employer shall implement the program and the joint planning committee and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of the committee shall cooperate with and assist the employer in implementing the program."

This section explicitly outlines the employer's primary responsibility: to "implement the program" once it has been developed. This is a direct and unambiguous statement of their obligation. Furthermore, it details the collaborative nature of this process. It states that the joint planning committee, along with any trade union or redundant employees who were involved in appointing the committee members, are required to
"...cooperate with and assist the employer in implementing the program." This highlights that the implementation is not solely the employer's burden but a shared responsibility involving all stakeholders who contributed to its creation. The use of "cooperate with and assist" emphasizes the active and supportive role of the other parties.

### Section 4 of the Labour Program Administrative Monetary Penalties (AMP)

#### Following a Labour Program Review Decision of the AMP
"If the decision states that:  there is no violation:       the Labour Program will cancel the notice of violation and you are not required to pay the penalty   a violation was confirmed and/or the amount of penalty is upheld (confirmed or varied), then you must do one of the following:       pay the amount of the penalty, or if you disagree with the decision, you may appeal the decision in writing. You must do so within 15 days after the day on which the Labour Program served the review decision. You must send the request for appeal to the Board and it must contain a statement of the grounds of appeal     Note that if you do not pay the full amount of the penalty or do not request an appeal, you will be considered to have committed the violation. You will be liable to pay the penalty amount set out in the decision letter. You may also be publicly named on the Labour Program Website."

While this section focuses on the employer's response to an AMP decision, it indirectly touches upon their broader responsibilities. If a violation is confirmed and the penalty is upheld, the employer has a clear obligation to either pay the penalty or file an appeal within 15 days. This demonstrates their accountability for addressing any non-compliance identified during the Labour Program's review.

### Section 8.2 of Labour Standards - Employer Compliance with Federal Labour Standards

#### Escalating Compliance and Enforcement Actions
"If it finds that an employer is operating below these conditions, the Labour Program may take a number of escalating compliance and enforcement actions, including:  assurance of voluntary compliance: An employer's written commitment to the Labour Program that they will correct one or more contraventions within a specified period of time. A contravention may be:         monetary, or  non-monetary   letter of determination: A formal written request that the employer correct the non-compliance situation. For example, the Labour Program may ask the employer to:         pay wages or other amounts owing immediately, or  implement appropriate workplace policies and practices   payment order: If you do not voluntarily comply, the Labour Program may issue a payment order to you or to a director of the corporation concerned to collect unpaid wages. The Labour Program will add an administrative fee to the amount owed in this payment order collecting money: If you or your director do not pay a payment order, the Labour Program may collect the amounts owed from:         your debtors, your financial institution, or the debtors or financial institution of one or more directors of your corporation   compliance order: As of January 1, 2021, the Labour Program may issue a compliance order to stop non-compliance. This order prevents reoccurrence of any contravention of the Code and its Regulations, including a contravention related to an ‘excess hours’ permitadministrative monetary penalty: As of January 1, 2021, the Labour Program may issue a notice of violation with an administrative monetary penalty (AMP). The Labour Program may issue the notice if you do not correct a contravention of the Code filing in federal court: The Labour Program may file a payment order and a notice of violation in federal court to ensure that it is enforceable as a judgment of that court. The Labour Program may also publish information on the Government of Canada website concerning an employer to whom a payment order or notice of violation has been issued  prosecutions: If you do not correct a contravention with the Code or Regulations, the Labour Program may choose to prosecute you. The Labour Program may also take this route if you are fully aware of your legal obligations and still willfully break the law. Repeat contraventions indicate an intentional or willful action. If found guilty, you may be subject to the following fines:         a corporation may be liable to a fine of up to:             $50,000 for the first offence $100,000 for the second offence, and $250,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences   an employer who is not incorporated may be liable to a fine of up to:             $10,000 for the first offence $20,000 for the second offence, and $50,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences     public naming of employers: The Labour Program will publish information about employers who violate the Code, including:         all payment orders of $5000 or greater filed in federal court administrative monetary penalties (some exceptions apply for category “A” violations), and  prosecutions..."

This section details the employer's responsibility to correct any contraventions identified during an investigation. It outlines a range of escalating actions the Labour Program can take, starting with assurance of voluntary compliance and progressing to payment orders, compliance orders, administrative monetary penalties, filing in federal court, and even prosecutions. The employer's failure to do so can result in significant financial penalties and public naming on the Labour Program website. The employer is ultimately accountable for ensuring compliance with federal labour standards.

## Regulatory Actions of the Governor in Council under this Division

### Section 111: Broad Scope of Regulatory Authority

Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code Regulations grants the Governor in Council extensive power to make regulations concerning the delivery of information to and from the Minister and various conciliation bodies. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may make regulations (a) prescribing to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received; (b) prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent; (c) designating, with respect to any notice or request authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, the officer who may give or send the notice or request on behalf of the Minister; (d) prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining; (e) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (f) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit; (h) [Repealed, 1998, c. 26, s. 51] (i) prescribing the form and content of any written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4) and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a request; (j) prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister; (k) prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof; and (l) prescribing the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a)."

This section reveals that the Governor in Council can regulate virtually every aspect of the communication process involving the Minister and affiliated bodies. The regulations can cover "any notice, request or report" and their "form and manner" of delivery. Furthermore, it can specify who is authorized to send these communications and the content they must include. The regulations can also address procedural matters such as filing copies of orders and decisions with the Minister and the public's access to these documents.

### Section 158: Application to Federal Crown Corporations

Section 158 specifies a particular area of regulatory action: directing that this Part applies to employment on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"The Governor in Council may, by regulation, direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province, including a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This indicates that the Governor in Council can tailor the application of this Division to specific federal Crown corporations, particularly those involved in nuclear safety and control. This allows for the creation of regulations that are relevant to the unique operational context of these corporations.

### Section 266: Exclusion from Application

Section 266 outlines the Governor in Council's ability to exclude certain employment from the application of this Part. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This power to exclude is significant as it allows the Governor in Council to create exceptions to the general rule of application. For example, it could exclude certain activities within a nuclear safety corporation from the requirements of this Division.

### Section 121.1 and 265: Application to Provincial Crown Corporations

Sections 121.1 and 265 reiterate the Governor in Council's ability to direct that this Part applies to employment on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.
"The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

These sections, similar to Section 158, highlight the Governor in Council's capacity to apply this Division to specific federal Crown corporations, particularly those operating within the nuclear safety and control framework.

### Section 266: Regulations Relating to Labour Standards

Section 266 further elaborates on the Governor in Council's regulatory power by stating that it can make regulations
"...relating to labour standards in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."
"On the recommendation of the Minister, the Governor in Council may make regulations relating to labour standards in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)."

This allows for the creation of regulations that address specific labour standards issues that are relevant to the employment covered by the regulations made under Section 111, 158, 121.1, and 265. These regulations can be tailored to the unique needs of the federal Crown corporations operating within the nuclear safety and control Act's purview.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can sections related to termination of employment not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions Where Sections on Termination of Employment Do Not Apply to Redundant Employees Represented by a Trade Union

### Section 229: Application of Sections 214 to 226

Section 229 outlines two primary conditions under which sections 214 to 226 of the Canada Labour Code do not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union.

#### Condition 1: Collective Agreement Provisions
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the trade union and the employer are bound by a collective agreement containing (a) provisions that (i) specify procedures by which any matters relating to the termination of employment in the industrial establishment at which those employees are employed may be negotiated and finally settled, or (ii) are intended to minimize the impact of termination of employment on the employees represented by the trade union and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment; and (b) provisions that specify that those sections do not apply in respect of the employees represented by the trade union."

This condition hinges on the existence of a collective agreement that explicitly addresses the termination of employment. The agreement must contain provisions for negotiation and settlement of termination matters, and it must also state that sections 214 to 226 do not apply to the employees represented by the trade union. This demonstrates a proactive approach to managing layoffs within a unionized workplace, where the collective agreement provides a framework for minimizing negative impacts on employees.

#### Condition 2: Technological Change
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the termination of the employment of those employees is the result of technological change as defined in subsection 51(1) and sections 52, 54 and 55 apply or would, but for subsection 51(2), apply to the trade union and the employer."

This condition links the non-application of sections 214 to 226 to technological change. If the redundancy is a direct result of technological advancements, and the trade union and employer are bound by a collective agreement that includes provisions for technological change, then those sections do not apply. This acknowledges that technological change can lead to job losses, and that collective agreements can provide mechanisms for addressing these situations.

### Section 215: Employee Representatives in Group Termination of Employment

Section 215 further elaborates on the appointment of employee representatives to a joint planning committee in group terminations, particularly when redundant employees are represented by a trade union.

#### Condition 1: Trade Union Representation
"Where all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of the joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents."

This condition is straightforward: if all redundant employees are represented by a trade union, each union gets to appoint at least one member to the joint planning committee. This ensures that the interests of all represented employees are heard and considered during the termination process.

#### Condition 2: No Trade Union Representation
"Where no redundant employees are represented by a trade union, the employees are entitled to appoint all the members of a joint planning committee who are to be their representatives."

This condition addresses the scenario where no single trade union represents all the redundant employees. In this case, the employees themselves have the right to appoint all the members of the joint planning committee. This provides a mechanism for the employees to directly advocate for their interests.

#### Condition 3: Some Trade Union Representation
"Where some but not all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, (a) each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents; and (b) the employees that are not represented by a trade union are entitled to appoint at least one member of a joint planning committee as their representative."

This condition covers the situation where multiple unions represent different groups of redundant employees. Each union gets to appoint at least one member, and the employees who are not represented by a union also get to appoint at least one member. This ensures that all employee groups have a voice on the joint planning committee.

### Section 30: Lay-offs That Are Not Termination for the Purposes of Severance Pay

Section 30 provides a list of lay-off scenarios that are not considered terminations for severance pay purposes. While not directly addressing the trade union representation condition, it offers a related context for understanding when termination rules might not apply.
"For the purposes of Divisions IX, X and XI of the Act and subject to subsection (2), a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of the employee’s employment by his employer where (a) the lay-off is a result of a strike or lockout; (b) the term of the lay-off is 12 months or less and the lay-off is mandatory pursuant to a minimum work guarantee in a collective agreement; (c) the term of the lay-off is three months or less; (d) the term of the lay-off is more than three months and the employer (i) notifies the employee in writing at or before the time of the lay-off that he will be recalled to work on a fixed date or within a fixed period neither of which shall be more than six months from the date of the lay-off, and (ii) recalls the employee to his employment in accordance with subparagraph (i); (e) the term of the lay-off is more than three months and (i) the employee continues during the term of the lay-off to receive payments from his employer in an amount agreed on by the employee and his employer, (ii) the employer continues to make payments for the benefit of the employee to a pension plan that is registered pursuant to the Pension Benefits Standards Act or under a group or employee insurance plan, (iii) the employee receives supplementary unemployment benefits, or (iv) the employee would be entitled to supplementary unemployment benefits but is disqualified from receiving them pursuant to the Employment Insurance Act ; or (f) the term of the lay-off is..."

This section reiterates the technological change condition, linking it to lay-offs as opposed to terminations. It also includes a condition specifically mentioning lay-offs that are mandatory under a collective agreement with a minimum work guarantee. These conditions highlight the flexibility that collective agreements can provide in managing layoffs, potentially allowing certain lay-offs to fall outside the scope of termination rules.

individual_results.answer:
## Employer Obligations Upon Termination of Employment

### Notice and Severance Pay

Section 230(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the primary obligation of an employer when terminating an employee's employment. It states:
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This provision mandates that the employer must provide either written notice of termination with the equivalent of at least the applicable number of weeks' wages in lieu of notice, or a combination of both. The applicable number of weeks of notice or wages in lieu of notice is determined by the employee's length of continuous employment with the employer, as detailed in subsection (1.1).

Furthermore, Section 230(1) specifies that severance pay is required in instances of individual and group termination of employment. It clarifies:
"As an employer, you are required to pay severance pay in instances of individual and group termination of employment. Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..."

### Additional Requirements for Group Terminations

Section 230(2) introduces additional requirements that apply specifically to group terminations of employment. It mandates that the employer must provide notice to several entities:
"If an employer is bound by a collective agreement that contains a provision authorizing an employee whose position becomes redundant to displace another employee on the basis of seniority, and the position of an employee who is so authorized becomes redundant, the employer must give at least the applicable number of weeks’ notice set out in subsection (1.1) in writing to the trade union that is a party to the collective agreement and to the employee that the employee’s position has become redundant."

This notice must also include information about the reason(s) for the group termination of employment.

### Exceptions to Severance Pay

Section 230(2) also outlines specific exceptions to the severance pay requirement. It states:
"Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..."

These exceptions ensure that severance pay is not automatically triggered in all termination scenarios.

### Employer's Duty to Provide a Written Statement of Benefits

Section 230(2.2) places an additional obligation on the employer to provide a written statement of benefits to the terminated employee. It specifies:
"An employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement. The statement must be given to the employee (a) in the case of an employee who receives notice under paragraph (1)(a), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment; (b) in the case of an employee who receives wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(b), not later than the date of the termination of their employment; and (c) in the case of an employee who receives a combination of notice and wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(c), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment unless the period of notice is shorter, in which case, the day on which notice is given to the employee of the date of the termination of their employment."

This statement ensures the employee has a clear understanding of their final compensation and benefits.

### Employer's Obligation to Provide a Written Statement of Reasons for Dismissal

Section 230(4) details the employer's obligation to provide a written statement of reasons for dismissal upon receiving an unjust dismissal complaint. It states:
"Upon receipt of an unjust dismissal complaint, the complainant or the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement may request in writing that the employer provide a written statement. The statement must give the reasons for the dismissal, and it must be provided within 15 days after the request is made. It is the employer’s responsibility to demonstrate that the complainant’s dismissal was for valid reasons (disciplinary, etc.)."

This statement is crucial for the employee to understand the basis for their termination and to potentially pursue further action if they believe the dismissal was unjust.

## Employer Obligations and Restrictions After Termination Notice

### Section 230(1) - Employer's Duty to Provide Notice or Wages in Lieu

Section 230(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the primary obligation of an employer following the provision of a termination notice. It states:
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This provision establishes a clear choice for the employer: either provide the legally required notice in writing, pay wages in lieu of notice for the equivalent period, or a combination of both. The "applicable number of weeks" is further detailed in subsection (1.1), ranging from two weeks for employees with at least three consecutive months of continuous employment to eight weeks for those with at least eight consecutive years. This ensures that the employer meets the minimum statutory requirements for providing advance warning of an impending termination.

### Section 231 - Restrictions on Changes to Terms and Conditions of Employment

Section 231 places significant restrictions on an employer's ability to alter an employee's terms and conditions of employment after providing a termination notice. It specifies:
"Where notice is given by an employer pursuant to subsection 230(1), the employer (a) shall not thereafter reduce the rate of wages or alter any other term or condition of employment of the employee to whom the notice was given except with the written consent of the employee; and (b) shall, between the time when the notice is given and the date specified therein, pay to the employee his regular rate of wages for his regular hours of work."

This means that the employer cannot unilaterally reduce wages, change job duties, or otherwise negatively impact the employee's employment package between the date of the notice and the termination date, unless the employee provides written consent. Furthermore, the employer is obligated to continue paying the employee their regular rate of wages for their regular hours worked during this notice period. This protects the employee's financial stability during the transition.

### Section 232 - Statement of Benefits

Section 232 mandates that an employer provide a written statement of benefits to the terminated employee. It states:
"An employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement. The statement must be given to the employee (a) in the case of an employee who receives notice under paragraph (1)(a), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment; (b) in the case of an employee who receives wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(b), not later than the date of the termination of their employment; and (c) in the case of an employee who receives a combination of notice and wages in lieu of notice under paragraph (1)(c), as soon as possible, but not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of their employment unless the period of notice is shorter, in which case, the day on which notice is given to the employee of the date of the termination of their employment."

This statement is crucial for the employee to understand their entitlements upon termination. It must include details on accrued vacation pay, outstanding wages, severance pay (if applicable), and any other benefits or pay owed. The timing of the statement's delivery is also specified, ranging from as soon as possible but no later than two weeks before termination for employees receiving notice, to no later than the date of termination for employees receiving wages in lieu of notice.

### Section 233 - Severance Pay Obligations

Section 233 details the severance pay obligations of an employer upon individual or group termination of employment. It states:
"As an employer, you are required to pay severance pay in instances of individual and group termination of employment. Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment  **Reasons for dismissal** Upon receipt of an unjust dismissal complaint, the complainant or the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement may request in writing that the employer provide a written statement. The statement must give the reasons for the dismissal, and it must be provided within 15 days after the request is made. It is the employer’s responsibility to demonstrate that the complainant’s dismissal was for valid reasons (disciplinary, etc.).  **Mediation** The Labour Program will first attempt to resolve the complaint. This may include assisting the parties to settle the complaint through mediation. If the parties choose not to participate in mediation or cannot resolve the complaint, the Head of Compliance and Enforcement will send the complaint to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (Board) who will hear the matter and make a determination."

This section clarifies that severance pay is generally required for both individual and group terminations of employment where the employee has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous service. The exceptions to this rule are outlined, including lay-offs that do not result in termination, employment contracts with end dates, dismissals for just cause, or terminations initiated by the employee. It also addresses the employer's obligation to provide a written statement of reasons for dismissal if an unjust dismissal complaint is received, and the Labour Program's initial attempt at mediation.
