## Conditions for Employer Termination After Employee Continued Work

### General Rule Regarding Notice and Wages
"An employer who terminates the employment of an employee must give the employee (a) notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date; (b) wages in lieu of notice, at their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work, for at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1); or (c) any combination of notice and amounts of wages in lieu of notice so that the total of the number of weeks of notice in writing and the number of weeks for which wages are paid in lieu of notice is equivalent to at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1)."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental obligation of an employer to provide either written notice or wages in lieu of notice to an employee before the termination takes effect. The notice period is determined by the employee's length of continuous employment with the employer, ranging from two weeks to eight weeks. The employer can also provide a combination of notice and wages in lieu of notice, ensuring the total equivalent to the legally required notice period.

### Lay-off Becoming Termination
"A lay-off becomes a termination of employment when the conditions of temporary lay-off no longer apply. A lay-off can also become a termination if an employee does not return to work when recalled. If this occurs, the employee is considered to have terminated their employment."

This passage clarifies a specific scenario where a temporary lay-off can evolve into a permanent termination. It states that a lay-off ceases to be temporary when the conditions under which it was implemented are no longer in effect. Furthermore, a lay-off can become a termination if the employee fails to report for their recalled duties. In such a case, the employee is legally considered to have terminated their own employment.

### Employer Obligations Upon Lay-off Becoming Termination
"If a lay-off becomes a termination of employment, the individual termination of employment requirements apply."

This sentence directly links the lay-off becoming a termination to the application of the standard individual termination of employment requirements outlined in Section 230. This means that if a lay-off transitions into a permanent termination due to the employee's failure to return to work, the employer is still obligated to provide the legally mandated notice or wages in lieu of notice.

### Conditions for Employer Termination After Employee Continued Work

Based on the provided documents, the conditions that must be met for an employer to terminate an employee's employment if the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the date specified in the initial termination notice are as follows:

1.  **Initial Termination Notice:** The employer must have provided the employee with a written notice of termination, specifying the date of termination and the applicable notice period (determined by the employee's length of continuous employment).
2.  **Employee Continued Work:** The employee must have continued to work for more than two weeks after the date specified in the initial termination notice.
3.  **Lay-off Becoming Termination:** The employer must be able to demonstrate that the lay-off that was initially temporary has become a permanent termination due to the employee's failure to return to work when recalled.
4.  **Individual Termination Requirements:** If the lay-off becomes a permanent termination, the employer is still obligated to provide the employee with the legally mandated notice or wages in lieu of notice.

In essence, the employer cannot terminate the employee's employment simply because the employee continued to work for an extended period after the initial notice. The lay-off must have transitioned into a permanent termination due to the employee's non-compliance with the recall instructions. Even then, the employer must still adhere to the standard individual termination of employment requirements.

## Employer Obligations Upon Termination of Employment in Canada

### Severance Pay Requirements

An employer in Canada is generally required to pay an employee severance pay upon termination of employment if the employee has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment. This is explicitly stated in multiple documents.
"As an employer, if you terminate the employment of an employee, you must provide the employee who has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with severance pay." This quote from WORKPLACE-3_5, WORKPLACE-3_6, and LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6 establishes the foundational obligation.

The amount of severance pay is calculated as the greater of two options:
"Severance pay is the greater of the following:  2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..." This passage from LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6 details the two calculation methods. The employee is entitled to either two days' wages for each full year of service, or five days' wages at their regular rate of pay.

### Exceptions to Severance Pay

There are specific circumstances where severance pay is not required. These exceptions are outlined in WORKPLACE-3_5, WORKPLACE-3_6, and LABOUR-REPORTS-8_6.
"Severance pay is not required when:  the employee’s lay-off does not result in a termination of employment the employee’s employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends the employee is dismissed for just cause, or the employee terminates their own employment..." These points clarify the situations where severance is not mandated.

"In addition, you must provide a notice of termination or a pay in lieu of notice." This quote from WORKPLACE-3_5 and WORKPLACE-3_6 highlights this requirement. If the employer provides a notice of termination, they must also provide the employee with pay in lieu of notice if the notice period is less than what is legally required.

### Employer Responsibilities Regarding Dismissal Reasons

When an employee files an unjust dismissal complaint, the employer has a responsibility to provide a written statement detailing the reasons for the dismissal.
"Upon receipt of an unjust dismissal complaint, the complainant or the Labour Program’s Head of Compliance and Enforcement may request in writing that the employer provide a written statement. ## Section 236 of the Canada Labour Code: Types of Regulations

### Purposes of Regulations under Section 236

Section 236 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the broad range of regulations that the Governor in Council can enact for the purposes of Division XI, which deals with severance pay.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations for the purposes of this Division (a) prescribing circumstances in which a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of the employee’s employment by his employer; (b) [Repealed, R.S., 1985, c. 9 (1st Supp.), s. 12] (c) establishing methods for determining whether severance benefits provided to an employee under a plan established by an employer are equivalent to any benefits required to be paid to the employee under this Division; and (d) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment and the expression “regular hours of work”."

This passage details four specific areas where regulations can be made. The first concerns lay-offs, specifying
"...circumstances in which a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of the employee’s employment by his employer..." This indicates the ability to create definitions and rules around the distinction between lay-offs and terminations for severance pay purposes. The second point, marked as repealed, suggests a previous area of regulation that is no longer in effect. The third area focuses on the equivalence of severance benefits provided by an employer plan to those required under the severance pay provisions of the Canada Labour Code. This highlights the power to establish methodologies for comparison and determination. Finally, the fourth area is dedicated to defining absences from employment that would not break the continuity of employment and the meaning of "regular hours of work," both of which are crucial for severance pay calculations.

### Application of Section 236 to Provincial Crown Corporations

Section 265 and Section 236 both address the application of this Division to provincial Crown corporations.
"Section 265 The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that this Part applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act . 1996, c. 12, s. 4 1997, c. 9, s. 125 Marginal note: Exclusion from application..."
"Section 236 The Governor in Council may make regulations for the purposes of this Division (a) prescribing circumstances in which a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of the employee’s employment by his employer; (b) [Repealed, R.S., 1985, c. 9 (1st Supp.), s. 12] (c) establishing methods for determining whether severance benefits provided to an employee under a plan established by an employer are equivalent to any benefits required to be paid to the employee under this Division; and (d) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment and the expression “regular hours of work”."

These sections state that the Governor in Council can direct that this Division applies to employment within a provincial Crown corporation whose activities are regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act. This demonstrates that the regulations made under Section 236 are not limited to private sector employers but can also extend to Crown corporations.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions under which an employer is required to reimburse an employee for work-related expenses, and are there any exceptions to this rule?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Employer Reimbursement of Work-Related Expenses

### Eligibility Criteria

Section 23.1 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations outlines the factors to consider when determining whether an expense is work-related. These factors are:
"(a) whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work; (b) whether the expense enables an employee to perform work; (c) whether incurring the expense is required by the employer as a condition of employment or continued employment; (d) whether the expense satisfies a requirement for the employee’s work imposed by an occupational health or safety standard; and (e) whether the expense is incurred for a legitimate business purpose and not for personal use or enjoyment."

This indicates that an expense is eligible for reimbursement if it is directly related to the employee's job duties, helps them perform those duties, is mandated by the employer, is necessary for occupational health and safety, or is for a valid business reason.

### Time Limits for Reimbursement

Employers have specific timeframes within which they must reimburse reasonable work-related expenses. For unionized employees, the time limit is
"...specified in a collective agreement  or written agreement, or if there is no agreement, within 30  days after the employee submits their expense claim to the employer..." For non-unionized employees, the time limit is
"...specified in a collective agreement  or written agreement, or if there is no agreement, within 30  days after the employee submits their expense claim to the employer..." These deadlines are designed to ensure timely compensation for legitimate work expenses.

### Exceptions to Reimbursement

Several exceptions exist where an expense is not eligible for reimbursement.
"An expense is not eligible for reimbursement when:  a written agreement between a non-unionized  employee and their employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example:  A written agreement specifies that a non-unionized employee is required to pay  for:  	 the replacement cost of lost uniforms penalties incurred for non-cancellation of a hotel  reservation  a collective  agreement or written agreement between a unionized employee’s trade union and  the employer requires the employee to pay the expense      Example: A collective agreement specifies that  employees are required to pay for:                 safety footwear costs in excess of their annual  safety footwear allowance eye exam fees to get safety glasses..."

This means that if an employee is contractually obligated to pay for an expense, it will not be reimbursed. Additionally, expenses incurred for personal use or enjoyment are also excluded.

### Reasonableness of Expenses

Section 23.1(2) of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations details eight factors to consider when determining whether an expense is reasonable. These factors mirror some of the work-relatedness criteria but with a focus on whether the expense is within the bounds of what is typically reimbursed in similar industries and whether the employer authorized it in advance.
"Whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work  Expenses connected to the employee’s performance of work are more likely to be reasonable.     Example: Uniforms  required by the employer     Whether the expense enables an employee to perform work  Expenses  incurred to enable an employee to work are more likely to be reasonable.     Example: Road  transportation expenses such as fuel or tolls incurred by transport truck  drivers     Whether the  expense is incurred at the request of the employer  Expenses an  employer requests or directs an employee to incur are more likely to be  reasonable. individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to take a medical leave of absence, and what protections are afforded to them during this time?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances Entitling an Employee to Medical Leave of Absence

### General Entitlement
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine."

This section of the Canada Labour Code (CLC) establishes the fundamental right of an employee to take medical leave of absence. It explicitly lists the primary reasons for which an employee can be granted this leave: personal illness or injury, organ or tissue donation, medical appointments during working hours, or quarantine. The leave can extend up to 27 weeks.

### Additional Entitlements Based on Collective Agreements or Employment Contracts
"...substantially equivalent to the period provided for in subsection (1.21)..."

This passage highlights that employees covered by collective agreements or individual employment contracts may receive medical leave with pay that is comparable to the 27-week unpaid leave provided by the CLC. This indicates that the specific terms of medical leave can vary depending on the terms of the employment relationship.

### Entitlements Based on Continuous Employment
"Subject to subsection (1.21) and the regulations, an employee earns, as of the first day on which this subsection applies to the employee, (a) after completing 30 days of continuous employment with an employer, three days of medical leave of absence with pay; and (b) following the period of 30 days referred to in paragraph (a), at the beginning of each month after completing one month of continuous employment with the employer, one day of medical leave of absence with pay."

This section details how an employee accrues medical leave with pay based on continuous employment. After 30 days of continuous employment, they earn three days of medical leave with pay. Following this, they earn one day of medical leave with pay at the beginning of each month after completing one month of continuous employment. This accrual continues up to a maximum of 10 days per calendar year, subject to regulations.

## Protections Afforded During Medical Leave of Absence

### Wage Continuation
"Each day of medical leave of absence with pay that an employee takes must be paid at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work, and that pay is for all purposes considered to be wages."

This passage is crucial as it guarantees that an employee receives their regular wages during their medical leave. It clarifies that the pay is considered wages for all purposes, ensuring that their financial stability is maintained.

### Benefits Accumulation
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division accumulate during the entire period of the medical leave of absence."

This protection ensures that an employee's benefits and seniority are not negatively impacted by their medical leave. Their pension, health, and disability benefits continue to accrue, and their seniority is preserved throughout the leave period.

### Employment Opportunities
"An employee is entitled, on written request, to be informed in writing of every employment, promotion or training opportunity that arises during the period when the employee is on a medical leave of absence under this Division and for which the employee is qualified, and on receiving that request, the employer must provide the information to the employee."

This provision safeguards an employee's career progression. They have the right to be informed of any job openings, promotions, or training opportunities that arise during their medical leave and for which they are qualified. The employer is obligated to provide this information promptly.

### Prohibition Against Discrimination
"Subject to subsection (7), an employer is prohibited from dismissing, suspending, laying off, demoting or disciplining an employee because the employee intends to take or has taken a medical leave of absence or taking such an intention or absence into account in any decision to promote or train the employee."

This strong protection prevents employers from retaliating against employees for taking medical leave. It explicitly prohibits any adverse employment actions, including termination, suspension, demotion, or disciplinary measures, based on the employee's medical leave. Furthermore, it prohibits employers from considering an employee's medical leave when making decisions about promotions or training.

### Return to Work
"For the purposes of calculating benefits, other than benefits referred to in subsection (8), of an employee who is absent from work due to medical leave under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence."

This provision ensures that an employee's employment history is not disrupted by their medical leave. Their employment on their return to work is considered continuous with their employment before the leave, which is important for benefit calculations and seniority.

individual_results.question: What are the obligations of an employer towards an employee who is absent from work due to a work-related illness or injury, and what benefits should continue to accumulate during the absence?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Obligations Towards an Employee Absent Due to Work-Related Illness or Injury

### Section 239.1: Prohibition and Employer Obligations

Section 239.1 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly prohibits employers from taking adverse action against an employee due to their absence from work for work-related illness or injury. It states,
"Subject to subsection (4) and to the regulations made under this Division, no employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because of absence from work due to work-related illness or injury." This provision establishes a fundamental right for employees to take medical leave without fear of retaliation.

Furthermore, Section 239.1 outlines the employer's obligation to subscribe to a plan that provides wage replacement. It specifies,
"Every employer shall subscribe to a plan that provides an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury with wage replacement, payable at an equivalent rate to that provided for under the applicable workers’ compensation legislation in the employee’s province of permanent residence." This ensures that the employee's income is protected during their recovery period.

### Section 239.1(2): Return to Work Obligation

Section 239.1(2) details the employer's responsibility to facilitate the employee's return to work. It states,
"...the employer shall, where reasonably practicable, return an employee to work after the employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury." This obligation extends to reassignment to a different position with different terms and conditions of employment if the employee is unable to perform their previous duties.

### Section 239.1(4): Benefits Accumulate

Section 239.1(5) is crucial as it clarifies which benefits continue to accumulate during the employee's absence due to work-related illness or injury. It states,
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury shall accumulate during the entire period of the absence." This ensures that the employee's benefits are not negatively impacted by their medical leave.

### Section 239.1(6) and (7): Employee Contributions

Sections 239.1(6) and (7) address the employee's responsibility for benefit contributions during the absence. They state,
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (5), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any absence due to work-related illness or injury unless, at the beginning of the absence or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." and
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (5) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not absent, unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time." These sections establish a clear expectation for the employee to continue making contributions if required, while the employer is obligated to maintain its contributions at a comparable level.

### Section 239.1(8): Deemed Continuous Employment

Section 239.1(8) further protects the employee's benefits by deeming their employment continuous with their time before the illness or injury. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (6) and (7), the benefits shall not accumulate during the absence, and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This prevents a gap in benefit accrual due to the medical leave.

### Section 239.1(9): Deemed Continuous Employment for Other Benefits

Section 239.1(9) extends the deemed continuous employment provision to other benefits. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating benefits, other than benefits referred to in subsection (5), of an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury, employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This ensures that the employee's benefits are not negatively affected by the medical leave, even those not directly tied to contributions.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer's long-term disability plan under the Canada Labour Code, and are there any exceptions to these requirements?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Long-Term Disability Plan Requirements under the Canada Labour Code

### General Insurance Requirement

Section 239.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes a primary requirement for employers offering long-term disability (LTD) plans:
"Every employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan must insure the plan with an entity that is licensed to provide insurance under the laws of a province." This quote is central to understanding the current legal landscape for LTD plans. It is not a discretionary provision; it is a mandatory obligation. The provision is further reinforced by the Jobs, Growth and Long-term Prosperity Act, which introduced this insurance requirement for all LTD plans offered by employers.

### Exceptions to the Insurance Requirement

While insurance is generally required, there is an exception outlined in Section 239.2(2).
"However, an employer may provide those benefits under a long-term disability plan that is not insured, in the circumstances and subject to the conditions provided for in the regulations." This exception is not broad. It is contingent upon meeting specific criteria detailed in the regulations. The regulations would specify the limited circumstances under which an LTD plan can be offered without insurance. However, the text does not elaborate on these circumstances.

### Additional Considerations from Part III of the Code

Part III of the Canada Labour Code also addresses LTD plans, although it does not impose a general obligation to provide them. It does state that employers who offer LTD plans must insure them with a licensed insurance company. This aligns with the specific requirement in Section 239.2(1). Furthermore, Part III mandates the accumulation of pensions, health, and disability benefits, as well as seniority, during an employee's absence from work for certain purposes, such as work-related injury or illness. This provision indirectly supports the importance of LTD plans by ensuring that employees have continued access to benefits during periods of disability.

### Employer Responsibilities Related to LTD Plans

Beyond insurance, employers have other responsibilities related to LTD plans. They must maintain the confidentiality of LTD plan documents, including start and end dates, interruption details, medical certificates, and notices issued. They must also provide detailed reasons for an employee's absence due to work-related illness or injury. Finally, they must notify the employee of their return to work or the reasons why they cannot return. These responsibilities are detailed in the "Employer compliance with federal labour standards" section of Labour-Reports-8_7.

individual_results.question: What are the conditions and time limitations for an employee to file a complaint about an unjust dismissal under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Filing an Unjust Dismissal Complaint

### Employment Duration and Collective Agreements

Section 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the initial conditions for filing an unjust dismissal complaint. It states:
"Subject to subsections (2) and 242(3.1), a person who has been dismissed and considers the dismissal to be unjust may make a complaint in writing to the Head if the employee (a) has completed 12 consecutive months of continuous employment by an employer; and (b) is not a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement."

This indicates that an employee must have worked for the same employer for at least 12 consecutive months to be eligible to file an unjust dismissal complaint. Additionally, they must not be part of a group of employees covered by a collective agreement. These two conditions must be met simultaneously.

### Time Limitations for Filing an Unjust Dismissal Complaint

Section 240(2) specifies the strict time limit for filing an unjust dismissal complaint:
"Subject to subsection (3), a complaint under subsection (1) shall be made within ninety days from the date on which the person making the complaint was dismissed."

This means that an employee must file their unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days of their dismissal. However, subsection (3) provides an opportunity for the Head to extend this period under certain circumstances.

### Extension of Time

Section 240(3) details the conditions under which the Head may extend the 90-day time limit:
"The Head may extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made in that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint but that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; or (b) in any circumstances that are prescribed by regulation."

The Head can extend the time limit if the complaint was initially made to an official without the proper authority, but the complainant reasonably believed they did. Alternatively, the Head can extend the time limit based on circumstances outlined in regulation.

### Limitation on Substantially Similar Complaints

Section 240(1.1) includes a limitation on filing a complaint based on substantially the same facts as a complaint that has already been withdrawn. It states:
"For greater certainty, the fact that an employer complies with Divisions X and XI does not (a) affect the employee’s rights under this Division; or (b) prevent the Board from deciding under paragraph 242(3)(a) that the dismissal was unjust or from making any order under subsection 242(4), including a reinstatement order."

This passage clarifies that if a complaint based on substantially the same facts has been withdrawn, a new complaint based on those same facts will not be permitted.

### Time Limit for Monetary Complaints

Section 12_1 outlines the time limit for filing a monetary complaint:
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you."

This means that if an employee is dismissed unjustly and believes they are owed unpaid wages, vacation pay, or other amounts, they must file their monetary complaint within six months of the last day their employer was legally obligated to make that payment.

### Time Limit for Non-Monetary Complaints

Section 12_1 also specifies the time limit for filing a non-monetary complaint:
"You must file your non-monetary complaint within 6 months from the day you were aware of the issue."

This indicates that if an employee is unjustly dismissed and believes they have experienced a non-monetary issue, such as not receiving a response to a request for a flexible work arrangement, they must file their non-monetary complaint within six months of becoming aware of the issue.

### Time Limit for Unjust Dismissal Complaints (Reiteration)

Section 12_1 reiterates the 90-day time limit for filing an unjust dismissal complaint:
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal."

This reinforces the 90-day deadline, while also mentioning the possibility of an extension by the Head under specific circumstances.

individual_results.question: What are the steps and obligations for an employer and the Head when handling a complaint related to the dismissal of a person described in subsection 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Steps and Obligations for Employer and Head in Handling an Unjust Dismissal Complaint

### Filing a Complaint

#### Who Can File a Complaint?

Section 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines who can file a complaint. It states:
"Subject to subsections (2) and 242(3.1), a person who has been dismissed and considers the dismissal to be unjust may make a complaint in writing to the Head if the employee (a) has completed 12 consecutive months of continuous employment by an employer; and (b) is not a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement." This indicates that an employee who meets these two criteria can initiate the complaint process.

#### Time Limit for Filing a Complaint

Section 240(2) specifies the time limit for filing a complaint:
"Subject to subsection (3), a complaint under subsection (1) shall be made within ninety days from the date on which the person making the complaint was dismissed." This means the complaint must be submitted to the Head within 90 days of the dismissal date.

#### Head's Role Upon Receiving a Complaint

Section 240(2) further details the Head's initial responsibilities:
"On receipt of a complaint made under subsection 240(1), the Head must endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint." This highlights the Head's proactive approach to facilitating a resolution between the complainant and the employer.

### Employer's Obligations

#### Providing Reasons for Dismissal

Section 241(1) mandates that if an employer dismisses a person described in subsection 240(1), they must provide a written statement explaining the reasons for the dismissal.
"If an employer dismisses a person described in subsection 240(1), the person who was dismissed or the Head may make a request in writing to the employer to provide a written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal, and any employer who receives such a request must provide the person who made the request with such a statement within 15 days after the request is made." This obligation is triggered by a request from either the complainant or the Head.

#### Responding to Head's Assistance

Section 240(2) also states that the Head may assist the parties to the complaint to settle it. The employer is expected to cooperate with this effort.

#### Board Referral

Section 240(3) outlines the Head's actions if a complaint is not settled within a reasonable time.
"If a complaint is not settled under subsection (2) within the period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances, the Head must, on the written request of the person who made the complaint that the complaint be referred to the Board, deliver to the Board the complaint made under subsection 240(1), any written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal provided under subsection (1) and any other statements or documents that the Head has that relate to the complaint." This indicates that the Head can refer the complaint to the Board if settlement efforts fail.

### Head's Obligations

#### Extending the Time Limit

Section 240(3) grants the Head the authority to extend the 90-day time limit for filing a complaint under certain circumstances.
"The Head may extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made in that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint but that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; or (b) in any circumstances that are prescribed by regulation." This flexibility allows the Head to accommodate situations where the complainant may have mistakenly sought assistance from an inappropriate official.

#### Deeming a Complaint Withdrawn

Section 240(5) specifies that if the Head does not receive a written request to refer the complaint to the Board within the extended period, they may deem the complaint withdrawn.
"Subject to the regulations, if the person who made the complaint does not, within the period set out in the notice, make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board, the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn." This provides a mechanism for closing a complaint if the complainant does not actively pursue it.

#### Assisting Parties to Settle

Section 240(2) reiterates the Head's duty to endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle it. This is a continuous obligation throughout the complaint handling process.

#### Providing Notice

Section 240(4) details the Head's obligation to provide written notice to the complainant if they have not replied to a written communication within a reasonable period, or if a longer period has elapsed.
"If the person who made the complaint does not reply to a written communication from the Head within a period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances and a period of at least 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, have elapsed from the day on which the complaint was made, the Head may give written notice to the person who made the complaint that they have the period of 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, set out in the notice to make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board." This notice informs the complainant of the remaining time to request Board referral.

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board suspend or reject a complaint, and what steps must it take in these situations?
individual_results.answer:
## Suspension of a Complaint

### Circumstances for Suspension

The Board can suspend consideration of a complaint "at any time, in whole or in part" if it is satisfied that the complainant must take certain measures before the Board may continue to deal with it. This is outlined in Section 241.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
"If the Board is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

### Steps Taken During Suspension

When a complaint is suspended, the Board is obligated to notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice
"...the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures." This ensures the complainant is aware of their obligations and the timeframe for fulfilling them.
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures."

### End of Suspension

The suspension concludes when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken. This provides a clear trigger for the Board to resume its work on the complaint.
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

## Rejection of a Complaint

### Circumstances for Rejection

The Board may reject a complaint "in whole or in part" under several circumstances, as detailed in Section 241.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code. These include:
"(a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..."
"(b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period."

### Steps Taken During Rejection

When a complaint is rejected, the Board must notify the complainant in writing and provide "reasons" for the decision. This ensures transparency and allows the complainant to understand why their complaint was not pursued.
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the complainant in writing, with reasons."

### Additional Rejection Scenarios

Section 246.2(3) provides an additional scenario for rejection, stating that the suspension of a complaint ends when the measures specified in the notice under subsection 246.1(2) have been taken. This implies that if these measures are not taken within the specified period, the complaint can still be rejected.

### Rejection of Complaints Related to Reprisals

Section 246.2(3) also addresses the rejection of complaints related to reprisals. It reiterates that the suspension of a complaint ends when the measures specified in the notice under subsection 246.1(2) have been taken. This suggests that if these measures are not taken within the specified period, the complaint can still be rejected.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Board take if it decides that a person has been unjustly dismissed, and what factors might it consider in making its decisions?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Actions Upon Finding Unjust Dismissal

### Remedies the Board Can Order
"If the Board decides that a complainant has been unjustly dismissed, the Board may, by order, require the employer who dismissed the complainant to:   pay the complainant compensation, not higher than the amount of money that is equal to what would have been paid by the employer if they had not dismissed them  reinstate the complainant in their employment, and  order the employer, in a fair way, to resolve or reduce any consequences of the dismissal..."

This section directly addresses the Board's potential actions. It outlines three primary remedies the Board can impose on the employer. The first is financial compensation, capped at the amount the employer would have paid had the dismissal not occurred. The second is reinstatement to the former position. The third is a broader order to address any negative impacts of the dismissal in a "fair way." These remedies are designed to rectify the injustice suffered by the complainant.

### Factors the Board Considers in its Decisions

### Seriousness of the Problem
"Adjudicators will consider a number of factors when deciding whether or not the dismissal was justified. For example, he or she may consider:   Seriousness of the problem: Did the action/inaction of the employee have serious or only minor consequences for the employer?"

The Board employs a multi-faceted approach to its decision-making process. One key factor is the "seriousness of the problem" caused by the employee's actions or inactions. The Board assesses whether the consequences for the employer were significant or relatively minor. This helps determine the appropriate level of intervention needed.

### Degree of Orientation
"Degree of orientation: Had the workplace rules been clearly explained? Was the employee informed about the employer's job performance expectations?"

The Board also evaluates whether the employee was adequately informed about workplace expectations. This includes whether the rules were "clearly explained" and whether the employee received feedback on their job performance. A lack of clarity or communication can weaken the employer's justification for dismissal.

### Past Discipline
"Past discipline: Has the employee been disciplined for improper workplace behaviour in the past?"

The Board considers the employee's disciplinary history. If the employee has been previously disciplined for similar behavior, it may strengthen the employer's case for dismissal. Conversely, a clean disciplinary record could weigh against the employer's position.

### Employee's Work History
"Employee's work history: Has the employee's work performance been satisfactory in the past?"

The Board assesses the employee's overall work performance. A history of "satisfactory" performance could make the dismissal seem unwarranted.

### History of Organization's Disciplinary Practice
"History of organization's disciplinary practice: Have other employees who engaged in similar improper conduct been disciplined for it?"

The Board examines the organization's past disciplinary actions. If similar misconduct has been met with consistent discipline, it could influence the Board's decision.

### Extenuating Circumstances
"Extenuating circumstances or mitigating factors: Was the employee facing pressures such as personal problems or provocation which may have led to the improper behaviour?"

The Board is willing to consider "extenuating circumstances or mitigating factors" that may have contributed to the employee's improper behavior. This could include personal problems or provocation.

### Past Unjust Dismissal Decisions
"Adjudicators might also rely on past unjust dismissal adjudication decisions when deciding your case. They are not obligated to follow those decisions, but they can serve as helpful guides. You do not have to refer to past decisions when making your arguments, but can if you like. Past adjudication decisions can be found at your local Labour Program office or in on-line legal databases such as LexisNexis and SOQUIJ, which can be subscribed to for a fee. Information about past unjust dismissal decisions can also be found in labour and employment law textbooks, which may be available at your local library."

The Board may refer to past unjust dismissal decisions as "helpful guides," although it is not bound to follow them. These decisions can provide context and precedent for the current case.

individual_results.question: What is the status of the Board's orders in relation to judicial review?
individual_results.answer:
## Judicial Review of Board Orders

### Finality of Board Orders

Several sections of the Canada Labour Code establish the finality of Board orders and decisions in relation to judicial review. Section 22(1) explicitly states,
"Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This passage is crucial as it sets the overarching principle of non-reviewability. It clarifies that judicial review is strictly limited to very specific circumstances outlined in the Federal Courts Act.

CLC-156 also reinforces this point, stating,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This is a concise and direct reiteration of the finality of Board actions.

CLC-243 further emphasizes this by stating,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This is a strong and unambiguous declaration of the Board's orders' immunity from judicial scrutiny.

### Prohibition of Court Proceedings to Question Board Proceedings

Beyond the finality of the orders themselves, the Code actively prevents courts from intervening in the Board's own processes. Section 243(2) declares,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 242." This passage is particularly important as it prohibits any attempt by a court to halt or alter the Board's deliberations or decisions.

CLC-146.1(4) echoes this sentiment, stating,
"If the Board issues a direction under paragraph (1)(b), the employer shall, without delay, affix or cause to be affixed to or near the machine, thing or place in respect of which the direction is issued a notice of the direction, in the form and containing the information that the Board may specify, and no person may remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Board." CLC-251.12(4) provides another layer of protection, stating,
"The order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This is a repetition of the finality principle found in other sections, further solidifying its importance.

### Exceptions to Judicial Review

While the Board's orders are generally final and immune from judicial review, there are limited exceptions. Section 22(1) mentions that review is possible
"...in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This indicates that judicial review is only available on very narrow grounds, such as jurisdiction or exceeding its authority.

CLC-156(1) also includes this exception, stating,
"...every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act." This is a direct parallel to Section 22(1), confirming the limited scope of judicial review.

### Enforcement of Board Orders

CLC-243(1) and CLC-146.1(4) both address the enforcement of Board orders, which is a consequence of their finality. CLC-243(1) states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This finality is what allows for the enforcement mechanisms outlined in CLC-146.1(4), such as the employer being required to post a notice of the Board's direction.

CLC-146.1(4) details the employer's obligation to post a notice of the Board's direction, stating,
"If the Board issues a direction under paragraph (1)(b), the employer shall, without delay, affix or cause to be affixed to or near the machine, thing or place in respect of which the direction is issued a notice of the direction, in the form and containing the information that the Board may specify, and no person may remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Board." This enforcement is a direct result of the Board's orders being final and not subject to judicial review.

individual_results.question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Board Orders in the Federal Court

### Finality of Board Orders

Section 156(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions. It states,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This provision is fundamental to understanding how Board orders can be enforced in the Federal Court. It means that once a Board order is issued, it is not subject to appeal or judicial review in any other court.

### Filing in the Federal Court

Section 23(1) outlines the process for enforcing Board orders in the Federal Court. It specifies that
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court..." This filing must occur within 14 days from the day the order is made or the day compliance is provided for, whichever is later.

### Registration of the Order

Section 23(2) details what happens after the Board files the order in the Federal Court. It states,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This registration is crucial because it transforms the Board order into a judgment of the Federal Court.

### Enforcement Proceedings

Section 244(1) further clarifies the enforcement process. It says,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This indicates that any party impacted by a Board order can initiate enforcement proceedings in the Federal Court by filing a copy of the order.

### No Review by Certiorari

Section 22(2) reinforces the finality of Board orders by explicitly stating,
"Except as permitted by subsection (1), no order, decision or proceeding of the Board made or carried on under or purporting to be made or carried on under this Part shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground, including the ground that the order, decision or proceeding is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board to make or carry on or that, in the course of any proceeding, the Board for any reason exceeded or lost its jurisdiction." This passage is particularly relevant as it directly addresses the question by asserting that Board orders are not subject to review by certiorari or any other form of judicial review in the Federal Court.

individual_results.question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make for the purposes of Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code, and what aspects of employment complaints can these regulations address?
individual_results.answer:
## Regulations under Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 111: Broad Regulatory Powers

Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council extensive regulatory authority. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may make regulations (a) prescribing to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received; (b) prescribing in what form and manner any notice or report that is authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, a conciliation commissioner, a conciliation board or an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall be given or sent and what shall constitute sufficient service of such notice or report on the person to whom it is given or sent; (c) designating, with respect to any notice or request authorized or required to be given or sent by the Minister, the officer who may give or send the notice or request on behalf of the Minister; (d) prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining; (e) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (f) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit; (h) [Repealed, 1998, c. 26, s. 51] (i) prescribing the form and content of any written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4) and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a request; (j) prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister; (k) prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof; and (l) prescribing the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a)."

This section reveals that the regulations can cover a wide array of administrative processes related to employment complaints. They can dictate
"...any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received..." including the "form and content" of specific notices like those to commence collective bargaining (d), under section 71 (e), and under section 87.2 (f). Furthermore, they can address the
"...manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister..." and the
"...circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof..." The regulations can also govern the
"...manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a).", indicating control over the dissemination of dispute resolution outcomes.

### Section 248: Inquiries

Section 248 outlines the Minister's power to cause an inquiry to be made into employment in an industrial establishment. It states that
"The Minister may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This regulation allows for the formal investigation of employment issues, which could be a precursor to or a component of a broader complaint process.

### Section 121.1 and 265 & 266: Application of Provincial Laws to Nuclear Crown Corporations

Sections 121.1, 265, and 266 address the application of provincial labour standards to nuclear Crown corporations. They permit the Governor in Council to direct that this Part (Division 11) applies to employment within such corporations. This means that regulations made under Division 11 can be extended to cover the specific employment conditions within these federally regulated nuclear entities.

### Section 266: Exclusion from Application

Section 266, while related to provincial Crown corporations, also touches upon the regulatory power of the Governor in Council. It states that the Governor in Council
"...may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..." This indicates that regulations made under Division 11 can be specifically excluded from applying to certain nuclear Crown corporations.

In summary, the Governor in Council can make regulations for Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code that address a comprehensive range of administrative aspects related to employment complaints, including the form and manner of notices, requests, and reports, the designation of officers to deliver these communications, the content of specific notices (like those for collective bargaining), the filing of orders and decisions with the Minister, public access to copies of these documents, and the release of conciliation reports. These regulations can also be applied to nuclear Crown corporations, with the possibility of specific exclusions.

individual_results.question: What is the effect of sections 240 to 245 on an employee's civil remedies against their employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Effect of Sections 240 to 245 on Civil Remedies

### Section 246

#### Application of Section 189
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division."

This statement from Section 246 establishes a foundational principle regarding the relationship between unjust dismissal complaints and civil remedies. It indicates that the provisions within Divisions XIV to XIV.1, which deal with unjust dismissal, do not diminish or interfere with an employee's existing civil options against their employer. Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code is invoked to ensure that these complaint mechanisms operate alongside, rather than in place of, the traditional legal avenues for seeking redress for wrongful dismissal.

### Section 246.1

#### Limitation on Subsequent Complaints
"An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under either subsection 240(1) or 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn."

This limitation in Section 246.1 directly addresses the potential for redundant complaints. It prevents an employee from filing a new unjust dismissal complaint based on substantially the same set of facts as a previous one, unless the earlier complaint has been formally withdrawn. This promotes efficiency in the Board's processing of complaints and avoids unnecessary duplication of effort. It is relevant to the question because it clarifies that the complaint process under unjust dismissal does not preclude an employee from pursuing civil remedies if they have already filed a complaint based on the same issues, provided that the prior complaint has been withdrawn.

### Section 240

#### Conditions for Filing a Complaint
"Subject to subsections (2) and 242(3.1), a person who has been dismissed and considers the dismissal to be unjust may make a complaint in writing to the Head if the employee (a) has completed 12 consecutive months of continuous employment by an employer; and (b) is not a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement."

Section 240 outlines the eligibility criteria for an employee to file an unjust dismissal complaint with the Head. It specifies that the employee must have completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer and must not be a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement. This ensures that the complaint process is accessible to employees who meet certain tenure requirements and are not covered by a collective bargaining agreement. While this section doesn't directly address civil remedies, it sets the stage for the complaint process, which can ultimately lead to civil remedies if the Board finds the dismissal unjust.

### Section 245

#### No Suspension or Affectation of Civil Remedies
"No civil remedy of an employee against his employer is suspended or affected by sections 240 to 245."

This passage from Section 245 is the most direct answer to the question. It unequivocally states that the provisions within Divisions XIV to XIV.1 do not have any impact on an employee's existing civil remedies against their employer. This means that even if an employee files an unjust dismissal complaint with the Head under Sections 240 to 245, they still retain the right to pursue traditional legal avenues for seeking compensation or reinstatement if the Board rules in their favour. The quote is crucial because it explicitly confirms the independence of the complaint process from civil remedies.

individual_results.question: What recourse do employees have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities?
individual_results.answer:
## Recourse for Employees Facing Disciplinary Action in Response to Protected Activities

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a broad prohibition against employers taking disciplinary action against employees for exercising their rights under the Part. It states:
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section directly addresses the question by explicitly listing protected activities that cannot result in disciplinary action. These activities include testifying in proceedings, providing information to authorities about health and safety conditions, and acting in accordance with the Part or seeking its enforcement. The use of the word "or" indicates that each of these activities provides an independent avenue of protection against retaliation.

### Section 246.1: Complaint to Board for Reprisals

Section 246.1 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for employees to file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken action against them in response to protected activities. It details the types of reprisals that can be the subject of a complaint, including dismissal, suspension, lay-off, demotion, financial penalties, or any other disciplinary action.
"...employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96; (a.1) [Repealed, 2021, c. 26, s. 25] (b) dismissing, suspending, laying off, or demoting the employee, imposing a financial or other penalty on the employee, or otherwise taking any disciplinary action against the employee, because the employee (i) has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part; (c) taking into account the fact that the employee has taken any of the actions referred to in subparagraphs (b)(i) to (iv) in any decision with respect to the promotion or training of the employee; or (d) threatening to take any of the reprisals referred to in paragraph (b) or (c)."

This section is crucial because it confirms that disciplinary action taken *because* an employee exercised their rights under the Part is a form of reprisal that can be the subject of a complaint to the Board. It specifically mentions reprisals taken
"...because the employee (i) has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part..."

### Section 133: Complaint to Board for Contravention of Section 147

Section 133 of the Canada Labour Code also allows employees to file a complaint with the Board if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to protected activities. It states:
"An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This section reinforces the availability of the Board as a recourse for employees facing disciplinary action in retaliation for exercising their rights under the Part. It confirms that such a complaint can be made in writing to the Board.

### Section 147.1: Abuse of Rights

Section 147.1 of the Canada Labour Code provides a limited exception to the general prohibition on disciplinary action. It states:
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This section allows for disciplinary action if an employee has "wilfully abused" their rights under sections 128 and 129. However, it is important to note that this exception is narrow and requires a demonstration of "wilfully abused" rights. It does not generally protect employees from disciplinary action for engaging in protected activities in good faith.

In summary, employees in Canada have multiple avenues of recourse under the Canada Labour Code if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to protected activities. Section 147 provides a broad prohibition on such retaliation, while Section 246.1 outlines the process for filing a complaint with the Board. Section 133 also allows for such complaints. Section 147.1 provides a narrow exception for employees who have "wilfully abused" their rights under sections 128 and 129.

individual_results.question: What can the Board do if it believes an employee needs to take certain actions before it can continue to handle their complaint, and what information must it provide to the employee in this situation?
individual_results.answer:
## Board Actions When Employee Needs to Take Actions

### Section 251.02(1)(b) of the Canada Labour Code
"A complaint may be suspended at any time, in whole or in part, pursuant to subsection 251.02(1) if the Head is satisfied that the complainant must take certain measures within a specific time period before the complaint can be dealt with."

This section outlines the Board's ability to suspend a complaint. The Board can do so if it determines that the complainant is obligated to fulfill specific actions within a defined timeframe. The Board's satisfaction with this requirement is the trigger for the suspension.

### Section 251.05(1)(b) of the Canada Labour Code
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee did not take the required measures within the specified time period, the complaint can be rejected."

This passage directly addresses the Board's action when an employee fails to meet the required measures within the given timeframe. It states that the complaint can be rejected if the Head is convinced of this non-compliance. This demonstrates the Board's follow-through mechanism when an employee is given a task and fails to complete it.

### Section 251.05(1)(c) of the Canada Labour Code
"The complainant may be issued a letter requiring communication if:  they do not reply to a written communication within a reasonable period of time, and at least 30 days have elapsed from the date the complaint was received by the Labour Program  The letter will advise that they have 30 days to indicate, in writing, that they wish to pursue their complaint. If no response is received, the complaint may be rejected."

This section details the Board's communication with a complainant who does not respond to a written request. It explains that a letter will be sent, informing the complainant of their 30-day window to indicate their desire to continue the complaint. The Board's action upon receiving no response is to reject the complaint. This highlights the Board's proactive approach to ensuring complainants engage with the process.

### Section 251.05(1)(a)(iv) of the Canada Labour Code
"**Other means available to the employee to resolve the complaint that should be pursued [subparagraph 251.05(1)(a)(iv)]**..."

This section discusses the Board's rejection of a complaint when other avenues for resolution exist. It emphasizes that the Board will consider whether the complainant has pursued other options, such as other government bodies or collective agreements.
"Prior to the rejection of a complaint on this ground, suspension of the complaint under section 251.02 of the Code should be considered as the primary option until the other means available to the complainant have been pursued and concluded."

This passage is crucial as it specifies the Board's recommended first step before outright rejection due to other available means. It suggests suspending the complaint while the complainant explores these other options.
"In order to reject a complaint, it is necessary to demonstrate that other means are not only available, but that those other means are appropriate for resolving the complaint."

This passage further clarifies the Board's burden when considering rejection due to other means. It requires a demonstration that the complainant has explored these options *and* that they are suitable for addressing the complaint's underlying issue.
"Example: An employee subject to a collective agreement files a complaint for termination and severance pay. Upon investigation, the employer alleges that the employee was dismissed. There was no termination such as a lack of work or discontinuance of a function. It appears that in reality the employee is challenging the dismissal by filing a complaint for termination and severance pay. Since the underlying subject-matter of the complaint is to challenge the dismissal, the allegations related to termination and severance pay should be rejected pursuant to subparagraph 251.05(1)(a)(iv). This is because there are other means available to the employee to resolve the real subject-matter of the complaint. The complainant has recourse to challenge the dismissal through their collective agreement."

This example illustrates the Board's application of the rejection rule. It shows that if another avenue exists to address the complaint's core issue, the Board may reject the initial complaint.

### Section 133(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This section outlines the process for an employee to formally lodge a complaint with the Board. It specifies that the complaint must be in writing and detail the alleged contravention.

### Section 133(2) of the Canada Labour Code
"The complaint shall be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

This passage sets a strict time limit for filing a complaint. It states that the complaint must be submitted within ninety days of the complainant becoming aware of the alleged action or circumstances.

### Section 133(3) of the Canada Labour Code
"A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be, in relation to the matter that is the subject-matter of the complaint."

This section provides an exception to the ninety-day rule for complaints related to the exercise of rights under sections 128 or 129. It requires the employee to have complied with specific obligations or the Head to have received relevant reports before the complaint can be filed.

### Section 134(1)(a) of the Canada Labour Code
"If, under subsection 133(5), the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening that section and may, if applicable, by order, require the employer to (a) permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention; (c) pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee; and (d) rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention, not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer."

This section details the Board's potential actions when it determines an employer has contravened section 147. It outlines a range of remedies, including reinstatement, compensation, and rescinding disciplinary action.

### Section 134(5) of the Canada Labour Code
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This passage explains the Board's initial approach to a complaint. It states that the Board will attempt to facilitate a settlement between the parties. If this fails or a settlement isn't reached within a reasonable timeframe, the Board will proceed to hear and determine the complaint.

### Section 134(6) of the Canada Labour Code
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This section clarifies the evidentiary weight of a complaint made under section 133 in respect of rights under sections 128 or 129. It states that the complaint itself is evidence of the contravention, and the party denying the contravention has the burden of proving it didn't happen.
