individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Board reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Board Rejection of a Complaint

### Section 246.3: General Grounds for Rejection

Section 246.3 outlines several specific circumstances under which the Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1).
"The Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee, (iv) there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator, or (vi) in respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process..."

This passage details a broad range of reasons for rejection. It includes situations where the complaint falls outside the Board's authority, is deemed baseless, has already been resolved through other means, or is covered by a collective agreement with a dispute resolution process. The Board's satisfaction with any of these grounds is sufficient for rejection.

### Section 246.3(b): Failure to Take Board Measures

Section 246.3(b) provides a more specific ground for rejection, relating to the Board's suspension of consideration of a complaint.
"(b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 246.2(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 246.2(2) were not taken within the specified time period."

This indicates that if the Board suspends a complaint due to measures the employee is required to take, and those measures are not completed within the given timeframe, the Board may reject the complaint. This highlights the Board's role in managing the progress of a complaint and its willingness to dismiss it if the employee fails to comply with its directives.

### Section 246.1(3): Prior Withdrawal of Substantially Same Complaint

Section 246.1(3) also lists grounds for rejection, including a prior withdrawal of a substantially similar complaint.
"A complaint referred to in subsection (1) shall be made to the Board not later than 90 days after the day on which the employee knew or, in the Board’s opinion, ought to have known of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

While this section primarily addresses the timing of a complaint, it indirectly supports rejection. If a complaint based on substantially the same facts was previously withdrawn, the Board may reject the new complaint as well, particularly if the withdrawal was due to it being incomplete or containing an error.

### Section 246.2(2): Failure to Take Board Measures

Section 246.2(2) details the Board's obligation to notify an employee of suspended consideration and specify the measures they must take and the timeframe for doing so.
"(2) If the Board suspends a complaint, the Board shall notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

This section reinforces the Board's process for handling suspended complaints. If the employee fails to meet the Board's requirements within the specified timeframe, the Board may reject the complaint.

### Section 246.3(b): Failure to Take Board Measures (Repeated)

Section 246.3(b) is a repetition of the ground for rejection related to the failure to take Board measures within the specified timeframe, further emphasizing its importance.

## Board Actions Upon Justified Reprisal Complaint

### Section 246.4: Board Orders for Justified Reprisal Complaint

Section 246.4 outlines the specific actions the Board can order an employer to take if it determines a complaint of reprisal is justified. It states:
"If the Board determines that a complaint under subsection 246.1(1) is justified, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal and, if applicable, to (a) permit the employee who has made the complaint to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate the employee; (c) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the reprisal, have been paid by the employer to the employee; (d) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer; and (e) do any other thing that the Board considers equitable for the employer to do to remedy or counteract any consequence of the reprisal."

This section details a comprehensive set of remedies the Board can impose. These include restoring the employee to their former position, reinstating them to their job, providing financial compensation for lost wages and penalties, and ordering the employer to take any other action deemed fair to address the harm caused by the reprisal. The use of quotation marks directly reflects the Board's potential to order the employer to "cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal" and to provide compensation
"...not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the reprisal, have been paid by the employer to the employee..."

### Section 246.5: Finality of Board Decisions

Section 246.5 addresses the status of the Board's decisions, declaring them
"...final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." It further elaborates on this finality by stating:
"Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court. Marginal note: No review by certiorari , etc. (2) No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Division."

This quotation emphasizes the lack of avenues for judicial review of the Board's determinations regarding reprisal complaints. The Board's orders are binding and cannot be challenged in the courts. This finality is crucial for ensuring that the Board's interventions are effective in deterring reprisal and providing redress to affected employees.

individual_results.question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Board Orders in the Federal Court

### Finality of Board Orders

Section 156(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of Board orders and decisions. It states,
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This provision is fundamental to understanding how Board orders can be enforced in the Federal Court. It means that once a Board order is issued, it is not subject to appeal or judicial review in any other court.

### Filing in the Federal Court

Section 23(1) outlines the process for enforcing Board orders in the Federal Court. It specifies that
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court..." This filing must occur within 14 days from the day the order is made or the day compliance is provided for, whichever is later.

### Registration of the Order

Section 23(2) details what happens after the Board files the order in the Federal Court. It states,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This registration is crucial because it transforms the Board order into a judgment of the Federal Court.

### Enforcement Proceedings

Section 244(1) further clarifies the enforcement process. It says,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This indicates that any party impacted by a Board order can initiate enforcement proceedings in the Federal Court by filing a copy of the order.

### No Review by Certiorari

Section 22(2) reinforces the finality of Board orders by explicitly stating,
"Except as permitted by subsection (1), no order, decision or proceeding of the Board made or carried on under or purporting to be made or carried on under this Part shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground, including the ground that the order, decision or proceeding is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board to make or carry on or that, in the course of any proceeding, the Board for any reason exceeded or lost its jurisdiction." This passage is particularly relevant as it directly addresses the question by asserting that Board orders are not subject to review by certiorari or any other form of judicial review in the Federal Court.

individual_results.question: What are the requirements for an employer to pay wages to an employee according to the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Wage Payment Requirements Under the Canada Labour Code

### Regular Payday and Vacation Pay

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific requirements for employers regarding the payment of wages and vacation pay.
"Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work." This passage directly addresses the employer's obligation to pay wages on a consistent schedule and to provide vacation pay when it is due. It also specifies a 30-day timeframe for vacation pay upon termination of employment.

### Pay Basis and Minimum Wage

The Code addresses situations where employees are not paid on an hourly basis.
"If your employer does not pay you on an hourly basis, you must receive at least the equivalent of the minimum wage. Where the basis of your pay is not time (for example, you may be paid an  annual salary or in accordance with a mileage rate), the Minister of Labour may  fix a rate that is equivalent to at least the minimum wage. This rate is  determined by dividing the amount of salary you received (excluding any  vacation pay, general holiday pay, and overtime pay) by the number of hours  worked you performed." This indicates that even employees with annual salaries or mileage-based pay are entitled to at least the minimum wage equivalent. The Minister of Labour has the authority to calculate this equivalent rate.

### Reporting to Work at the Call of the Employer

The Code also specifies that employees who report to work at the employer's call must receive wages for at least 3 hours at their regular rate.
"If you report to work at the call of your employer, you must receive wages for at least 3 hours at your regular rate of wages. This applies whether or not your employer asks you to do any work after reporting to work." This provision ensures that employees who are called in for work are compensated for their time, even if they are not assigned any tasks.

### Exemptions for Apprentices and Employees Receiving Room and/or Board

The Code includes exemptions to the minimum wage for apprentices and employees receiving room and/or board.
"If you are registered under and paid according to a provincial apprenticeship act, your employer is exempt from the application of the minimum wage. If your employer provides you with room and/or board, and you accept that arrangement, your employer may reduce your wages below minimum wage. Your employer cannot reduce your wages more than:  50 cents, for each meal, and 60 cents, per day, for living quarters..." This clarifies that apprentices are not subject to the minimum wage, and employees receiving room and/or board can have their wages reduced by a maximum amount for meals and living quarters.

### Getting Paid for Work

The Code reiterates the employer's obligation to pay wages on the regular payday and to provide vacation pay when it is due.
"Your employer must pay your wages on the regular payday established. Any vacation pay you are owed must be paid at the time you take your vacation. If your employment ends and you are owed vacation pay, your employer must pay it within 30 days after your last day of work." This passage reinforces the importance of timely wage and vacation pay.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which an employee who is a member of the reserve force is entitled to a leave of absence from their employment?
individual_results.answer:
## Entitlement to Reserve Force Leave of Absence

### Section 247.5: General Entitlement

Section 247.5 outlines the general circumstances under which a reserve force member is entitled to a leave of absence. It states:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

This section clearly establishes that eligibility for reserve force leave hinges on having completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, or a shorter period specified for their employee class. Once this threshold is met, the employee is entitled to leave for a wide range of reserve force activities, including deployments, military skills training, and duties called upon under various National Defence Acts.

### Section 247.5(1.1): Maximum Leave Duration

Section 247.5(1.1) places a limit on the total duration of leave taken under certain categories. It specifies:
"Leaves taken by an employee under paragraphs (1)(a) to (d) can total no more than an aggregate of 24 months in any 60-month period."

This means that an employee cannot take a combined total of 24 months of leave for deployments, military skills training, training ordered under the National Defence Act, or duties called upon under section 275 of the National Defence Act within any 60-month period of continuous employment. This provision aims to balance the reserve force obligations of employees with their civilian careers.

### Section 247.5(4): Adverse Effect on Public Health or Employer Hardship

Section 247.5(4) provides an exception to the 24-month aggregate leave limit. It states:
"...an employee is not entitled to a leave of absence under this Division if, in the opinion of the Head, it would adversely affect public health or safety or would cause undue hardship to the employer if the employee, as an individual or as a member of a class of employees, were to take leave."

This exception allows the Head to deny leave if it would have a negative impact on public health or safety or create an unreasonable burden for the employer. This ensures that the reserve force leave provisions are not used in a way that is detrimental to the broader interests of society or the workplace.

### Section 247.95: Prohibition Against Discrimination

Section 247.95 prohibits employers from discriminating against reserve force members. It states:
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them."

This provision ensures that reserve force members are treated fairly by their employers and are not penalized for their service. It also prevents employers from considering reserve force commitments in decisions related to promotions or training.

### Section 247.96: Prohibition Against Refusal of Employment

Section 247.96 further reinforces the prohibition against discrimination by stating:
"No person may refuse to employ a person because they are a member of the reserve force."

This provision prevents employers from refusing to hire individuals because they are reserve force members. It ensures that reserve force members have the same opportunities for employment as anyone else.

### Section 247.97: Regulations

Section 247.97 grants the Governor in Council the power to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Division. This includes the ability to specify absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment, define "military skills training," and set out the terms and conditions for the application of certain paragraphs. This flexibility allows the regulations to adapt to the evolving needs of the reserve force and the workplace.

individual_results.question: What are the notice and communication requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Notice and Communication Requirements for Leave of Absence under Division XV.2

### Section 247.6: Notice to Employer

Section 247.6 outlines the mandatory notice requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence under this Division.
"An employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks’ notice to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer of the length of the leave."
This passage clearly states that an employee must provide at least four weeks' written notice to their employer before the leave commences. This notice must also include the intended duration of the leave.

### Section 207: General Notice Requirements for Leave

Section 207 provides a more general overview of notice requirements for leaves of absence under other Divisions of the Canada Labour Code, which are relevant as they may apply to this Division as well.
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."
This section reiterates the four-week written notice requirement, emphasizing that a valid reason must be provided for not meeting this deadline. It also specifies that the notice must include the intended length of the leave.

### Section 207.3: Notice of Change in Length of Leave

Section 207.3 addresses the specific requirement to notify the employer of any changes to the length of the leave.
"Every employee who is on a leave of absence from employment under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9 shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with a notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave that they intend to take."
This passage highlights the need to promptly inform the employer of any adjustments to the leave duration. It also specifies that this notice must be in writing.

### Section 207.01: Minimum Periods of Leave

Section 207.01 clarifies that a leave of absence under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 may only be taken in one or more periods of not less than one week’s duration. While not a direct notice requirement, this provision influences the timing of the initial four-week notice, as the leave must be in at least one week-long period.

### Section 207.4: Documentation

Section 207.4 mentions that the employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave and of any changes to the leave length. This is a follow-up to the initial notice, providing further context.
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

### Section 247.6: Valid Reason for Notice Delay

Section 247.6 also addresses the scenario where a valid reason exists for not providing the four-week notice.
"If there is a valid reason for not providing notice in accordance with paragraph (1)(a), the employee shall notify the employer as soon as practicable that the employee is taking a leave of absence."
This passage indicates that if a valid reason prevents the employee from giving the four-week notice, they must still inform the employer as soon as possible.

### Section 247.6: In Writing

Section 247.6 reinforces the requirement for all notice and other information provided to the employer to be in writing.
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, any notice or other information to be provided by the employee to the employer under this section is to be in writing."

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who takes a leave of absence for military purposes in terms of providing documentation to their employer and notifying them of their return to work?
individual_results.answer:
## Employee Responsibilities Regarding Military Leave Documentation and Return to Work Notification

### Written Notice and Documentation Required
"To take this leave, you must provide a 4 weeks’ written notice to your employer indicating:  the length of the leave, unless you gave a valid reason not to do so, and your intention to extend or shorten the leave, unless you have a valid reason not to do so  Your employer can request within 3 weeks after the start date of the leave, proof that you qualify for this leave. In this case, you must provide documentation approved by the Chief of the Defence Staff or their Commander, unless there is a valid reason not to do so. If you did not specify the length of the leave before it started and you give the employer less than 4 weeks’ notice of the end date, your employer may delay your return to work by up to 4 weeks after receiving notice. Any waiting period before returning to work is considered as part of the leave."

This section outlines the initial notification requirements for an employee taking military leave. The employee must provide a written notice of at least four weeks in advance, specifying the intended duration and any potential extensions or shortenings. The employer then has the right to request documentation confirming the leave's eligibility within three weeks of the start date. This documentation must be either prescribed by the Chief of the Defence Staff or their Commander or approved by them. The employee is obligated to provide this documentation within three weeks of the leave's commencement, unless a valid reason exists.

### Return to Work Notification
"Upon your return to work, your employer must reinstate you in your former position or give you a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits. If you are no longer able to perform the function of the original position, or those of a comparable position, your employer may assign you to a different position with different terms and conditions of employment.  If, during a leave period, your employer reduces the wages and benefits of a group of employees as part of a reorganization plan and if you are reinstated in that group you will receive no more than the wages and benefits that you would have received if you had been at work during the reorganization. If your employer increases the wages and benefits for your group during the leave, you would be entitled to the increases upon your return to work. Your employer must inform you of any change to wages and benefits resulting from a reorganization by sending you a notice to your last known address. If you encounter difficulties upon returning to your civilian position, it is suggested that you discuss the situation with your employer and include the information in this web page. If problems persist, contact a regional Labour Program Officer, who will be able to answer any questions and give advice to both parties on the requirements of this legislation.  If a collective agreement is in place but is silent on the leave of absence for members of the reserve force, your employer must still grant you the leave, because the collective agreement must include provisions that are at least equal to those of the Code."

This section details the employer's responsibilities upon the employee's return to work. The employer is legally obligated to reinstate the employee to their former position or a comparable one with the same wages and benefits. If the original position is no longer feasible, a different position with equivalent terms and conditions may be offered. The employee is entitled to any wage or benefit increases that occurred during the leave period. The employer must notify the employee of any changes to wages and benefits resulting from a reorganization. If the employee faces difficulties reintegrating into their civilian position, they are advised to discuss it with their employer and document the issues. Further assistance can be obtained from a regional Labour Program Officer. Importantly, the employee is still entitled to the leave even if a collective agreement is silent on the matter, as the agreement must at least meet the standards of the Canada Labour Code.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employee's employment status and position when they return to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division?
individual_results.answer:
## Employment Status and Position Upon Return from Reserve Force Leave

### Continuous Employment and Benefits

Section 247.91 addresses the continuity of employment and benefits for employees returning from reserve force leave. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave." This means that the employee's time spent on leave is counted as part of their overall continuous employment with the employer. This is significant because it impacts the calculation of benefits such as seniority, vacation time, and pension.

Section 247.91 further elaborates on this continuity by saying,
"The seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall accumulate during the leave." This ensures that the employee's seniority is not lost while they are on leave and is added to their seniority upon their return. This can be beneficial for future promotions or benefits eligibility.

### Resumption of Employment in Same Position

Section 247.93 outlines the employer's obligation to reinstate the employee to their previous position upon their return. It specifies,
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins." This is a fundamental right for employees returning from reserve force leave.

Section 247.93(2) provides an exception to this rule, stating,
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location." This ensures that even if the original position is no longer available, the employee is placed in a position that is equivalent in terms of pay, benefits, and location.

### Not Able to Perform Work

Section 247.94 addresses situations where the employee is no longer able to perform the functions of their previous position or a comparable one. It states,
"Subject to the regulations, if an employee is not able to perform the functions of the position that they occupy before the leave begins — or those of a comparable position, with the same wages and benefits and in the same location — the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment." This allows the employer to accommodate the employee's changed abilities by assigning them to a different role. However, it also ensures that the new position is comparable in terms of pay, benefits, and location.

### Prohibition Against Discrimination

Section 247.96 reinforces the protection against discrimination based on reserve force membership or leave. It states,
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them." This ensures that employees returning from reserve force leave are not penalized for their service.

Section 247.96(2) extends this protection to prospective employees, stating,
"No person may refuse to employ a person because they are a member of the reserve force." This prevents employers from discriminating against reserve force members during the hiring process.

individual_results.question: What protections are provided to employees who are members of the reserve force and take a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Protections for Reserve Force Members Taking Leave of Absence

### Entitlement to Leave

Section 247.5(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the entitlement to leave for reserve force members. It states:
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."
This provision establishes a clear right to leave for reserve force members who meet the minimum continuous employment requirement. The leave can be for a wide range of activities, including deployments, training, and recovery from service-related injuries.

### Resumption of Employment

Section 247.92 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the resumption of employment after a leave of absence. It states:
"Section 189 applies for the purposes of this Division."
Section 189 of the Canada Labour Code guarantees an employee the right to be reinstated to their former position or a comparable one with the same wages and benefits upon their return from a leave of absence. This is further elaborated upon in Section 247.93(1):
"At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins."
Section 247.93(2) provides an exception to this rule:
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location."
These sections collectively ensure that reserve force members are protected upon their return to work, with a strong presumption of reinstatement to their previous role.

### Wages and Benefits

Section 247.95(1) protects employees from wage or benefit reductions that occur during their leave of absence as part of a reorganization plan. It states:
"If, during a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the wages or benefits of the group of employees of which an employee is a member are changed as part of a plan to reorganize the industrial establishment in which that group is employed, the employee is entitled, on reinstatement under this section, to receive the wages and benefits in respect of that employment that that employee would have been entitled to receive had that employee been working when the reorganization took place."
This provision ensures that reserve force members do not suffer financial setbacks during their leave due to company restructuring. Section 247.95(2) mandates that employers provide this notice to employees as soon as is practicable.

### Prohibition Against Discrimination

Section 247.96(1) prohibits employers from taking into account an employee's reserve force membership or intention to take leave in decisions related to promotion or training. It states:
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them."
Section 247.96(2) further reinforces this protection by prohibiting employers from refusing to hire someone because they are a reserve force member. These prohibitions create a level playing field for reserve force members in terms of career advancement and employment opportunities.

### Additional Protections

Section 247.97 grants the Governor in Council the power to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Division. This allows for the creation of specific protections tailored to the unique needs of reserve force members, such as specifying what constitutes an operation for the purposes of leave entitlement or defining "military skills training."

individual_results.answer:
## Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code: Purpose of Regulations

### Overview

Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad authority to make regulations for carrying out the purposes of Division XV.2, which pertains to Leave of Absence for Members of the Reserve Force. The purpose of these regulations is to provide detailed rules and clarifications on the eligibility, duration, and conditions of such leave.

### Specific Areas Covered by the Regulations

The regulations under section 247.97 cover a wide range of aspects related to Reserve Force leave, as detailed in the numbered paragraphs.

#### Defining Continuity of Employment
"...specifying the absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment for the purpose of subsection 247.5(1)..." This regulation aims to clarify which absences, even those related to Reserve Force duties, will not negatively impact an employee's seniority or benefits upon their return to regular employment.

#### Defining Operations and Activities
"...specifying what constitutes or does not constitute an operation for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(a)..." and
"...setting out the activities for the purposes of paragraph 247.5(1)(b)..." These regulations provide precise definitions of what constitutes Reserve Force operations and activities, which are relevant to determining eligibility for leave.

#### Military Skills Training

individual_results.question: What protections does the Canada Labour Code provide to employees regarding genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results?
individual_results.answer:
## Canada Labour Code Protections for Genetic Testing and Disclosure

### General Entitlement Against Genetic Testing and Disclosure

The Canada Labour Code establishes fundamental protections for employees concerning genetic testing. Section 247.98(2) explicitly states,
"Every employee is entitled not to undergo or be required to undergo a genetic test." This right is further reinforced by Section 247.98(3), which grants employees the entitlement
"...not to disclose or be required to disclose the results of a genetic test." These provisions are foundational, ensuring employees have autonomy over their genetic information.

### Prohibition on Discriminatory Actions Based on Genetic Test Results

The Code strongly prohibits employers from engaging in discriminatory actions based on genetic test results. Section 247.98(4) details these prohibited actions:
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Division, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee (a) because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee." This comprehensive prohibition covers a wide range of adverse employment actions, directly addressing the potential for genetic testing to be used as a basis for unfair treatment.

### Restrictions on Third-Party Disclosure of Genetic Test Results

The Code places strict limitations on the disclosure of genetic test results by third parties. Section 247.98(5) declares,
"No person shall disclose to an employer that an employee has undergone a genetic test, or disclose to an employer the results of a genetic test, without the written consent of the employee." This provision safeguards employees from having their genetic information shared with their employer without their explicit permission.

### Consent Requirements for Genetic Test Collection and Use

Section 247.98(6) mandates that employers must obtain the written consent of the employee before collecting or using the results of a genetic test. This consent requirement is paramount to protecting employee privacy and control over their genetic data. It ensures that genetic information is not used against the employee without their knowledge or agreement.

### Time Limits for Filing Genetic Testing Complaints

The Labour Code specifies time limits for filing genetic testing complaints. Section 247.99(1) states,
"An employee who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 247.98(4) may make a complaint in writing to the Head." Section 12_2 further elaborates on this, stating,
"**Complaints related to genetic testing** If your complaint is related to the following prohibited actions, you must file your complaint no later than 90 days after the date on which you knew of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint:  on the basis of a genetic test result because you refused to take a genetic test, or  because you refused to disclose the results of a genetic test..." This 90-day limit applies to complaints alleging discriminatory actions based on genetic test results. For complaints related to third-party disclosure of genetic test results, the time limit is 6 months from the date on which the subject matter of the complaint arose.

### Extension of Time to File a Genetic Testing Complaint

Section 247.99(2) provides a mechanism for extending the time to file a genetic testing complaint under certain circumstances. It states,
"You may be eligible for an extension of time to file a complaint if you filed a complaint:   with another government official under the wrong complaint category, or  that was incomplete or contained an error..." This extension is available if the initial complaint was made with the incorrect category or was deficient in some way.

### Reprisal Complaints

Section 247.98(7) addresses reprisals against employees for exercising their genetic testing rights. It states,
"...take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee (a) because the employee refused a request by the employer to undergo a genetic test; (b) because the employee refused to disclose the results of a genetic test; or (c) on the basis of the results of a genetic test undergone by the employee." This provision protects employees from retaliation for refusing genetic testing or disclosing their results.

individual_results.answer:
## Steps an Employee Can Take if They Believe Their Employer Has Taken Action Against Them in Contravention of Subsection 247.98(4)

### Filing a Complaint with the Board

An employee who believes their employer has taken action against them in contravention of subsection 247.98(4) can file a complaint in writing to the Board.
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96; (a.1) [Repealed, 2021, c. 26, s. 25] (b) dismissing, suspending, laying off, or demoting the employee, imposing a financial or other penalty on the employee, or otherwise taking any disciplinary action against the employee, because the employee (i) has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part; (c) taking into account the fact that the employee has taken any of the actions referred to in subparagraphs (b)(i) to (iv) in any decision with respect to the promotion or training of the employee; or (d) threatening to take any of the reprisals referred to in paragraph (b) or (c)."

This passage explicitly states that a complaint can be made if the employer has taken action
"...has made a complaint under this Part, other than a complaint under section 240, (ii) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee to the Head or provided any other assistance to the Minister or the Head in the exercise or performance of the Minister’s or the Head’s powers, duties and functions under this Part (ii.1) has provided information regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of any employee or provided any other assistance to an external adjudicator or a member of the Board in the exercise or performance, in accordance with subsections 12.001(2) or 14(5), of the powers, duties or functions conferred on the Board by this Part, (iii) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part, or (iv) has exercised, or sought to exercise, any right conferred on the employee by this Part..." These actions constitute reprisals prohibited by subsection 247.98(4).

### The Role of the Head

The Head plays a role in handling the complaint by examining beyond the initial allegations.
"The Head should examine beyond the initial allegations of a complaint and assess the underlying subject-matter."

This indicates that the Head will investigate the substance of the complaint to determine if it falls under the purview of subsection 247.98(4).

### The Role of the Board

The Board's role is multifaceted. It receives the complaint, considers the evidence, and can make orders.
"...any order under that section, including a reinstatement order."

This passage highlights the Board's power to issue remedies, such as reinstating the employee. Furthermore, the Board can consider whether the employer's action was in contravention of subsection 247.98(4).
"...if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the reprisal was not taken, the burden of proof is on that party."

This passage indicates that the Board will assess the evidence presented by both sides to determine if the employer's action was a reprisal. The Board will place the onus on the party alleging the reprisal to prove it.

### Additional Steps

An employee can also seek legal advice and representation to assist them in filing the complaint and navigating the Board's process. They can also report the employer's actions to other relevant authorities, such as the Human Rights Tribunal.

individual_results.question: What is the effect of an order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code, and how does it interact with the court system?
individual_results.answer:
## Effect of an Order Made by the Board under Section 247.99

### Finality of the Order

Section 247.991(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the finality of an order made by the Board under this section. It states,
"Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This means that once an order is issued, it cannot be challenged in the judicial system. 

This finality is further reinforced in Section 247.991(2), which prohibits any court action to question, review, prohibit, or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 247.99.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 247.99." This comprehensive prohibition ensures that the Board's orders are not subject to judicial interference.

### Interaction with the Court System

Section 247.991(3) and (4) detail the process for enforcing an order made by the Board under this section within the Federal Court.
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 247.99(8), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file a copy of the order in the Federal Court, exclusive of reasons." This indicates that an order can be registered in the Federal Court, giving it the "same force and effect" as a judgment obtained in that Court. 

Section 247.991(4) elaborates on this, stating,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (3), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This means that the order can be enforced through the standard court processes, such as garnishment or seizure of assets.

Section 247.991(5) clarifies that the making of a complaint under subsection 247.99(1) does not suspend or affect an employee’s civil remedies against their employer.
"The making of a complaint under subsection 247.99(1) does not suspend or affect an employee’s civil remedies against their employer." This ensures that an employee's ability to pursue other legal avenues against their employer is not hindered by the Board's order.

### Enforcement of Orders

Section 246.6(1) and (2) further address the enforcement of Board orders.
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under section 246.4, or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This mirrors the process outlined in Section 247.991(3) and (4), allowing for the registration and enforcement of Board orders in the Federal Court.

Section 246.6(2) emphasizes the legal standing of a registered Board order:
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This reinforces the ability to use the court system to compel compliance with the Board's orders.

### Section 244 and 244(1)

Section 244(1) and (2) of the Canada Labour Code also discuss the enforcement of Board orders. They state,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This is identical to the enforcement provisions found in Section 246.6(1) and (2) and Section 247.991(3) and (4), confirming the same court-based enforcement mechanism.

Section 244(2) further clarifies the legal effect of a registered Board order:
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This reiterates the ability to use the court system to enforce the Board's orders.

### Section 247.992

Section 247.992 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations. These regulations can cover a wide range of aspects related to the Board's orders, including
"...prescribing circumstances for the purposes of paragraph 247.99(3)(b); (b) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 247.99(6); (c) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1); and (d) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 247.99(6.1)." This regulatory power allows for the detailed operationalization of the Board's orders and the enforcement mechanisms outlined in other sections of the Code.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Minister take to investigate employment in industrial establishments, and who can be appointed to carry out this investigation?
individual_results.answer:
## Minister's Actions to Investigate Employment in Industrial Establishments

### Section 12.07: Measures the Minister Can Take

Section 12.07 outlines the various actions the Minister can undertake upon receiving a request for an inquiry.
"On receipt of the request, the Minister may take one or more of the following measures: (a) obtain, in an informal and expeditious manner, any information that the Minister considers necessary; (b) refer the matter for mediation, where the Minister is satisfied that the issues in relation to the request may be appropriately resolved by mediation; (c) request the Governor in Council to have an inquiry held under section 12.08; or (d) advise the Chairperson that the Minister considers that it is not necessary to take further measures under this section."
This indicates that the Minister has a range of options, from gathering preliminary information to formally requesting an inquiry from the Governor in Council or suggesting mediation.

### Section 12.08: Appointment of Inquirer

Section 12.08 details who can be appointed to conduct the inquiry when the Minister requests it.
"On receipt of a request referred to in paragraph 12.07(c), the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, appoint a judge of a superior court to conduct the inquiry."
This passage explicitly states that the Governor in Council, acting on the Minister of Justice's recommendation, can appoint a judge of a superior court to lead the inquiry.

### Section 248: General Authority for Inquiries

Section 248 provides a broader statement of the Minister's authority to investigate employment.
"The Minister may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."
This section confirms the Minister's power to initiate inquiries into employment conditions in any industrial establishment and to appoint individuals to carry them out.

### Section 12.09: Powers of the Inquirer

Section 12.09 describes the extensive powers vested in the judge appointed to conduct the inquiry.
"The judge has all the powers, rights and privileges that are vested in a superior court, including the power (a) to issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry; and (b) to administer oaths and examine any person on oath."
This passage highlights the judge's ability to compel testimony and evidence, ensuring a thorough investigation.

### Section 12.10: Staffing the Inquiry

Section 12.10 explains that the judge can assemble a support team.
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses."
This allows the judge to bring in experts to assist with the complex aspects of the inquiry.

### Section 138: Special Committees

Section 138 outlines the Minister's ability to appoint special committees to assist or advise on occupational health and safety matters.
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies."
This provides a mechanism for the Minister to leverage external expertise and perspectives on specific issues.

### Section 248: Appointment of Inquirer (Repeated)

Section 248 reiterates the Minister's authority to cause an inquiry to be made and to appoint one or more persons to hold it.
"The Minister may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."
This reinforces the Minister's central role in initiating and staffing employment investigations.

individual_results.question: What powers does the Head have to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code, and who can assist or be delegated these powers?
individual_results.answer:
## Head's Powers to Gather Information and Conduct Inspections

### Section 249: Delegation of Powers

Section 249 outlines the Head's broad power to delegate their own powers. It states,
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part." This indicates that the Head can empower others to carry out their information-gathering and inspection responsibilities.

Furthermore, Section 249(1.1) details the Head's obligation to provide a certificate of authority to any person to whom powers, duties, or functions are delegated.
"The Head shall furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated under subsection (1) a certificate of authority and, when entering any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business the person, shall, when requested, show the certificate to the person in charge of that place." This certificate serves as proof of the Head's authorization for the delegated individual to conduct inspections and gather information.

### Section 248: Inquiries

Section 248 grants the Head the power to
"...cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment..." and to
"...appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry." This power is specifically for gathering information, as inquiries are a formal process of investigation.

Section 248(2) elaborates on the Head's authority within an inquiry:
"A person appointed pursuant to subsection (1) has all of the powers of a person appointed as a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act..." This means that the Head can appoint individuals with extensive powers to compel testimony, examine documents, and conduct investigations.

### Section 250: Administering Oaths

Section 250 specifies that the Head can
"...administer all oaths and take and receive all affidavits and statutory declarations required with respect to the Head’s powers set out in subsection 249(2) and certify to the administration, taking or receiving of them." This power is crucial for ensuring the reliability and legal standing of the information gathered during inspections and inquiries.

### Section 249(2): Specific Powers During Inspections

Section 249(2) lists a comprehensive set of powers the Head can exercise during an inspection. These powers directly relate to information gathering:
"(a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee; (b) take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a); (c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment; (c.1) require any employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan that must be insured in accordance with subsection 239.2(1) to furnish proof that the plan is insured in accordance with that subsection; (d) require an employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment; and (e) require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made."

These powers allow the Head to delve into a wide range of employment-related information, from financial records to employee statements.

### Section 249(3): Assistance During Inspections

Section 249(3) clarifies who can assist the Head during an inspection:
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations." This obligation to provide "reasonable assistance" ensures that the Head has the support needed to conduct thorough inspections.

Section 249(4) further specifies that
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary." This allows the Head to bring in experts or other personnel to aid in the inspection process.

### Section 249(5): Evidence Precluded - Head

Section 249(5) protects the Head from being required to testify in civil suits or proceedings regarding information obtained during inspections.
"The Head shall not be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions." This ensures that the Head can conduct inspections without fear of being compelled to disclose confidential information.

### Section 249(6): Evidence Precluded - Other Persons

Section 249(6) extends this protection to others who assist the Head.
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), and no person who has accompanied or assisted such a person or the Head in carrying out their duties and functions, shall be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions or in accompanying or assisting the person, except with the written permission of the Head." This encourages cooperation with inspections by shielding those who assist from potential testimony.

### Section 249(7): Not Liable

Section 249(7) provides immunity from personal liability for actions taken in good faith under the Head's authority.
"Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part." This encourages the Head and their delegated agents to act decisively during inspections without fear of personal repercussions.

individual_results.question: What happens if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this impact potential prosecution?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Failure to Pay Wages: Consequences and Prosecution

### Section 289: Payment Responsibility
"If a person or a department pays the penalty set out in a notice of violation, the person or the department is considered to have committed the violation and proceedings in respect of it are ended."

This section outlines the immediate consequence of an employer failing to pay a penalty imposed under the Canada Labour Code. It states that if the employer complies with the penalty, the violation is considered resolved, and further legal action ceases. This highlights the importance of timely payment as a way to avoid more severe repercussions.

### Section 290: Failure to Act
"A person or a department that neither pays a penalty imposed under this Part nor requests a review or an appeal in the specified time is considered to have committed the violation and is liable for the penalty."

This section elaborates on the failure to act, clarifying that it is also treated as a violation. It emphasizes that the employer's inaction – neither paying the penalty nor seeking a review – results in them being held liable for the full amount. This underscores the proactive nature of addressing a violation; simply waiting for enforcement action will not mitigate the financial burden.

### Section 274: Liability of Parties to Violation
"If a corporation or a department commits a violation, any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."

This section broadens the liability beyond the corporation or department itself. It identifies individuals within the organization who can be held personally liable for the violation, even if they did not directly commit the act. These individuals include officers, directors, agents, mandataries, senior officials, and anyone with managerial or supervisory responsibilities. The penalty for these individuals is the same as that for the corporation or department.

### Section 14: Director's Liability
"Sometimes, wage recovery from an employer is unlikely or impossible. In this case, the Labour Program may hold the corporation’s directors liable for amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director. Corporate directors are jointly and individually liable for employees’ wages and other amounts to which employees are entitled, up to a limit equivalent to 6 months’ wages."

This section specifically addresses the situation where wage recovery from the employer is improbable. It states that the Labour Program can hold the corporation's directors jointly and individually liable for the unpaid wages, up to a limit of six months' wages. This is a significant consequence for directors, as it can result in substantial personal financial responsibility for the employer's failure to pay.

### Section 15: Prosecution
"...if you are fully aware of your legal obligations and still willfully break the law. Repeat contraventions indicate an intentional or willful action. If found guilty, you may be subject to the following fines:         a corporation may be liable to a fine of up to:             $50,000 for the first offence $100,000 for the second offence, and $250,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences   an employer who is not incorporated may be liable to a fine of up to:             $10,000 for the first offence $20,000 for the second offence, and $50,000 for the third (and subsequent) offences     public naming of employers: The Labour Program will publish information about employers who violate the Code, including:         all payment orders of $5000 or greater filed in federal court administrative monetary penalties (some exceptions apply for category “A” violations), and  prosecutions..."

This section details the potential for criminal prosecution. It outlines the circumstances under which the Labour Program may choose to prosecute, including repeated violations or willful disregard for the Code. It also specifies the fines that can be imposed on corporations and unincorporated employers upon a guilty verdict. Furthermore, it mentions the public naming of employers who violate the Code, which can have a significant reputational impact. The inclusion of "prosecutions" as a point for public naming indicates that prosecution is a serious enforcement tool.

individual_results.question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records, and what information must be included in the report?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Head to Order an Internal Audit

### Section 251.001(1) - General Authority for Internal Audits
"Subject to the regulations, the Head may, in writing, for the purpose of verifying compliance or preventing non-compliance with this Part, order an employer to, in accordance with the order, (a) conduct an internal audit of its practices and books, payrolls and other records to determine whether the employer is in compliance with any provision of this Part or the regulations; and (b) provide a report of the results of the audit to the Head."

This section establishes the Head's broad power to issue internal audit orders. The order must be in writing and be for the specific purpose of either verifying compliance with the Canada Labour Code or preventing future non-compliance. The order will mandate the employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices, books, payrolls, and other records. Crucially, the order will also specify that the employer must submit a report detailing the audit's findings to the Head. The phrase "in accordance with the order" indicates that the audit's scope and content will be defined by the Head's specific instructions.

### Section 251.001(2) - Information to be Included in the Report
"The Head shall, in the internal audit order, specify (a) any industrial establishment and class of employees to which it applies; (b) the period of time to be covered by the internal audit; (c) the provisions of this Part or the regulations with respect to which the internal audit was ordered; (d) the date by which the employer is to provide the report; and (e) the form of the report."

This subsection details the mandatory information that the Head must include in the internal audit order. It must clearly define the scope of the audit, including the specific industrial establishment and employee class it covers, the time period to be audited, the particular provisions of the Code or regulations being examined, the deadline for report submission, and the required format for the report. This ensures that the audit is focused and addresses the Head's concerns effectively.

### Section 251.001(3) - Additional Information the Head May Specify
"The Head may also specify in the order that the report is to contain any information that the Head considers appropriate."

This subsection provides the Head with flexibility to request additional information beyond what is explicitly listed in subsection (2). The Head can instruct the employer to include any other data or analysis that it deems relevant to assessing compliance. This allows the Head to tailor the audit to its specific needs and gather a comprehensive understanding of the employer's practices.

### Section 251.001(6) - Non-Compliance Findings
"If the employer determines that it had not complied with any provision referred to in the order, the employer shall set out in the report the nature of the employer’s non-compliance and the steps that have been or will be taken by the employer to comply with the provision."

This subsection outlines the employer's obligation when the internal audit reveals a failure to comply with a provision of the Code or regulations. The employer must detail the specific nature of the non-compliance and the corrective actions it has already taken or plans to implement to achieve compliance. This transparency allows the Head to assess the employer's commitment to rectifying the issues identified in the audit.

### Section 251.001(7) - Wages and Other Amounts Owed
"If the employer determines that any wages or other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part are owed, the employer shall also state in the report the name of the employee, the amount owed for the period of time covered by the internal audit, the method used to determine the amount owed and any payment subsequently made to the employee with respect to that amount owed."

This subsection addresses the employer's responsibility to report any outstanding wages or other amounts owed to employees. The employer must provide detailed information about the employee, the amount owed, the calculation method, and any payments made to date. This ensures that the Head is aware of any wage arrears and can take appropriate action to ensure employees receive their rightful compensation.
