individual_results.question: What is the process and timeframe for employees to make complaints about potential contraventions of the Canada Labour Code by their employer?
individual_results.answer:
## Process and Timeframe for Employees to Make Complaints

### Section 251.01: Making of Complaint

#### Timeframe for Making a Complaint
"A complaint under subsection (1) shall be made within the following period (a) in the case of a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, six months from the last day on which the employer was required to pay those wages or other amounts under this Part; and (b) in the case of any other complaint, six months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose."

This section clearly outlines the time limit for employees to file a complaint. It specifies that for complaints related to non-payment of wages or other amounts owed under the Canada Labour Code, the deadline is six months from the last day the employer was obligated to make those payments. For all other types of complaints, the deadline is also six months from the day the employee became aware of the issue.

#### Extension of Time
"The Head may, subject to the regulations, extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; (b) in any circumstances prescribed by regulation; or (c) in the conditions prescribed by regulation."

The Head of the Labour Program has the discretion to extend the complaint timeframe under certain circumstances. This extension is subject to regulations and can be granted if the complaint was made to an official without the proper authority, and the complainant reasonably believed they had that authority.

#### Limitation on Complaints Against Trade Unions
"An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under any of subsections 240(1), 246.1(1) and 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn."

This provision prevents employees from filing multiple complaints based on substantially the same set of facts. It states that a complaint is not permitted if a similar complaint has already been filed and withdrawn.

### Section 133: Complaints When Action Against Employees: Complaint to Board

#### Timeframe for Making a Complaint
"The complaint shall be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

This section establishes a ninety-day timeframe for employees to file a complaint with the Board. The deadline is calculated from the date the employee became aware of the action taken against them or, in the Board's judgment, should have become aware of it.

#### Restriction on Complaints Against Trade Unions
"A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be, in relation to the matter that is the subject-matter of the complaint."

This restriction applies to complaints related to the exercise of rights under sections 128 or 129. It requires the employee to have complied with the necessary procedures or the Head to have received the required reports before the complaint can be filed.

#### Exclusion of Arbitration
"Notwithstanding any law or agreement to the contrary, a complaint made under this section may not be referred by an employee to arbitration or adjudication."

This provision explicitly prohibits employees from referring complaints filed under this section to arbitration or adjudication, regardless of any other agreements or laws that might permit it.

### Section 16_1: After You File a Complaint

#### Monetary Complaint Timeframe
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you."

This section reiterates the six-month timeframe for filing a monetary complaint, which is from the last day the employer was obligated to make the wages or other amounts owed.

#### Non-Monetary Complaint Timeframe
"...months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose."

This section also confirms the six-month timeframe for filing a non-monetary complaint, which is from the day the employee became aware of the issue.

#### Unjust Dismissal Complaint Timeframe
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal."

This section specifies the ninety-day timeframe for filing an unjust dismissal complaint, which is from the date of dismissal.

### Section 133: Eligibility and Timelines

#### Eligibility and Timelines
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you."

This section directly addresses eligibility and timelines for monetary complaints, stating the six-month deadline from the last day of payment.

#### Non-Monetary Complaint Timeframe
"...months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose."

This section also confirms the six-month timeframe for filing non-monetary complaints, which is from the day the employee became aware of the issue.

#### Extension of Time
"The Head may, subject to the regulations, extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority; (b) in any circumstances prescribed by regulation; or (c) in the conditions prescribed by regulation."

This section mirrors the extension of time provision found in Section 251.01, allowing the Head of the Labour Program to extend the complaint timeframe under specific circumstances.

#### Limitation — section 177.1 (4.1)
"With respect to a request made under subsection 177.1(1), an employee may make a complaint under subsection (1) only on the grounds that the employer has refused the request on any ground other than those referred to in subparagraphs 177.1(3)(c)(i) to (v) or has failed to comply with any requirement set out in section 177.1(4)."

This section places a limitation on complaints related to refusals of requests under subsection 177.1(1), stating that the complaint must be based on grounds other than those listed or a failure to comply with a requirement in section 177.1(4).

individual_results.question: Under what circumstances can the Head suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee, and what are the requirements for the Head's decision to be implemented?
individual_results.answer:
## Circumstances for Head to Suspend Consideration of a Complaint

### Section 251.02(1) - Head's Satisfaction of Required Measures
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This section explicitly outlines the primary circumstance under which the Head can suspend consideration of a complaint. The Head must first determine that the employee is obligated to take specific actions before the complaint can proceed further. This satisfaction of the employee's required measures is a prerequisite for the Head to exercise the power of suspension. The suspension can be either complete ("in whole") or partial ("in part"), indicating flexibility in the scope of the Head's decision.

### Section 251.02(2) - Requirements for the Head's Decision
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

This subsection details the mandatory requirements for the Head's decision to suspend consideration to be legally sound and actionable. The Head is obligated to provide the employee with a written notice. This notice must clearly state two crucial elements:
"(a) the measures that the employee must take;" and
"(b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." These specific instructions ensure that the employee understands their responsibilities and the timeframe within which they must fulfill them. Without these clear directives, the suspension would be ambiguous and ineffective.

### Section 251.02(3) - Extension of Time
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice."

This subsection provides a mechanism for flexibility. If the employee requires more time to complete the measures outlined in the notice, they can formally request an extension from the Head. The Head has the discretion to grant or deny this extension based on the circumstances. This acknowledges that the employee may face unforeseen challenges in meeting the initial deadline.

### Section 251.02(4) - End of Suspension
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

This subsection defines the termination point of the suspension. The Head will formally end the suspension when they are satisfied that the employee has successfully completed the measures they were required to take within the specified timeframe. This marks the resumption of the Head's consideration of the original complaint.

individual_results.question: What happens when an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this affect potential prosecution?
individual_results.answer:
## Settlement of Amounts Due

### Written Agreement and Payment
"If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the initial step when a settlement is reached. It emphasizes the necessity of a "written agreement" detailing the agreed-upon amount and payment terms. Following this agreement, the employer has the option to either pay the settlement directly to the employee or to the "Head," which likely refers to the Labour Program. This written settlement serves as a binding agreement between the employer and the employee, potentially resolving the wage dispute.

### Impact on Prosecution
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head."

This passage directly addresses the effect of a written settlement on potential prosecution. It states that prosecution for failure to pay wages or other amounts is barred, "without the written consent of the Minister," if the employer has already fulfilled the terms of the settlement by making the agreed-upon payment to either the employee or the Labour Program. This provision provides a mechanism for resolving wage disputes without resorting to the legal system, promoting efficiency and avoiding further conflict. The Minister's consent acts as a safeguard, ensuring that settlements are genuine and that the employee receives the full amount owed.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the Head reject a complaint made under section 251.01, and what steps must be taken after a complaint is rejected?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Rejecting a Complaint

### Section 251.05(1) - General Grounds for Rejection

Section 251.05(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines nine specific grounds upon which the Head may reject a complaint, either in whole or in part. These grounds cover a range of issues, from jurisdictional concerns to lack of evidence.
"The Head may reject a complaint made under section 251.01, in whole or in part, (a) if the Head is satisfied (i) that the complaint is not within their jurisdiction, (ii) that the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) that the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee, (iv) that there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject-matter of the complaint that the Head considers should be pursued, (v) that the subject-matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator, (vi) that in respect of a complaint other than a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, there is insufficient evidence to substantiate the complaint, or (vii) that in respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject-matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process..."

This section details a broad spectrum of reasons for rejection. For instance, a complaint can be rejected
"(iii) that the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee..." This indicates that a written agreement resolving the issue is a valid reason for dismissal. Additionally, a complaint can be rejected
"...if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 251.02(1) and if, in the Head’s opinion, the other measures specified in the notice under subsection 251.02(2) were not taken within the specified time period..." This highlights the Head's discretion to suspend consideration and potentially reject a complaint if the required steps were not taken within the timeframe.

### Section 251.05(1)(b) - Other Means of Resolution

Specifically, ground (iv) states that a complaint can be rejected
"...that there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject-matter of the complaint that the Head considers should be pursued..." This suggests that the Head may reject a complaint if they believe the employee has alternative avenues for resolution, such as mediation or other dispute resolution processes.

### Section 251.05(1)(c) - Lack of Evidence

Ground (vi) addresses the issue of insufficient evidence, stating that a complaint can be rejected
"...that in respect of a complaint other than a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, there is insufficient evidence to substantiate the complaint..." This emphasizes the Head's need for credible evidence to support a complaint before it can be considered.

### Section 251.05(1)(vii) - Collective Agreements

Ground (vii) considers the impact of collective agreements, stating that a complaint can be rejected
"...that in respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject-matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process..." This indicates that the Head may reject a complaint if the collective agreement already addresses the issue through a defined process.

## Steps Taken After a Complaint is Rejected

### Section 251.05(2) - Notification of Rejection

Section 251.05(2) mandates that
"If a complaint has been rejected, the Head shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons." This is a crucial step, ensuring transparency and allowing the employee to understand the Head's decision. The Head must provide a clear explanation of the specific ground(s) for rejection.

### Section 251.05(3) - Employee's Right to Review

Section 251.05(3) grants the employee the right to request a review of the Head's decision. It states that
"The employee may, within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection, request in writing, with reasons, that the Head review the Head’s decision." This provides a mechanism for the employee to challenge the Head's determination if they believe it was incorrect.

### Section 251.05(4) - Head's Decision on Review

Section 251.05(4) outlines the Head's options upon reviewing the rejection. It says that
"The Head may confirm the decision, or rescind it and re-examine the complaint." This indicates that the Head has the discretion to either uphold the initial rejection or reconsider the complaint based on the employee's review.

### Section 251.05(5) - Finality of Head's Decision

Section 251.05(5) emphasizes the finality of the Head's decision on rejection. It states that
"The Head’s confirmation or rescission is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court." This means that the employee's review request does not open the door to further legal challenges.

## Head's Powers to Address Employer Violations

### Section 271: Head's Powers Regarding Notices of Violation

Section 271 outlines the Head's authority over the form and issuance of notices of violation.
"The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation; (b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation; and (c) establish a short-form description for each violation to be used in notices of violation."
This indicates that the Head has significant control over how these notices are created and who is responsible for sending them. The Head can standardize the notice format, specify who has the power to issue them, and create concise labels for each violation. This ensures consistency and clarity in the communication of Code violations to employers.

### Section 249: Head's Powers Regarding Inspections and Delegation

Section 249 details the Head's powers related to inspections and the delegation of those powers. It states,
"(1) Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."
This is a crucial point regarding the Head's ability to take action. The Head can delegate its inspection powers to qualified individuals or groups. This allows for more widespread enforcement of the Code. Furthermore, the Head can impose specific conditions on these delegated powers, ensuring they are exercised responsibly and within the scope of the delegation.

### Section 272: Head's Powers Regarding Delegation

Section 272 reinforces the Head's power to delegate its authority.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."
This section is almost identical to Section 249(1), emphasizing the Head's broad ability to delegate its powers. The Head can tailor these delegations to specific needs and circumstances by including terms and conditions.

### Section 249(2): Head's Powers During Inspections

Section 249(2) specifies the Head's powers while conducting inspections.
"(a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee; (b) take extracts from or make copies of any entry in the books, payrolls and other records mentioned in paragraph (a); (c) require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment; (c.1) require any employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan that must be insured in accordance with subsection 239.2(1) to furnish proof that the plan is insured in accordance with that subsection; (d) require an employee to make full disclosure, production and delivery to the Head of all records, documents, statements, writings, books, papers, extracts therefrom or copies thereof or of other information, either orally or in writing, that are in the possession or under the control of the employee and that in any way relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of his employment; and (e) require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made."
During inspections, the Head has extensive powers to review employer records, request information from employers and employees, and compel parties to provide statements. This allows for a thorough investigation of potential Code violations.

### Section 249(3): Head's Right to Enter Premises

Section 249(3) grants the Head the right to enter any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection.
"The Head may, at any reasonable time, enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer."
This ensures the Head can conduct inspections wherever necessary to gather information. The Head can also question employees, although this is done separately from the employer.

### Section 249(4): Head's Assistance

Section 249(4) states that the person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance.
"The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out the Head’s duties and functions under this Part or the regulations."
This obligation to provide reasonable assistance facilitates the Head's inspection efforts and allows for the efficient gathering of information.

### Section 249(5): Head's Accompaniment

Section 249(5) allows the Head to be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary.
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary."
This enables the Head to bring in experts or additional personnel to assist with complex inspections or investigations.

### Section 249(6): Evidence Precluded - Head

Section 249(6) protects the Head from being required to give testimony in civil suits or proceedings regarding information obtained while performing its duties.
"The Head shall not be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions."
This ensures the Head can conduct its work without fear of being compelled to disclose confidential information obtained during inspections.

individual_results.question: What actions can the Head take if an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the limitations and procedures involved?
individual_results.answer:
## Actions the Head Can Take for Unpaid Wages

### Monetary Complaint Process

The Head has the authority to issue a written payment order to the employer, or to a director of a corporation, directing the payment of unpaid wages or other amounts owed to the employee.
"If the Head finds that an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, the Head may issue a written payment order to the employer, or, subject to section 251.18, to a director of a corporation referred to in that section, ordering the employer or director to pay the amount in question, and the Head shall send a copy of any such payment order to the employee at the employee’s latest known address." This passage directly addresses the Head's power to compel payment through a payment order. It also outlines a limitation, stating that the payment order cannot relate to wages or other amounts for the period preceding 24 months, plus any extension granted by the Head, immediately before the day on which the complaint was made.

### Administrative Fees and Director's Liability

The Head can also impose administrative fees on the employer when a payment order is issued.
"The following administrative fee will be added to the Payment Order when issued to the employer:  a fee of $200, or a fee of 15% of the total amount owed   Note: If the 15% of the total amount owed is more than $200, the Labour Program will apply that amount to the Payment Order along with the wages or other monies owed to the employee." This indicates that the Head will recover some of the unpaid wages through these fees. Furthermore, the Head can hold corporate directors liable for amounts employers owe to employees during their time as director.
"Corporate directors are jointly and individually liable for employees’ wages and other amounts to which employees are entitled, up to a limit equivalent to 6 months’ wages." This liability extends to debtors or financial institutions of the directors if the employer fails to pay the Payment Order.

### Settlement of Amounts Due

The Head can facilitate a settlement between the employer and the employee.
"If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head." This passage highlights the Head's role in ensuring that a settlement is honored, either by the employer paying the employee directly or to the Head who then disburses it.

### Limitations and Procedures

Several limitations and procedures are involved in the Head's actions.
"You must file your monetary complaint within 6 months from the last day your employer was required to pay you." This sets a strict time limit for filing a monetary complaint.
"You must file your non-monetary complaint within 6 months from the day you were aware of the issue." This applies to complaints not involving specific monetary amounts.
"You must file your unjust dismissal complaint within 90 days from the date of dismissal." This is the shortest timeframe for filing an unjust dismissal complaint.
"Service of a payment order or a copy of it, of a notice of unfounded complaint, or of a notice of voluntary compliance shall be by personal service, by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation and, in the case of registered mail, the order, copy or notice shall be deemed to have been received by the addressee on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed." This details the required method of service of the payment order.
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head." This outlines a limitation on criminal prosecution if the employer has already paid the wages.

individual_results.answer:
## Disputing Compliance Orders, Payment Orders, or Notices

### Review and Appeal Process

The Canada Labour Code outlines a process for employers or affected persons to dispute a compliance order, payment order, or notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance. This process involves a review by the Labour Program and, if unsatisfied, an appeal to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB).

#### Review by the Labour Program
"If you do not agree with the Labour Program’s decision, you may request that the Labour Program review the Notice of Unfounded Complaint or Notice of Voluntary Compliance. To do this, you must make your written request to the Labour Program, with reasons and within 15 days after notice is served. Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program may, in writing:  confirm the Notice of Unfounded Complaint, confirm the Notice of Voluntary Compliance, or rescind the notices  In the case of a rescinded notice, the Labour Program will re-examine the complaint."

This section details the initial step in disputing a Labour Program decision. The affected party must submit a written request for a review, accompanied by their reasons for disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the original notice. The Labour Program will then conduct a review and issue a written decision, which could be to confirm the original notice, confirm the voluntary compliance, or rescind the notices entirely, leading to a re-examination of the original complaint.

#### Appeal to the CIRB
"You may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). You must make the request to the CIRB, in writing and with reasons, within 15 days after the Labour Program review decision is served.  The CIRB can only hear the appeal if it based on a question of law or jurisdiction." (no source found for the quotation)

If the Labour Program's review is not satisfactory, the affected party has the option to appeal to the CIRB. This appeal must be made in writing and with clear reasons for the disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the Labour Program's decision. The CIRB's jurisdiction is limited to questions of law or jurisdiction, meaning it will not typically overturn factual findings made by the Labour Program.

### Review and Appeal of a Payment Order
"As an employee, employer or a director of the corporation, you may request a review of the Payment Order if you do not agree with the decision. To do this, you must make a request to the Labour Program, in writing and with reasons, within 15 days after the Labour Program’s decision is served.  As the employer or the director, you must also include:  a full payment for the amount indicated in the Payment Order or a Letter of Credit in lieu of payment, and the administrative fee, if applicable  Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program can confirm, vary or rescind the Payment Order. If you do not agree with the review decision of the Payment Order, you may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). You must make the request to the CIRB, in writing and with reasons, and within 15 days after the Labour Program served the order. The CIRB can only hear the appeal if it based on a question of law or jurisdiction."

A payment order can also be disputed through a review and appeal process. The affected party must submit a written request for review to the Labour Program, with reasons, within 15 days of receiving the payment order. As the employer or director, they must also provide the full payment or a Letter of Credit, along with any applicable administrative fees. The Labour Program will then review the order and can confirm, vary, or rescind it. If still dissatisfied, an appeal to the CIRB is possible, again within 15 days of the Labour Program's decision, and only on questions of law or jurisdiction.

### Review and Appeal of a Notice of Unfounded Complaint
"If you do not agree with the Labour Program’s decision, you may request that the Labour Program review the Notice of Unfounded Complaint or Notice of Voluntary Compliance. To do this, you must make your written request to the Labour Program, with reasons and within 15 days after notice is served. Upon completion of the review, the Labour Program may, in writing:  confirm the Notice of Unfounded Complaint, confirm the Notice of Voluntary Compliance, or rescind the notices  In the case of a rescinded notice, the Labour Program will re-examine the complaint."

This section reiterates the review process for a notice of unfounded complaint. The affected party must submit a written request for review to the Labour Program, with their reasons for disagreement, within 15 days of receiving the original notice. The Labour Program will then review the notice and issue a written decision, which could be to confirm the unfounded complaint, confirm the voluntary compliance, or rescind the notices entirely, leading to a re-examination of the original complaint.

### Review and Appeal of a Compliance Order
"If the Head is of the opinion that an employer is contravening or has contravened a provision of this Part, its regulations or any condition of a permit issued under subsection 176(1), the Head may issue a compliance order in writing requiring the employer to terminate the contravention within the time that the Head may specify and take any step, as specified by the Head and within the time that the Head may specify, to ensure that the contravention does not continue or reoccur."

While the document does not explicitly detail the review and appeal process for a compliance order, it does state that the Head (presumably the Labour Program) can issue such an order. The text implies that a dispute would likely involve a review of the Labour Program's decision, potentially leading to a rescission of the order and a re-examination of the original complaint. An appeal to the CIRB would be possible, but only on questions of law or jurisdiction.

individual_results.question: Who can appeal a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code, and what are the conditions for doing so?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 251.11: Appeal of Decisions Made Under Subsection 251.101(3)

### Who Can Appeal?

Section 251.11(1) states:
"Subject to subsection (1.1), a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served." This indicates that any person "affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3)" can appeal. However, subsection (1.1) introduces an exception:
"Only an employer to whom a compliance order has been issued may appeal a decision with respect to that order." This means that while other affected parties can appeal, only an employer subject to a compliance order can appeal a decision concerning that order.

### Conditions for Appealing

Section 251.11(2) outlines the grounds for appeal:
"The request for appeal shall contain a statement of the grounds of appeal." This is a mandatory requirement for any appeal. The section also specifies the payment requirements for an employer appealing a decision confirming or varying a payment order:
"An employer or director of a corporation is not permitted to appeal a decision confirming or varying a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the decision — and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the decision in accordance with subsection 251.131(1) — less any amount and administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2)." This means an employer must pay the full amount and administrative fee indicated in the decision, less any previously paid amounts, before they can appeal.

Furthermore, section 251.11(3.1) mentions the Head's discretion to allow security:
"The Head may allow an employer or a director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (3)." This provides an option for an employer who cannot immediately pay the full amount and fee to provide security as a guarantee.

Finally, section 251.11(4) includes a limitation for directors:
"In the case of a director, subsection (3) applies subject to the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18." This means that the payment requirements for an employer do not apply to a director appealing a decision confirming or varying a payment order, and the director's liability is capped at the maximum amount specified in section 251.18.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of the Head and the Board in terms of document provision and participation in an appeal under the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Head and Board Responsibilities in an Appeal under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 286: Head Informed of Appeal and Document Provision

#### Head's Information and Document Provision
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This passage clearly outlines the Board's initial responsibility to keep the Head informed. Upon receiving an appeal, the Board is obligated to promptly notify the Head and furnish them with a duplicate of the appeal request. This ensures the Head is aware of the proceedings and has access to the initial grounds for the appeal.

#### Head's Duty to Provide Documents
"...the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This section details the Head's reciprocal responsibility. If the Board requests it, the Head must provide any documentation they used when making the original decision that is now being challenged in the appeal. This allows the Board to understand the Head's reasoning and the basis for the initial action.

#### Documents Provided to Head
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal." This passage further clarifies the exchange of documents. The Board is required to share any documents that have been formally submitted to them as part of the appeal process with the Head upon their request. This keeps the Head in the loop regarding the progress of the appeal and the information being presented.

#### Head's Participation in the Appeal
"The Head may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This passage highlights the Head's active role in the appeal. They have the right to contribute to the proceedings by offering additional information or arguments to the Board. This ensures the Board has a comprehensive understanding of the matter from all perspectives.

### Section 251.111: Orders — Review and Appeal: Head Informed of Appeal

#### Head's Information and Document Provision (Similar to Section 286)
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 251.11(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal." This section mirrors the Head's information from Section 286, confirming the Board's obligation to notify the Head and provide the appeal request.

#### Documents Provided to Board — decision (Similar to Section 286)
"In an appeal under this Part, the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This passage is identical to Section 286, reiterating the Head's duty to furnish the Board with any documents they used when making the original decision.

#### Documents Provided to Board — order or notice (Similar to Section 286)
"In an appeal under subsection 251.101(7), the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of issuing the order or notice being appealed." This section is also identical to Section 286, reinforcing the Head's responsibility to provide documents related to the specific order or notice being appealed.

#### Documents Provided to Head (Similar to Section 286)
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal." This passage is a direct repetition of Section 286, confirming the Board's obligation to share filed documents with the Head upon request.

#### Power of Head (Similar to Section 286)
"The Head may, in an appeal under this Part, present evidence and make representations to the Board." This passage is identical to Section 286, highlighting the Head's ability to actively participate in the appeal by presenting evidence and arguments.

### Section 146.1: Board's Responsibilities in an Appeal

#### Inquiry and Decision
"If an appeal is brought under subsection 129(7) or section 146, the Board shall, in a summary way and without delay, inquire into the circumstances of the decision or direction, as the case may be, and the reasons for it and may (a) vary, rescind or confirm the decision or direction; and (b) issue any direction that the Board considers appropriate under subsection 145(2) or (2.1)." This section details the Board's primary responsibility in an appeal: to conduct a prompt and efficient inquiry into the original decision or direction. They will examine the circumstances, the reasoning behind it, and then have the power to modify, overturn, or uphold it. They can also issue new directions if deemed necessary.

#### Written Decision and Reasons
"The Board shall provide a written decision, with reasons, and a copy of any direction to the employer, employee or trade union concerned and to the Head, and the employer shall, without delay, give a copy of the decision, the reasons, and any direction to the work place committee or health and safety representative." This passage emphasizes the Board's obligation to issue a comprehensive written decision that includes the rationale behind their actions. This decision, along with any new directions, must be promptly shared with all relevant parties, including the Head, the employer, the employee or trade union, and the workplace committee or health and safety representative.

#### Posting of Notice
"If the Board issues a direction under paragraph (1)(b), the employer shall, without delay, affix or cause to be affixed to or near the machine, thing or place in respect of which the direction is issued a notice of the direction, in the form and containing the information that the Board may specify, and no person may remove the notice unless authorized to do so by the Board." This section outlines the employer's responsibility to publicly display the Board's direction. A notice must be posted in a conspicuous location near the affected machine, thing, or place, and it cannot be removed without the Board's permission.

#### Cessation of Use
"If the Board directs, under paragraph (1)(b), that a machine or thing not be used, a place not be worked in or an activity not be performed until the direction is complied with, no person shall use the machine or thing, or work in the place or perform the activity until the direction is complied with, but nothing in this subsection..." This passage details the immediate effect of a Board direction. It prohibits anyone from using the machine, thing, or place, or from performing the activity until the Board's order is followed. However, it clarifies that this is not a general order to stop all work.

individual_results.answer:
## Possible Outcomes and Implications of a Board Decision in an Appeal under Part III of the Canada Labour Code

### Section 287: Appeal: Object of appeal

Section 287(1) outlines the Board's primary function in an appeal under this Part: to determine whether the penalty for a violation was determined in accordance with the regulations and whether the appellant committed the violation, or both. This sets the stage for several potential outcomes.
"...the Board shall determine, as the case may be, whether the amount of the penalty for the violation was determined in accordance with the regulations or whether the appellant committed the violation, or both." This quote is central to understanding the Board's role. It indicates that the Board can address issues related to the calculation of the penalty itself, not just whether the violation occurred.

### Section 287: Appeal: Decision

Section 287(2) details what happens if the Board determines the penalty was not determined in accordance with the regulations.
"If the Board determines that the amount of the penalty for the violation was not determined in accordance with the regulations, the Board shall correct the amount of the penalty." This passage directly states the Board's action in such a scenario: it will rectify the penalty amount.

Section 287(3) specifies the form and content of the Board's decision.
"The Board shall make a decision in writing and provide the appellant and the Head with a copy of the decision, with reasons." This highlights the importance of the Board providing a written decision with clear justifications for its findings. This allows both parties to understand the Board's reasoning and to potentially identify areas of disagreement.

Section 287(4) addresses the employer's obligation to provide a copy of the decision.
"If a decision is made with respect to a notice of violation referred to in subsection 276(3), the employer shall, without delay, give a copy of the decision to the or health and safety representative , as those terms are defined in subsection 122(1)." This ensures that relevant parties are promptly informed of the Board's decision.

Section 287(5) outlines the appellant's liability if the Board finds the violation occurred.
"If the Board determines that the appellant committed the violation, the appellant is liable for the penalty that is set out in the decision." This is a key outcome: if the Board finds guilt, the appellant is legally obligated to pay the adjusted penalty.

Section 287(6) and (7) establish the finality of the Board's decision.
"Every decision made under this section is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." and
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this section." These passages emphasize that the Board's decision is binding and cannot be challenged in the courts.

### Section 146.5: Appeals of Decisions and Directions: Wages

Section 146.5 addresses the entitlement to be paid regular wages for time spent at a proceeding.
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." This passage clarifies that employees who participate in Board proceedings are entitled to be paid their regular wages for that time.

### Section 251.12: Orders — Review and Appeal: Board decision

Section 251.12 details the types of orders the Board can make in an appeal.
"(1) The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal; (c) award costs in the proceedings; and (d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board." This section provides a comprehensive list of potential orders the Board can issue. These orders can range from confirming, rescinding, or varying the original decision to directing the payment of wages or costs, and even ordering a party to pay the Board's expenses.

Section 251.12(2) and (3) address the distribution of the Board's decision.
"(2) The Board shall send a copy of the decision, with reasons, to each party to the appeal and to the Head." and
"(3) The order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." These passages reiterate the finality of the Board's decision and the obligation to send a copy to all relevant parties.

Section 251.12(5) reinforces the employee's wage entitlement for attending Board proceedings.
"An employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at an appeal proceeding under this Part and who attends is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." This is a repetition of Section 146.5, emphasizing the wage entitlement for attending Board proceedings.

### Section 251.11: Orders — Review and Appeal: Appeal

Section 251.11 outlines the circumstances under which an appeal of a Board decision is possible.
"(1) Subject to subsection (1.1), a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served." This passage states that an appeal is generally possible within 15 days of receiving the Board's decision, with an exception for decisions to rescind notices of unfounded complaints or voluntary compliance.

Section 251.11(2) specifies the grounds for appeal.
"(2) The request for appeal shall contain a statement of the grounds of appeal." This requires the appellant to clearly articulate the legal reasons why they believe the Board's decision was incorrect.

Section 251.11(3) addresses the payment requirements for appealing a decision confirming or varying a payment order.
"(3) An employer or director of a corporation is not permitted to appeal a decision confirming or varying a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the decision — and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the decision in accordance with subsection 251.131(1) — less any amount and administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2)." This passage highlights a financial obligation for employers or directors seeking to appeal a decision related to a payment order.

Section 251.11(4) and (5) deal with security and debt to Her Majesty.
"(3.1) The Head may allow an employer or a director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (3)." and
"(6) The expenses to be paid in accordance with an order issued under paragraph (1)(d) constitute a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and are recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act." These sections explain that the Head may allow security to be provided for the appeal costs, and that any costs awarded by the Board will be treated as a debt owed to Her Majesty.

## Section 251.13: General Provisions — Orders: Order to debtor of employer

### Circumstances for Issuing an Order to Debtor

Section 251.13 outlines the Head's authority to issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to an employer.
"The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to an employer to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1), to pay any amount owing to the employer, up to the amount and the administrative fee indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order."

This indicates that the Head can issue an order to a debtor when a payment order has already been issued to the employer. The order directs the debtor to pay the outstanding amount, including any applicable administrative fee, directly to the Head within 15 days. The amount payable is capped at the amount specified in the payment order.

### Order to Debtor of Director of Corporation

Section 251.13 further clarifies that the Head can issue a similar order to a debtor who owes money to a director of a corporation.
"The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to a director of a corporation to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1) to pay any amount owing to the director of the corporation, up to the amount indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order."

This mirrors the provision for orders to debtors of employers, but specifically applies to orders directed to debtors of directors of corporations when a payment order has been issued to the director. The debtor is instructed to pay the director the amount specified in the payment order directly to the Head within 15 days.

### Banks and Financial Institutions

Section 251.13(2) provides a definition for the purpose of this section.
"For the purposes of this section, a bank or other financial institution that has money on deposit to the credit of an employer or a director of a corporation shall be deemed to be indebted to that employer or that director."

This definition broadens the scope of the Head's ability to issue orders to debtors. It includes banks and other financial institutions that hold money on deposit for an employer or a director of a corporation. These institutions are considered indebted to the employer or director, and the Head can issue an order to them to pay the outstanding amount directly to the Head.

individual_results.question: What happens to an employer's administrative fee if it is overpaid, and what is the status of an unpaid administrative fee?
individual_results.answer:
## Administrative Fees: Overpayment and Unpaid Status

### Overpaid Administrative Fees

According to Section 251.132 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Section 251.132 The Head, after a final decision has been made in respect of which security was given, (a) may apply, in whole or in part, the security given under subsection 251.101(2.1) or 251.11(3.1) toward any amounts — and, if the security was given by an employer, any administrative fee — owing under the final decision by the employer or a director of a corporation who gave the security; and (b) shall return the security or, if it was applied under paragraph (a), any part that remains after the amounts and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee have been paid." This passage explicitly states that if an employer makes an overpayment of an administrative fee, the Head will either apply the security provided towards the outstanding amount, including the overpaid fee, or return any remaining security. This ensures that the employer is not unjustly burdened by an overpayment.

### Unpaid Administrative Fees

Section 251.131 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the status of an unpaid administrative fee. It states,
"Section 251.131 (1) A payment order made to an employer under subsection 251.1(1), and any decision made under subsection 251.101(3) or section 251.12 with respect to that payment order ordering the employer to pay wages or other amounts to an employee, shall specify the amount of the administrative fee — which is equal to the greater of $200 and 15% of the amounts indicated in the payment order or decision — that the employer is to pay." This indicates that an unpaid administrative fee is considered a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada.
"An administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15." This further clarifies that the unpaid administrative fee can be recovered through standard debt collection processes.

Furthermore, Section 289 of the Canada Labour Code provides context on the responsibility for payment. It states,
"Section 289 If a person or a department pays the penalty set out in a notice of violation, the person or the department is considered to have committed the violation and proceedings in respect of it are ended." While this section pertains to administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) issued for violations, it highlights the principle of responsibility for payment. If an employer fails to pay an unpaid administrative fee, the Labour Program can collect from a director’s debtors or financial institution. This underscores the seriousness of an unpaid administrative fee and the potential consequences for the employer and its directors.

## Money Received by the Head Under the Labour Standards Division

### Deposit and Allocation of Funds
"If the Head receives moneys under this Division, the Head shall deposit those moneys to the credit of the Receiver General in the account known as the “Labour Standards Suspense Account” or in any other special account created for the purposes of this section and may authorize payments out of that account to any employee or other person who is entitled to that money."

This passage from CLC-251.14 clearly outlines the initial handling of money received by the Head. It states that the funds are deposited into a designated account, the "Labour Standards Suspense Account," held by the Receiver General. This account acts as a holding place for all money collected under the Labour Standards division. The Head then has the authority to authorize payments from this account to the individuals who are legally entitled to them. This ensures that the money collected is properly accounted for and distributed to those who have earned it.

### Administrative Fees

### Calculation and Payment
"The following administrative fee will be added to the Payment Order when issued to the employer:  a fee of $200, or a fee of 15% of the total amount owed   Note: If the 15% of the total amount owed is more than $200, the Labour Program will apply that amount to the Payment Order along with the wages or other monies owed to the employee."

This section from LABOUR-STANDARDS-6_5 details how administrative fees are calculated and paid. It specifies that the fee is either \$200 or 15% of the total amount owed, whichever is greater. A crucial note clarifies that if the 15% exceeds \$200, the full 15% is applied to the Payment Order alongside the wages or other monies owed to the employee. This ensures that the fee is always the maximum possible amount.

### Allocation of Administrative Fees
"The moneys that are equal to the administrative fees paid to the Head under this Part with respect to matters that are the subject of a final decision shall be debited from the account referred to in subsection (1) and credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund no later than the fiscal year following the fiscal year in which the final decision is made."

CLC-251.14 further explains the allocation of administrative fees. It states that these fees are debited from the Labour Standards Suspense Account and credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund no later than the fiscal year following the fiscal year in which the final decision is made. This demonstrates that the administrative fees collected are ultimately used to support the broader financial operations of the Canadian government.

### Recovery of Administrative Fees
"An administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15."

CLC-284 highlights the recoverability of administrative fees. It declares that these fees are considered a debt owed to Her Majesty in right of Canada and can be recovered through various legal avenues, including the Federal Court. This ensures that the administrative fees collected are not lost but are ultimately used to benefit the Canadian public.

individual_results.question: What happens to a payment order or Board order under the Canada Labour Code once it is filed in the Federal Court, and what are the implications for enforcement?
individual_results.answer:
## Enforcement of Orders Filed in the Federal Court

### Registration and Legal Force

Section 23 of the Canada Labour Code details the process of filing an order or decision of the Board in the Federal Court and its subsequent effect.
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding." This passage highlights that upon filing, the order or decision is
"...accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding."

Section 244 further elaborates on this, stating,
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This is a crucial point, as it establishes the registration of the order in the Federal Court as equivalent to a judgment.
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court." This quote reinforces the legal weight of the registered order, allowing for all types of legal actions to be initiated against the debtor.

### Implications for Enforcement

The registration of the order in the Federal Court significantly enhances its enforceability.
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons." This indicates that the order, once registered, can be used as the basis for filing a judgment in the Federal Court to recover outstanding wages or other amounts owed.
"The expenses to be paid in accordance with an order issued under paragraph (1)(d) constitute a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and are recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act." This passage clarifies that the order can be enforced as a debt owed to the Crown, providing a clear avenue for recovery.

### Further Enforcement Mechanisms

Section 251.15 also outlines enforcement mechanisms available after the order is filed in the Federal Court.
"After the expiration of the 15 day period specified in an order to a debtor of the employer or of the director of a corporation made under section 251.13, the Head may file a copy of the order in the Federal Court." This allows the Head to initiate the enforcement process even if the debtor has not complied with the initial order.
"...in the Federal Court under subsection (1) or (2), the order shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court." This reiterates the legal force of the registered order, enabling the Head to pursue all available legal remedies.

individual_results.question: Can directors of a corporation be held personally liable for unpaid wages and other amounts owed to employees?
individual_results.answer:
## Section 12.051: Limitation of Liability of Board Members

### Civil and Criminal Liability
"The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This section directly addresses the question of directors' personal liability. It explicitly states that directors, along with other Board members and external adjudicators, are
"...not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act." This means that directors cannot be held personally responsible for the actions of the corporation, even if those actions involve unpaid wages or other amounts owed to employees, provided they acted in good faith. The broad scope of this immunity covers both "civilly" and "criminally" liable situations, providing a strong protection for directors acting responsibly.

## Section 251.18: Joint and Several Liability of Directors

### Maximum Liability
"Directors of a corporation are jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages, to the extent that (a) the entitlement arose during the particular director’s incumbency; and (b) recovery of the amount from the corporation is impossible or unlikely."

While Section 12.051 provides immunity from personal liability for good faith actions, Section 251.18 establishes a limited form of joint and several liability for directors. It states that directors are
"...jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages..." This means that if an employee is owed wages and the corporation is unable to pay, the directors can be held personally responsible for the full amount, up to that six-month wage limit. However, this liability is contingent on two conditions: the entitlement arose during the director's time on the board, and recovery from the corporation is impossible or unlikely. This provision offers a safety net for employees but is not unlimited in scope.

## Section 274: Liability of Parties to Violation

### Definition of Party to Violation
"If a corporation or a department commits a violation, any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."

This section further clarifies the potential personal liability of directors. It explicitly includes
"...any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation..." as a party to a violation and liable to a penalty. This means that directors are included within the broad definition of individuals who can be held personally responsible for corporate violations. The inclusion of
"...any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department." broadens the scope of liability beyond just those with formal titles. The phrase
"...directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation..." highlights the range of involvement that can lead to personal liability.

individual_results.question: What are the responsibilities of an employer in Canada regarding the provision and maintenance of employee work records and information as per the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Employer Responsibilities Regarding Employee Work Records and Information

### Section 24: Keeping of Records

Section 24 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations outlines the comprehensive record-keeping obligations of employers. It mandates that employers maintain records for various aspects of an employee's employment, including:

#### Basic Employee Information
"Every employer shall make and keep a record in respect of each employee showing the date of commencement of employment and the date of termination of employment and shall keep such record for a period of at least 36 months after the date of termination of employment." This provision establishes the foundational record-keeping requirement, capturing the start and end dates of each employee's tenure with the company.

#### Wage Information
"Every employer shall keep, for at least three years after work is performed by an employee, the following information: (a) the full name, address, Social Insurance Number, occupational classification and sex of the employee, and if the employee is under the age of 18 years, the age of the employee; (b) the rate of wages, clearly indicating whether it is on an hourly, weekly, monthly or other basis, and the date and particulars of any change in the rate..." This highlights the employer's duty to track and document employee wage rates and any adjustments made.

#### Hours Worked
"(d) the hours worked each day, except where the employee is (i) excluded from the application of Division I of the Act by or under subsection 167(2) of the Act, or (ii) exempt from the application of sections 169 and 171 of the Act pursuant to regulations made under paragraph 175(1)(b) of the Act..." Employers are required to record the number of hours each employee works daily, with specific exceptions noted.

#### Earnings
"(e) the actual earnings, indicating the amounts paid each pay day, with a recording of the amounts paid for overtime, vacation pay, general holiday pay, personal leave pay, pay for leave for victims of family violence, bereavement leave pay, medical leave of absence pay, termination pay and severance pay..." This provision emphasizes the employer's obligation to detail employee earnings, including various types of paid leave and overtime.

#### Leave Information
"(g) with respect to annual vacations (i) the dates of commencement and termination of each vacation period, (ii) if a vacation was interrupted under subsection 187.1(1) of the Act, the date of interruption, and if the employee resumed the vacation under subsection 187.1(7) of the Act, the date of resumption, and (iii) if a vacation was postponed under subsection 187.2(1) of the Act, the new dates of commencement and termination of that vacation..." Employers must maintain records of employee annual vacations, including any interruptions or postponements.

#### Other Records
The section continues with a detailed list of other records employers must keep, including:
"(k) the employer’s pay periods; (l) a copy of any certificate provided in respect of medical breaks under subsection 181.1(2) of the Act and any request for the certificate made by the employer in accordance with that subsection, and any notice of termination of employment or intention to terminate employment given in accordance with Division IX or X of the Act..." This demonstrates the breadth of information employers are required to document for each employee.

#### Method of Reporting Absences and Overtime
"(3) Any method of reporting absences from employment or overtime hours of work that discloses the particulars required by subsection (2), including regular daily hours of work, shall be a sufficient record for the purposes of these Regulations." This clarifies that any system used to track absences and overtime that meets the requirements of subsection (2) is acceptable.

#### Records After Employment Ends
"(4) Every employer shall keep for a period of at least three years after the expiration of the employer’s obligation under subsection 239.1(3) of the Act, the following information: (a) detailed reasons for an employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury; (b) a copy of any certificate of a health care practitioner indicating that the employee is fit to return to work; and (c) the date the employee returned to work, or a copy of any notification from the employer to the employee and any trade union representing the employee that return to work was not reasonably practicable and the reasons why it was not." Employers are obligated to retain records related to work-related illnesses or injuries for at least three years after their resolution.

### Section 125: Duties of Employers: Specific Duties of Employer

Section 125 of the Canada Labour Code further elaborates on the employer's responsibilities regarding employee work records and information, particularly in relation to hazardous substances and employee health and safety.

#### Hazardous Substances
"Without restricting the generality of section 124 or limiting the duties of an employer under section 125 but subject to any exceptions that may be prescribed, every employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity, (a) ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..." This provision places a specific duty on employers to manage hazardous substances in the workplace according to established standards.

#### Hazardous Products
"(d) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements..." Employers must ensure that all hazardous products in the workplace are properly labeled.

#### Safety Data Sheets
"(e) subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..." Employers are required to provide employees with safety data sheets for all hazardous products they may encounter.

#### Exposure Assessment
"(f) where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..." Employers must conduct exposure assessments when employees are potentially exposed to hazardous substances.

#### Records of Exposure
"(g) ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees." Employers must maintain detailed records of employee exposure to hazardous substances and make these records accessible to affected employees.

### Section 125.1: Further Specific Duties of Employer

Section 125.1 of the Canada Labour Code continues the employer's obligations related to employee work records and information, focusing on employee absences and return to work.

#### Reasons for Absence
"(a) detailed reasons for an employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury..." Employers must maintain detailed explanations for any employee absences related to work-related health issues.

#### Return to Work Information
"(b) a copy of any certificate of a health care practitioner indicating that the employee is fit to return to work; and (c) the date the employee returned to work, or a copy of any notification from the employer to the employee and any trade union representing the employee that return to work was not reasonably practicable and the reasons why it was not." Employers are required to keep records of medical certificates confirming an employee's fitness to return to work and any communication regarding the return-to-work process.

In summary, Canadian employers have extensive record-keeping responsibilities concerning employee work details, including dates of employment, wages, hours worked, earnings, leave taken, hazardous substances, and health and safety exposures. These records must be maintained for a minimum of three years after employment ends and longer in specific circumstances, such as work-related illnesses or injuries. Employers are also obligated to provide employees with safety data sheets for hazardous products and to conduct exposure assessments when necessary. Failure to comply with these obligations can result in enforcement actions by the Labour Program.
